(2017) report that in 2005, publications around the subject of ecosystem services numbered in the realm of 200, a figure based on an analysis using data from SCOPUS and Web of Science. Eleven years later, in 2016, this number lay at approximately 3000. Significant large-scale studies, analyses, and programs also followed, such as TEEB, which aimed to quantify the costs of a decline in ES stemming from a failure to halt the global loss of biodiversity (Kumar, 2012). [SOURCE: Page_69]

The majority of analyses on ES conducted over the past two decades adheres to the structure outlined in the MEA report (see Figure 1.2), which subdivides ecosystem services into four general types: provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting. To begin with, provisioning ES are the most readily visible benefits humans derive from ecosystems in the form of goods - food, raw materials for production and energy generation, but also medicinal resources and, on a more general level, genetic resources that may be of future use. Regulating services contribute to the provision of an environment in which both humans and ecosystems can prosper. They include, for instance, climate regulation through carbon sequestration, air and water purification, flood protection, biological disease control, and waste decomposition. More abstract but no less important are cultural ES. These encompass the cultural, spiritual, historical, and recreational value of ecosystems and the natural environment. Benefits which fall into this category can range from ecotourism and ecotherapy to the heritage and religious value of important natural sites. Finally, supporting services such as nutrient cycling, soil formation, and primary production form be basis of ecosystem functioning and thus the provision of all other types of ES. In some categorizations, including the one used in this thesis, they are subsumed under regulating services (Jacobs, 2002; Grunewald and Bastian, 2015). [SOURCE: Page_69]

69 [SOURCE: Page_69]

Figure 1.2: Conceptualization of the role of ecosystem services according to the MEA. Image reproduced under Creative Commons Licensing. [SOURCE: Page_70]

Building on this classification and further developing the ES concept, many studies have contributed in-depth sub-classifications in various disciplines to the scientific discourse on ES over the years. One such sub-focus which is particularly relevant for the purposes of this thesis are hydrological ES (HES), alternatively termed water ES (ESS). Brauman et al. (2007), for instance, specifically discusses the biophysical generation of hydrological services such as in-situ water supply for hydropower generation, recreation, transportation, and the supply of fish, the mitigation of water-related damage such as floods, as well as the benefits derived from diverted water supply for agricultural, commercial, and municipal use. HES have been highlighted in several studies, due to the prominent interface between ES science and policymaking in freshwater ecosystems (Harrison-Atlas et al., 2016). [SOURCE: Page_70]

However, despite the broad establishment of the ES concept in the scientific community, its application is frequently still a matter of dispute (Grizzetti et al., 2016). In particular, the development of ES indicators in order to quantify, monetize, and assess ES still arouses con- [SOURCE: Page_70]

70 [SOURCE: Page_70]

tentious discourse. While specially designed ES models such as INVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs) and ARIES (ARtificial Intelligence for Ecosystem Services) exist, many studies challenge whether they are sufficient to quantify ES that rely on a complex nexus of factors, such as is commonly the case for HES, and question whether integrating ES into discipline-specific models instead would not entail more methodological benefits (Hallouin et al., 2018). The very type of valuation and the various analytical elements involved are often under discussion. Hackbart et al. (2017), for instance, concludes that the current state of knowledge about HES gives "the false impression that the ecosystem services valuation is sufficiently consolidated to support decisions about payments for ESw". [SOURCE: Page_71]

This thesis follows the general methodology outlined in Grunewald and Bastian (2015) for the analysis and evaluation of ES. The general procedure of the application of the ES concept has been outlined briefly in the introduction above and will be further expanded in Section 4.3.3. A thorough characterisation of the area of interest is provided in Chapter 4.3 together with a definition of terminology and a selection of ES to be evaluated. The evaluation procedures and indicators chosen are outlined in Chapters 4.3 and 6, alongside the basis for biophysical assessment and an approximation of monetary evaluation. Furthermore, spatial and temporal aspects are considered through distributed modelling as outlined in Chapter 6, as well as scenario building, a common approach to identify losses and gains in ESw (Ávila-García et al., 2020). However, further steps suggested in Grunewald and Bastian (2015), such as a differentiated cost/benefit analysis, a consideration of trade-offs, knowledge communication, and recommendations for ES management and monitoring are not within the scope of this thesis. [SOURCE: Page_71]

1.3.4    The Necessity for Interdisciplinary Work and Transdisciplinary Ap- proaches in a Development Context [SOURCE: Page_71]

In the previous sections of this chapter, the terms "interdisciplinary" and "multidisciplinary" have been used largely synonymously. However, there are differences between these terms. "Interdisciplinary" is sometimes defined as describing the intersection between two disciplines, while "multidisciplinary" emphasizes that participation and cooperation of multiple disciplines. By and large, though, these terms are used to refer to approaches that combine methods and [SOURCE: Page_71]

71 [SOURCE: Page_71]

theoretical frameworks from multiple disciplines. In contrast, "transdisciplinary" denotes the involvement of non-academic stakeholders in the process of knowledge production (Rigolot, 2020). [SOURCE: Page_72]

This PhD took place in the frame of a broader transdisciplinary research project financed by the French Development Agency (AFD), which aimed to rehabilitate Preks and increase one particular type of ES - the provisioning of water for agricultural purposes. The thesis took the AFD project as an entry point to further explore both the hydrological functioning of the Prek system and the other ES it provides. Furthermore, the research presented here has benefited from the insights gained by researchers from other disciplines, from sociologists to geohydrologists, working in the framework of the same project, through methods such participatory games (Venot et al., 2022) and chemical water quality analysis (Tweed et al., 2020). The results of their research have served as a foundation for both the fieldwork approach presented below (cf. Chapter 4), and as an aid in the construction of the model presented in Chapter 6. [SOURCE: Page_72]

On a meta-scale, an interdisciplinary approach also allows for advanced reflection on the limitations of individual methodologies and the foundational assumptions that underlie method- ological choices. This is invaluable in terms of gaining insights into the cultural constructs and power relations on which the knowledge ultimately generated is often contingent, and into the "unequal material and socio-economic effects of discursive and methodological framings" (Venot et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_72]

As with the domain of socio-hydrology, this thesis strives to demonstrate an awareness rather than a full incorporation of these views. As outlined in the introduction and detailed further below, a multi-method approach encompassing classical statistical hydrological analysis, interviews, remote sensing, and computational modelling was utilized to answer the research questions outlined in Section 1.1. However, no in-depth meta-analysis of the interactions between these methods was undertaken, nor was an approach from the perspective of science and technology studies (STS) employed. These analyses were within the purview of studies conducted in the framework of the same project, some even within the same case study area, such as Venot and Jensen (2021), which draws on STS and critical water research to explore the multiplicity of Preks and construe them in the context of a "socionatural mosaic landscape", and Venot et al. (2022), which examines the use of serious games as a participative way of generating knowledge. [SOURCE: Page_72]

72 [SOURCE: Page_72]

2 The Research Site: Introducing the Mekong, its (Cambodian) Delta, and the Preks [SOURCE: Page_73]

While the methods presented below are transferable, and can thus be applied to river basins and deltaic areas facing similar challenges, a thorough understanding of the Mekong basin’s unique configuration is necessary to comprehend the approaches chosen to address research questions of this thesis. This chapter aims to set the stage, as it were. It introduces the Mekong, Southeast Asia’s largest river, tracing its course from its spring on the Tibetan plateau to its delta in the South China Sea, introducing its traditional hydrological dynamics, and giving a brief outline of its economic and ecological importance, as well as of the multiple pressures it faces and the varying projections of its future development. The subsequent section then focuses on the Mekong Delta in Cambodia and Vietnam, giving in-depth insights into its hydrology, geology, biodiversity, and socio-economic characteristics. Most immediately relevant to this thesis, it also [SOURCE: Page_73]

73 [SOURCE: Page_73]

provides an initial overview of the Prek system of the Cambodian Mekong delta, which is the centerpiece of this dissertation. [SOURCE: Page_74]

2.1     Southeast Asia’s Centering Line - The Mekong [SOURCE: Page_74]

The Mekong river’s headwaters originate on the Tibetan Plateau in China, in the Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve (SNNR) of Qinghai province. The reserve is also known as Three Rivers Nature Reserve, as two other major Asian rivers also take their spring here - the Yangtze and the Huang He (Yellow) River. The SSNR was China’s first national park (Li et al., 2012). From here, the Mekong runs over a length of over 4,800 kilometers through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam, making it the 12th longest river in the world (Nhan and Cao, 2019). In China, the river carries the name Lancang or Lancang Jiang River. From its spring in Qinghai province at an altitude of over 5,200 m (Campbell, 2009), the river flows through the Tibetan Autonomous Region and on into China’s Yunnan Province, where its channel descends steeply through deep canyons. In this section of its course, also known as the Three Rivers Region, the Mekong is once more in close proximity to two other major rivers. At one point, the distance between the Mekong, the Yangtze, and the Salween Rivers is less than 120 kilometers (Eyler, 2019; Wang et al., 2017), though the rivers are separated by high mountain ranges. No tributaries enter the Mekong in this section of its course. Further South, the Mekong also passes in close proximity to the Red River, which forms one of the most vital waterways in northern Vietnam. [SOURCE: Page_74]

In southern Yunnan province, the Mekong leaves the narrow confines of gorges. Its valley opens out, its floodplain widens, and its flow velocity decreases. In this section, the river continuously drops in elevation, between 3000 and 2000 meters above sea level, and transitions to mid- and lowland reaches. At the southern tip of Yunnan, the Mekong briefly flows along the border with Myanmar, then leaves China. Subsequently, it forms the border between Laos and Myanmar for approximately 100 kilometers before reaching the Golden Triangle. This name is used to refer to the tripoint where the borders of Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand meet. Furthermore, this is the location of the confluence between the Mekong and the Ruak River, which forms the border between Thailand and Myanmar further upstream. This area in the [SOURCE: Page_74]

74 [SOURCE: Page_74]

Northeast of Myanmar and the North of Thailand and Laos is also known as the Northern Highlands. Here, several large tributaries flow into the Mekong, such as the the Nam Ta, Nam Ou, Nam Soung and Nam Khan on its left bank, and the the Nam Mae Kok and Nam Mae Ing on its right bank (Piman and Shrestha, 2017). [SOURCE: Page_75]

After the Golden Triangle, the Mekong passes through a series of rapids, also known as Khon Pi Luang Lin and Grundy-Warr (2020), and flows through Laos for about 400 kilometres, before defining the border between this country and Thailand for another 850 kilometers. Here, the Mekong passes through the low-lying Khorat Plateau, with an average elevation of only 200 m. In this region, the confluences between the Mekong and several important tributaries can be found, such as the Songkhram and Mun rivers on its right bank, and the Nam Ca Dinh, Se Bang Fai, and Se Bang Hiang on the left bank. South of the Laotian capital of Vientiane, if once more passes into the country’s interior. After passing the city of Pakse, it turns south and crosses into Cambodia (Kondolf et al., 2018; Molle et al., 2009). Here, at the border between Laos and Vietnam, a natural fault line intersects the river in the Four Thousand Island (Siphandone) area, resulting in a series of waterfalls that makes the river impassable to boats. [SOURCE: Page_75]

This border area is characterised by three tributaries of the Mekong - the Se Kong, Se San, and Sre Pok. Together, they form a transboundary river basin (also known as the 3S RIVER BASIN), which spans across Laos, Vietnam, and Cambodia, and drains into the Mekong. The 3S Basin provides an important contribution to the Mekong in terms of discharge and sediment load, accounting for 17-20% of the river’s flow, and 20% of its sediment input (Piman et al., 2013a; Shrestha et al., 2016). As will be explained in more detail below, it also plays a crucial role in terms of aquatic biodiversity, providing habitats and migration routes for fish. [SOURCE: Page_75]

Further south in Cambodia, one of the most outstanding features of the Mekong River Basin can be found - the Tonle Sap system. The centerpiece of this system is the Tonle Sap Lake, a seasonal freshwater lake connected to the Mekong through the Tonle Sap River. It is located in an extensive lacustrine and alluvial floodplain system, in a depression formed by the tectonic dynamics of the Indian an Eurasian Plate. The lake’s core characteristic is the seasonal variation of its extent and water volume. During the dry season, it drains into the Mekong via the Tonle Sap River. As the water level in the Mekong rises during the annual Monsoon season, the river’s flow reverses and replenishes the lake. Studies estimate that the average extent of the lake’s [SOURCE: Page_75]

75 [SOURCE: Page_75]

Overall, the Mekong river basin drains a total area of 795,000 km^2 . It is divided into the Upper Mekong Basin (UMB), which includes the Tibetan Plateau, the Three Rivers Area, as well as its basin area in Yunnan province and Myanmar. The UMB only contributes an average of 18% of the Mekong’s annual discharge, even though it accounts for 23.2% of the river basin’s surface area (186,356 km^2 ) and the first 1,800 km of the river’s length (Mekong River Commission, 2019). The reason for this is that tributary systems in the UMB are typically small. During the dry season, however, this contribution is higher, accounting for 45% of river flow. In addition, the UMB also carries major ecological importance for downstream areas, since the the majority of sediment input into the river system originates in this region. However, the UMB’s steep riverbed gradients and narrow gorges provide an advantageous framework for the development of hydroelectric infrastructure (Stone, 2011; Hecht et al., 2018). To date, seven dams have been completed on the Upper Mekong, with over 20 more in their planning or construction phase (Stimson Center, 2022). The resulting economic, ecological, and hydrological impacts are explored in further detail below. [SOURCE: Page_77]

The Lower Mekong Basin (LMB) encompasses the Northern Highlands, the Khorat Plateau, the Tonle Sap Basin, and the Mekong Delta. Similar to the UMB, the Northern Highlands provide attractive opportunities for hydropower development. For instance the Xayaburi Dam, which began its operation in 2019, is located in Laos in this area. In contrast, the Khorat Plateau, Tonle Sap Basin, and especially the Mekong Delta are characterised by lower terrain gradients. However, these areas, in particular the Mekong’s floodplains in Cambodia and Vietnam, constitute an essential element in the Mekong system in terms of biodiversity and food security. Agricultural productivity in the LMB provides food security for over 90 million people, and the region is home to the world’s largest inland fishery (Piman et al., 2013b; Nhan and Cao, 2019). However, both fisheries and agricultural productivity in the LMB depend on established hydrological cycles, which have seen significant changes in recent years. [SOURCE: Page_77]

2.1.1    The Mekong’s Traditional Hydrological Dynamics [SOURCE: Page_77]

The Mekong presents a complex systems in terms of hydrology, with high inter- and intra-annual variations in its discharge. The most marked characteristic in terms of hydrology is the annual mono-modal flood pulse in its discharge during the monsoon period, which is typical for tropical [SOURCE: Page_77]

77 [SOURCE: Page_77]

rivers (Junk et al., 1989). The Mekong Basin’s climate is fundamentally influenced by the south- west monsoon, with a dry season lasting from December to May, and a wet season lasting from June to November (Mekong River Commission MRC, 2005; Delgado et al., 2012a). Rainfall in the basin is distributed along an east-to-west gradient, with highlands in Laos and Cambodia receiving as much as 3,000 mm of precipitation per year. In contrast, the Khorat Plateau in Thailand can be classified as semi-arid, with annual rainfall amounts of merely 1,000-1,600 mm, and annual rainfall on the Tibetan Plateau can amount to as little as 600 mm. In total, over 75% of the river’s discharge is generated by precipitation during the wet season between July and October (Hoang et al., 2019). Dry season flows, in turn, depend on glacial meltwater from the Lancang river basin to a considerable degree, which is why the UMB’s contribution to discharge is proportionally higher during the months between December and May. [SOURCE: Page_78]

During the wet season, wide swaths of the LMB, including the Tonle Sap Floodplain and the Mekong Delta in Cambodia and Vietnam, are inundated. This annual inundation, with a flood pulse typically beginning in late June or July, peaking in September, and receding in October and November, forms a major contribution to the high aquatic biodiversity, agricultural productivity, and rich fisheries of downstream systems (Hoang et al., 2018, 2019). The average annual benefits resulting from these regular inundations have been estimated to lie at USD 8-10 billion (Piman and Shrestha, 2017). However, extreme floods also pose a serious risk to the safety of downstream communities. While people in these areas have adapted to regular inundations in their agricultural practices, architecture, and everyday way of life, disproportionately extensive floods can still cause extensive damage to crops as well as infrastructure, and the loss of lives and livelihoods (Heng et al., 2021; Boretti, 2020; Kondolf et al., 2018; Kummu and Sarkula, 2008). The latest of these severe floods occurred in 2011, with one of the highest discharge values ever recorded in the LMB. Typically, these floods can be traced back to the impact of severe tropical storms and cyclones (Heng et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_78]

2.1.2    Ecological Importance [SOURCE: Page_78]

Globally speaking, the Mekong’s is one of the most biodiverse river basins in the world, beside the Amazon and the Congo (Winemiller et al., 2016). It stretches across a wide spectrum of habitat types and climate frameworks, from arid alpine to tropical lowland and deltaic ecosystems. [SOURCE: Page_78]

78 [SOURCE: Page_78]

Southeast Asia in general is considered a biodiversity hot-spot, characterised by considerable species diversity and high levels of endemism. In fact, this bio-region is home to the highest proportion of endemic and mammal species worldwide, as well as the second-highest proportion of endemic vascular plants (at country level) (Morand and Lajaunie, 2017). Partially, the reason for this is the region’s geological and paleoecological history, with tectonic plate dynamics as well as shifting paleo-climatic conditions and sea levels promoting diversification (Claude, 2017) [SOURCE: Page_79]

The ecology and biodiversity of the Mekong Basin is also closely linked to its hydrology, specifically its annual flood pulse. Many ecological processes within the basin’s fluvial system follow an annual cycle synchronised with the river’s flow dynamics. Consequently, the hydro- biological cycle between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems equally displays a distinct seasonality (Piman et al., 2013a; Junk et al., 1989). [SOURCE: Page_79]

The way that hydrological dynamics in the Mekong basin influence its biodiversity is best illustrated by looking at its diversity of fish species and their collective behavioural characteristics. While it is generally agreed that the diversity of fish in the Mekong is extraordinary, estimates of species numbers vary wildly. Coates et al. (2003) gives an estimated species number of 1200, while van Zalinge et al. (2004) states that there are over 2000 species to be found in the Mekong. According to Winemiller et al. (2016), the river is home to 599 species, 213 of them endemic. Hortle (2009a) gives a species number of 1100, 850 of which are freshwater fish. He further notes that some of the variations in estimates may well be due to taxonomic shifts, with species being split or lumped on the basis of new analyses, as well as the discovery of new species in the system. Baran et al. (2012), for instance, notes that in the decade between 2000 and 2001, 279 new species were found in the Mekong. However, Hortle (2009a) also notes what he calls "escalation bias", "where a figure is quoted that supports a commonly-held belief (the Mekong has ‘high’ biodiversity) while ignoring the actual counts of species from the system", which in turn "creates a credibility issue for those seeking to promote conservation of the system’s biodiversity, as well as highlighting the practical problems of classification and nomenclature facing those engaged in field studies or management of habitat for fisheries" (p.6). [SOURCE: Page_79]

While the exact estimates of species numbers may vary, some of them buoyed by escalation bias, the overall diversity of the system is not in doubt. As Eyler (2019) aptly summarizes: "Only the Amazon outranks the Mekong in terms of fish diversity, but the Amazon is near twice the [SOURCE: Page_79]

79 [SOURCE: Page_79]

length and its watershed nearly ten times the Mekong’s. No river on earth has more migratory fish than the Mekong" (p.11). [SOURCE: Page_80]

The role of the hydrological cycle in sustaining this diversity among fish species is pro- nounced. For instance, the annual flood pulse creates a wide range of shallow-water habitats on the floodplains of Cambodia and Vietnam, across the Tonle Sap Lake area and in the Mekong Delta. These habitats, with structural elements in the form of submerged vegetation, provide ideal habitats for population regeneration. Many fish species spawn either directly in the flood- plains or migrate there in their juvenile phases. As the floods recede, mature fish return to the river mainstream, its distributaries, lakes such as the Tonle Sap, as well as swamps (Halls and Hortle, 2021; Burbano et al., 2020). In addition, the annual flood provides an almost unlimited nutrient base for fish species, which has the capacity to sustain immense population sizes. The floods transfer nutrients from the river main stream to the adjacent floodplains. Simultaneously, mineralized nutrients are released from the inundated soils. In turn, these nutrients form the basis of the growth of periphyton, phytoplankton, and subsequently zooplankton, valuable food resources for fish (Hortle, 2009b). Furthermore, certain fish species continue their growth as long as sufficient nutrient levels are available. Consequently, the Mekong supports some of the world’s largest fish species, such as the Mekong Giant Catfish Pangasianodon gigas and the giant freshwater stingray Urogymnus polylepis (Eyler, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_80]

2.1.3    Socio-Economic and Political Significance [SOURCE: Page_80]

Overall, approximately 66 million people live in the Lower Mekong Basin alone, including almost the entire population of Laos and Cambodia, a third of the population of Thailand, and a fifth of the population of Vietnam. However, population distribution is uneven. For instance, the Upper Mekong Basin is comparatively sparsely populated, excepting Jinghong, the capital of the prefecture of Xishuangbanna, with a population of half a million. Along the majority of the river, small villages and towns form the centers of population, alongside a few large urban capitals like Vientiane and Phnom Penh. In the Mekong Delta, a contrasting situation can be found. Here, the river is bustling with traders and floating markets, and its banks, as well as those of the man-made canals, are lined with continuous rows of houses. Population density in the delta tallies in at 425 people per square kilometer, five times higher than in the UMB [SOURCE: Page_80]

80 [SOURCE: Page_80]

(Eyler, 2019). In recent years, urban centers along the Mekong have seen considerable rates of expansion. Between 2008 and 2017, for example, the population of the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh grew from 1.3 to 2 million people. During the same time span, the population of Vientiane increased by 400%, from 208,000 to almost 800,000 Eyler (2019). [SOURCE: Page_81]

Impressive as these numbers may be, however, the Mekong Basin provides food security for an even larger number of people. Especially the fertile floodplains in Cambodia and Vietnam are hubs of agricultural production. The Vietnamese Mekong Delta, for instance, is the source of 75% of the country’s rice production, even though it occupies less than 12% of its land surface (Eyler, 2019). Through exports the Delta provides nutrition for an estimated 200 million people (Minderhoud et al., 2017). [SOURCE: Page_81]

Along the Mekong itself, the majority of the population - especially the rural population - depends on the river for their livelihoods or part of their diet. 40% of the basin’s population lives within 15 km of the river’s mainstream (Soukhaphon et al., 2021). In the LMB, 80% of the population are small-scale farmers, with an average of 1.8 ha on which to cultivate their crops. They substitute their diet with fish caught for household consumption as well as products from local forests (Carew-Reid and Taylor, 2017). In Cambodia, for instance, 60% of the protein in people’s diet comes from fish caught in the Mekong system, including the Tonle Sap Lake and the delta Ahmed et al. (1998). Overall, the Mekong is the most productive system of inland fisheries in the world, with an annual catch of 2.3 million tonnes, at a value of USD 11 billion (Mekong River Commission, 2019). Campbell and Barlow (2020) further note that the economic importance of fisheries in the Mekong basin is likely undervalued due to the fact that a large proportion of the catch is taken in by artisanal and subsistence fishers. [SOURCE: Page_81]

In addition, the Mekong also carries a large political and social importance in the region. Historically, the river has acted as a border in several sections. For instance, it has traditionally delineated the zones of influence of the Vietnamese and Thai kingdoms in Southeast Asia. This delineation has deeply permeated popular conscience. In northeast Thailand, for example, a Thai province bordering the Mekong carries the name of "Loei", which translates as "the beyond" (Eyler, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_81]

In general, political relations in the Mekong Basin are traditionally marked by a large degree of isolation. Historically, overland travel in the area was difficult. In the mid-19th century, for [SOURCE: Page_81]

81 [SOURCE: Page_81]

example, French explorer Henri Mahout noted that a journey by land from Saigon to Luang Prabang in the north of Laos took longer than a voyage by sea from Saigon to Paris (Eyler, 2019). This inhibited trade relations between Southeast Asian countries and limited the sphere of influence of central governments. It also contributed towards the large diversity in ethnicities, languages, and political systems in the region, especially in the mountainous uplands. These latter areas have been described as refuges for ethnic minorities retreating from the expanding influence from the Chinese, Vietnamese, and Thai in the lowlands. Some scholars have even coined a particular term to describe these high-elevation areas of the Mekong Basin - Zomia, used to denote Southeast Asia’s mainland massif (Scott, 2009). The social and political diversity of this region is illustrated by official statistics. Yunnan Province in the UMB is the home to 26 of the 56 officially recognized ethnic groups in China. The Laotian part of the Mekong Basin is home to 149 official ethnic groups, whose languages stretch across 8 linguistic families (Eyler, 2019). As Scott (2009) emphasizes, the influence of central governments in this area is traditionally limited, as difficult terrain conditions impede the enforcement of centralist policies as well as the deployment of both civil servants and the military (Giersch, 2010) In the 21st century, technology as well as modern infrastructure projects have done much to bridge the remoteness of the region. However, a considerable degree of isolation from central governance and control remains. For instance, the Golden Triangle is one of the world’s hot-spots for the production of illicit drugs - with farmers producing opium and carrying it down narrow mountain paths that provide protection from policing (Luong, 2020). [SOURCE: Page_82]

In addition, tensions exist between upstream- and downstream countries on the Mekong in terms of water management, which are partly due to political and geographical fragmentation having entered into popular consciousness. One of the major points of conflict is the development of hydropower and irrigation infrastructure upstream, which modifies flow and sediment load to the detriment of downstream countries. China, Thailand and Laos have already completed construction on numerous hydropower plants on both the Mekong’s mainstream and its tributaries, the consequences of which are already being felt. In addition, Thailand is diverting considerable volumes of water from the Mekong mainstream for large-scale irrigation projects. Furthermore, upstream land management practices, especially deforestation have negative downstream impacts (cf. Section 3.4.1.7). [SOURCE: Page_82]

To a certain degree, this conflict stems from a lack of awareness. For example, in China [SOURCE: Page_82]

82 [SOURCE: Page_82]

the Mekong also carries the name Lancang or Lancang Jiang River, as noted above. This terminological discrepancy has led to some confusion, as many people in China were not aware until relatively recently that the Mekong and the Lancang were, in fact, the same river. This cognitive disconnect is exemplified in a 2006 documentary, Where Have All the Fish Gone, which examines the effects of hydropower construction on the Lancang. Here, a Chinese diplomat goes on record to say that he fails to understand the preoccupation of downstream countries with developments on the Lancang river - since they cannot affect the Mekong, as they are two different rivers (Eyler, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_83]

However, over the past decades, the conflicts over water management have thrown into sharp relief the need for intergovernmental coordination in the region, and have increased the awareness of the Mekong as one complex, interconnected system. Attempts at coordination and mediation between Southeast Asian countries exist, most notably in the form of the Mekong River Commission (cf. Section 2.1.5). Nonetheless, tensions persist, as each country prioritizes its own interests in the face of the fast economic growth in the region. [SOURCE: Page_83]

2.1.4     Pressures on the River: Between Climate Change and Economic Development [SOURCE: Page_83]

In recent years, the pressures that the Mekong River has faced have been manifold. They range from the development of hydropower infrastructure and destructive practices such as riverbed mining, over the cascading effects of changing land practices, to more large-scale shifts in precipitation and temperature patterns over the basin due to global change. The effects of these pressures, acting in tandem on the river system, partially balance and partially magnify each other (Hecht et al., 2018). [SOURCE: Page_83]

2.1.4.1   Hydropower Development [SOURCE: Page_83]

One of the most widely-studied drivers of change on the Mekong is the development of hy- dropower dams, especially upstream in the Chinese part of the basin, and in Laos, where the Mekong’s mainstream passes through narrow gorges, which offer ideal conditions for dam [SOURCE: Page_83]

83 [SOURCE: Page_83]

construction from the point of view of geotechnics and civil engineering. Overall, the Mekong Basin has a cumulative potential for hydropower generation of 268,000 GWh/year. Currently, approximately half is being exploited, and the basin has sometimes been referred to the "battery of Southeast Asia" (Schmitt et al., 2019). At the moment, eleven dams are operating on the Mekong’s mainstream, and 130 on its tributaries. A further 36 are currently being constructed, and a further 291 are in their planning stages, though both planning and construction on some has been delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and its various economic consequences (Stimson Center, 2022). In addition to hydropower generation, many dams also fulfill a water provisioning role for agricultural systems. Water from their reservoirs is diverted for irrigation purposes during the dry season (Hecht et al., 2018). [SOURCE: Page_84]

Dam construction in the Mekong basin began in the 1960s. In November 1965, the first hydropower dam in the region was opened - Nam Pung Dam, in the Sakon Nakhorn Province in northeastern Thailand. This was followed by a series of other dams throughout Thailand and Laos. However, hydropower dam development was slowed by the Cold War throughout the 1960s, 70s, and 80s. It was only in the early 1990s, that hydropower infrastructure development sped up, with construction commencing on the Pak Mun Dam on the Mun River in Thailand in 1990. The first dam on the Mekong’s mainstream was completed in 1993 in China - the Manwan Dam. Towards the end of the 1990s, dam construction was once more slowed due the the 1998-99 Asian financial crisis, which led to a decrease in demand for hydropower (Jacobs, 2002; Soukhaphon et al., 2021). After the turn of the millennium, construction began once more in earnest, with more ambitious, large-scale projects, and at a greater speed. In 2008, the Mekong basin was still one of the least regulated in the world, with the total active storage capacity of hydropower stations along its main course and tributaries amounting to a mere 2% of its annual discharge, at 8.6 km^3 . In the late 2010s, however, several large reservoirs, many financed by Chinese investors, began to impound and commence hydropower generation. By 2025, active reservoir storage is expected to increase tenfold in comparison to its 2008 value, to over 86.8 km^3 (Hecht et al., 2018). In the UMB, the economic value of hydropower is estimated at an annual USD 4 billion, while an MRC Council Study (Mekong River Commission, 2018b) estimates gains from hydropower development to tally in at a cumulative USD 160 billion by 2040 in the LMB. [SOURCE: Page_84]

84 [SOURCE: Page_84]

and flows during the wet season to decrease by 16% by 2050 on the Mekong mainstream. In Räsänen et al. (2017) already reported an increase in discharge of 121–187% during the peak dry season in northern Thailand, while wet season discharge decreased by 32–46%. Many studies have also examined the effects in tributary systems, such as the 3S river basin. Here, Piman et al. (2016) project a 98% increase in dry season flows if seven large proposed dams are built. In the lowland areas, Dang and Tran (2016) projects an increase in dry season water levels by up to 70% and a decrease in wet season water levels by up to -6%. [SOURCE: Page_86]

In addition, the numerous dams on the Mekong’s main stream and its tributaries reduce the sediment load in the river, with negative impacts for downstream areas, especially the river’s deltaic floodplains. Bussi et al. (2021) predict that dams will reduce the sediment flux to the Mekong Delta by 50% under the most realistic development scenario in the next twenty years. Kondolf et al. (2014) even found that if all currently planned dams are constructed to their full capacity, 96% of sediments that would usually reach the delta to be deposited on its floodplains would remain trapped in reservoirs. This is expected to have pronounced adverse effects on ecosystems and agriculture in the delta, which depend on the nutrient input from sediment deposition during the annual Monsoon inundations. For instance, phosphorus concentrations are projected to decrease by 47 to 53% and nitrogen concentrations between 57 and 62% (Piman and Shrestha, 2017).In addition, a lack of sedimentation can pose an existential threat to the delta, which is facing both land subsidence and sea level rise (Minderhoud et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_86]

Furthermore, hydropower dams have more immediate negative effects on ecosystems and individual species. As mentioned above, the majority of Mekong fish species are migratory. Hydropower infrastructure disrupts the river continuum and cuts numerous species off from their spawning grounds. For instance, Laos’ Xayaburi dam, with a capacity of 1285 MW, has been criticised for imperiling the migratory route of the Mekong Giant Catfish and the Giant Pangasius Catfish. Moreover, hydropower dams reduce the nutrient levels in the water, as outlined above, thus restricting the nutritional basis available for aquatic species (Yoshida et al., 2020; Campbell and Barlow, 2020). While some projects have taken measures to mitigate these negative impacts on aquatic species, many of them have fallen short. For example, at the Pak Mun Dam on the Mun River in Thailand, a fish ladder was added after the construction of the actual dam had been completed. It was reportedly poorly designed and unsuccessful in allowing larger numbers of fish to migrate upstream (Baird et al., 2020). According to the Mekong River Commission, the [SOURCE: Page_86]

86 [SOURCE: Page_86]

negative effects from hydropower infrastructure could lead to a decline of fisheries by 2040 that could cost a cumulative USD 23 billion (Soukhaphon et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_87]

Finally, hydropower infrastructure has also had negative impacts on the communities living in their immediate vicinity, as well as cascading upstream and downstream effects. Entire communities have been resettled to create space for dam construction, some of them to unsuitable areas. Fish yields have fallen considerably in many places due to the disruption of aquatic ecosystems, threatening food security. Water quality, too, has reportedly declined in many areas adjacent to dams. For example, in the area of the Yali Falls Dam, villagers have reported negative health impacts linked to poor water quality, including stomach infections, rashes, and eye irritations. In 2009, toxic blue-green algae were found in the dam’s reservoir (Yoshida et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_87]

2.1.4.2   Land Use Change [SOURCE: Page_87]

Another factor that is causing major shifts in the hydrology of the Mekong basin and, by extension, its delta, is land use and land cover (LULC) change. As the economy of the Mekong sub-region grew in the course of recent decades, traditional land use patterns have been succeeded by new uses, many of them causing a cascade of consequences that manifests large-scale impacts on hydrological processes. [SOURCE: Page_87]

The most evident and widely-studied instance of land use change in the Mekong Basin is deforestation. The entirety of the Mekong region has seen high rates of deforestation for the past six decades. Hirsch (2010) noted that between the early 1960s and the late 1990s, Thailand lost half of its forest cover, while Laos’ decreased from covering two thirds of the country’s surface to one half. Furthermore, Vietnam lost two million hectares of forests during the Second Indochina War alone, due to concerted chemical deforestation operations and bombings by the US Air Force. Lacombe and Pierret (2013) note that even thirty years later, in 2002, degraded forest still covers those areas that were bombed heavily during the war. In Cambodia, one of the highest rates of deforestation has been observed, especially with the beginning of unregulated logging operations after the collapse of the Khmer Rouge Regime. Lohani et al. (2020) note an overall forest loss of 19% in the country since 1993. The same study furthermore found that the [SOURCE: Page_87]

87 [SOURCE: Page_87]

rate of loss is increasing, doubling its pace after 2011. In the entirety of the LMB, Leinenkugel et al. (2015) 2015 find an annual forest loss rate of 0.4% between 2001 and 2011. Potapov et al. (2019) find that between 2000 and 2017, 9.4% of the region’s overall forest cover disappeared, but that 16.6% of forests extant at the end of this period were stand replacement following reforestation. This study too highlights the particularly high rate of forest loss in Cambodia, at 22.5%. According to a report by the FAO (Costenbader et al., 2015), the major driving factors of forest loss in the region are agricultural expansion, especially high-value cash crops such as oil palms and cocoa, the construction of infrastructure such as dams and roads, the extraction of resources like minerals and gas, unsustainable and unregulated logging practices, and forest fires. However, the predominance of these factors in the loss of forests, as well as the rates of that loss exhibit a large spatial heterogeneity. [SOURCE: Page_88]

Overall, the effects of this change in land cover are far-reaching, especially in hydrological terms. Forests regulate processes such as water flow and infiltration, they impact the dynamics of seasonal flooding, as well as nutrient cycling. Generally, forest loss decreases evapotranspiration and thus increases the annual basin water yield, alongside erosion. However, when forests are converted to intensive cropland, the reverse can be the case, with increased evapotranspiration fuelled by irrigation decreasing the overall water yield (Netzer et al., 2019). Ultimately, LULC developments are one of the largest uncertainty factors in the future hydrological developments in the Mekong Basin. For instance, Shrestha et al. (2017) compares three different LULC scenarios and their impact on the future hydrological development of the 3S Basin. The results indicate major variations between scenarios, with a decrease in annual streamflow ranging between 3 and 22% and a change in annual sediment load varying between -8% and +249%. [SOURCE: Page_88]

2.1.4.3   Climate Change [SOURCE: Page_88]

Climate change is another significant driver of change in the Mekong Basin, with the impacts of shifts in temperature and precipitation already evident in various manifestations across the region, and more severe effects forecast for the medium- to long-term future. In fact, the LMB has been identified as one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change on a global basis (Mercado and Asia Times, 2021; Eyler, 2019) [SOURCE: Page_88]

88 [SOURCE: Page_88]

The most immediate impact of climate change across the Mekong basin lies in the increase in average temperatures throughout the year. Projections see an overall increase in temperatures between 0.4 °C and 3.3 °C across the basin by the year 2060 (Mekong River Commission, 2021; IPCC, 2013). [SOURCE: Page_89]

In addition, precipitation patterns are changing as well, with high-intensity rainfall events becoming more frequent and the temporal and spatial distribution of rainfall shifting. Whether the overall development of rainfall patterns is towards increased or decreased annual rainfall sums varies according to which climate scenario is being analysed, with some projections predicting an average decrease of 16% while others prognosticate an increase of 17% (Mekong River Commission, 2021, 2018b) [SOURCE: Page_89]

These changes are likely to cause a riptide of effects for ecosystems, agriculture, and human settlements (Johnston et al., 2020; Trisurat et al., 2018; Try et al., 2020). To compensate the adverse impacts, adaptations in agricultural practices such as technological improvements in irrigation systems will be necessary. Furthermore, economic effects on sectors such as hydropower production and navigation are to be expected (Mekong River Commission, 2018a). More fundamental impacts are also expected on processes such as soil erosion, with increases of up to 17% predicted by 2060, and flooding in the deltaic areas (cf. Chapter 2.2.3.1) (Mekong River Commission, 2021). [SOURCE: Page_89]

Part of the reason for the severe effects of climate change on the Mekong region is that it is not only regional processes that are fundamentally altered. Large-scale ocean-atmospheric processes such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), and monsoon cycles impact hydroclimatic conditions in the Mekong Basin (Mekong River Commission, 2021; Kiem, 2017). [SOURCE: Page_89]

A final aspect of the impact of climate change on the hydroclimatic development of the Mekong basin that needs to be mentioned at this point is that the effects of several of the processes described thus far counteract each other. For instance, Yun et al. (2020) found that climate change in the basin would increase flood magnitude by 14% and flood incidence by 45%, while hydropower development would decrease them by 16% and 36% respectively. [SOURCE: Page_89]

89 [SOURCE: Page_89]

2.1.5     The Mekong River Commission - Between Governance and Mediat- ing Conflicting National Interests [SOURCE: Page_90]

As outlined above, many conflicting interests are related to the development of the Mekong region, with upstream valorisation often infringing on the potential benefits of downstream riparian states. [SOURCE: Page_90]

To mediate conflicts arising from this field and provide support for sustainable development and management, the Mekong River Commission (MRC) was founded in 1995 by LMB countries - Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam (Piman et al., 2013a). Its stated aim is to "promote, support, cooperate, and coordinate in the development of the full potential of sustainable benefits to all riparian states and the prevention of wasteful use of the Mekong River Waters." Its mandate includes various sectors, encompassing agriculture (especially irrigation), climate change adaptation, drought monitoring, fisheries, flood control, hydropower, and navigation (Mekong River Commission MRC, 1995). [SOURCE: Page_90]

Over the past twenty-seven years, the MRC has evolved into a well-established independent intergovernmental body coordinating the exchange of knowledge and resources across the LMB. It regularly releases State of the Basin reports to outline the main development advances and challenges facing the Mekong, it maintains large-scale hydrological models predicting the future of the river, and it provides a central point of access to extensive data on the Mekong system for parameters ranging from water levels and river discharge to evapotranspiration, sediment load, and zoo-plankton abundance 1 . [SOURCE: Page_90]

However, the MRC has also faced harsh criticism in the past, with some even seeing it as a wholly "failed institution" due to its lack of success in preventing unsustainable dam projects from posing a threat to communities and ecosystem services (Eyler, 2019). Principally, this is due to the MRC’s limited institutional reach. It lacks the power to overrule member states, as well as mechanisms to resolve disputes between stakeholders. Furthermore, the fact that key riparian countries like Myanmar and China are not members of the MRC impedes its reach (Cronin et al., 2016; Hirsch et al., 2006; Suhardiman et al., 2012). 1 Information is available via the MRC’s Data Portal and has been used extensively in the analyses for this thesis, [SOURCE: Page_90]

see Figure 2.4 [SOURCE: Page_90]

90 [SOURCE: Page_90]

2.2     The Mekong Delta: A Hub of Human Activity, Hydrolog- ical Dynamics, and Biodiversity [SOURCE: Page_92]

The delta of the Mekong, which fans out across southern Cambodia and Vietnam, is one of the most productive areas in the world in terms of agriculture and fisheries. This region of fertile alluvial soils has been a hub of human activity for millennia. Currently, it is home to over 19 million people, and 10,000 km^2 of rice paddies. However, the Delta is also facing a wide array of challenges, ranging from population pressure and soil acidification to changes in the Mekong’s runoff regime and thus the annual monsoon inundations (Stewart and Coclanis, 2011). In that, it is epitomatic of the threats looming over (tropical) deltas worldwide, especially those seeing intensive agriculture (Szabo et al., 2016; Renaud et al., 2013; Loucks, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_92]

This section outlines the characteristics of the Mekong Delta, with a particular focus on its Cambodian part. It gives an overview of the Delta’s geographical location, its geology and pedological characteristics, and its value in terms of biodiversity. Then, it proceeds to review the recent literature available on the Delta’s hydro-geological dynamics and its socio-economic development. Finally, the various challenges affecting the Mekong Delta as a whole are outlined. [SOURCE: Page_92]

2.2.1    Geographical Location [SOURCE: Page_92]

The exact delineations of the Mekong Delta vary, but it takes its origin at the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Here, the Tonle Sap river flows into the Mekong. Only a few kilometers downstream, the Mekong’s first distributary, the Bassac river, diverges from the mainstream, marking the start of the delta (Renaud et al., 2013). It then stretches across the southern Cambodian provinces of Takeo, Kandal, and Prey Veng, as well as the Southern Vietnamese provinces of An Giang, Bac Lieu, Ben Tre, Ca mau, Dong Thap, Hau Giang, Kien Giang, Long An, Soc Trang, Tien Giang, Tra Vinh, Vin Longh and Can Tho City. [SOURCE: Page_92]

Overall, the Mekong’s catchment area spans 760 000 km^2 . Its delta stretches over circa 55 000 km^2 (Mekong River Commission MRC, 2005), 40 000 km^2 of which are in Vietnam (Stewart and Coclanis, 2011). In terms of area, the Mekong Delta is the third largest deltaic plain in the world, after the Amazon and Ganges- Brahmaputra Deltas (Coleman and Roberts, 1989). [SOURCE: Page_92]

92 [SOURCE: Page_92]

initiating delta progradation^3 . Since the beginning of its formation, the Mekong Delta has prograded over 220 km into the South China Sea, at an average long-term rate of 30 m per year (Hanebuth et al., 2012). In deeper sediment layers, however, evidence of earlier subaqueous^4 phases of delta development are still evident. The current coastal zone of the Mekong Delta as well as its subaqueous section have been formed over the course of the last 1,000 years. In comparison to other deltas in the wider region, such as that of the Yangtze, the Pearl River, and the Red River, these are relatively young deltaic forms (Liu et al., 2017). [SOURCE: Page_94]

In terms of sediment typology, the Holocene sediment deposition left behind largely un- consolidated, fine-grained, clayey sediments (Zoccarato et al., 2018). These sediments contain arsenic (As), bound in Fe(III) (oxyhydro)oxides. Problematically, geohydrological conditions in the Mekong Delta promote dissimilatory reductive dissolution of these Fe(III) complexes, coupled with the anaerobic oxidation of organic matter, and thus the release of geogenic As into the groundwater contained in the Mekong Delta’s alluvial aquifers (Stopelli et al., 2020). This is problematic since these aquifers are the main source of water supply in the Mekong Delta, for household consumption as well as agricultural activity and industry (Duy et al., 2021) (see Chapter 2.2.3.3). [SOURCE: Page_94]

As for the soils of the Mekong Delta, there are three main types: alluvial, acid sulfate, and saline. The first of these, alluvial soils, tend to be located along main rivers and cover approximately 31% of the delta. These are the most agriculturally productive soils. In contrast, acid sulfate soils are acidic and only possess limited fertility. They make up ca. 41% of the delta. The third type, saline soils, covering ca. 19% of the delta, are located in areas where the water table is low, and saline intrusion during the dry season is frequent (Torell and Salamanca, 2003). In terms of international soil classifications, the soils in the Mekong Delta correspond to Fluvisols, Gleysols, Luvisols, Acrisols, Arenosols and Plinthosols according to the World Reference Base system, and to Entisols, Inceptisols, and Ultisols of USDA Soil Taxonomy system. As for mineralogy, the dominating clay mineral is muscovite in more recent alluvial soils and kaolinate in old alluvial soils (Nguyen et al., 2015). 3 Progradation is the process in which a river supplies sediment to coastal and shelf areas in faster than marine [SOURCE: Page_94]

processes can disperse it. Consequently, regressive sedimentary deposits begin to form(Coleman and Roberts, 1989). 4 The subaqueous parts of a delta lie below low-tide elevation and extend towards deeper marine areas. River [SOURCE: Page_94]

sediments are deposited until depths of 300 m and over a width of up to several tens of kilometers. (Coleman and Prior, 1982) [SOURCE: Page_94]

94 [SOURCE: Page_94]

2.2.3     Overall Hydro(geo)logical Dynamics [SOURCE: Page_95]

As mentioned above, part of the reason for the Mekong Delta’s fertility and productivity comes from the periodic deposition of sediments during the annual monsoon inundations. This illustrates the large significance of hydrological dynamics for the economic and ecological lifeblood of the area. In addition to sediment deposition, groundwater recharge is an important process linked to this defining feature of the Mekong Delta’s hydrology. [SOURCE: Page_95]

2.2.3.1   Annual Monsoon Inundations [SOURCE: Page_95]

Every year during the flood season, which typically lasts from July until November, considerable swaths of the delta are inundated. This is the result of the Mekong and its distributaries over- topping their banks and inundating the floodplains. The exact extents of inundations vary inter-annually. [SOURCE: Page_95]

According to Toan (2014) 35-50% of the Vietnamese Delta is flooded every year, with inundations reaching depths of up to 4.0 m, and lasting for three to six months. Dinh et al. (2019) found that in the hydrological year 2016/2017, flood extents rose consistently starting at the beginning of August, with 25-30% of the Delta inundated by September, and 46% at the flood peak in mid-October. This study further underlined that Vietnamese Provinces most affected by inundations were An Giang, Dong Thap, Long An, Kien Giang and Can Tho. The reason for this, Dinh et al. (2019) postulate, is that inundations emanate principally from the main branches of the Mekong centered in these provinces. Other studies record far smaller overall flood extents in the delta. Kuenzer et al. (2013), for instance, found a maximum flood extent of 13.4% of the delta area for the 2007 wet season. [SOURCE: Page_95]

It must be noted, that these annual monsoon inundations are not the only type of flood in the Mekong Delta. In fact, previous research has identified three more flood types in the region (Delgado et al., 2012b; Tri, 2012; Apel et al., 2012). The first of these results from the artificial distribution of flood waters via an extensive network of canals regulated through control structures such as sluice gates and dykes. The second additional flood type is the result of extreme local precipitation events. Floods of the third type in the coastal provinces and result [SOURCE: Page_95]

95 [SOURCE: Page_95]

from high tides during storms. Kuenzer et al. (2013) notes that most floods in the delta are a result of a combination of these flood types. However, it must be noted that this is only true for the Vietnamese part of the Mekong Delta. In the Cambodian part, no coastal areas are present, and the dense system of hydraulic infrastructure that characterizes the landscape of the Vietnamese Mekong Delta is absent here. Nonetheless, short-term inundations can also result from heavy precipitation on the Cambodian side of the border. [SOURCE: Page_96]

In itself, the impact of the Vietnamese system of dykes and gates on flood and sediment dynamics has been the subject of scientific interest. Triet et al. (2017) found the dyke system to impact flood dynamics downstream, increasing flood hazards due to the risk of dyke breaks. This study found an average increase of 9–13 cm in water levels at flood peak in the central Delta, and an increase in duration of 15 days. Duc Tran et al. (2018) noted that upstream dyke systems increase peak water levels in areas located in the downstream reaches of the delta. Furthermore, Quoc Thanh et al. (2019) found that the network of dykes also led to a decrease in minimum water levels and impacted tidal fluctuation on the Mekong’s main branches. [SOURCE: Page_96]

Another aspect of the flood dynamics in the Mekong Delta that needs to be highlighted is that inundations do not only carry positive implications. In general, the local population, especially those working in the agricultural sector, are adapted to and even dependent on the annual inundations. However, when these inundations deviate from their usual patterns, they can cause serious damage and loss of life and livelihoods. For example, if inundations arrive sooner than anticipated, they can damage crops that have not yet been harvested (cf. Section 4.3.4). If floods have a higher magnitude than usual, they can damage infrastructure, from hydraulic control structures to farmsteads (Hoang et al., 2018). For instance, the historic 50-year flood in 2000 resulted in estimated economic losses in excess of US$ 200 million (Cosslett and Cosslett, 2014). [SOURCE: Page_96]

2.2.3.2   Sediment Dynamics [SOURCE: Page_96]

As outlined above, one of the main benefits of annual inundations in the Mekong Delta is the deposition of nutrient-rich sediments, which enhance the fertility and productivity in the region. Historically, in its unregulated state, the Mekong transported 160 Mt of suspended sediments [SOURCE: Page_96]

96 [SOURCE: Page_96]

annually (Bussi et al., 2021). A considerable percentage of this sediment load would eventually be deposited on the floodplains, as flow velocities decreased or ceased entirely during inundations. In the early 2000s and 2010s, Hung et al. (2014) described an average annual deposition of 6.86 kg/m^2 in Tam Nong district in Dong Thap province of the Vietnamese Mekong delta, which corresponds to approximately 6 mm in depositional height. [SOURCE: Page_97]

However, the amounts of deposited sediments in the Delta have been continuously declining for several decades. Upstream hydropower development on the mainstream is one of the reasons for this development, as sediments become trapped in reservoirs. Another factor is the further development of hydraulic infrastructure in the Vietnamese part of the delta. For instance, Manh et al. (2014) note that the rates of sediment deposition on floodplains of the Cambodian delta is up to six times higher - from 19 to 23% of the annual sediment load recorded at the Kratie measurement station maintained by the MRC - rather than the 1 to 6% deposited in the heavily enclosed floodplains in Vietnam. [SOURCE: Page_97]

According to Manh et al. (2015), the combination of various drivers will significantly decrease the Mekong’s sediment load until the middle of the century. A comparison of scenarios revealed that even median changes would result in an overall decrease in floodplain sedimentation by 40%. Maximum-change scenarios in all drivers would lead to a 95% reduction in the rates of sediment deposition in the delta. Similarly, Bussi et al. (2021) note that the decline in suspended sediment flux would reach 50% at the apex of the delta if all currently planned hydropower projects on the Mekong were built. [SOURCE: Page_97]

2.2.3.3   Groundwater Dynamics [SOURCE: Page_97]

In the Mekong Delta, groundwater is an important resource, especially during the dry season, serving as a basis for household water supply as well as for irrigation in agriculture. Typically, people use private tube-wells to access ground water, with more than 1 million of these shallow wells reported across the delta (Danh and Khai, 2015). Their depths reach 80-120 m. In addition, there are groundwater abstraction wells penetrating into depths of 200-450 m, which belong to official water supply plants. In total, daily groundwater abstraction was estimated at 2.5 million m^3 in 2015 (Minderhoud et al., 2017; Duy et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_97]

97 [SOURCE: Page_97]

The source for these groundwater abstractions is a multi-layered aquifer system in the Delta’s alluvial basin. Due to the various stages of sediment deposition during the formation of the delta, the stratigraphy of the aquifers is complex. Furthermore, there are older stratigraphic units under the deltaic forms of the Holocene, with aquifers dating back to the Pleistocene, Pliocene, and Miocene (Wagner et al., 2012). According to Duy et al. (2021), these aquifers, composed of sand and gravel, form four layers, separated by aquitards consisting of silt and clay, at depths of 0-49 m, 31-193 m, 153-381 m, and 275-550 m. Broadly, the hydraulic conductivity of the aquitards lies at 3-40*102 m/s, while the aquifers exhibit a hydraulic conductivity of 1-20*102 m/s (Wagner et al., 2012; Minderhoud et al., 2017; Hung Van Pham et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_98]

Past studies have found shallow groundwater dynamics to be closely linked to the river system and to inundation dynamics in the floodplains. Kazama et al. (2007) found that reductions in inundation extents lead to severe reductions in groundwater storage in the Cambodian part of the Mekong Delta. Modelling three flood seasons, the authors found that a 19% decrease in inundation areas in 1993 led to a 31% reduction in groundwater storage. For 1998, these numbers were 44% and 42% respectively. In contrast, deeper groundwater layers in the Mekong Delta are relatively uninfluenced by surface water dynamics. Hung Van Pham et al. (2019), for instance, found that most fresh groundwater in the Mekong Delta was recharged 60,000 - 120,000 years ago. During this time, sea levels were relatively low and top layers exhibited high hydraulic conductivity. However, during the Holocene a clayey sedimentary layer was deposited that now inhibits groundwater recharge of the deeper aquifers. [SOURCE: Page_98]

Groundwater management efforts in the Mekong Delta, especially in Vietnam, have been disparate over the past few decades, leading to overexploitation, which, in turn, causes a cascade of negative impacts (Renaud and Kuenzer, 2012; Danh and Khai, 2015; Wagner et al., 2012). One of the consequences has been a decline in groundwater levels, with average rates of decline ranging between 0.01 and 0.55 m/year over the past twenty years (Duy et al., 2021; Erban et al., 2014). Another effect is land subsidence. To a certain extent, subsidence in deltaic areas such as the Mekong Delta is natural. Due to the overburden of the gravitational load, underlying sediments are compacted through pore collapse. However, this process is accelerated significantly by aquifer depletion as a result of groundwater exploitation. Pores that were formerly filled by groundwater are exposed to compaction, leading to increases in subsidence rates. In their landmark 2017 study, Minderhoud et al. (2017) found that the Mekong Delta sank by an average [SOURCE: Page_98]

98 [SOURCE: Page_98]

18 cm over the past quarter century. Furthermore, the authors highlight that subsidence rates have been increasing, with average rates currently at 1.1 cm per year, and peak rates at 2.5 cm per year. [SOURCE: Page_99]

2.2.4       Socio-Economic Factors [SOURCE: Page_99]

The Mekong Delta carries an economic importance in both Cambodia and Vietnam that is disproportionate to the relative surface area it occupies in either country. The Delta’s high agricultural productivity has even earned it the moniker of being the "rice bowl" of the region. In fact, the Mekong Delta is a globally important source of rice, shrimp, and Catfish exports (Olson and Morton, 2018). [SOURCE: Page_99]

The Mekong Delta contributes 75% of Vietnam’s total production in the sectors of agriculture, fisheries, and forestry. Furthermore, 50% of the country’s agricultural exports come from the Delta, in particular 90% of its rice exports (Liao et al., 2016). In fact, the Vietnamese Mekong delta contributes a total of 15% to global rice exports, accounting for 5.7 million tons of milled rice in 2018, and exceeding a value of 2.5 $ billion (Quyen et al., 2018). In Cambodia, agriculture makes up 23.5% of the country’s total GDP, with over 33% of the working population employed in the sector (National Institute of Statistics, 2020). Cambodia’s total rice production in the 2019–20 season reached 10.9 million metric tons, slightly lower than the previous season’s harvest due to unfavourable weather conditions. Average yield per hectare lay at 3.09 metric tons (World Bank, 2021). In Vietnam, agriculture accounted for 15% of the GDP. Fisheries comprise 10-15% of Vietnam’s GDP in the Agricultural, Fishery and Forestry Sector. In Cambodia, fisheries account for approximately 10% of GDP (Yoshida et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_99]

Furthermore, it must be noted that for the population of the Mekong Delta, agriculture and fisheries play a key role in ensuring livelihoods. Even if their primary economic activities lie else- where, such as in garment manufacturing or tourism, many people fish and maintain agricultural activities to meet household needs. Furthermore, economic activities have become diversified, with many people moving away from full-time farming and towards seeking employment in industries such as tourism and construction. However, part-time agricultural activities are often maintained (Vandôme, 2020). In Cambodia, for instance, 67% of families living on the Mekong [SOURCE: Page_99]

99 [SOURCE: Page_99]

floodplains who have agricultural holdings report that agriculture makes up a higher or similarly high percentage of their household income as other economic activities (World Bank, 2021). [SOURCE: Page_100]

2.2.5    Biodiversity and Conservation [SOURCE: Page_100]

Despite being, as outlined above, heavily modified by human activity in terms of land cover and hydrology, the Mekong Delta can still boast substantial levels of biodiversity. Significant mam- mals from the point of view of conservation include the Hairy-nosed Otter (Lutra sumatrana), the Small Clawed Otter (Aonyx cinerea), and the Dugong (Dugong dugong) (Campbell, 2012). [SOURCE: Page_100]

Furthermore, the wetlands of the delta serve as an important habitat for numerous species of birds. Buckton and Safford (2004) reviewed the avifauna of the delta between 1988 and 2004 and found a total of 247 bird species, half of which can be considered wetland-dependant, and twenty of which were listed globally as threatened or near-threatened. Species of interest include the South-East Asian Sarus Crane (Grus antigone sharpii), the Indian Cormorant (Phalacrocorax fuscicollis), and the Little Cormorant (Phalacrocorax niger). [SOURCE: Page_100]

In terms of fish biodiversity, approximately 460 species can be found in the Mekong Delta. As noted above, the Mekong River is the second most biodiverse riverine habitat in the world, after the Amazon. The Delta contributes a large share of this biodiversity, as both freshwater and marine species are present here. The predominant species groups are carps, barbs, minnows (cyprinids), and gobies (gobiids). Furthermore, four endemic species can be found in the Mekong Delta: the Dwarf Catfish (Akysis filifer, the Mekong Sea Catfish (Hemipimelodus daugueti), the Mekong Goby (Stenogobius mekongensis), and the Mekong Blind Sole (Typhlachirus elongates) (Tran, 2016; Vidthayanon, 2008). [SOURCE: Page_100]

In terms of vegetation it must be noted that many natural habitation types such as natural grasslands, sedge-lands, and regularly flooded forests have been replaced by agricultural areas or destroyed during the Vietnam War. For instance, data from the 1950s documents approximately 200,000 hectares of Mangrove forests in the Mekong Delta, most of which were destroyed by exfoliants during the 1960s and 70s (Tran, 2016). Since the end of the war, conversion into rice paddies and shrimp aquaculture has led to a further reduction of these habitats, which is particularly detrimental since they have a high floristic diversity (Truong and Do, 2018; Duke, [SOURCE: Page_100]

100 [SOURCE: Page_100]

2.2.6    Hydraulic Infrastructure: The Canals of the Vietnamese and Preks of the Cambodian Mekong Delta [SOURCE: Page_102]

As outlined in previous sections, the Mekong Delta has undergone extensive human modifications in terms of hydraulic infrastructure. How exactly this modification has taken shape, however, varies considerably between the Cambodian and the Vietnamese part of the delta. [SOURCE: Page_102]

In Vietnam, an extensive network of dykes, canals, and hydraulic control infrastructure such as gates exists today. In total, the dyke network in this part of the Delta has a length of over 13,000 km, 8,000 km of which are low dykes (crest levels 1.5 - 4.0 m a.s.l). High dykes, (crest levels 4.0 - 6.0 m) are concentrated in Gi-ang and Dong Thap provinces (Triet et al., 2017). [SOURCE: Page_102]

This network of canals and dykes in the Mekong Delta has a long history. While pre-colonial textual evidence is sparse, oral histories and archaeological evidence point towards canals being built at large scale as early as prior to 700 CE. For instance, ancient canals were discovered by a French archaeologist in 1931 while looking at aerial photographs of the region around Chau Doc. These canals reach a length of over 100 km, stretching from the coast of the Delta to Angkor Borei, across the border in Cambodia (Paris, 1931; Biggs, 2004). [SOURCE: Page_102]

However, it was only in the early 19th century that a systematic series of major public works initiated by the court of the Nguyen Empire more permanently shaped the delta landscape. These included the Bao Dinh canal, which widened a waterway first created in 1705, the Vinh Te canal, and the Thoai Ha canal. The latter two projects aimed to increase the Nguyen’s control over Vietnam’s border with Cambodia (Biggs, 2004). During the French colonial rule, canals were regarded as a tool to tie the Mekong Delta more intimately into the colonial state. The years between 1866 and 1930 saw an extensive expansion of waterways (Biggs, 2004, 2010). Overall, 174 million m^3 of earth were dredged - a scale comparable to the construction of the canals in Suez and Panama during the same period, at 260 and 210 million m^3 respectively. The situation during World War II the Vietnam War led to a fragmentation of the majority of hydraulic projects and a surge in small-scale local adaptation projects initiated by farmers. After 1975, projects initiated by the central government in the sectors of irrigation, land reclamation, and rice production revived and recentralized the construction of hydraulic infrastructure, with over 10,000 km of canals being built (Huu Nguyen et al., 2016; Biggs, 2004, 2011; Benedikter, [SOURCE: Page_102]

102 [SOURCE: Page_102]

2014). [SOURCE: Page_103]

Figure 2.7: Excavation of the Cho Cao canal, ca. 1878, attributed to Émile Gsell, courtesy of the Université Côte d’Azur (ark:/17103/5hfh). In 1875 the French colonial authorities decided to construct a canal connecting Cua Tiêu to the Vaïco river as a transport route for rice by steamship. [SOURCE: Page_103]

On the Cambodian side of the border, the system of hydraulic infrastructure is less extensive, largely lacking a systematic network of dykes and control infrastructure such as gates. Instead, the defining characteristics are Preks. Located along the banks of the Bassac and the Mekong, these large-scale, trapezoidal canals form a connection between the river and the low-lying floodplains. They do so by breaching the elevated river banks, which were formed through centuries of sediment deposition (Kazama et al., 2007). The majority of these canals was constructed during the early 20th century. Unlike for the hydraulic infrastructure on the Vietnamese side of the border, an in-depth review of the Preks is as of yet lacking. Some aspects of their history, through the lens of engineering reports across the centuries, will be explored in Section 4.2. In addition to the Preks, a network of smaller-scale canals exists on the floodplains of the Cambodian Mekong Delta. Some of them are connected to the Preks and thus, by extension, to the river mainstream. The origin of these canals largely lies in the period of the Khmer Rouge regime in the 1970s. During this time, extensive resettlement and public work projects aimed to extend Cambodia’s network of canals by forced manual labour. According to a UN survey from the 1990s, approximately 75% of Cambodia’s canal networks originate from these work programmes (Fuller, 2008). [SOURCE: Page_103]

103 [SOURCE: Page_103]

2.2.7    Challenges in the Delta: From Subsidence to Salinity Intrusion [SOURCE: Page_104]

From the previous sections in this chapter it emerges that the Mekong Delta is currently facing a multitude of challenges that pose existential threats to its ecological balance and economy and, consequently, the livelihoods of its population. Most serious are changes in the hydrological regime of the Mekong, climate change, and land subsidence. To make matters worse, various facets of these threats amplify each other’s effects. [SOURCE: Page_104]

For instance, the Mekong Delta is in serious danger of becoming entirely inundated year- round due to a combination of land subsidence, sediment starvation, and sea level rise. As noted above, Minderhoud et al. (2017)’s results indicate that the entire Delta has already sunk approximately 18 cm over the past 25 years as a result of land subsidence. Part of that subsidence is due to natural sediment compaction due to overburden. Part of it, however, is also due to groundwater extraction at unsustainable rates. Simultaneously, sedimentation on the floodplains, which would normally counteract subsidence by raising land, is declining due to sediments becoming trapped in upstream hydropower reservoirs. Moreover, economic activities such as riverbed mining further reduce sediment load and increase erosive processes. In addition, sea level rise driven by climate change is further decreasing the relative elevation of the delta. Minderhoud et al. (2019) found that the average elevation of the Delta is a mere 0.8 m above sea level, rather than the previously assumed 2.6 m. Consequently, large swaths of the Delta will fall below sea level if current rates of sea level rise continue, or if they accelerate. For example, Minderhoud et al. (2019) states that over 70% of the population in the Delta would be displaced following a sea level rise of 1 meter. [SOURCE: Page_104]

Another problem that is aggravated by the processes described above is salinity intrusion into the delta. Several studies and reports have highlighted that saline sea water now intrudes further inland, especially during the dry season, than previously reported (Trung et al., 2020; Toan, 2014). This causes considerable difficulties for farmers who use the freshwater from the rivers and canals for irrigation. Part of the reason for this more extensive salinity intrusion is climate change, in particular shifts in precipitation patterns and sea level rise. Eslami et al. (2019) also report that channel incision resulting from sediment starvation and riverbed mining significantly increases tidal amplification and salinity intrusion. As a consequence, farmers in the Mekong Delta have been forced to adapt agricultural practices and livelihood models, for instance by [SOURCE: Page_104]

104 [SOURCE: Page_104]

adopting the prawn rice rotational crop (Paik et al., 2020; Loc et al., 2021). [SOURCE: Page_105]

Apart from trapping sediments that could counteract land subsidence and prevent channel incision, upstream hydropower construction also has more direct negative effects on the Mekong Delta. Agriculture and fisheries are affected by its altered hydrological regime, decreasing wet season flows and thus inundation extents. Yoshida et al. (2020) found that if all 11 proposed mainstream dams in the LMB were to be constructed, the fish yields would decrease by 366,570 t and 267,429 t annually in Vietnam and Cambodia respectively. This would have severe economic impacts, the authors point out, with losses ranging from 6% to 9% of GDP in the Agriculture, Fishery and Forestry sector in Vietnam, and exceeding 3% of total GDP in Cambodia. Furthermore, this study also highlights that while total loss under this scenario would be smaller in Cambodia than in Vietnam, the vulnerable volume would be greater in the former country. [SOURCE: Page_105]

2.2.8    From the Regional to the Local: Understanding Delta-Wide Changes in the Prek System in Cambodia [SOURCE: Page_105]

As this chapter has outlined, the Mekong region as a whole and its delta in particular is facing a range of far-reaching changes, many of which have negative implications for its ecosystems and the livelihoods of its inhabitants. More broadly, many of these processes - from conflicts over hydropower development to subsidence are representative of similar issues that (tropical) deltas worldwide are facing. [SOURCE: Page_105]

From the literature cited in the preceding sections, it is clear that many of these processes of change and their impacts have been studied extensively at supra-regional and regional scales. However, few studies so far have assessed their impacts at more local scales, especially in the Cambodian Mekong Delta.
