In the following chapters, this thesis zooms in first on the Cambodian part of the Mekong Delta, then on an even smaller case study area. First, the hydrological groundwork will be laid to understand large-scale processes and land use patterns in this part of the delta. Then, the focus will fall entirely on the landscape-defining features of the case study area - the Preks, and the ecohydrological system of which they form the basis. [SOURCE: Page_105]

105 [SOURCE: Page_105]

106 [SOURCE: Page_106]

3 Understanding Large-Scale Hydrological Processes in the Region: Past Changes and Current Reality [SOURCE: Page_107]

To assess the regional and local impacts of the basin- and delta-wide changes outlined above, it is necessary to take a step-wise approach - to "zoom in", as it were, progressively. This chapter discusses the hydrological characteristics of the Cambodian Mekong Delta. It also strives to assess the hydrological changes that the region has experienced over the past decades. Thus, it lays the groundwork for the understanding of local-scale analyses of ecohydrological and sociohydrological processes, as well as their formal modelisation in subsequent chapters.1 1 Part of this chapter is based on a paper published in: Orieschnig, C., Venot, J.P., Massuel, S., Eang, K.E., [SOURCE: Page_107]

Chhuon, K., Lun, S., Siev, S. and Belaud, G., 2022. A Multi-Method Approach to Flood Mapping: Reconstructing Inundation Changes in the Cambodian Upper Mekong Delta. Journal of Hydrology, p.127902. [SOURCE: Page_107]

107 [SOURCE: Page_107]

The processes that are examined in this chapter are changes in river flow, precipitation, inundations, and, to a certain extent, land use. Changes in river flow are assessed through a statistical analysis of the water levels of the Mekong and its distributary, the Bassac river. In the Cambodian Mekong Delta, time series of water level measurements stretch back as far as 1926, in the form of daily manual measurements. More modern, near-realtime records at a time step of 15 minutes exist since 2008 at some stations. A trend analysis and break point detection was carried out at four hydrological stations maintained my the MRC in order to pinpoint patterns of change in the hydrological series. Furthermore, the data at several local stations was compared to better understand upstream and downstream dynamics. Similar analyses were implemented for the time series of precipitation measurements. In addition, several sources of precipitation measurements were compared - manual and automatic in-situ measurements at various stations in the area, as well as remotely sensed precipitation measurements. [SOURCE: Page_108]

Detecting changes in regional inundation patterns proved to be a more difficult challenge due to the paucity of data that allows analyses on this subject. Satellite images provide a valuable avenue to assess how the temporal dynamics and extents of annual inundations have changed in the Cambodian Mekong Delta. However, images with sufficient temporal and spatial resolution to satisfactorily track highly dynamic processes such as inundations have only been consistently recorded since 2014. In order to track floods that lie farther back in time, a new method was developed to link locally measured water levels with flood maps derived from satellite images. Once this water level - flood link (WAFL) was established, it was used to re-construct a time series of daily inundation extents going back to 1991. The accuracy of the link itself was checked using a high-resolution digital elevation model, as well as historical remote sensing imagery. [SOURCE: Page_108]

A final element of the regional context that needs to be understood in the framework of this thesis is the general shift in land use, reflecting economic trends and influencing ecohydrological processes. To this end, a classification of natural vegetation was carried out using historical Landsat images and spectral indices. This classification was also used to draw conclusions on the impact of vegetation on the performance of WAFL. [SOURCE: Page_108]

108 [SOURCE: Page_108]

3.1     Delineating the Areas of Interest [SOURCE: Page_109]

The study area for which the aspects discussed above is explored in more detail in this chapter is located ca. 50 km south of the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh, in the floodplains adjacent to the Mekong and the Bassac river, one of the Mekong’s deltaic distributaries. It can further be subdivided into two zones, denominated A and B. [SOURCE: Page_109]

Zone A is located on the right bank of the Bassac. In the North and West is delineated by the Stung, a small stream that debranches from the Bassac. Its southern limit is formed by the Vinh Te canal, which in itself forms the border to Vietnam. This zone’s landscape is fundamentally characterised by Prek channels, which establish a connection between the main rivers and their floodplains by breaching the river banks, elevated by sediment deposition. The terrain characteristically slopes away from the river banks towards the floodplains to the West, and from the banks of the Preks to the inter-Prek areas in the North and South. The elevated terrain areas along the banks of the Bassac and the Preks are called Chamkar in the local language and are rarely flooded. Here, flood-sensitive crops such as fruit trees and vegetables are grown. The lower-lying areas in the floodplains are called Boeung. These are flooded on a regular basis during the rainy season and are cultivated with crops such as rice and maize during the dry season. While flooded, they serve as nurseries for a large variety of fish species (Hortle, 2009b). In addition, these floodplain areas are criss-crossed by a rectangular network of canals that were excavated during the Khmer Rouge period in the 1970s. This landscape configuration and its socio- and eco-hydrological characteristics will be explored further in subsequent chapters. [SOURCE: Page_109]

Zone B differs from Zone A in that its landscape is less defined by Preks and more by large interior floodplains at its center. This zone is bracketed between the Mekong in the East and the Bassac in the West. In the North, its border is formed by a dyke and a canal, and in the South, as in Zone A, by the Vinh Te canal and the border to Vietnam. While Preks do exist in Zone B, along both the Mekong and the Bassac, their lengths are shorter and the distances between them bigger. Instead, the defining landscape elements are the extensive floodplains at the center of Zone B. Here too, a network of Khmer Rouge canals is embedded in the floodplain. In addition, there are shallow, artificial reservoirs, also excavated at the same time. In these areas, rice cultivation dominates. In addition, fishing used to be a predominant activity here at sufficient water levels, with fish benefiting from the broad expanses of submerged natural vegetation. [SOURCE: Page_109]

109 [SOURCE: Page_109]

3.2.1    Data Availability: Mekong River Commission Time Series and In- Situ Loggers [SOURCE: Page_111]

The hydrological data used in this analysis, and in the wider context of the thesis, comes from several stations maintained by the MRC, as well as water level measurements taken with a series of differential pressure loggers (Onset Hobo MX2001) in a sub-section of Zone A, which corresponds to the smaller-scale study area on which Chapters 4.3 and 6 focus. These loggers were installed in 2020 by a team from IRD and ITC in the course of the project of which this thesis forms a part. The locations of all measurement stations are given in Figure 3.2, except for two stations in Phnom Penh, which are located approximately 50 river kilometers upstream of Koh Kehl (cf. Figure 3.1). Furthermore, a pressure logger that was installed near the hydrological station at Koh Khel is equally not visible in the map since its location coincides with that of the MRC station. [SOURCE: Page_111]

The loggers have been collecting information at a temporal resolution of 15 minutes since late spring 2020, though with varying consistency as will be explained in subsequent chapters. The MRC stations, too, have different periods of coverage. Table 3.1 gives the specifics for each water level measurement station in the vicinity of the areas of interest and shown in Figure 3.2, including the measurement interval and the temporal range of measurements. Here, it can be seen that several water level measurement stations ceased their activity in 2005-2006, such as Kompong Trabek, Stung Slot, and Tuk Chhoo, as well as the measurement of daily minimum and maximum water levels in Chau Doc and Tan Chau. These measurements will thus not be considered any further. Furthermore, some measurement stations, such as Angkorborey, Phnom Penh Port, Koh Khel, Chau Doc, and Tan Chau provide both manual and telemetry measurements. Manual measurements are nominally taken at an interval of 1-6 days, though for the stations in the study area twice-daily measurements have been provided since 2006, and once-daily measurements were recorded before then. Telemetry measurements, in contrast, provide near-realtime data at an interval of 15 minutes. While this data resolution is useful for gaining insights into daily dynamics such as the propagation of tidal influence, they span shorter durations than the daily time series. For instance, telemetry data goes as far back as 2008 at Phnom Penh Chaktomuk and 2010 at Chau Doc, but only to June 2021 at Koh Kehl. In contrast, manual measurements at Neak Luong provide a fairly consistent time series since 1926. [SOURCE: Page_111]

111 [SOURCE: Page_111]

For the purpose of the analysis in this section, water level time series at six MRC stations were used: Phnom Penh Chaktomuk, Koh Kehl, Angkorborey, and Neak Luong in Cambodia and Tan Chau and Chau Doc in Vietnam. The Koh Kehl and Chau Doc stations measure data on the Bassac, Tan Chau and Neak Luong on the Mekong. The Phnom Penh Chaktomuk station is located near the diffluence of the Mekong and the Bassac and can thus be seen to represent water levels in both rivers. The Angkorborey measurement station is located further inland in the Cambodian floodplain and measures the water level in the Prek Ambel, a distributary of the Bassac. Long-term daily data from the Neak Luong, Koh Khel, Tan Chau, and Chau Doc stations on the Mekong and the Bassac were used for an analysis of hydrological trends in these rivers just upstream and downstream of the area of interest. [SOURCE: Page_112]

Furthermore, near-realtime water levels at Phnom Penh Chaktomuk, Koh Khel, and Chau Doc were harnessed for a simplified HEC-RAS model to examine the amplitude and dynamics of tidal influence in this river section.2 To complement these insights, near-realtime (NRT) data from Phnom Penh, Angkorborey, Koh Khel, Chau Doc, and the logger in the study area located on the Bassac were used to compare sub-daily dynamics and tidal influences upstream and downstream of the areas of interest. [SOURCE: Page_112]

At Koh Khel, a continuous time series of daily water level measurements since autumn 1991 is available. At Neak Luong, a series is available since 1926, which is, apparently, remarkably complete save for two larger gaps in 1946 and 1952-3. For this series, the tests were carried out twice: once on the entirety of the series, and once on a shortened series corresponding to the same duration as that available at Koh Khel. At both Chau Doc and Tan Chau, series are available since 1980 and the analysis was conducted on the entirety of the series. [SOURCE: Page_112]

Furthermore, river cross sections provided by the MRC at Koh Khel and Chau Doc^3 were used to estimate the geometry of the river between these two sections in order to construct a hydraulic model in HEC-RAS to simulate the water level slope on the Bassac. In addition to these profiles, two profiles near Koh Khel and Koh Thom, measured with an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) in 2018 were used. 3.2.2.2    Change Point and Trend Analysis [SOURCE: Page_116]

To analyze the long-term hydrological trends in river water levels, a trend analysis was imple- mented using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test (Hamed and Ramachandra Rao, 1998). Then, a change point detection was carried out using the Pettitt test (Pettitt, 1979), Buishand’s range test (Buishand, 1982), and the standard normal homogeneity test (Alexandersson (1986)). This approach follows the analyses by Mallakpour and Villarini (2016), Yun et al. (2020), and Zhou et al. (2019). The parameters tested were the dates of the flood rise and recession, the overall flood duration, the duration of water levels above local threshold^4 , the average water level during the flood, and the maximum water level, along with the date at which it was reached each year. [SOURCE: Page_116]

These parameters reflect the immediate considerations of farmers with regard to their cul- tivation practices. The date of the flood arrival, for example, determines whether early wet season crops can be harvested in time, or whether they will suffer damage from the oncoming inundations. Similarly, the date of the flood recession dictates when crops can be planted on the formerly inundated fields and the extent to which they will depend on irrigation at the end of their growing cycle. The dates of the flood rise and recession - and thus the overall flood duration - were defined on the basis of the rate at which water levels rise and fall (∆wl). The date of the largest positive ∆wl was taken as the start of the flood, the date of the largest negative ∆wl as the date of recession. The number of days between these two dates was taken as the flood duration. All elevations are given in the local Ha Tien 1960 elevation datum. [SOURCE: Page_116]

3.2.3      Results and Discussion [SOURCE: Page_116]

The comparisons of near-realtime and daily water levels are given in Figures 3.5 and 3.7. From the comparison of NRT data, at the end of November 2020, it emerges that tidal influence can be registered at all stations, though at different amplitudes. In Chau Doc, daily water level variations 4 Local thresholds of 5 m at Koh Khel, 4 m at Neak Luong, and 2 m at both Tan Chau and Chau Doc were chosen. [SOURCE: Page_116]

A local threshold of 4 m rather than 5 m was set at Neak Luong because there were several years in the time series when water levels did not exceed 5 m at all. The downstream thresholds of 2 m similarly take account of the lowest water level exceeded every year as well as the water surface slope. [SOURCE: Page_116]

116 [SOURCE: Page_116]

according to the tides reach amplitudes of up to 1 m. At Phnom Penh, in contrast, the variation is only several centimeters. It is notable that the tidal influence is clearly discernible at the station in the case study area on the Bassac mainstream, but hardly noticeable in Angkorborey, even though the latter station is further downstream in absolute terms. Furthermore, it is important to note that the average registered water levels decline much more sharply between stations further downstream than between Phnom Penh and Koh Khel. For instance, the average water level during the period shown in Figure 3.5 (27/11/2020 - 30/11/2020) is 3.20 m in Phnom Penh and 2.98 m at Koh Khel. This results in a difference of 22 cm over ca. 50 river kilometers, meaning an average slope of the water surface of 0.4 cm per kilometer. In contrast, the average water level registered by the logger in the study area is 2.37 m, even though it is only ca. 21 river kilometers downstream of Koh Khel. This means that there is a total decline of 61 cm, which translates to 2.9 cm per river kilometer. Similarly striking is the difference between the logger in the case study area and the station at Chau Doc, which tallies in at 92 cm, or 1.8 cm per river kilometer.5 It can furthermore be observed that at Chau Doc, both the diurnal and the semi-diurnal tidal regimes that influence the Mekong Delta can be observed. According to Dung et al. (2011) and Phan et al. (2019), the Mekong Delta sees two tidal influences: the semidiurnal tide originating in the South China Sea and the diurnal tide, stemming from the Gulf of Thailand^6 [SOURCE: Page_117]

Similarly, propagation times vary. For example, on 28/11/2020, the maximum water level at Chau Doc at high tide is registered at 21:30. At the logger in the case study area, this maximum level is registered at 06:30 on 29/11/2020, eight hours later. In contrast, the maximum water level at Koh Khel is registered only three hours later. Between Koh Khel and Phnom Penh, the delay is a mere five and a half hours, with the maximum water level being reached at 15:00. This means the average propagation speed of the tidal wave between Chau Doc and the logger is 6.4 km/h, between the logger and Koh Khel 7 km/h, and between Koh Khel and Phnom Penh ca. 9.1 km/h. [SOURCE: Page_117]

at approximately 5 m (min:-0.3 m on 01/06/2010, max: 4.89 m on 23/09/2000). This lines up well with the values reported by (Lanh, 2005), as well as Dung et al. (2011), which give the seasonal amplitude at Tan Chau and Chau Doc at 3-5 m. Furthermore, as Figure 3.7 illustrates, the seasonal water level dynamics at Angkor Borey more closely mirror those at Chau Doc than at Koh Khel, even though it is located an approximately equal distance (40 river km) between the two. [SOURCE: Page_121]

Furthermore, the daily data also illustrates that the water slope along the Bassac is far steeper during the flood season, as could be expected due to the backwater effect. This becomes especially evident when looking at the long-term time series available at Phnom Penh, Koh Khel, and Chau Doc, shown in Figure 3.8. At the peak of the flood season, up to 6 m separate the water level elevations between Phnom Penh and Chau Doc, while during the dry season this difference decreases to approximately 0.5 m. Equally notable is the evolution of the water level slope between Phnom Penh and Koh Khel, which is practically non-existent during the height of the dry season, with only a few cm of difference in water elevation between the two stations, even though they are separated by over 50 km. During the wet season, in contrast, this difference reaches over 4.5 m. It is notable that the water levels at Phnom Penh and Koh Khel evolve in almost perfect sync, with small water level differences between the two stations, during the majority of the flood rise. Then, however, the levels at Koh Khel peak at 6 - 6.5 m while those at Phnom Penh continue to rise. This points towards a threshold for floodplain connectivity in the section between these two stations, which leads to significant attenuation effects at Koh Kehl. [SOURCE: Page_121]

One more phenomenon that can be observed is a bi-weekly oscillation in water levels at all stations, which becomes particularly evident during the height of the dry season. An example is given for the months of January to June 2020 in Figure 3.9. It is likely that these oscillations are due to the lunar cycle. Previous studies have reported that the lunar phases have an impact on the observed migratory behaviour of several fish in the Mekong system (Poulsen et al., 2004; Baird et al., 2020), especially the delta, though it appears that no detailed studies on the effect exist yet. [SOURCE: Page_121]

Finally, the comparison of daily water levels between stations also evidences a triple-peaking pattern, especially at Phnom Penh and Koh Khel. This pattern is particularly visible when looking at the long-term time series in Figure 3.8. A first, sharp peak typically occurs relatively early in the wet season, followed by an equally sharp, short descent before the flood rise continues. Then, [SOURCE: Page_121]

121 [SOURCE: Page_121]

as the flood nears its peak, the water levels at Koh Khel, which have thus far risen almost in sync with those at Phnom Penh, decrease slightly before peaking a few days later. At Phnom Penh, the water levels continue to rise sharply for another few days, then decrease slightly, and finally peak. It can be conjectured that these peaks are related to thresholds for floodplain connectivity, or perhaps even the reverse flow of the Mekong into the Tonle Sap Lake. [SOURCE: Page_122]

The results of the analysis of long-term hydrological trends related to flood characteristics are given in Figures 3.10 to 3.14. The water level time series at Koh Khel shows trends towards a later flood rise and an earlier flood recession (the latter is significant at p <0.1). Most significant is the decrease of the duration of water levels at over 5 m (p=0.022). A break point is detected by all three homogeneity tests for the hydrological year 2007/08. [SOURCE: Page_122]

The water level series at Neak Luong since 1926 exhibits significant trends towards a later flood arrival (p=0.03), decreasing maximum water levels (p<0.001), and decreasing flood durations at over 5 m (p<0.001). The short time series (1990-2020) shows a trend towards an earlier flood recession (p=0.06), a shorter flood duration (p=0.09), and especially a decreasing average water level during the flood (p=0.03), as well as a decrease in the incidence of water levels above 4 m (p=0.03). Significant break points were detected 17 years into the time series, which corresponds to the break 2009/10. [SOURCE: Page_122]

At both Tan Chau and Chau Doc, break points were detected for the hydrological year 2007/08. In addition, there is a significant decreasing trend in terms of maximum water levels and flood durations of over 2 m at Tan Chau (p<0.001). [SOURCE: Page_122]

Overall, it emerged from the analyses that the hydrological year 2007/2008 significantly separates two statistically homogeneous periods characterised by different flood durations, dates of flood rise and recession, and flood peaks. This closely mirrors trends observed in basin-wide studies, with shorter flood durations and lower wet season water levels, and a break point in 2008 (Yun et al., 2020; Heng et al., 2021). Consequently, the years pre- and post-2008 were used as comparison periods for the analysis of long-term trends in land cover and inundation dynamics (see Chapter 3.4). When comparing some flood characteristics of the pre- and post-2008 periods, several common trends emerge (see Table 3.2). Flood durations decrease by approximately 16-32 days and average peak water levels decrease by between 10 and over 50 cm. While it must be noted that many of these differences are not statistically significant, certainly in part due to [SOURCE: Page_122]

122 [SOURCE: Page_122]

3.3.1     Data Availability: Local Rainfall Measurements vs. Remotely Sensed Series [SOURCE: Page_128]

Overall, there are eleven precipitation stations either within or in the vicinity of the areas of interest in the Cambodian Mekong Delta. Eight of them were installed by the Mekong River Commission and two by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) (see Figure 3.15). One was installed in the course of the project in the framework of which this thesis was conducted. [SOURCE: Page_128]

The MRC stations are Koh Khel, Prey Lvear, Angkorborey^7 , and Koh Thom West of the Bassac, Peam Raing (Leuk-Dek) between the Bassac and the Mekong, and Neak Luong and Peam Chor East of the Mekong. These stations form part of the MRC observation network and coincide with the hydrological stations at Koh Kehl and Neak Luong. The UNDP installed two measurement stations West of the Bassac, one at Khao Thum^8 and one at Borey Cholsar. They were installed as part of the project Strengthening Climate Information and Early Warning Systems in Cambodia to Support Climate Resilient Development and Adaptation to Climate Change, funded through the GEF-Least Developed Countries Fund. In the course of this project, 24 Automatic Weather Stations (AWS) and 29 Automatic Hydrological Stations (AHS) were installed across Cambodia. In March 2019, they were handed over to the Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology (MOWRAM), which has maintained them since then (UNDP, 2021). Finally, one station on the western bank of the Bassac river was installed in 2020 in the course of the project of which this thesis forms a part, in cooperation between the IRD and the ITC. [SOURCE: Page_128]

One considerable limitation on the reliability of the data listed above, however, is the duration over which the various stations provide data as well as their sensor type and temporal resolution. In terms of sensors and temporal resolution, two basic types exist - manual instruments providing once- or twice-daily data, and automatic stations providing near-realtime information every 15 minutes. Furthermore, some stations exhibit gaps during those periods for which they do nominally provide data. The manual measurements at Angkorborey, for instance, are listed as lasting from from 2001 to 2007 in the metadata provided by the MRC. However, data 7 Angkorborey (Angkor Borey in its alternative anglicised spelling.) is given twice in the map because two [SOURCE: Page_128]

different stations were maintained at different points in time in similar locations. 8 Here, it is likely that the name of the station is a variation of "Koh Thom". The UNDP does not provide exact [SOURCE: Page_128]

location data - it is thus difficult to pinpoint whether these two stations truly coincide. [SOURCE: Page_128]

station at Koh Khel, and the field station at Prek Chann in the case study area are used. These were chosen because they are located at the intersection of Zone A and B. Since rainfall events can be highly localized, this spatial proximity to both sub-zones is an important factor. Furthermore, these stations continue to provide either consistent time series stretching back several years, or reliable high-resolution NRT data. [SOURCE: Page_130]

The second data type used for precipitation analysis in this thesis is remotely sensed data in the form of CHIRPS. CHIRPS stands for Climate Hazards group Infrared Precipitation with Stations. It is a quasi-global dataset spanning latitudes from 50 °S to 50 °N, at the resolution of 0.05 °. Data is provided at daily, pentadal (5-day), and monthly resolution. Originally, CHIRPS was created in order to support the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) of the United States Agency for International Development. It further developed approaches previously used with success in thermal infrared precipitation products such as the Rainfall Estimate (RFE$_2$) dataset by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) or the TAMSAT African Rainfall Climatology And Time series (TARCAT) by the University of Reading. At its core, CHIRPS provides global Cold Cloud Duration (CCD) rainfall estimates based on the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission Multi-satellite Precipitation Analysis version 7 (TMPA 3B42 V$_7$) and station data incorporated through smart interpolation (Funk et al., 2015). 3.3.3    Results and Discussion [SOURCE: Page_132]

The results of the analysis of rainfall data are given in Figures 3.17 to 3.21, as well as Table 3.4. One observation that emerges even from a purely visual comparison is that there is considerable heterogeneity between stations, both on a daily and monthly level. Looking at Figure 3.17, which shows the daily rainfall amounts registered in October 2021 at the three in-situ stations, as well as the values extracted from CHIRPS, it emerges that CHIRPS tends to overestimate rainfall amounts on days on which the in-situ stations register low or no precipitation. In contrast, it fails to capture high-intensity events such as those registered on the 1st , the 5th , and the 17th at Koh Khel. Similar observations can be made when looking at the monthly rainfall sums for 2021, shown in Figure 3.18. During the first three months of the year, CHIRPS registers far higher rainfall amounts than the in-situ stations. During months with higher rainfall values, in contrast, it is in relatively good agreement with at least one in-situ station - with Koh Thom in April, Koh Khel in May, Koh Thom again in June, and so forth. It is noteworthy that the in-situ stations show similarly high deviations amongst themselves as in comparison to CHIRPS. In April 2021, for instance, when both CHIRPS and the UNDP station at Koh Thom registered total rainfall values of almost 200 mm, both the MRC station at Koh Khel and the field station at Prek Chann barely registered half that amount. Similarly, in May, the in-situ station at Koh Khel and CHIRPS both registered just below 150 mm rainfall, while the field station hovered around 100 mm and the UNDP station barely surpassed 50 mm. Both the monthly and daily comparison reveal that the discrepancies between the in-situ stations do not follow a fixed pattern which could be explained through instrument bias, for instance. [SOURCE: Page_132]

132 [SOURCE: Page_132]

The fact that the agreement between individual stations and CHIRPS data is no higher than the agreement between the in-situ stations themselves is also highlighted by Table 3.4, which shows the RMSE for the comparison of monthly precipitation sums since 2020 between all data sources. The smallest overall RMSE was reached in the comparison between MRC data at Koh Khel and CHIRPS data, followed by the comparison between MRC data and measurements collected at the field station at Prek Chann. In contrast, the highest RMSE was evidenced by the comparison between UNDP and MRC data. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Further insights into the dynamics of rainfall are provided by Figure 3.19. Here, all dates of 2021 for which data for all four stations was available (223 days) were sorted into categories depending on how many mm of rainfall were registered at each station. The results show that the patterns are generally similar between the three in-situ stations, especially between the UNDP and MRC station. CHIRPS, on the other hand, evidently slightly overestimates the number and magnitude of low-intensity rainfall events and underestimates high-intensity events. [SOURCE: Page_133]

Overall, these results points towards considerable spatial heterogeneity in terms of rainfall events in the study area. The stations at Prek Chann and Koh Thom lie 6.5 km apart but still register significantly different rainfall sums for individual events, as can be seen in the comparison of daily values in October 2021. Some of that might be due to local conditions at the stations, though no systematic bias can be detected between them. In terms of spatial configuration, the station at Koh Khel is located approximately 13.5 km further North. For individual rainfall events, it exhibits similarly unsystematic variations in comparison to values measured at other in-situ stations. When it comes to the comparison of the magnitude and frequency of rainfall events, though, Figure 3.19 shows that the UDNP and field station exhibit slightly more similar patterns, with the MRC station registering a few more medium-intensity events. This similarity might be due to their spatial proximity. [SOURCE: Page_133]

When it comes to CHIRPS, it is notable that with regard to RMSE values, it is a fairly good predictor for local rainfall values, especially for the MRC an field station, with RMSE results of 42.03 mm and 54.93 mm respectively. These values are similar to those reported by Dandridge et al. (2019), which compared the use of different satellite-based precipitation products in Southeast Asia and found that for elevations between 0 and 100 m, CHIRPS showed an average RMSE of 85.41 mm in comparison to local stations. The same study also noted [SOURCE: Page_133]

3.4     Identifying Inundation Dynamics and Trends Through Satellite Imagery [SOURCE: Page_137]

As outlined in the introductory chapter to this thesis, inundations play an essential role in the hydrological cycle of the Mekong Delta. They furthermore contribute to a wide range of regulating ecosystem services that support the biodiversity and agricultural productivity of the Mekong Delta, from depositing nutrient-rich sediments on the floodplains to recharging shallow aquifers (Kondolf et al., 2018; Boretti, 2020; Kummu and Sarkula, 2008; Dang et al., 2018). It is therefore crucial to understand the temporal and spatial patterns of inundations in the area of interest to this thesis - and how they have changed over the past few decades. However, several obstacles had to be overcome in order to gain insights into these aspects at the local scale. [SOURCE: Page_137]

Previous research existed on the how hydrological changes in the Mekong basin impacted annual inundations in the Mekong Delta, especially their incidence, duration, and spatial pattern of annual inundations. However, these studies were set at larger scales, often focused on Vietnam, and based on different hydrological and hydrodynamic models or on past series of remote sensing imagery (Heng et al., 2021; Try et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020; Mohammed et al., 2018; Burbano et al., 2020). Each of the proposed modeling approaches comes with its own limitations and simplifying assumptions, as well as with a challenge regarding parametrisation in the relatively data-sparse region of the Mekong Basin. In terms of remote sensing, freely accessible, consistent long-term image time series such as Landsat and MODIS can provide some insights into how the spatial patterns of inundations have shifted (Aires et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2016; Fayne et al., 2017). However, many of these series are limited in terms of the temporal and spatial resolution of images, and, in the case of optical images, exhibit data sparsity during the wet season due to cloud cover. They also have difficulties accounting for water areas dissimulated by natural vegetation. Due to the limitations inherent in each approach, the existing studies are unable to produce both sufficiently extensive time series and adapted spatial and temporal resolutions for analysing long term flood dynamics at local scales. [SOURCE: Page_137]

An alternative path is now available in the form of the Sentinel constellation by the European Space Agency (ESA). Its Sentinel-1 and 2 satellites, launched between 2014 and 2017 (Potin et al., 2019), provide freely available optical and SAR data, at a return period of five to six days [SOURCE: Page_137]

137 [SOURCE: Page_137]

and a spatial resolution of up to 10 m. This makes Sentinel a valuable basis to better understand dynamic hydrological processes, such as inundations, at local scales. Both Sentinel-1 and -2 data have been widely used in hydrological applications, separately and in combination (Twele et al., 2016; DeVries et al., 2020; Tsyganskaya et al., 2018). On the floodplains of the Mekong delta, Quang et al. (2019) and Pham-Duc et al. (2017) both use Sentinel-1 to track annual inundations. However, the disadvantage of the Sentinel series lies in its comparatively short duration, which makes it impossible to observe long-term trends. [SOURCE: Page_138]

To address these challenges, a new method was developed in the course of this thesis to analyse long-term flood dynamics in the Cambodian upper Mekong delta, in order to infer the impact of basin-wide hydrological alterations on local hydro-ecological systems. To circumvent barriers of data sparsity and limitations of any single method, a multi-method approach was employed to reconstruct a time series of daily inundation extents, based on local water level measurements since 1991 and on Sentinel-derived flood maps. It hinges on the construction of a Water Level - Flood Link (WAFL), as is outlined below. [SOURCE: Page_138]

3.4.1    Materials and Methods [SOURCE: Page_138]

An overview of the methodology employed in this analysis is given in Figure 3.22. [SOURCE: Page_138]

The multi-method approach outlined here is based on local knowledge acquired in the course of fieldwork and through exchanges with other researchers working in the area. Besides in-situ measurements, the researchers working on the project of which this thesis forms a part acquired an in-depth qualitative understanding regarding the development projects implemented in the area, local agricultural practices, and local hydrological processes.This understanding provided the context for this approach. [SOURCE: Page_138]

At the core of this methodology is the establishment of a water level - flood link (WAFL). This is achieved by deriving a time series of inundation extents from Sentinel-1 and -2 imagery, and then linking them to locally-measured water levels using a correlation model to take into account propagation delay times. As a subsequent step, a time series of inundation extents is back-calculated on the basis of WAFL. [SOURCE: Page_138]

138 [SOURCE: Page_138]

For this study, interferometric wide swath (IW) images in VV and VH polarization at 10 m resolution are used. The image bands of which a Sentinel-1 tile consists are given in Table 3.5 [SOURCE: Page_140]

Like Sentinel-1, the ESA’s Sentinel-2 collection consists of a pair of satellites. Sentinel-2A was launched in 2015, followed by Sentinel-2B in 2017. Both satellites have a return period of 10 days, resulting in a combined Sentinel-2 image frequency of 5 days. The constellation provides multi-spectral optical imagery for a total of 12 spectral bands ranging from the blue to the short wave infrared spectrum. All Sentinel-2 bands are given in Table 3.6 below. [SOURCE: Page_140]

Both Sentinel-1 and -2 images were used to generate a series of flood maps for the area of interest for the period 2017-2020. 2017 was chosen as a starting point because the Sentinel satellite constellation was fully in place beginning that year. For this purpose, the series of Sentinel-1 and 2 images available on Google Earth Engine (GEE, Gorelick et al. (2017)) was analysed. [SOURCE: Page_140]

First, images were subjected to multiple pre-treatments. Sentinel-2 images were atmospheri- cally corrected using the sen^2cor algorithm (Main-Knorn et al., 2017) and clouds were masked based on the QA band. Sentinel-1 images underwent pre-processing based on the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-1 toolbox. Metadata was updated with a restituted orbit file, border noise and thermal noise were removed, and radiometric calibration and orthorectification were applied. In addition, a refined Lee speckle filter (Lee, 1983) was implemented. [SOURCE: Page_140]

3.4.1.2   Landsat [SOURCE: Page_141]

As briefly mentioned above, the Landsat satellites maintained by the North American Space Agency (NASA) provide optical imagery. The standout characteristic of this satellite series is its consistency over multiple decades. The first Landsat satellite was launched in 1972 - Landsat 1 - since then, the mission has provided a consistent archive of earth observation imagery. Landsat 1 - 3, carrying a Multi-spectral Scanner (MSS) provided a spatial resolution of 60 m and four spectral bands in the green, red, and near infrared (1 and 2) spectrum for the period between 1972 and 1983. Landsat 4 and 5 also both still carried MSS onboard, but were also equipped with a Thematic Mapper that recorded a larger variety of spectral bands, seven in total. They provide earth observation scenes at a spatial resolution of 30 m between 1982 and 1993, and 1984 and 2012 respectively. They were succeeded by Landsat 79 , launched in 1999, and Landsat 8, launched in 2013 (Tollefson, 2013). In September 2021, NASA launched Landsat 9. First images from the mission were released at the beginning of November (NASA Earth Observatory, 2021; Masek et al., 2020). The return period of Landsat is 16 days, which allows for the monitoring of processes with moderate temporal dynamics, but places some restrictions on observing highly dynamic processes such as floods. Nonetheless, Landsat has been used for a wide range of 9 Landsat 6 was lost in a launch failure in October 1993. [SOURCE: Page_141]

Then, an unsupervised K-means classification approach was chosen (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007; Frank et al., 2016) to identify flooded areas in both Sentinel-1 and -2 images. This classification approach was selected because it can be applied equally to optical and SAR images, and because no local calibration of threshold values is required. As the training period for the classifier, a time window during the 2018 wet season - from September 25 to October 01 - was used due to the large flood extents and sharp contrast between open water and dry areas at this time. Validation of the flood classification was carried out using a total of 2340 points, set manually on the basis of SPOT-6 high-resolution imagery, on four different dates at different stages during the flood cycle: 2017/01/29, 2018/06/24, 2018/08/04, and 2019/01/27. On this basis, a confusion matrix and the kappa coefficient (Congalton, 1991) of the classification were calculated. After validation, the classifier was applied to the entire collection of Sentinel images, and the extents of open water areas were extracted for each image. Finally, the time series of inundation extents was exported, smoothed using a 3-day rolling mean, and scaled down to a daily time step using linear interpolation. [SOURCE: Page_144]

3.4.1.5   Establishing a Water Level - Flood Link (WAFL) [SOURCE: Page_144]

In the dynamics of inundations on large floodplains, a temporal lag is typically observed between the change in river water level and the change in flood extent (Zhang et al., 2017). Time is needed [SOURCE: Page_144]

144 [SOURCE: Page_144]

to fill the water bodies when the river flood occurs, accounting for a temporal lag between the flood dynamics and the river water levels. Similarly, the flood recession on the floodplains is out of phase with the river water level drop, since inundated areas decrease more slowly due to the retention of water by dykes and other floodplains structures. This results in hysteresis effects on the relationship between river water levels and the inundated surfaces (Hughes, 1980; Kummu et al., 2014). Lag times are controlled by the ease with which water can flow between the river and the floodplains, depending on hydraulic controls such as dykes, canals, bank heights, local topography, and water level gradients. Physically-based models require geometric data of the main hydraulic connections and dykes, which are not accessible at this scale. Even high- resolution DEMs are often insufficient in terms of horizontal resolution and vertical accuracy to capture the hydraulic controls by dykes in the area, many of which are below 1 m in height. Due to the low terrain gradient, a water level rise of a few centimetres is enough to act as a tipping point for water to spill over certain dykes and induce several hectares of additional inundated surfaces. [SOURCE: Page_145]

To account for this lag time, the correlative method for flood curves developed by Lamagat et al. (1993) was used. Initially developed to identify correlations between gauging stations, this approach has been used with satellite data series in both the Tana river delta in Kenya by Leauthaud et al. (2013), and at the Niger and Senegal rivers by Bader et al. (2016) (flooded areas) and Belaud and Bercher (2010) (satellite altimetry). It was developed to model the propagation of flood waves, specifically in areas with low slope gradients and observable hysteresis effects in rating curves - such as deltaic floodplains. This approach combines kinematic elements with statistical methods. Its main advantage is that it identifies optimal correlation factors not between the overall time series of flood extents and water levels in the river, but between a set number of sub-sections of the time series. Consequently, it can account for the varying time delays depending on the phase of the flood cycle. Therefore, the time delay is expressed as a function of the river water level, while the flood extent at a given time is a function of the water level observed some days before. [SOURCE: Page_145]

Once the delay times had been made explicit, each inundation map was extracted from the time series of Sentinel-1 and 2 images and assigned a corresponding water level. Then, a flood count and water level link parameter were calculated for each pixel in the areas of interest. The approach used to achieve this is depicted in Figure 3.24. The binary flood maps - flooded pixels [SOURCE: Page_145]

145 [SOURCE: Page_145]

having been assigned a value of 1 - were stacked. Subsequently, the sum of times each pixel was registered as flooded was calculated. As a result, pixels that represent permanent water areas, which are always detected as flooded, have a flood count equal to the number of images in the analysis. Pixels on elevated terrain areas that are never flooded have a flood count of zero. Next, flood counts are linked to water levels measured at Koh Khel. Each pixel was assigned the lowest water level (cm resolution) at which it was detected as being inundated. [SOURCE: Page_146]

Figure 3.24: Logic workflow for creating the water level - flood link (WAFL). Example of an area with 4 pixels, and 4 images corresponding to 4 different water levels at Koh Khel. Blue areas represent flooded pixels. [SOURCE: Page_146]

3.4.1.6   Comparing the Flood Link With Inundation Extents Derived from Landsat and TanDEM-X [SOURCE: Page_146]

Since the link was established on the basis of relatively recent images from the second half of the 2010s it became necessary to ascertain to which extent it was capable of delivering accurate estimates of inundated areas based on water levels from the 1990s and the 2000s. To this end, two approaches were chosen. The first was a comparison of inundation extents generated on the basis of the WAFL with those directly derived from Landsat images from the period 1991-2020. The second was to use the TanDEM-X (12m) Digital Elevation Model (DEM), which is based on SAR imagery collected in the early 2010s, to generate estimates of flood extents and compare them with those generated on the basis of WAFL. [SOURCE: Page_146]

In order to assess the accuracy of the WAFL, the inundation extents that it found were [SOURCE: Page_146]

146 [SOURCE: Page_146]

compared with two other sources of information on inundations: inundation maps derived from historical Landsat imagery and inundation extents estimated from the TanDEM-X elevation model. [SOURCE: Page_147]

For the comparison with Landsat, a total of 94 optical Landsat-5 and -8 images were used. [SOURCE: Page_147]

To derive inundation maps from Landsat images, the same spectral indices as for Sentinel were calculated, and the images were then partitioned into flooded and dry areas by an unsuper- vised k-means algorithm. These maps were then compared with the inundation extents generated using the WAFL and the water level observed at the date the image was taken. First, the total inundated area was derived for each of the 94 images and compared to the calculated inundated area. Second, six Landsat images from flood seasons during the period of interest (1991-2020) were chosen to identify discrepancies in spatial inundation patterns. These images, at a time step of about five years, were selected because they provide rare cloud-free wet-season scenes. They date from 1991/11/29, 1995/11/05, 2000/08/31, 2005/08/21, 2013/09/12, 2015/09/11, and 2020/11/28. [SOURCE: Page_147]

The second method of testing the applicability of WAFL was to derive inundation maps from the TanDEM-X (12 m resolution) elevation model, provided by the German aerospace agency (Rizzoli et al., 2017). This DEM was used to assess the extent of inundation patterns as if they were solely linked to differences in detectable terrain elevation in the study area. To establish the comparison, flood extents were generated from the DEM by super-imposing a planar water surface onto the DEM and classifying all areas that were beneath the elevation of that surface as flooded. The planar water surface itself takes into account a North-South slope, based on water level measurements at Koh Khel and in-situ measurements at the western end of a Prek at the center of Zone A. Similar to the Landsat measurements, a comparison of the size of inundated areas was carried out, along with spatially explicit comparisons of the distribution of inundations. [SOURCE: Page_147]

The comparison was also performed locally, directly based on in-situ measurements. The in-situ water level measurements were carried out using a differential pressure logger (Onset Hobo MX2001), with a complete time series available from September 2020 to April 2021 at 15-minute intervals. First, a pseudo water level in the floodplains within a radius of 1km of the logger was generated. This was achieved using inundation extents detected through Sentinel images, and the DEM-derived elevation-area curve of the zone, and based on the assumption that [SOURCE: Page_147]

147 [SOURCE: Page_147]

3.4.1.7   Land Use Classification: Detecting Natural Vegetation [SOURCE: Page_149]

Finally, vegetation is another element that remains to be tested to assess the applicability of the WAFL. Natural vegetation, such as shrubland and forests, can easily obscure open water surfaces due to canopy cover, especially in optical remote sensing imagery (Tsyganskaya et al., 2018; Pekel et al., 2016; Plank et al., 2017). Therefore, discrepancies between calculated and observed inundated areas might also be due to this obscuring effect, rather than the performance of the classification method. In Cambodia especially, it is known that forest loss has been a notable issue over the past few decades. Driven by economic developments and the Cambodian government’s policy of land concessions, forested areas decreased by 12.4% between 2000 and 2012 alone (Davies et al., 2015). Lohani et al. (2020), evaluating forest loss in Cambodia between 1993 and 2017, found that, overall, 19% of primary forest was lost, that the rate of deforestation is accelerating, and that the majority of deforestation is centered in the floodplain, with 31% of forests there having been lost since the 1990s. [SOURCE: Page_149]

To assess the long-term change of land cover in the area of interest and to gauge the extent of these changes on the detection of inundations, an approach relying on a simple thresholding method using the NDVI was chosen. The NDVI was calculated for composite Landsat images for the dry seasons 1990/1991, 2000/2001, 2010/2011, and 2020/2021 for the months between March and May, which are the driest in the region. Then, areas exhibiting an NDVI of over 0.55 (Nath and Acharjee, 2013; Hashim et al., 2019) were classified as likely forest and shrubland. Further on in the analysis, the obscuring effect of canopy cover was taken into consideration by considering low-lying areas classified as natural vegetation, which were otherwise surrounded by open water surfaces, as likely flooded. [SOURCE: Page_149]

3.4.1.8   Flood Dynamics Analysis: Calculating Inundation Durations and Incidences [SOURCE: Page_149]

As a final step in this analysis, flood extent maps were used to generate inundation durations and incidences for each pixel (10 m) in the study area for the comparison periods identified on the basis of the hydrological time series. The term "inundation incidence" refers to the percentage of years in each of the two comparison periods during which any one pixel was flooded. Six different incidences were calculated: the overall annual inundation incidence (the % of years [SOURCE: Page_149]

149 [SOURCE: Page_149]

during the period that a given pixel is flooded, regardless of the date), along with inundation incidences at dates of interest to agricultural practices in the area, identified on the basis of interviews with stakeholders. These are the 15th of July, the 31st of July, the 15th of August (of importance for harvesting early wet season crops), the 31st of August, and the 25th of September (of importance for rainy season cultivation and planting of recession crops). [SOURCE: Page_150]

3.4.2     Results [SOURCE: Page_150]

3.4.2.1   Detection of Inundation Extents [SOURCE: Page_150]

In total, 119 Sentinel-2 and 360 Sentinel-1 images, taken between 2017/01/01 and 2020/12/31 were processed. This means that, on average, one image is available every three days. An example of an inundation map derived from a Sentinel-2 image on the basis of the k-means classification is given in Figure 3.26 below. The average accuracy of the classification of flooded areas lay at 96.5%, with a Kappa value of 0.785. However, it must be mentioned that these values at least partly result from the fact that the validation data used was itself derived from remote sensing imagery. Though it was set on the basis of high-resolution imagery, and with first-hand knowledge of the study area in mind, the validation points were still only set in unambiguous areas. Consequently, areas such as flooded vegetation or inundated rice fields prior to planting that cannot be easily discriminated as either flooded or not in satellite imagery are underrepresented, and their ambiguities missing from the validation results. [SOURCE: Page_150]

Dynamics of inundation extents in Zone A and B, detected on the basis of optical and SAR Sentinel imagery and in relation to water levels at Koh Khel, are shown in Figure 3.27. A good general correspondence between the dynamics of the two curves can be observed. A time delay between the dynamics of the water level curves and the response of the inundated areas can be clearly seen. Large inundated areas correspond to high water levels several days prior, justifying the use of the Lamagat model as explained in the previous section. [SOURCE: Page_150]

150 [SOURCE: Page_150]

3.4.2.2   The Water level flood link (WAFL) [SOURCE: Page_152]

The water level flood link (WAFL) was calculated in accordance with the methodology described above. It is given in Figure 3.28, alongside the TanDEM-X elevation model. As can be seen, the WAFL shows similar elevation gradients to those seen in the DEM. [SOURCE: Page_152]

Figure 3.28: Side-by-side comparison of the water level at which each pixel becomes flooded, according to the WAFL, and the TanDEM-X terrain elevation model. [SOURCE: Page_152]

3.4.2.3   Comparison of Calculated Inundation Extents with Flood Maps Derived from Sentinel and Landsat and Influence of Natural Vegetation [SOURCE: Page_152]

In terms of comparing the inundation extents calculated using the WAFL with flood maps derived from Sentinel- and Landsat images, there is widespread agreement, though idiosyncratic variations remain. [SOURCE: Page_152]

152 [SOURCE: Page_152]

Figure 3.29, shows the agreement between WAFL- and Sentinel-2 derived inundation extents at three dates during the flood seasons in 2018, 2019, and 2020. The 2018 image is partially obscured by clouds that are misclassified as dry areas in the Sentinel-derived inundation map. For the 2019 and 2020 images, average classification accuracies lie at 90.60%. [SOURCE: Page_153]

The agreement between the calculated flood extents based on WAFL and those observed in the 94 Landsat images used in this analysis is shown in Figures 3.30 and 3.31. It emerges that in terms of overall inundated areas, there is a strong agreement between the two methods. As Figure 3.30 shows, there are some deviations in years that saw heavy floods, during which calculated inundation extents are lower than those obtained through Landsat classification. [SOURCE: Page_153]

In addition, it can be noted that the spatial distribution of inundations varies between the two methods of detection and that the deviations are more extensive the further back in time the points of comparison lie. For example, Figure 3.31 shows that WAFL-derived inundation maps detect extensive inundated areas in Zone B, while these areas are dry according to the Landsat classification. In contrast, areas of medium elevation in Zone A (transition zones between Boeung and Chamkar) appear as flooded in the 1990s and early 2000s in Landsat images, but are registered as dry by WAFL. The strong agreement between the total water surfaces obtained by the two methods may thus be contingent. This hypothesis will be further investigated in the discussion section. [SOURCE: Page_153]

153 [SOURCE: Page_153]

Figure 3.31: Comparison of inundation extents derived from the WAFL and Landsat-5 and -8 images [SOURCE: Page_156]

156 [SOURCE: Page_156]

is more likely to be due to the planting of fruit trees such as mango, whose areas, according to interviews and agricultural statistics, have sharply increased over the last 10 years. [SOURCE: Page_158]

Furthermore, the analysis of the extents of natural vegetation shows that there is an extensive overlap between those areas that are detected as flooded in WAFL-derived maps, but not by those generated directly from Landsat images. The Overlap line of Table 3.9 shows that upwards of 93% of pixels that exhibit these discrepancies coincide with the detected extents of natural vegetation. This indicates that the floods that are actually present may be masked by canopy cover and are thus undetectable by Landsat imagery. If one considers that all forest pixels that overlap with areas being detected as dry by Landsat and wet by the WAFL are indeed flooded, agreement scores between the two methods for detecting flood extents increase from an average of 79.75% to 87.16% for Zone A, and from 68.49% to 87.18% for Zone B. [SOURCE: Page_158]

3.4.3     Discussion [SOURCE: Page_164]

3.4.3.1   Local Hydrological Trends and their Reflection of Basin-Wide Changes [SOURCE: Page_164]

Hydrological trends in the Cambodian upper Mekong delta closely mirrored those observed in basin-wide studies, with shorter flood durations and lower wet season water levels. Furthermore, the division of comparison periods into a pre- and post-2008 series mirrors the break point found in basin-wide studies, such as Yun et al. (2020) and Heng et al. (2021). [SOURCE: Page_164]

3.4.3.2   Inundation Mapping Using Sentinel: Between Biases and the Value of Observing Local Dynamics [SOURCE: Page_164]

In terms of inundation dynamics, curves of flood extents closely correspond to those of locally measured river water levels, both for Zone A and B. The most noticeable difference between the two zones is that the delay time between the two curves is larger for Zone B than for Zone A, which may be due to its larger width, as well as the relatively shorter length of the Preks connecting the river to the floodplains. In combination, these terrain characteristics mean that floods take longer to reach the center of Zone B than of Zone A. Another resulting characteristic that can be observed for both Zones is that shorter flood durations result in lower maximum inundation extents. This means that even if the peak water levels of two years match up closely, the peak inundation extents won’t be the same if the flood duration is shorter. [SOURCE: Page_164]

3.4.3.3   Validity of the WAFL: Balancing Natural Vegetation, Sedimentation, and Terrain Correspondence [SOURCE: Page_164]

The comparison between WAFL-derived inundation extents and flood maps extracted from Sentinel-2 imagery reveals several advantages and drawbacks of the proposed methodology. First, it clearly illustrates the benefit of using the WAFL-reconstructed inundation extents for the image during the 2018 flood season. The optical Sentinel-2 images at this date show several gaps, left by cloud masking. However, not all clouds were properly detected by the masking algorithm and those that remain are falsely classified as dry areas in the Sentinel-derived flood map, leading [SOURCE: Page_164]

164 [SOURCE: Page_164]

to inconsistencies with the WAFL classification. The drawbacks of the methodology are most clearly revealed in the image from the 2020 flood season. Here, it is visible that the agreement of the two flood classifications is considerably higher in Zone A than in Zone B. Particularly, the WAFL classification in Zone B fails to capture some of the areas detected as inundated in the Sentinel-2 images. This may be due to the fact that water level dynamics in this year deviated considerably from the previously observed norm, with an early peak followed by a lowering of levels, before abruptly rising again towards the season’s main peak. It can be conjectured that the correlative relationship established to characterise the delay time between water levels and the response of inundated areas failed to adequately capture this development. Whether this is an isolated response is hard to assess, since similar early peaking patterns cannot be found anywhere else in the data. [SOURCE: Page_165]

In terms of which factors most impact the detection of floods and the applicability of the WAFL, natural vegetation emerges as the central element in the comparison with Landsat images. This is particularly apparent as the binary classification into flooded and not flooded areas that was chosen in this approach limits the possibility of detecting flooded vegetation. Overall, the comparison with Landsat-derived inundation maps highlights the potential of the WAFL for re- constructing past inundation extents. In general, while the WAFL also has some issues mistaking areas with natural vegetation for dry areas, even when they are flooded, this misclassification is much less frequent than with Landsat. There are two main reasons for that. First, Sentinel-1 SAR has the capacity to detect water under vegetation layers (Tsyganskaya et al., 2018). And second, at the time the Sentinel images were recorded (2017-20) there was already much less natural vegetation in the study area than at the time that many of the Landsat images used in this analysis were taken (cf. Figure 3.32). [SOURCE: Page_165]

A second discrepancy in the comparison with Landsat is observed on higher-lying terrain in the study area. Here, Landsat continually registers inundations in the 1990s and early 2000s, which the WAFL fails to capture. That may be due to the fact that at the time that the Landsat images were recorded, these areas actually were flooded regularly, but that by the time the Sentinel-images were taken, this had changed. Some possible explanations for that could be the construction of local infrastructure (such as small dams and dykes), the natural deposition of sediments, or the raising of land through geotechnical projects. (It is not rare to see farmers raising the level of their land to build houses or plant trees.) The regular distribution of this [SOURCE: Page_165]

165 [SOURCE: Page_165]

discrepancy in flood prevalence between Landsat and WAFL-derived maps seems to speak more for the second option. In terms of sediment deposition on the floodplains of the Mekong delta, Hung et al. (2014) found an average annual deposition of 6.86 kg/m^2 in the Vietnamese Mekong delta in Tam Nong district in Dong Thap province. This corresponds to an annual increase of 6 mm in height. These deposition rates are likely to be higher on the Cambodian side of the border due to the absence of dams and dykes. According to Manh et al. (2014), deposition on the Cambodian floodplains is indeed up to six times higher than in Vietnam, ranging from 19 to 23% of the annual sediment load at Kratie, rather than the 1 to 6% deposited in the compartmentalised floodplains in Vietnam. [SOURCE: Page_166]

When it comes to the comparison of the WAFL with TanDEM-X and the inundation extents derived on both bases, using a planar water surface superimposed on the DEM on the basis of in-situ water levels, seems to be a valid approach on a local scale. From a physical perspective, it appears that the water level registered by the logger could be construed to represent the inflow into the Boeung area, while the pseudo water level derived from Sentinel can be seen as the storage response, with local hydrological processes mirroring the dynamics of those of a reservoir (the Boeung) filling and emptying. This is typical for flood storage cells: the inflow-outflow is governed by the difference in levels between the main connection point and the mean level in the area. The delay is directly linked to the volume of water stored in the considered area and the flow rate. When there is no obstacle in the considered area, the delay is very short and water level can be considered as horizontal (propagation effects are not visible at a daily time step). When dykes limit the flow propagation, the filling of the area is made possible by small openings in dykes (usually made by farmers to irrigate their rice fields). Then it takes a longer time to fill the area. During flood recession, the processes are inverted: water level decreases rapidly in the Preks that are well-connected to the Bassac, while water is stored in the floodplains. Water is kept as long as possible in rice fields (by clogging the dykes) and recedes progressively by gravity (surface and subsurface drainage) and evapotranspiration. [SOURCE: Page_166]

However, the accuracy of this approach diminishes considerably when applied at the scale of the entire study area. At this scale, the assumption of a horizontal water surface slope no longer holds. Even when superimposing a sloped water surface over the entire DEM and taking into account correlations between the station at Koh Khel and the logger, the discrepancy remains high due to the complexity of the hydrological processes in the area. Broadly, this leads to an [SOURCE: Page_166]

166 [SOURCE: Page_166]

overestimation of inundated extents derived from TanDEM-X. However, the use of the DEM does have the advantage of absolutely removing the interference of natural vegetation, as evidenced by the discrepancies in the center of Zone B observed in Figure 3.35. [SOURCE: Page_167]

3.4.3.4   Decreasing Flood Incidence and Durations in the Cambodian Mekong Delta: Pat- terns and Impacts [SOURCE: Page_167]

Despite limitations in the detection of the full flood extents in the 1990s and early 2000s, the analysis clearly shows a pronounced decrease in the incidence and duration of floods, especially in July and the first half of August. Large swaths of the study area, which were regularly flooded during these months in the 1990s, now remain dry until the second half of August. Taken together with the trends of earlier flood recession and the shorter flood durations outlined above, this means that overall, inundations in the Cambodian Mekong delta arrive later, recede earlier, and have lower magnitudes. [SOURCE: Page_167]

To a certain extent, this is in line with previous basin-wide studies such as Yun et al. (2020) and Hecht et al. (2018) that investigated the impacts of climate change and hydropower development. Their main findings were that a lower wet season discharge was to be expected in the future as a result of these developments, along with a higher dry season discharge. In terms of inundations, however, these higher dry season discharges do not balance the lack of inundations during the wet season that are key for the ecological functioning of the floodplains. Similarly, the results are in line with observations by Aires et al. (2020), who found a declining trend in inundation extents in their analysis of the Vietnamese and Cambodian Mekong delta using MODIS data.The same study also found inundations to be delayed by about two weeks in the Cambodian part of the Mekong delta. The present study indicates a longer delay, which may be due to differences in both the time frame and the spatial resolution of the data used. Figure 3.37 indicates that the incidences with which pixels were flooded in late July prior to 2008 are now only attained in late August or early September. Similar parallels exist in the work of Heng et al. (2021). In their modelling study of the Cambodian floodplains - one of the few taking this region as its focus - the authors conclude that total flood extent is projected to decline by 18% by 2040. [SOURCE: Page_167]

These alterations are anathema to the formerly predictable hydrological regime of the re- [SOURCE: Page_167]

167 [SOURCE: Page_167]

gion, and are likely to have wide-reaching consequences for agriculture and fisheries. Greater variability in the dates of the flood arrival and its recession may, for instance, result in shifts in the planting and harvesting times for recession crops and an increased need for irrigation water (Erban and Gorelick, 2016). As far as fisheries are concerned, the later onset of floods and overall decrease in inundation durations limit the period during which fish populations can regenerate in the shallow waters on the floodplains (Hortle, 2009b). Compounded with the decrease in natural vegetation, which provides valuable structural habitat features, this is likely to negatively impact fish population dynamics.Vu et al. (2021) showed a close correlation between the long-term decline in commercial fish catches and declining peak water levels in the Mekong delta. Furthermore, local-level data obtained by the authors from fishermen in the area show fish catch to be much lower in years when the water level at Koh Khel exceeds 4 m for a lower number of days. These changes in inundation extents and durations are likely to impact food security in the region. Burbano et al. (2020), for example, link the shorter flood durations in the Tonle Sap region and the Mekong delta floodplains to shifts in dietary protein from fish to meat, and, consequently, land use changes resulting from the need to accommodate cattle. [SOURCE: Page_168]

Shorter inundation durations and lower incidence also reduce the spatial and temporal extent of the terrestrial-aquatic interface that many regulating ecosystem services depend on. This includes processes such as pest regulation, nutrient deposition, and soil and ground water recharge (Brown and My Phung, 2010; Chen et al., 2011). [SOURCE: Page_168]

Finally the analysis also shows that, even though large changes have occurred in the basin over the past three decades, the link between river water levels and inundation extents has remained relatively static. In contrast to the major changes on the Mekong itself, its hydraulic connections to its floodplains seem to have changed comparatively little, which may be related to the still limited development of water control infrastructure in the Cambodian upper Mekong delta. [SOURCE: Page_168]

168 [SOURCE: Page_168]

3.5     Conclusion : Characterising the Hydrological Dynamics of the Cambodian Mekong Delta [SOURCE: Page_169]

Overall, it can be summarized that the Cambodian Mekong Delta has seen significant shifts in hydrological patterns over the past few decades. While precipitation patterns have remained rela- tively stable on average, river water levels and, consequently, inundations have seen considerable changes. Trends point toward a later arrival of the flood and a shorter overall duration. [SOURCE: Page_169]

The WAFL has been found to delineate inundation extents with acceptable accuracies. For one thing, it has a smaller propensity for mistaking flooded vegetation for dry areas than inundation maps derived from Landsat images. For another, it is based on actual physical observations and thus avoids overestimating inundation extents, a pitfall to which flood maps derived from superimposing a sloped water surface on the TanDEM-X DEM are prone. In terms of improving the approach, it is possible to envision an additional layer of correction of the Sentinel-derived maps on the basis of TanDEM-X to remove any remnants of vegetation interference, as well as the improvement of the water surface slope on the scale of the floodplains. Furthermore, a spatialisation of delay times could lead to more regionally adapted results. And finally, a correction based on long-term sedimentation rates is conceivable. [SOURCE: Page_169]

Based on the identification of a change point in the local hydrological series in 2008 that conforms to previous basin-wide studies linking this change to acceleration of hydropower development on the Mekong mainstream, inundations durations and incidences between two periods, 1991-2008 and 2009-2020 were compared. This comparison showed a small decrease in overall inundation incidence as well as a sharp decrease in inundation incidence at specific dates in July and the first half of August. The results also indicate a decrease in average inundation durations of up to 39 days per year. Overall, this is likely to have considerable adverse impacts on agricultural cycles, fish reproduction, and regulating ecosystem services such as soil and ground water recharge. [SOURCE: Page_169]

Considering all the limitations outlined above, the WAFL offers a valuable path to recon- structing a consistent time series of inundation extents going back to the 1990s. For the purpose of assessing long-term changes in spatial inundation patterns this is invaluable - especially [SOURCE: Page_169]

169 [SOURCE: Page_169]

considering the alternatives of having only sparse amounts of contemporary optical data, data with insufficient spatial and temporal resolution, or no spatial data at all. [SOURCE: Page_170]

On a more general level, the analyses in this chapter has also allowed a better understanding of some overall characteristics of the hydrology of the region, from the propagation of tidal influence upstream to the likely impact that the impact of connections to floodplains have on the attenuation of flood peaks on the mainstream of the Bassac. [SOURCE: Page_170]

Finally, this chapter has also provided a thorough evaluation of the hydrological data available for the area, both in-situ and derived from earth observation approaches. This serves as a valuable basis for the analyses presented in subsequent chapters, and especially for the modeling approach presented in Chapter 6. [SOURCE: Page_170]

170 [SOURCE: Page_170]

4 Understanding Preks - their Origins, Management, and Significance for Local Agroecosystems [SOURCE: Page_171]

Following the thorough analysis of regional hydrological and land cover dynamics in the Cambo- dian Mekong delta presented in the previous chapter, this chapter will "zoom in" to a local level. At this level, several research questions outlined for this thesis that relate to more small-scale processes will be addressed. In particular, this chapter will discuss what role local infrastructure in the form of Preks plays in catalyzing regional processes at a local level, what ecosystem services the people in the Prek area benefit from, and how these are linked to hydrological processes. [SOURCE: Page_171]

In order to do address these issues, a multi-method approach combining interviews with local [SOURCE: Page_171]

171 [SOURCE: Page_171]

stakeholders, archival research, and remote sensing was used. This chapter first introduces the small-scale case study area in which field work was carried out and which forms the center of the analyses presented in this part of this thesis. Then, it delves into the defining landscape feature in this area - the Preks. An overview will be given of their general characteristics, origins, and history, with a particular focus on the recent development projects that aimed to improve their functionalities. Next, one of the core elements of this thesis will be presented - the fieldwork and interviews that were carried out with farmers and local officials in the case study area. In particular, insights into ecosystem services, agricultural practices, water management, and local governance of the Prek system will be outlined. Finally, a remote sensing analysis of land cover in the case study area that combines optical and SAR images will be presented. As will be outlined below, many of the benefits that the local population derives from Preks are related to agriculture. Therefore, it is crucial to understand land use practices and patterns in the region. Partly, this is achieved through interviews with farmers, which allow for the characterization of cropping practices. However, to gain a better spatialized understanding of cultivation cycles, remote sensing is used. The overall approach of this analysis, with a particular focus on the comparison of classification methods, is outlined and results are presented. [SOURCE: Page_172]

4.1     Case Study Area: Location and Characteristics [SOURCE: Page_172]

The case study area in which the local-level analyses presented in this chapter, as well as for the modelling approach outlined in the following chapter, were conducted is shown in Figure 4.2. It is located at the center of the larger Zone A, which was described in the previous chapter. In the East, its border is formed by the Bassac, in the West by the Prek Ambel. Overall, this area encompasses ten Preks. From North to South, they are Prek Cham Kroum, Prek Me Srok, Prek Lok, Prek Pok, Prek Hom, Prek Nou, Prek Put, Prek Chann, Prek Touch, and Prek Thom. They connect the Bassac to the floodplains in the interior of the study area, or to the Prek Ambel in the West. These varying Prek configurations are a principal reason why this area was chosen as the case study area for this thesis. Some connect to larger water courses, such as Prek Cham Kroum, which forms the northern border of the delineated study area, and Prek Thom, which forms the southern border. Others, such as Prek Put, end in a dead end in the study area. A third type, finally, connects to a network of smaller-scale canals in the floodplains. Furthermore, some Preks [SOURCE: Page_172]

4.2     Exploring the History of Preks: From Historical to Mod- ern Engineering Reports [SOURCE: Page_175]

Part of understanding the diverse roles that Preks fulfill today, especially in terms of cultural ecosystem services, is to acquire a sense of their historical importance in the region, their original development, and what they have come to mean for the local population. This section looks at the history of the Preks through the lens of reports written by engineers in various periods, beginning in the early 20th century. To collect these sources, archival research was carried out in the National Archives of Cambodia in Phnom Penh in 2020. It must be noted that, unfortunately, many documents from the period of the French Protectorate and the years after World War II were destroyed during the regime of the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s. For the National Library, the proportion of records that were exterminated during that time lies at 80%. It is reasonable to assume that similar percentages apply to the National Archives. These missing documents are conspicuous when trying to follow cross-references in the files, or when searching through collections of maps and images with missing entries. Most of the documents that were examined stem from the time between 1900 and 1935. In addition to the physical records in the National Archives in Phnom Penh, the digital archives of the French National Library were consulted, as well as the Archives d’Outre Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, which host many documents related to the country’s colonial past. [SOURCE: Page_175]
