4.2.1    From Indigenous Discoveries to Colonial Priority [SOURCE: Page_176]

The oldest written sources on the Cambodian Preks stem from the time of the French colonial administration in the early 20th century. The history of French colonial presence in Cambodia begins in 1863, when officers from the French navy stationed in neighbouring Vietnam persuaded King Norodom to relinquish control over Cambodian foreign affairs through a treaty with France. This control was progressively extended through a series of reforms until both the King’s resistance and a local guerilla rebellion were overcome in 1897 and the French representation in Phnom Penh assumed authority over the executive. Even though Cambodia was nominally a Protectorate of France, rather than a colony, the King’s authority had been reduced to a minimum and the French administration took charge of the affairs of the state. Cambodia effectively remained integrated into French Indochina until after World War II (Tully, 2005). [SOURCE: Page_176]

One of the principal priorities of the French administration was the modernization of the country, especially with regard to infrastructure such as roads, canals, and railways, and agricul- tural practices. The aim, ultimately, was to make colonies accessible, increase productivity, and gain profit from the land. Civil engineers and agronomists played a major part in this enterprise. In fact, several institutions, societies, and schools were founded particularly for the purpose of educating colonial engineers, such as the École nationale supérieure d’agriculture coloniale (1902) and the Société française des ingénieurs coloniaux (1895) (Vacher, 1999). [SOURCE: Page_176]

On the floodplains of the Mekong in Cambodia, one of the primary challenges that these colonial engineers and agronomists faced was that much of the land in the area was low-lying and marshy, and remained water logged for long periods. The space for growing high-value crops such as cotton was therefore limited. One of the solutions to this problem were the Preks - or canaux de colmatage in the French terminology. Colmatage, in general, refers to the process of raising land through improving the conditions for sedimentation. [SOURCE: Page_176]

The first organised studies on the concept of colmatage that appear on the record began in 1906. A first suggestion for such a study was discussed in an exchange of correspondence between Captain Gatard, the head of the Service Hydraulique Agricole, and the head engineer of the Direction Générale des Travaux Publics (File Nr. 5656 in the National Archives of Cambodia). [SOURCE: Page_176]

176 [SOURCE: Page_176]

Gatard feels that a deepening of the Prek channels to increase agricultural potential is essentially inefficient. He believes that it would bring sediments, yes, but that the main issue for agricultural productivity is a lack of water during the dry season. He further states that cultivation is only possible very near the stream (where water is provided through capillarity) or in the lowlands where water from the flood is retained the longest. In fact, he even states his fear that colmatage might ruin the rice fields that are located in those areas. Instead, he proposes building a large number of small reservoirs in the lowlands for the provision of irrigation water during the dry season. He also speaks out in favour of better control over water inflow and outflow in the Preks, for example using stoplogs, and believes that sediment deposits in the Preks themselves have positive effects since they contribute to the retention of flood water for use during the dry season. Overall, he opposes the further study of colmatage systems. [SOURCE: Page_177]

Nonetheless, such a study was implemented at Stung Trang, near Kratie. It appears that the general consensus was that the topographical configuration of the area was well-suited to the purposes of the study. Precise elevation measurements and profiles were created, water samples taken, water levels measured, and temperatures measured. Detailed descriptions of the methods and results, as well as the formulae derived to describe colmatage are available in a report from the 28th of May 1909 by the Service Hydraulique Agricole (M. Jumeau, File Nr. 5654). Overall, the results seem to have been promising, though there was some criticism later on (report by M. Moreau, 15th of June 1909, same file) that the topographical configuration was very particular and that further studies were necessary before a generalisation of results was possible. It is mentioned that a second field study, at Prey Veng, was underway at the time. [SOURCE: Page_177]

Most immediately useful for the purposes of this thesis is a study conducted by Lieutenant Raymond Barthélemy (Administrateur Des Services Civils), first published as a report in 1908, and later re-published in the Revue Indochinoise in 1913 (Barthélemy, 1913). His aim was to describe the general principles of the Prek/Chamkar system, using both the field experiment at Stung Trang and observations at already existing Preks. In his report he emphasizes that he heavily involved locals in his study: [SOURCE: Page_177]

Dans cette étude, nous avons tenu le plus grand compte des observations des habitants, ils ont été pour nous des guides excellents, cette question du percement de canaux de colmatage les intéresse vivement, non seulement ils ont toujours [SOURCE: Page_177]

177 [SOURCE: Page_177]

consenti à nous renseigner lorsque nous avions recours à eux, mais ils sont le plus souvent d’eux-mêmes venus au devant de nous pour nous demander de comprendre dans nos projets des preks qu’ils nous indiquaient pour nous montrer les meilleurs emplacements et la manière la plus économique d’y exécuter les travaux. - Premières études de colmatage du Mékong, File Nr. 25754, p.7 1 [SOURCE: Page_178]

Furthermore, through his interactions with the locals, he also gathered a legend of the origins of the Preks, which is given in more detail in the typewritten version of the report (File 8990): [SOURCE: Page_178]

Les Tiams^2 avaient autrefois trouvé un procéde de se procurer cette terre pré- cieuse; voici la légende qui m’a été racontée par de vieux Cambodgiens. Le Che Tiam Ania Khou, aieul du Gouverneur Tiam de Kanchor habitait il y a un siècle (NB: early 1800s) le petit village de Dey Dos, sur la rive droite du Mékong; sa maison avait vue sur le fleuve et derrière elle se trouvait un grand beng qui se remplissait tous les ans au moment des crues, mais assez tardivement. Ania Khou avait acheté dans la province de Sambor une superbe pirogue qui était fort lourde, son idée était de faire pénétrer cette pirogue dans le grand beng qui était derrière sa maison et de l’utiliser pour le transport des bois et des paillottes blanches qu’il irait chercher à la montagne en traversant le beng. Mais les flancs de la berge sont presque à pic à Dey Dos, et tous ses efforts pour hisser la pirogue, pour lui faire franchir le bourrelet, furent vains; elle était trop lourde et la berge trop abrupte du côté du fleuve. Ania Khou eut alors l’idée de creuser un canal d’une profondeur de sept ou huit coudées (NB: ca. 3.5-4 m) et d’une largeur égale à celle de la lourde pirogue, pensant de profiter du moment de la plus haute crue de l’année pour faire pénétrer sa pirogue par ce canal dans le grand Beng. Le plan d’Ania Khou réussit à merveille et lorsque la crue eut atteint le niveau du fond du canal, les eaux du fleuve se précipitèrent dans le Beng dont le niveau était encore de plusieurs mètres en contre-bas, la pirogue fut violemment poussée vers la nappe d’eau dormante et y flatta, mais il advint que les eaux du fleuve se précipitaient avec tant de force, qu’elles élargirent le canal 1 See Appendix C for translations. 2 It seems like Tiam might be a spelling variant of Cham. Kompong Cham, for example is denoted as ‘Kompong [SOURCE: Page_178]

Tiam’ in several old maps in the archive. Furthermore, later on in the text, Barthelemy uses the phrasing “par plusieurs Tiams et Cambodgiens”, which suggests a duality between these two groups and makes it likely that it is indeed the Muslim minority group that is referred to here. [SOURCE: Page_178]

178 [SOURCE: Page_178]

qui, en deux mois, atteignit une largeur de soixante coudées (NB: ca. 30 m). De plus, les eaux limoneuses du fleuve se précipitant dans des eaux plus claires et qui n’étaient pas à la même température, déposaient rapidement leur limon et lorsque la décrue arriva, le vieux Tiam ne fut pas peu surpris de voir que la superficie de terre cultivable avait considérablement augmenté derrière sa maison et qu’un double bourrelet de terre fertile était nettement dessiné au débouché du nouveau prek dans le Beng. [SOURCE: Page_179]

Barthélemy goes on to summarise that in subsequent years, many followed this example and breached the banks of the Mekong to create Preks, until several mésroks and governors placed restrictions on such projects since they interrupted the circulation on the paths along the river. It was only under the Résident Supérieur Luce (Luis-Paul Luce, 1856-1931, Résident Supérieur du Cambodge 1900-01 and 1905-11) that construction of the Preks was assigned a higher priority in the context of furthering agriculture than the continuity of roads. According to Barthélemy, the measures proposed by Luce regarding the construction of the Preks was met by strong approval of the local population.3 [SOURCE: Page_179]

In his report, Luce furthermore describes the general functioning and morphology of Preks. He mentions the way that Boeungs function as buffers during the wet season, attenuating the flood peak, and even goes as far to liken the great Cambodian lakes to gigantic Boeungs. He also formulates several laws on the functioning of Preks – the first one, for example, stating that there is always a temporal delay between the rise and fall of water levels in the main stream and the Boeungs. Furthermore, several factors that can have positive and negative impacts on the process of colmatage, such as temperature differences, the presence of vegetation etc. are considered. Finally, Barthélemy outlines some general principles that need to be adhered to when constructing Preks – for example that their entry level should be no lower than the mainstream water level on the 15th of July, since the sediment-laden waters needed for colmatage only arrive in the second half of that month. [SOURCE: Page_179]

Barthélemy’s conclusions are that the construction of Preks is a valuable measure to increase 3 The conflict of interests between Preks and roads are also mentioned in other files. For example, one report [SOURCE: Page_179]

notes that during the construction of colonial road VII in Kandal, several Preks were closed off. The same report also includes observations about how land quickly became infertile in the region due to a lack of nutrient input from the flood. [SOURCE: Page_179]

179 [SOURCE: Page_179]

Figure 4.5: Figure from Lt. Barthelemy’s report, illustrating sediment deposition in the Boeung following a Prek’s construction. [SOURCE: Page_181]

In later exchanges about concrete measures for projects by the Direction Hydraulique Agri- cole (File 5654), Barthélemy goes into more detail on the projects he envisions, giving estimates of the lengths of Preks required and the ensuing costs. In this file, a great number of details is available – such as the general price of Chamkar land, which is given at 50 piastres for 1 masenkongseng (Cambodian unit of area measurement. This corresponds to ca. 2,000 francs per hectare.) The costs for the Preks that are proposed vary between just over 100, to just over 1000 piastres, with lengths varying between 50 m and 790 m. It is further estimated that a single Prek can create at least six hectares of land per year. Taking into account the price for Chamkar land, Barthélemy concludes that a Prek could pay for its own construction in the very first year. [SOURCE: Page_181]

An important takeaway from these figures is that the Preks that were proposed at the time do not correspond to the channels that are known today, most of which amount to several kilometers in length and evolved over time from the original breaches. The lengths proposed by Barthélemy are much shorter, constituting, in most cases, only a breach in the river bank. [SOURCE: Page_181]

Apart from the information about the concrete development of Preks, some insights could be gained into the development of irrigation initiatives during this period. [SOURCE: Page_181]

Through the letters of Martin Flacourt, the Head of the Services Agricoles et Commerciaux, it is evident how irrigation became a more and more important part in increasing the agricultural capacity of Cambodia during the early 20the century. [SOURCE: Page_181]

181 [SOURCE: Page_181]

File 5654 includes reflections about projects that were being undertaken in 1909-10 to increase irrigation capacities. At the time, some manual irrigation practices were to be found across the country, but most agriculture was rainfed. It appears that an irrigation programme was launched in 1903, with a view towards stabilising agricultural production. As the report states: [SOURCE: Page_182]

Il ne s’agit donc pas ici de conquérir, pour un peuple qui ne saurait les exploiter, de nouveaux terrains propres à la culture, mais simplement de régulariser, au moyen des irrigations, une récolte qui ne dépend que de la quantité d’eau de pluie annuelle et aussi de sa répartition au cours du développement des diverses phases de la culture. - Rapport au sujet d’un programme de travaux d’hydraulique agricole (10th of May 1910, FileNr 5654), Direction Générale des Travaux Publics [SOURCE: Page_182]

From the same report it can further be gleaned that there were two trial areas for irrigation projects: Prek Chlong and Prek Thnot. Each project was subsidized with ca. 5 Million francs. Some conclusions that were drawn from these projects were, for example, that the maximum yield of 1 ha paddy rice with irrigation is 1.7 t. Furthermore, calculations about how to pay for irrigation infrastructure (for example through additional taxes on the raised rice production) are given. [SOURCE: Page_182]

However, the initiative for irrigation projects did not only come from government agencies. File Nr. 5652 details a 1907 initiative taken by 50 residents of Prek They/Prek Sdey village in Kasthom province, who came together in a sort of association to dig a canal of 5 km in length and 2-3 m in depth to irrigate large areas of Chamkar land. From letters exchanged between provincial representatives and the central government in Phnom Penh, it appears that in this case, an initial breach of the river bank already existed, but that the aim was to lengthen this channel. It is remarked, however, that the project is being implemented without a detailed plans in a “façon rudimentaire”. From the documentation it seems like there were quite some administrative troubles in getting the project approved, but that the group was persistent. [SOURCE: Page_182]

From these early documents, several insights into the development of Preks in the early 20th century can be derived. It becomes clear that the functioning of Preks was not, in itself, an invention by French engineers, but that it was well-known among the local population for at least a century, and, if the story recorded by Barthélemy is accurate, discovered by members of a [SOURCE: Page_182]

182 [SOURCE: Page_182]

minority group. Furthermore, it becomes evident that there was considerable enthusiasm on the side of the local population to see Prek and canal projects implemented - and that they took the initiative themselves in multiple cases. The fact that the construction of Preks was assigned a high priority by the colonial government is evidenced by the fact that they were given precedence over the continuity of roads. [SOURCE: Page_183]

However, these early documents also show that the Preks of the period are not equivalent to the Prek channels that exist today, neither in form nor purpose. Especially from the notes and observations on the ideal properties of Preks by Barthélemy, it can be seen that their main purpose was to increase sedimentation in the Boeung areas and create new fertile Chamkar land, though he also mentions the regulating effect on flood attenuation. As is outlined in the next section, Preks are now seen to fulfill a much larger range of ecosystem services, serving as a source of dry-season irrigation water chief among them. Anathema to this is Barthélemy’s suggestion to ensure that Prek entrances are no lower than the river water level in mid-July to prevent the inflow of sediment-poor water. [SOURCE: Page_183]

4.2.2    Post-Colonial Period and the Khmer Rouge [SOURCE: Page_183]

French colonial rule in Cambodia ended after World War II, in 1953. In theory, Cambodia had already declared its independence from France eight years earlier in March 1945. At the time, Japan was in control of much of Southeast Asia and urged colonial territories to make a bid for independence. However, when Japan surrendered in August 1945, Allied forces occupied Phnom Penh and French control was reinstated. The French only granted full independence to the country in 1953 after King Sihanouk had mounted a highly public campaign to apply international pressure on the colonial administration. Sihanouk subsequently abdicated in favour of his father in order to participate in politics. After becoming prime minister, however, he declared himself Chief of State and governed Cambodia under a one-party rule until 1970, a time also referred to as the Sangkum period. He was eventually removed through a coup d’état in 1970 and succeeded by Lon Nol, the Prime Minister, who declared the Khmer Republic. While there were many factors leading to the coup, one of the main reasons for was Sihanouk’s policy of neutrality and his toleration of North Vietnamese activities on Cambodian soil in the course of the war in neighbouring Vietnam. Lon Nol’s government abandoned this stance and took [SOURCE: Page_183]

183 [SOURCE: Page_183]

the side of the United States in the conflict. However, Cambodian communist forces mounted a resistance, claiming Sihanouk as a figurehead for their movement, and were subsequently subjected to extensive American carpet bombing in the East of the country (Tully, 2005; Kiernan, 2002). [SOURCE: Page_184]

No concrete information could be found on the development of Prek channels during this period. Part of the reason for this is that no documents covering these years were available in the National Archives of Cambodia. However, it can be assumed that the existing infrastructure of the Preks was maintained during this period, perhaps even extended. The reason why such conjecture seems reasonable is that agriculture held a high priority in the ideology of Sihanouk and the Sangkum period in general. Public figures were encouraged to perform manual agricultural labour and Sihanouk himself gifted farm equipment to villages and had himself photographed working in fields. In the 1960s, as much as 80% of the population was employed in agriculture (Ayres, 2000b,a). According to Dumas (1990), both farmer- and state-managed irrigation systems were expanded during this period. However, the provinces bordering Vietnam experienced considerable disruptions throughout the 1950s, 60s, and 70s as the Vietnam war continued to be fought. During this period, the United States dropped approximately 500,000 tons of explosive on Cambodia. Even at the beginning of the 21st century, almost 50% of villages report unexploded ordnance. Furthermore, bomb-induced deforestation in the course of the war shifted hydrological conditions in the area (Lacombe and Pierret, 2013). Nevertheless, Preks appear to have been maintained, as the current configuration of the landscape evidences that they continued to fulfill their original purpose. Today, elevated Chamkar areas have formed along the Preks, after a century of deposition processes. [SOURCE: Page_184]

While it is difficult to evaluate any measures that might have been taken to extend the system of Preks and canals in the Cambodian Mekong delta in the years 1953-1975, the years that follow held a dramatic shift that has been extensively documented. In 1975, Lon Nol’s government collapsed under the onslaught of the Cambodian communist forces. Subsequently, the country became Democratic Kampuchea, under the rule of the Communist Party of Kampuchea (CPK), alternatively known as the Khmer Rouge and led by Pol Pot (Tully, 2005). The Khmer Rouge aggressively pursued the ideal of creating a self-sufficient agrarian society entirely independent of Western influence. Directly after communist forces entered Phnom Penh in 1975, inhabitants were ordered to leave the nation’s cities and move to the countryside. Here, many were forced [SOURCE: Page_184]

184 [SOURCE: Page_184]

to participate in the construction of irrigation infrastructure which, the Khmer Rouge believed, was the key to increasing agricultural gains. However, the design of canals was not based on calculations grounded in civil engineering, or even on local experience values. Instead, a rectangular network of canals and dykes reaching from North to South and East to West was created, often spaced so as to create units of four hectares. Ultimately, the vision of the CPK was to create a nested canal network - arranged in 10 x 10 km grids, encompassing smaller 1 × 1 km grids, which, in turn, feature 100 m × 100 m grids - in order to supply sufficient irrigation water for rice production (Tyner et al., 2018; Tyner and Rice, 2020; Dumas, 1990; Coakley et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_185]

In short order, these structures were built, but without the use of heavy machinery. Instead, construction work was completed through forced manual labour under abject conditions, to the point where the rural labour camps in which people were forced to work became known as Killing Fields. In total, approximately 2 million Cambodians are estimated to have died in the four years until the Khmer Rouge regime was toppled, representing 25% of the population at the time (Tabeau and Zwierzchowski, 2013). Nonetheless, the construction of irrigation infrastructure was widely completed under these conditions Tyner et al. (2018) estimates that 7,000 kilometers of canals and dikes, as well as over 350 reservoirs were completed during the Khmer Rouge regime. However, many structures had averse rather than positive effects on local hydrological conditions. Due to the lack of control structures, rapid drainage of upland areas occurred in many parts of the country, alongside flooding of lowland areas. Often, improper design of these structures resulted in failure within a few years. Many eroded away in the course of subsequent floods. Most analyses considering the extent and effectiveness of the irrigation schemes implemented by the Khmer Rouge echo the standard total view (STV) defined by Michael Vickery, which characterizes it as a typical manifestation of a poorly managed regime ultimately doomed to failure (Vickery, 1984; Rice and Tyner, 2017; Dumas, 1990) [SOURCE: Page_185]

In the case study area of this thesis, a network of canals stemming from this period exists in the Boeung areas in the West and Southwest, as shown in Figure 4.2. Furthermore, the dyke that delineates the southern border of the study area appears to have originated at this time as well. The remnants of concrete gate structures that exist here are referred to as "Pol Pot" gates by the local population. One of these structures is shown in Figure 4.6. It is not known which, if any, measures the Khmer Rouge took to maintain or extend the Prek channels themselves during this [SOURCE: Page_185]

185 [SOURCE: Page_185]

unfamiliar with the rainfall and flood conditions of the new areas to which they have moved. Even farmers returning to their original lands are faced with changes in the hydrology of their new area. - p. 276 [SOURCE: Page_187]

In addition, land remained state-owned until 1989, and farmers had relatively few means to invest in the cultivation of their fields. Dumas (1990) observes that conditions improved slowly and that as resources actually owned by farmers increased, they began to perform water management on an individual basis. Part of these efforts became rehabilitating salvageable parts of irrigation structure from pre-Khmer Rouge times, which had not been maintained in the interim, as well as some Khmer Rouge canals. [SOURCE: Page_187]

Coordinated efforts by the government to improve agricultural practices and infrastructure began in the mid-1980s, under the auspices of the Ministry of Agriculture, particularly the De- partment of Hydrology. However, a significant obstacle to the development and implementation of projects was the lack of expertise, as a vast number of intellectuals and members of the educated echelons of society either been targeted and killed by the Khmer Rouge, or had fled the country. During this period, international organizations began to implement projects related to irrigation infrastructure in the region. For instance, (Dumas, 1990) mentions a small-scale irrigation programme in Kompong Cham that was set up in cooperation between the Department of Hydrology and the American Friends Service Committee, a Quaker organization. It is in the context of such rehabilitation and development projects that concrete information on the Preks becomes available once more during the 1990s. [SOURCE: Page_187]

After Vietnam withdrew from Cambodia in 1989 following pressure from both the US and the Soviet Union, a peace agreement was reached in 1991 that was endorsed by the UN Security Council. Subsequently, a peacekeeping operation that included both soldiers and civil servants was established in Cambodia under the control of a United Nations Transitional Authority. The 1990s continued to be tumultuous, including free elections followed by a coup led by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who still rules Cambodia to this day. It was only in the early 2000s that the situation began to stabilize on a more permanent basis, marked, not least, by Cambodia’s entry into ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) (Chandler and Overton, 2021). [SOURCE: Page_187]

It is during this period that development projects in the agrarian sector began to multiply [SOURCE: Page_187]

187 [SOURCE: Page_187]

rapidly. The French Development Agency (Agence Française du Développement, AFD), for instance, became involved in the country in 1993 (AFD, 2021), the Japan International Coop- eration Agency (JICA) in 1996, and the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) launched its Cambodia Agricultural Value Chain Program (CAVAC) in 2008 (DFAT). [SOURCE: Page_188]

Systematic Prek rehabilitation was first financed by AFD and implemented by MoWRAM between 1999 and 2003. This pilot project was carried out in the framework of a initiative called PADAP - Programme d’Appui au Développement de l’Agriculture Périurbaine. The project was centered around two canals in S’ang District and aimed to test rehabilitation measures and the effects on cropping developments. The initial study, led by AGRISUD International, received a positive evaluation in 2004, highlighting value gains, increased agricultural output, and initiatives by the local population. At the same time, JICA was also financing their first Prek rehabilitations. After an initial study on the functioning of the system was undertaken in 1996-1997, JICA financed the rehabilitation of four Preks on the right bank of the Mekong in 2001-2002. Following their initial project, AFD extended its Prek rehabilitation scheme through the Northwest Irrigation Sector Project (NWISP). The overall project aim was to intensify and diversify agricultural systems, as well as to make them more resilient. In this context, a polder was created in 2009-10 between Prek Ta Roat and Ta Ong in S’ang District, Prek Ambel Commune. In 2013, AFD launched the project WASP (Water and Agriculture Sector Programme) to rehabilitate almost thirty Preks in Kandal Province over the course of four years. Rehabilitation work on the first thirteen Preks was launched in 2015, in cooperation with the MoWRAM as well as the consulting agencies SOFRECO and SBK Research and Development. Work on these Preks was largely completed in 2017. This was followed by a second rehabilitation phase which targeted a total of twelve Preks and ended in 2020. In 2020, another project that includes rehabilitation efforts related to Preks was launched by MoWRAM and the AFD - Water Resource Management and Agro-Ecological Transition in Cambodia (WAT4CAM). Financed by the AFD and the European Union, its stated aim is to improve irrigation systems management and integrated water resources management in Cambodia. One of its four components is the Rehabilitation and completion of irrigation and drainage infrastructures, which includes the rehabilitation and modernization of 20 to 40 Preks (SOFRECO, 2017; Pratx, 2017; MoWRAM, 2021). [SOURCE: Page_188]

At this point it must be briefly outlined what Prek rehabilitation entails. Preks are, by design, [SOURCE: Page_188]

188 [SOURCE: Page_188]

trapezoidal channels that connect the river mainstream to the floodplains at a certain depth. Over time, however, sediments are deposited in the canals, reducing their cross section. Bank collapses and erosion can further impair the vector functionality of Preks. Rehabilitation projects primarily aim to reinstate this functionality by deepening the Prek beds and restoring - or even extending - its profile. In addition, rehabilitation projects typically include the construction or improvement of roads along the Prek. In some cases, control structures such as gates are also constructed to regulate the seasonal inflow of water from the river or outflow from the Boeung. Bank vegetation is removed (Pratx, 2017; SOFRECO, 2017). Figure 4.7 shows a comparison of Prek Chann and Touch in 2020, the former of which is rehabilitated, the latter of which isn’t. [SOURCE: Page_189]

One of the main questions in rehabilitation projects is the scale of earthenworks to be implemented. The deeper the bed of the Prek is lowered, the better water availability will be throughout the dry season, but the higher costs for geotechnical works are. For this reason, engineers during the WASP project distinguished between deep and shallow calibration projects. Deep calibration involves lowering the bed level to an elevation that guarantees year-round inflow, typically 0 m asl. Shallow calibration, in contrast, only lowers the bed level to 1.5 m asl. This allows inflow for most of the year. During the height of the dry season, however,pumps are neccessary to supply the Prek with water. A large pump is used to lift water from the Bassac into the Prek so that farmers can use their own smaller pumps to irrigate their fields with water from the Prek, which they also do along Preks that are deeply excavated. At some Preks that have not yet been rehabilitated, this practices already exists, with "water sellers" providing their service - and those of their pumps - in return for a seasonal fee from the farmers who benefit from the practice (SOFRECO, 2017). In the case study area of this thesis, two Preks have been rehabilitated, both in deep calibration - Prek Me Srok and Prek Chann. At Prek Chann, a gate was also constructed to control water flows (cf. Figure 4.9). [SOURCE: Page_189]

189 [SOURCE: Page_189]

problems have also occurred in the course of the projects, often related to a mismatch between the assumptions of engineers and the reality of stakeholder practices and hydrological processes. In several instances, bank collapses happened, which obstructed the flow of water in the Prek once more. This was the case at Prek Chann, for instance. The reasons for these collapses have been conjectured by engineers to be a combination of water pressure from the Chamkar soils and erosion effects (SOFRECO, 2017). Another frequent problem is erosion around control structures such as gates. If these are not opened in time during the wet season the shear forces of the water once they are opened can easily damage the structure, as shown in Figure 4.10b. [SOURCE: Page_191]

Finally, it also needs to be mentioned that the rehabilitation practices described above only appertain to official projects initiated in the framework of collaboration between the Cambodian government and various international actors. However, there are also local initiatives for Prek rehabilitation - or at least excavation. Sediment deposition in the Preks is one of the most commonly reported problems that restricts water inflow. Therefore, regular excavations are organized by some village chiefs to maintain the vector functionality of the Preks. In most cases, these excavations are limited to the heads of the Preks, where the majority of sedimentation happens (see interviews below). However, in the case study area one major locally-organized excavation project was observed during the field work. Here, several kilometers of Prek Thom at the southern end of the case study area were excavated. The results of excavation and the border between excavated and not excavated Prek stretches is shown in Figure 4.11. Sometimes these excavations also have economic motives, as the sediment that is extracted from the Preks can be sold to farmers wishing to raise their land as well as for construction purposes. These initiatives are also sometimes supported by the administration at the communes and district administration, and by the provincial offices of the MoWRAM. [SOURCE: Page_191]

191 [SOURCE: Page_191]

Crabtree, 2006). This is also the result of the initial pilot phase of the interviews in 2019. At the beginning of the fieldwork, two questionnaires were used – one for a closed survey and one for a semi-structured interview. After the first day, however, the questionnaires were merged into one due to the fact that once a conversation was begun, additional information was gained that could not have been recorded using only a closed-survey questionnaire. The new questionnaire combined elements from both the closed survey and the semi-structured interview. This also allowed for a statistical analysis of the results (though the sample size was limited due to the restrictions in fieldwork that arose in 2020), as well as the collection of important additional information that cannot be captured purely through closed-survey questions. [SOURCE: Page_194]

Broadly speaking, there were two phases of developing the interview structure. The first phase, during the June 2019 field trip, aimed to understand the types of ecosystem services linked to Preks and their hydrological functioning that locals benefit from (see Appendix 4 for a brief description of results from this initial phase). The second phase, starting in November 2019, strove to make these services quantifiable and to develop a more in-depth understanding of agricultural and water management practices. The questionnaires for this approach were piloted in November 2019 and applied in February-March 2020. Three different versions were developed - one for farmers, another for village chiefs, and the third for the heads of Prek User Committees (PUC), who are elected locally to be responsible for Prek water management. Generally, PUCs fall into the broader category of Water User Associations (cf. Ivars and Venot (2018)). 4 Further interviews were planned with representatives of the MoWRAM, the Chief of the Commune, and private water sellers. Unfortunately, these could not take place because fieldwork was cut short due to the pandemic. During the fieldwork in February and March 2020, a very extensive section on agricultural practices such as fertilizer and pesticide application, and tilling was included in the questionnaire. This later served as the basis for an agronomic analysis in an MSc thesis written in the framework of the COSTEA project (see Vandôme (2020)). During the interviews carried out in autumn 2020 and spring 2021, this section was scaled down considerably. Copies of all the questionnaires used can be found in Appendix E. [SOURCE: Page_194]

The interviews (see Figure 4.13) themselves were carried out in a variety of locations. Some were conducted directly in the fields of the farmers, which offered the advantage that they 4 These committees are established in the course of rehabilitation projects, to ensure proper maintenance of the [SOURCE: Page_194]

Prek once construction is finished. The head of the PUC is elected democratically. Their main task is to coordinate maintenance efforts between farmers who benefit from Preks For further details, see Section 4.3.6. [SOURCE: Page_194]

4.3.2    Geographic and Demographic Information on Respondents [SOURCE: Page_196]

In the first phase of fieldwork, 19 people were interviewed - two at each Prek except Prek Put, where only one respondent was located. In the second phase, eight village chiefs, the chief of one Prek User Committee (PUC at Prek Chann), and 675 farmers were interviewed. Among the farmers who were interviewed, two were not strictly speaking farmers. One was a Cham fisherman, who also owns some livestock but no land, and who lives in the Cham village at the end of Prek Cham Kroum. The other was a scavenger – a woman who owns no land herself, and who does not farm, but who collects the remains of crops after harvests from other people’s fields. The information gathered from these interviewees covers 149 plots, with 201 responses to which crops were cultivated, as one plot is sometimes used for the cultivation of several crops. This represents ca. 116 ha, which amounts to 2.7% of the study area. [SOURCE: Page_196]

Of the interviewed farmers, 24% were women and 76% were men. The distribution of their ages is shown in Figure 4.14. The age of the interviewees ranged from 28 to 72, with an average of 47 years, with the majority falling into the age groups of 31-40 and 51-60. Generally, it has to be noted that there might be a slight skewing of results due to the fact that Buddhist rules prevent farmers over 50 from either fishing or tending to livestock, according to information from respondents. Among the interviewees, 52% were over this age. [SOURCE: Page_196]

The geographical distribution of interviewed farmers along Preks in the study area is shown in Figure 4.15. As mentioned above, the distribution is uneven. The reason for this is that limited time was available for the interviews due to the pandemic. It must also be noted that most of the interviews at Prek Thom were conducted at its tail end, with farmers whose activities are centered in the Boeung areas. 5 37 during in February - March 2020, and the others between November and March 2021 by a colleague from [SOURCE: Page_196]

## RUA.

4.3.3     Outlining Ecosystem Services and their Relation to Prek Channels [SOURCE: Page_198]

Some information on the ecosystem services to which the Preks contribute existed already before fieldwork began. Engineering reports such as SOFRECO (2017) listed irrigation, transport by boat, sediment supply, mitigation of flood damage, domestic water supply, fishing, and sedimentation as the principle benefits of Preks in general and rehabilitated Preks in particular. [SOURCE: Page_198]

Generally, it has to be noted that the largest number of ecosystem services is used by those interviewees who are economically less well-off. For instance, in one village the most prosperous interview participant – who also happens to be a village chief – only uses the Prek for irrigation purposes, whereas the least well-off amongst the interviewees derive domestic water, irrigation water, major parts of their diet (in the form of bank vegetation and fish) as well as means of transport and nutrient-laden sediments from the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_198]

4.3.3.1   Provisioning Ecosystem Services [SOURCE: Page_198]

During the interviews, it became apparent that the majority of ecosystem services from which the local inhabitants benefit directly fall under the category of provisioning ecosystem services, though some interviewees explicitly remarked on regulating services as well, which will be examined in the next section. [SOURCE: Page_198]

Irrigation Water Supply Generally, it can be said that the main importance of the Prek for the interviewees lies in its provision of water for crop irrigation. Most of the interviewees grow crops such as mangoes, cucumbers, beans, corn or sugarcane in the Chamkar area of the Preks and rice in the Boeung (see Section 4.3.4 for a more in-depth profile). Most of these crops are irrigated regularly with water from the Preks or the canal system in the Boeung. [SOURCE: Page_198]

Alternative sources of irrigation water exist as well, though they are limited. For instance, some farmers pump from adjacent plots or small-scale ponds located in the inter-Prek areas (see Figure 4.16) just after the flood. In many cases, ponds were excavated to use the soil to raise land elsewhere. A secondary effect is that they can retain flood water after recession, which can be used for irrigation during the early dry season. Groundwater is rarely used for irrigation if it can [SOURCE: Page_198]

198 [SOURCE: Page_198]

are to be kept clear of vegetation as much as possible. [SOURCE: Page_200]

In addition, interviewees stated that they used the natural vegetation for fuel, fish traps and medicinal plants. [SOURCE: Page_200]

It was difficult for participants to estimate the frequency of usage of natural vegetation for food. Most said that they use the plants they find along the Prek or in the Boeung to supplement their diets a few times per week throughout the year. [SOURCE: Page_200]

Details on using bank vegetation as fuel were given by one farmer who was observed cutting trees along the Prek. He stated that he cuts trees that grow in front of someone else’s plot, but that he does not have to pay for it - though the veracity of that statement is questionable. He said that he cuts two trees per year, which result in two cubes of solid wood. Each cube could be sold for ca. 40,000 Riel, but he said he keeps it mostly for home use. [SOURCE: Page_200]

Another use for the bank vegetation is for constructing fish traps. Here, branches from trees that grow in the case study area are cut off and placed on a type of scaffolding in the water, a system locally called "samras". This offers an attractive shelter to fish, and they can be caught there more easily. [SOURCE: Page_200]

In terms of medicinal uses of bank vegetation, only one respondent said that she uses it for this purpose. The medicinal purpose in question was the use of dried herbs to soothe menstrual cramps. [SOURCE: Page_200]

A final point that must be noted on this issue is that there are apparently some concerns related to the use of natural vegetation. One farmer, in particular, noted that his family used to supplement their diets frequently with plants that grow along the Prek and on the Chamkars. However, he stated that they ceased to do so due to concerns over extensive pesticide use. Three more farmers also voiced concerns about using grass that grows along the Preks to feed their cattle out of concerns about pesticide contamination. [SOURCE: Page_200]

200 [SOURCE: Page_200]

he only fished there one time in total, which might be related to the short duration of the flood that year. [SOURCE: Page_204]

The general consensus is that the peak fishing period is between November and January, during flood recession. At this time, fish that have prospered in the flooded Boeung are channelled by the water that is draining to the Bassac. One interviewee stated that during this time, they could catch as much as 30-40 kg of fish in the Prek over the course of five days.One more aspect that was mentioned by multiple fishermen is that the catch in the canals and in the Boeung is also dependent on the phase of the moon. This is likely to be related to the varying water levels mentioned in Section 3.2.3 and the resulting currents. [SOURCE: Page_204]

One particular fishing practice needs to be mentioned. One interviewee stated that their family uses the Boeung plot they own partly for rice cultivation, but partly to rear fish. Part of the plot is lower than the other, and they refer to it as a ‘pond’. In this pond, they let fish mature, before using their pump to extract the water. This technique is also known as bear fishing. [SOURCE: Page_204]

Finally, the interviewee in the Cham village also noted that commercial fishing activities were prohibited from March onwards by the Fisheries Ministry, to protect fish procreation.7 [SOURCE: Page_204]

At this point it must be noted that the importance of fishing as an element of livelihoods appears to be much larger in neighbouring areas than in the case study area under scrutiny here. In the area bracketed by the Mekong and the Bassac, villages whose main economic activity is fishing exist, with fish traps set up almost permanently and some people - often of Vietnamese ethnicity - living on house boats nearby. These traps, though illegal, use vegetation arranged as shelters and food incentives to attract fish so that they can be caught. Even though they have theoretically been outlawed by the government, they can still be seen frequently in the region. 7 In fact, the official "closed fishing season" lasts from the beginning of June to the end of September, according [SOURCE: Page_204]

to information from the Ministry (Kunthear and Khmer Times, 2018; Sivutha and The Phnom Penh Post, 2021a) [SOURCE: Page_204]

204 [SOURCE: Page_204]

rehabilitation on preventing flood damage to crops. Farmers at rehabilitated Preks did not state that they experienced any difference in the impact of floods in comparison to before. The majority of farmers reported that they kept the areas of their plots that are flooded regularly clear of any crops that could be damaged during this time. Some mentioned extreme events that lay several years back and did result in larger damage, but none that they could relate to the Preks. [SOURCE: Page_206]

This indicates that there are few benefits of flood regulation in the Prek system on a local level - but that these are only effectively felt by downstream communities, as indicated in the hydrological analysis in Section 3.2. It also points towards the fact that the rehabilitation of a single Prek changes relatively little in the flood patterns at its tail end, which, in turn, can be seen as an indicator of the fact that the flood also arrives via neighbouring Preks and the canal network. [SOURCE: Page_206]

Sediment and Nutrient Cycling In contrast to regional flood retention, the benefit of sediment deposition is keenly felt by farmers in the study area. Eight of them noted that they used the sediments from the Preks to raise their lands and that they appreciated (partial) inundation of their plots during the flood season because it brought ‘good earth’ and kept their lands fertile. In addition, some also excavate the sediments from the Prek channels directly to sell at a profit - see the information provided by village chiefs in Section 4.3.6 for further information. [SOURCE: Page_206]

Ground- and Soil Water Recharge Groundwater is used relatively infrequently in the case study area due to concerns about arsenic contamination and the availability of clean drinking water from a communal pipe and Prek water for irrigation. Only in the area of Prek Put, which is dry for most of the year, do farmers still use wells regularly for irrigation, according to the information gathered in the interviews. For this reason, the direct effects of groundwater recharge by Preks and the floods that they catalyze were not a fruitful topic of discussion during the interviews. [SOURCE: Page_206]

However, two farmers did talk in depth about the benefits of soil water recharge. They stated that shorter flood durations over the past few years, but especially during the 2019-20 season, had left soils relatively dry. One farmer said that infiltration depths of the soils in his plots only reached 20-30 cm that year and that, consequently, he needed to irrigate sooner and more [SOURCE: Page_206]

206 [SOURCE: Page_206]

intensively to provide sufficient water for his crops. Apart from the shorter flood duration, he also said that the development of soil crusts that inhibit infiltration contributed to this issue. The reason for the development of these crusts, he believes, is the over-use of fertilizer and pesticides, which destroy soil structure. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Pest Regulation During the interviews, it emerged that for many farmers, crop losses due to pests were a more pressing concern than floods or droughts. Extended flooding can contribute to reducing several aspects of this concern. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Most importantly, several farmers stated that floods are a major contributing factor to the reduction of rat populations, which cause considerable damage to rice, vegetables, and even fruit trees. Especially for rice fields, rats are a concern. One farmer noted that his rice crop was decimated from 160 to 40 bags by rats last year. Other estimates of rice crop losses due to rats lie at 30%. To combat rats, farmers take measures such as electrical traps, rat poison, and setting off fireworks in the fields to scare them away. Also cutting away grass that grows on the borders of plots has been mentioned as a step to take to exterminate rats, since it deprives them of their shelters. The abundance of rats is a well-known problem in the region, and the focus of several initiatives for integrated pest management (Flor et al., 2018; Castilla et al., 2020; Jahn et al., 1999). [SOURCE: Page_207]

The most frequently mentioned natural factor for rat population control was regular flooding. In fact, the majority of farmers who engaged on the issue of pest control mentioned that a considerable negative impact of the short duration of the 2019 flood was the fact that rats were abundant during the following dry season. Overall, eight farmers stated that they believe floods contribute to the decimation of rat populations. When asked to elaborate, three farmers detailed that rat populations are particularly decimated when the flood water reaches up to the level of the road at the middle of the Prek, or over the crest of the Prek. One farmer also stated that a fast rise in water levels also contributes to the death toll among rats, since many of them have their nests in the banks of the Prek and do not have the time to retreat if the flood arrives quickly. [SOURCE: Page_207]

Another aspect of regular inundations’ contribution to pest control is that several farmers are of the opinion that large enough floods can also help reduce the damage done to crops by insects. One farmer also noted that he would welcome Prek rehabilitation because it would [SOURCE: Page_207]

207 [SOURCE: Page_207]

reduce stagnant water in the Prek, which is a breeding ground for insects. [SOURCE: Page_208]

4.3.3.3   Cultural Ecosystem Services [SOURCE: Page_208]

Investigating cultural ecosystem services related to the Prek system in the case study area proved to be difficult. Partially, this is due to the fact that they were only peripherally inquired after during the interviews. Partially, however, it is also likely that the historical context outlined above contributes to the fact that there are no readily evident local traditions, stories, spiritual practices, or songs related directly to the Prek channels, or the Prek system as a whole. Due to the major population movements in the aftermath of the Khmer Rouge period, many families have been living in the area only for one generation. In addition, it must be noted that such enquires are generally difficult, even more so when responses are translated. [SOURCE: Page_208]

To a certain extent, Prek channels provide recreational value to the local population. On multiple occasions, for example, children could be seen playing in the Preks when they had sufficient water - swimming and jumping from bridges. [SOURCE: Page_208]

It can also be surmised that the Preks contribute to the formation of a local and regional identity on a deeper level. Even though some farmers have plots at more than one Prek, the majority possesses a Chamkar and a Boeung plot at the same Prek at which their homestead is also located. This means that the majority of their life and labour is organized along the length of Prek channels. Villages and communities, too, are organized along the Preks. [SOURCE: Page_208]

However, to delve into the complexities of identity formation and the underlying social processes, a far more targeted and in-depth approach would be necessary. For this reason, cultural ecosystem services will not be considered further in the framework of this thesis. [SOURCE: Page_208]

4.3.4     Characterising Agricultural Practices [SOURCE: Page_208]

The data collected during the interviews allowed for an in-depth characterization of agricultural practices in the area, to further shed light on the role that Preks play in contributing to provisioning ecosystem services. An extensive account of a typology of farming systems in the study area, [SOURCE: Page_208]

208 [SOURCE: Page_208]

based on data collected in February and March 2020, is available in Vandôme (2020).8 This section provides an overview of the agricultural practices reflected in the entirety of the interview data collected in the course of this thesis. This will form an important element of the modelling approach presented in the next chapter, as average values are used as baseline inputs for the calculation of future likely yields. [SOURCE: Page_209]

4.3.4.1    Characteristics of Survey Respondents’ Holdings [SOURCE: Page_209]

In total, the 67 farmers who were interviewed in the course of this thesis own 149 plots, covering a total of 116 ha. On average, a farmer owns 2.5 plots (σ = 1.23). Part of the reason for this is historical. According to information by one interviewee in his 60s, each household was allocated a Boeung plot, a Chamkar plot, and a plot of land in the village when the Vietnamese relinquished control over the region in 1989 and individual land management became possible again, followed by private land ownership in 2001 (though many people still hold land use right on state-owned land, rather than actual ownership). Over the past forty years, property structures have shifted relatively little, though some respondents rent additional plots from farmers who no longer cultivate them themselves. In total, 84% of the plots of farmers who were interviewed belonged to them, 12% were rented, and 4% were shared between relatives. Recently, the sale of land has also become more common. Part of the reason for this is that outside investors are moving into the region, prominently from China.9 Seven was the maximum number of plots owned by a single farmer in the study area. [SOURCE: Page_209]

The average size of a plot in the study area is 0.8 ha (σ = 1.07 ha), with a maximum size of 8 ha. Generally, Boeung plots tend to be larger, at an average of 1.20 ha (σ = 1.28 ha) than either plots located in transition areas (x̄ = 1.05 ha, σ = 1.75 ha) or on Chamkars (x̄ = 0.46 ha, σ = 0.44ha). Typically, multiple crops are cultivated on a single Chamkar plot (x̄ = 1.41 on average, σ = 0.68) and plots located in the transition zone (x̄ = 1.28ha, σ = 0.47ha). In contrast, Boeung plots are almost exclusively cultivated with rice, though in several cycles. Figure 4.21 shows the distribution of crops among the different zones in the study area. 8 It must be noted that this data under-represents Boeung areas, as the interview focus was only shifted there in [SOURCE: Page_209]

autumn 2020. 9 Chinese companies and the government have (co-)financed several infrastructure projects in the region, including [SOURCE: Page_209]

in the case study area. The bridge across the Mekong at Koh Thom just North of the case study area is an example of this. [SOURCE: Page_209]

4.3.4.2       Average Cropping Practices [SOURCE: Page_211]

The average planting and harvest dates, irrigation practices, yield, and revenue for them are given in Table 4.4. Vandôme (2020) also produced a visual representation of the farming itineraries for the different crops, reproduced in Figure 4.22. Broadly, the crops grown in the study area can be organized into three groups - rice, fruit trees such as mango and lemut, and vegetables like different varieties of beans, eggplants, and cucumbers. [SOURCE: Page_211]

Vegetables The latter group - vegetables - are grown on Chamkars and on transition zone plots either during the dry season, or in sections of these plots for which flood frequencies are low. For some vegetable crops, the planting dates are mostly uniform, for instance for mung beans. In contrast, crops like cucumbers and eggplants are grown at various times of the year in various plots on Chamkars, in transition zones and in Boeungs. As Table 4.2 shows, vegetables are among the most profitable crops in the study area. However, they are also fairly labour-intensive to grow. Beans, for instance, are picked by hand. [SOURCE: Page_211]

One difficulty with information on vegetables is that many of them are not well-represented in the fieldwork dataset. For instance, only one farmer growing eggplants was interviewed, and only two interviewees provided information on growing bitter melon. This is one of the reasons why vegetables were grouped together as a single crop type in the modeling process - to reduce the uncertainty and noise in the data by averaging them out according to the area each crop occupies in the fieldwork data. [SOURCE: Page_211]

212 [SOURCE: Page_212]

Fruit Trees    In contrast, extensive information is available on the cultivation of fruit trees, especially mangoes (see Chapter 5). In total, 41 farmers provided information on the practices involved in growing mango trees. They are one of the most widely cultivated crops in the study area. In fact, especially on the Chamkar areas of the two northernmost Preks in the study area – Prek Cham Kroum and Prek Me Srok, it appears that little else is grown. [SOURCE: Page_213]

One of the farmers stated that five to ten years ago, there was a general switch to mangoes due to the high prices for the fruit back then. Some farmers also changed to planting mango trees because of what could be termed situational peer pressure. One of them said he switched from vegetables to mangoes because his plot is narrow, and he was afraid that the new trees of his neighbours would cast shade on his plot and inhibit the growth of his vegetables. [SOURCE: Page_213]

However, the price has since dropped. Furthermore, there are other issues mango growers are facing. Several farmers stated that they lost crops not only due to insects, droughts or floods, but also because hormones for inducing flowering in mango trees sometimes did not work. [SOURCE: Page_213]

As a consequence, some farmers are pursuing strategies to raise the quality of their products to increase the price. Most commonly, it was observed that young mango fruits were covered in paper bags. Farmers said that this was to protect their skin in order to be able to sell them to Thailand for as much as 1500 Riel per kg. [SOURCE: Page_213]

Other farmers are thinking about switching crops again. One interviewee told us that he wants to switch back to rice because mango is no longer very profitable and buying rice for family needs from the market is very expensive. However, he says that he is waiting for his neighbours to make the switch also, because he is afraid that if he is the only one planting rice in the midst of mangoes, rats will converge onto his plot. [SOURCE: Page_213]

Other fruit trees grown in the area include banana and lemut trees. However, only four plots that were (partially) used to grow these trees appeared in the data. Since their management is similar to mangoes in terms of irrigation and pesticide spraying, there were therefore lumped together with mangoes for the land use classification and the model described below. [SOURCE: Page_213]

Rice   Finally, there is rice - the most common crop in the study area, especially in the Boeungs. Overall, four different kinds of rice cultivation can be distinguished - recession rice, dry season [SOURCE: Page_213]

213 [SOURCE: Page_213]

rice, early wet season rice, and wet season rice. [SOURCE: Page_214]

Recession rice is the most widespread type of rice cultivation in the study area. As its name suggests, it is planted as the flood recedes from plots, usually when there are a few centimeters of water left, or when the soil is still very muddy from being submerged. This means that the planting and harvesting times for recession rice vary considerably, as is reflected in Table 4.4. In some plots, the flood sometimes recedes as early as the end of October, while it lingers until December in others. Generally, water availability is least problematic for this type of rice, since the soil is saturated at the beginning of cultivation, and water levels in the Preks and canals are still relatively high. In addition, there are still significant amounts of precipitation towards the end of the year. Still, if floods recede quickly, water levels in the Bassac are low, and rainfall insufficient, these crops can experience drought stress (see Section 4.3.4). In some cases, it can also be problematic if the flood recedes too late. In that case, recession rice can only be planted with a delay - and it misses out on natural precipitation during the latter part of the year. [SOURCE: Page_214]

Dry season rice can only be cultivated if sufficient irrigation water is available. It is usually an option on plots where recession rice could be planted and harvested relatively early - in December or January - or on plots that are close to canals and Preks that experience consistent inflow during the dry season. But even then, the expenses for pumping the required amounts of water are often prohibitive. Overall, this is not a common practice in the area - only seven farmers engage in it. [SOURCE: Page_214]

Far more common is the cultivation of early wet season (EWS) rice. Cultivation begins in April or May, when precipitation begins to set in. As the water levels in the river rise at the beginning of the wet season, irrigation becomes possible once more. The most critical issue with EWS rice is that it must be harvested before the arrival of the flood - usually July or early August. If this is not the case, the crop may be lost partially or completely. [SOURCE: Page_214]

Finally, there is wet season rice - which is grown on elevated plots while much of the case study area is flooded. It is partially rainfed and partially sustained through irrigation with water lifted from the full canals and Preks. Like dry season rice, though, this is not a common practice in the case study area, partially because it has the lowest average yields of all the different types of rice cultivation (cf. Table 4.4). [SOURCE: Page_214]

214 [SOURCE: Page_214]

Irrigation During the surveys, farmers were asked how frequently they irrigate their various crops and how long each irrigation session lasts. Most respondents were able to provide detailed information on these issues with a high degree of certainty. In addition, they were asked to explain their reasoning behind choosing to irrigate a plot or not. While some farmers named factors such as soil moisture and monitoring precipitation amounts, most said that it was a matter of routine that they adhered to because their neighbours also did. [SOURCE: Page_215]

To irrigate their crops, farmers use small pumps (see Figure 4.23a) that the majority owns themselves, though three respondents have mentioned renting them or sharing them with family members. These pumps are mobile and can be moved between plots (see Figure 4.23b). On average, farmers own one or two (average: 1.4) pumps. The average pump capacity lies at ca. 7.5 HP (5593 W). Most pumps used to pump water directly from a water source to the destination plots have between 5 and 7 HP. Pumps are placed at various elevations on the banks of Preks. To supply pumps, PVC pipes are used. To distribute water along fields, flexible plastic tubes are used in most cases (see Figure 4.23c and 4.23d). The reason for this is that it allows farmers greater flexibility in where to direct the flow of water (see Figure 4.23e). Furthermore, these tubes can be laid across the path on the banks of the Prek without impeding traffic - carts, tractors, and small motorbikes that farmers use for transport. [SOURCE: Page_215]

In some Preks where natural water inflow from the Bassac ceases during the dry season, water is pumped into the Prek during these times. In some places, this is being organised by village chiefs, in other places by private farmers. Sometimes the pumping is officially sanctioned, sometimes, it appears, the village chief is not even aware of it. Table 4.3 shows a summary of the current state of knowledge about pumping practices within the Prek as well as between the Prek and the Bassac or canals, from North to South. It must be emphasized, however, that this information may not be entirely reliable, as contradictions between what was reported by village chiefs and farmers, and what was observed in the field, were evident. [SOURCE: Page_215]

4.3.4.3       Livestock [SOURCE: Page_217]

Among the interviewees, 37 keep livestock. Most of them keep a small number of cows (3-4) to sell for meat, though two farmers also raised pigs. Several interviewees reported having given up on keeping livestock since it had become unprofitable. [SOURCE: Page_217]

Some of the farmers who raise cows also sell the manure they produce. One farmer said that he sold manure three times per year to Takeo. Another farmer detailed that they had to sell the manure to Takeo because farmers in Kandal prefer chemical fertilizers. Apparently, the farmers in Takeo use the manure to fertilize fields for the cultivation of rainy season rice. The farmer said that they have dams in Takeo to protect the area, and can spread the dung over a longer period of time before cultivation, without it being swept away by the flood [SOURCE: Page_217]

Farmers largely use hay from natural vegetation that grows in the Boeung, as well as rice straw to feed the cattle. Some of them also let the cattle graze along the Prek and in the Boeung (see Figure 4.24d). Most of them, however, seem to raise them directly at their houses. During the fieldwork, several farmers were also observed watering and washing their cattle in the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_217]

One concept that also occurred in relation to cattle was the practice of prowa cows. The interviewee in the Cham village at the end of Prek Me Srok raises cows who belong to someone else under prowa. Ultimately, the owner has the benefit of selling mature cows, but the farmer who raises them gets to keep some of the benefits, in this case every second calf born. [SOURCE: Page_217]

Four farmers who were interviewed also raise pigs. Most of the farmers interviewed also raise chickens at their houses. While the majority only raise chickens for family needs, and are [SOURCE: Page_217]
