There are several interesting aspects that emerged during the interviews related to crop losses due to floods. To begin with, several farmers stated that they lost their mango trees to floods not due to the roots of trees being damaged by excessive moisture, but because the mechanical stress uprooted them. One farmer, who lost 10 out of 200 trees in this way, noted that he usually puts up wooden constructions to support the trees, to prevent such losses. [SOURCE: Page_219]

On average, farmers lost ca. 38% of their yield when their plots were affected by floods. Most reported that the losses were not distributed evenly across their plots, but were centred at the back end of Chamkar plots, or the lower areas of Boeung plots. The estimates for water levels at the time when losses occurred ranged between 40 and 100 cm. [SOURCE: Page_219]

Another notable aspect is that several farmers also mentioned crops being used due to floods caused by heavy rains and the strong winds that accompany them. [SOURCE: Page_219]

Finally, two farmers also pointed out that they believe the main cause of the flood-related crop losses in their plots is bad drainage. [SOURCE: Page_219]

Drought In total, 33% of farmers who were interviewed reported crop losses due to droughts. Unlike for the losses caused by floods, drought losses occurred evenly distributed across the plots. Furthermore, the average percentage of yield lost was estimated by farmers to be slightly higher than for flood losses, at an average of 57%. [SOURCE: Page_219]

The majority of reported losses concerned rice. Either recession rice, which must have been planted late, was lost in February or March due to a lack of rainfall and a dearth of irrigation water. Or EWS rice was lost for the same reasons, mostly in May. [SOURCE: Page_219]

Other crops for which losses were reported are maize, green bean and mung bean. These ranged between 30 and 100% of the corp and occurred mostly at the height of the dry season, between April and May. [SOURCE: Page_219]

An in-depth analysis of the effects of drought in the study are is provided by Vandôme (2020), based on both field data and a modelling approach using the FAO software CROPWAT 8.0. [SOURCE: Page_219]

219 [SOURCE: Page_219]

Pests As mentioned above, for many farmers, pests are actually a bigger concern in terms of crop losses than either floods or droughts, with 83% of farmers who responded to the question reporting losses. To put this in numbers, farmers report that they have lost an average of 30% of (mostly rice) crops to rats, with losses reaching as far as 75%, and an average of 38% (mostly mangoes) to insects. In addition, crop loss risk factors compound each other. In very dry years, rat populations are higher. One farmer who lost their entire rice crop to an unexpected return of the flood in February 2018 also stated that they could not replant the crop because rats during this time of the year would have eradicated the young rice plants. [SOURCE: Page_220]

4.3.5    Assessing Alternative Roles: Perspective of a Landless Scavenger [SOURCE: Page_220]

One of the interviewees, does not own or farm any land herself, but still profits from agriculture by scavenging fields after harvest to look for produce that was left behind. She also fishes for snails in the canals behind the Preks and sells chickens. A particularly interesting aspect of this interview was that she was able to give a (subjective) comparison of agricultural production between Prek areas, since her scavenging activities take her to Prek Pok, Prek Chann, Prek Touch, as well as along the Prek Ambel and outside the study area. [SOURCE: Page_220]

As a scavenger, she collects rice and vegetables that are left behind after the farmers harvest on their plots. In doing so, she can collect considerable quantities of produce. Last year, she collected a total of 53 bags of rice, at a weight of 70-80 kg each. 43 of these bags were collected between January and March, and ten between April and June. To reach this amount of rice collected, she has to work practically every day between 7 am and 5 pm, sometimes aided by her elderly mother. She uses her bicycle for transport along the Preks, and her husband picks up the finished bags of rice on his motorcycle. Out of the 53 bags she collected, she keeps 10 for family needs throughout the year, and sells the rest for 1,000 Riel/kg to middlemen. She says that 2019 was an exceptionally good year for her because it was wet during the harvest period between January and March and the rice harvesting machines left a lot behind as a consequence. As a harvesting implement, she uses a hand sickle. [SOURCE: Page_220]

The interviewee also collects leftovers of white bean, green bean, and other vegetables. She keeps 3 kg of beans for family needs and sells the rest – for 4,500 Riel per kg of green bean and [SOURCE: Page_220]

220 [SOURCE: Page_220]

3,000 Riel per kg of white bean. Last year, she said she spent 4-5 days per month collecting these crops, and managed to collect ca. 10 kg per day. [SOURCE: Page_221]

When asked to compare agricultural production between Preks in the different years, she noted that crop yields at Prek Chann as well as the snail populations in the Prek and the canals behind it have increased since the rehabilitation. [SOURCE: Page_221]

A final note on scavenging activities that the she added is that they are apparently common in the area. She even stated that school students scavenge on the weekends to support school canteens. [SOURCE: Page_221]

In addition to selling the rice and vegetables she scavenges, the interviewee also raises and sells chickens. These live in the shrubland in the vicinity of her house, and in the natural vegetation along the Prek. She says she also feeds them paddy rice. Three times per year she can sell five to ten chickens, for 35,000 – 38,000 Riel per head. However, she also raises particularly expensive cocks (currently seven), which she can sell for 100,000 Riel each. [SOURCE: Page_221]

Apart from selling agricultural products and chickens, the interviewee also fishes in the Preks and the canals network in the Boeung, especially canal 24. She states that she fishes during the whole year, every weekend for ca. 6 hours. Each time, she says she manages to catch ca. 30 kg of snails and 1-2 kg of fish that accidentally get caught in her nets. As a fishing implement, she uses a bicycle wheel the spikes of which have been removed and replaced with a hand-woven string net. According to Ms. Hang, catch is mostly stable across the year, though peak fishing periods are during heat waves, since the animals then come out of their hiding places, and during flood recession. She sells the catch to middlemen from Phnom Penh – for 3,500 Riel per kg of snails and 7,000 Riel per kg of fish. [SOURCE: Page_221]

Finally, two interesting perspectives emerged from this interview related to hydrological issues. For one, the interviewee stated that she joined a meeting of the Cambodian People’s Party (CPP)in February 2020 at Prek Put at which it was suggested to fill the Prek up. Currently, there is only water in Prek Put in July and August, but this is not used for irrigation – also because it is of low quality since a pig farmer supposedly drains their wastewater into the Prek. The final decision over the future of the Prek lies with the head of the Pagoda which lies on its north bank. As a second point of interest, she also noted that the fields along Prek Put are often irrigated [SOURCE: Page_221]

221 [SOURCE: Page_221]

through wells, since the Prek cannot be used for water supply. [SOURCE: Page_222]

4.3.6     The Role of Local Governance: Outlining the Roles of Village Chiefs and Prek User Committees [SOURCE: Page_222]

4.3.6.1   Information from Village Chiefs [SOURCE: Page_222]

Overall, eight interviews with village chiefs and one interview with a PUC chief were conducted in the course of the fieldwork in February and March 2020. This section gives a summary of general aspects that emerged from the interviews, as well as a closer discussion of a few salient points. The information gleaned from these interviews illustrates how local communities influence water flows in the area. While these have not yet been accounted for in the model to be described below, they offer interesting insights into feedback loops to be incorporated into calculations later on. [SOURCE: Page_222]

General Observations The level of detail the village chiefs could provide on issues of Prek management, agriculture and general management procedures varied vastly. Some could provide the exact numbers of the villagers and confident estimates about crop production and Prek water usage, while others did not even know whether fields in their village area were flooded during the wet season. [SOURCE: Page_222]

On average, village chiefs are 66 years old and have held their positions for 17 years. All of them were men. They primarily define their tasks as managing village affairs and communicating problems at village level to the commune. Only one village chief stated that his primary task was to represent the CPP on a local level. All village chiefs mentioned that they paid particular attention to matters of infrastructure – in terms of road and Prek maintenance. Two of them also emphasized that they were particularly concerned with security issues, with one detailing that he was struggling to deal with illegal gambling, cockfights, drunken violence, and drugs. In terms of communication, all village chiefs said that they regularly interacted with the commune level to report any larger issues. One of them said that he had one monthly meeting with him, the others did not specify the intervals. Some village chiefs stated that there was a general assembly [SOURCE: Page_222]

222 [SOURCE: Page_222]

of village chiefs and the commune chief once per year and that it had been held at Koh Thom recently. [SOURCE: Page_223]

Rehabilitation At the Preks that have been rehabilitated, the village chiefs say that they are happy that the project was implemented, despite some of the difficulties that have arisen as a consequence, such as bank collapses. [SOURCE: Page_223]

At the Preks that have not yet been rehabilitated, several chiefs stated that they wanted their Preks to be rehabilitated. At Prek Thom and Prek Touch, an excavation is being organised by the village chiefs, though it only includes a deepening of the Prek and no road construction. [SOURCE: Page_223]

Water Use During the interviews, village chiefs made several observations related to water use that had not been included in the questionnaire, which are summarized here. [SOURCE: Page_223]

The village chief at Prek Chann stated that before rehabilitation, many people drilled wells, but used them only as a source of irrigation water, since the water quality was too bad for it to be used for household purposes. At Prek Chann, water from the Prek is also used for non-drinking household purposes like cleaning, washing laundry etc. Similarly, the village chief at Prek Me Srok has stated that since the completion of rehabilitation no pumping ventures have been necessary to supply the Prek with water. [SOURCE: Page_223]

Two village chiefs stated that (temporary) earthen dams are built across the Preks from time to time – at Prek Nou and Prek Put. At Prek Nou, the dams are used to channel water during the dry season, to supply pumps that lift water to distribution channels. At Prek Put, on the other hand, where there is generally little water, the dams are used as bridges by private farmers. It requires the permission of the village chief to build them, and he says he insists they have culverts to let the flood through in July and August. [SOURCE: Page_223]

As mentioned above, at Prek Nou, water, which flows naturally into the Prek, is pumped to distribution channels. These lie in the South of the Prek, and also supply fields that lie in the vicinity of Prek Put, since the latter Prek is dry for the majority of the year. Three pumping machines are used to lift the water from Prek Nou to the distribution channels. These pumps are operated by the village chief, a vice chief and a private person. Two of them have 24 HP, [SOURCE: Page_223]

223 [SOURCE: Page_223]

and one 38 HP. One pump operates on electricity, the other two on gasoline. According to one village chief, ca. 30 ha are supplied using these pumps. The one he operates is run for five to six hours every two weeks between December to March. [SOURCE: Page_224]

At Prek Pok, a pumping machine is used to supply the Prek with water between March and April. The village chief states that it is organised by the people who need water at this time, and that they report to him and he forwards the information to the commune level. [SOURCE: Page_224]

Agriculture The village chiefs interviewed, in addition to the questions asked during the interview, made various observations on the agriculture in the study area. Some of them are relayed here for the sake of completeness. [SOURCE: Page_224]

One village chief noted that there was a dramatic decrease in rice crops this year because of an overabundance of herbicide-resistant grass. He estimated the decrease to lie at 40%. [SOURCE: Page_224]

Several village chiefs commented on recent changes in crops. One of them noted that people were interested in cultivating fruit trees, but that for many investment costs were too high. As a consequence, he noted, people lost motivation and abandoned Chamkar plots. Another village chief noted the decrease in diversity in crops. He said that ca. 15 years ago, tobacco was the main crop on Chamkar areas, and was grown alongside potatoes, chilies, rice, white bean and maize. Now, mango is the main crop along the Prek, and rice is just cultivated in the short term. More fertilizer is needed, along with hormones and pesticides, and the investment costs for farmers to make the transition were considerable. He noted that ca. 10% of them did not make it and either rent out or sold their land. However, he also noted that due to the low water levels in the Prek, mangoes are the only crop that can be grown with a reasonable level of profitability. [SOURCE: Page_224]

Gate Operation at Prek Chann One of the main aims of the interviews with village and PUC chiefs was to discover the reasoning behind gate operation, as well as the patterns of its opening and closing, to incorporate the data into the hydrological model accordingly. Unfortunately, reliable-seeming information could only be gleaned from one village chief interviewed. The information provided by the PUC chief at Prek Chann (see note below) was inconsistent and in itself contradictory. [SOURCE: Page_224]

224 [SOURCE: Page_224]

According to Meas Chrik, 68, village chief of Por Andet village at Prek Chann, the gate operation is as follows: [SOURCE: Page_225]

The gate is closed completely in late June, when the water level in the Bassac begins to rise at the beginning of the rainy season. The reasons given for closing the gate at this time are: [SOURCE: Page_225]

• Avoiding the early floodwater in the Bassac, since this water includes many water plants and residues. [SOURCE: Page_225]

• Avoiding crop losses. Some farmers along the Prek are still cultivating at this point, and delaying the arrival of the flood gives them the opportunity to harvest at the appropriate time. [SOURCE: Page_225]

The gate is then opened ca. one and a half months later in August, but only to ca. 1.5 m above the bottom of the Prek to avoid fast inflow. Generally, the opening of the gate is executed very slowly to avoid erosion. The reasons given for opening the gate are: [SOURCE: Page_225]

• The deteriorating water quality in the Prek. Opening the gate allows for inflow from the now high-quality Bassac water. [SOURCE: Page_225]

• The high difference in water levels. According to Mr. Meas, the water level difference is ca. 3.5 m at this point between the Prek- and Bassac-side of the gate. If the difference is higher still, the danger of bank erosion during gate opening grows sharply. [SOURCE: Page_225]

In December, the gate is opened further still to ca. 3 m above the bottom of the Prek to keep the metal structure out of the water, since the village chief is worried about rusting. It remains in this position until the end of the dry season. [SOURCE: Page_225]

The opening and closing of the gate requires four to five people, chosen by the village chief. The equipment needed consists of a key and a lever that is connected with a wheel to operate the opening and closing mechanism. It is stored locally. The decision to open or close the gate is taken together with the PUC and the commune chief. [SOURCE: Page_225]

Mr Meas also notes that originally, one of the main purposes of the gate in his understanding was flood protection. However, since the completion of the rehabilitation, floods have generally [SOURCE: Page_225]

225 [SOURCE: Page_225]

been small according to his view. He doesn’t think that the gate is useful to keep water in the Prek but believes that water availability is now much better than before rehabilitation. [SOURCE: Page_226]

Locally Organized Prek Excavation        One topic that was discussed in detail with village chiefs were excavation activities at their Preks. A detailed description of the large-scale excavation that took place at Prek Thom is provided below. However, several other village chiefs also commented on excavations at their Preks. [SOURCE: Page_226]

At Prek Cham Kroum, the village chief stated that a project for a Prek-wide excavation had been proposed by him several times, to deepen the Prek and extend the profile. However, there is some opposition among the village population because several families along the Prek would have to be resettled. No resolution of the conflict has been reached. [SOURCE: Page_226]

At Prek Chann, some excavations were ongoing at the time of the field visit, to remove the material from bank collapses following rehabilitation. Otherwise, excavations at this Prek have ceased since rehabilitation. Equally, there have not been excavations at Prek Me Srok since the completion of rehabilitation, except for the work that is currently being done to fix bank collapses in the village area. However, the village chief says he is thinking about organising smaller excavations to repair bank collapses further along the Prek, which are not being repaired as part of the current project. [SOURCE: Page_226]

At Prek Lok, excavations take place every year in strategic places, like the head of the Prek. According to the village chief, the people report to him and he forwards information to the commune. In turn, the commune representatives come to observe the situation and reach a decision on excavation. The village chief states that funds for the excavation are provided by the government – an annual average of 1 million Riel. Furthermore, the chief says that he raises ca. 5,000 Riel per family per year to cover excavation costs. Costs are furthermore covered by selling the material that is excavated from the Prek. The material is sold in partial compensation by the private companies charged with the excavation of the Prek. Recipients are farmers in the vicinity of the Prek who aim to raise their land. It has furthermore been noted that due to the profitability of such ventures, the initiative for excavation has also come from private companies themselves. Excavation work at Prek Lok takes place between March and April. [SOURCE: Page_226]

226 [SOURCE: Page_226]

Excavation at Prek Thom and Prek Touch           One of the most remarkable observations in the study area during this field visit was the excavation that is ongoing at Prek Thom, in the south of the study area. Here, the entire Prek is being excavated in a sharp trapezoidal profile. [SOURCE: Page_227]

In an interview with the village chief it emerged that the project is driven by a private sector company. It is mutually beneficial to the company and the village, because the company gets to keep and sell the soil that is excavated, while the village profits from the improved Prek profile and better water inflow. [SOURCE: Page_227]

According to the village chief, the project was discussed in advance between the village chiefs of the affected villages, the commune chief, and the company. The company also provided a model of the proposed Prek profile as a decision basis. During this meeting, the village chief emphasized that he made sure the excavation would reach to the very end of the Prek. He also says that he consulted with the people in his village before making a final decision. [SOURCE: Page_227]

The people in the village, they said, would have preferred a French project, because rehabili- tations by French engineers usually also include roads, which this one doesn’t. They would have wanted the same sort of project as was implemented at Prek Chann – but without a gate. The village chief noted that in 2006/07 there were some talks about a rehabilitation project financed by international development agencies, but that ever came to pass. [SOURCE: Page_227]

For now, the villagers are purportedly happy with the excavation because of the prospect of improved water availability. According to the village chief, nobody had to be resettled. He furthermore said that the excavation started at the end of December and that the Prek is usually dry between January and July – so no major inconvenience for agriculture was expected. A private water seller who operated a pump at the Prek moved to another Prek outside the study area. The excavation is expected to be finished in April. [SOURCE: Page_227]

The village chief says that he expects some bank collapses, but none as severe as at Prek Chann. He says he believes the profile implemented at Prek Thom is safer because of the long slopes and the narrow bottom. The bed of the Prek is supposed to be lowered by 3 m along the whole length of the Prek. However, he also noted that there are no exact measurements or plans available. [SOURCE: Page_227]

227 [SOURCE: Page_227]

4.3.7    Summarizing the Results of Fieldwork [SOURCE: Page_229]

Overall, the interviews conducted in the course of fieldwork have provided a solid understanding of the general agricultural practices in the area, as well as of water management and the organizational difficulties the latter entails. They have outlined that providing irrigation water, especially during the dry season, is the principal priority of Preks in the eyes of the respondents. It has also emerged that many local stakeholders have a very nuanced understanding of the various regulating ecosystem services that the flood in the area contributes to, from pest regulation to sediment deposition. [SOURCE: Page_229]

Furthermore, one of the principal outcomes of the interviews has been to quantify and characterize ecosystem services - or at least to ascertain whether it was possible. For agricultural practices, which largely rely on the provision of irrigation water through the Preks and canals, extensive information has been collected and analyzed statistically to provide a basis for further analyses. In contrast, quantifying services such as the use of natural vegetation and fish catch has been difficult for several reasons. To begin with, practices have shifted considerably over the last years. According to multiple respondents, fish catch has declined dramatically and the use of natural vegetation now entails concerns of pesticide contamination. Another reason is that it was nigh impossible to calculate the average use of either resource due to a paucity of information. For instance, while all respondents could readily answer whether they fish in the Preks or use natural vegetation, estimating a frequency proved difficult for them, as their uses, over the past years, had changed considerably. [SOURCE: Page_229]

In contrast, an aspect on which much clarity could be gained was the attitude towards rehabilitation projects and general water management practices. It emerged that rehabilitation is generally seen in a positive light by local communities, and that water inflow into the Prek is seen as the main benefit, alongside the construction of better roads along the Prek, which allow for transport without having to rely on boats. The construction of inflow management structure such as gates, in contrast, is seen critically - for one thing because it limits transport possibilities, for another because they require management that, if carried out improperly, can lead to erosion and injury. [SOURCE: Page_229]

Another issue that became clearer is that many respondents don’t implicitly associate the [SOURCE: Page_229]

229 [SOURCE: Page_229]

rehabilitation state of "their" Prek with the arrival or recession of the flood as a whole. This suggests that flow dynamics in the Boeung play an essential role during the early flood phase. [SOURCE: Page_230]

Overall, the interviews have yielded a clearer understanding of local land cover dynamics, water management practices, and ecosystem services. However, as mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, all of this is presents a snapshot of a fraction of the case study area. In order to better quantify provisioning services in particular, a more spatialized understanding of key aspects of flood and land cover dynamics is necessary. The methodology of WAFL, presented in the last chapter, can provide the former based on water levels in the Bassac river. To provide the latter - an understanding of land cover distribution in the study area as a whole - another approach was utilized. The next section of this chapter aims to outline the path that was taken to assess land cover dynamics in the case study area as a whole through remote sensing. [SOURCE: Page_230]

4.4     Conclusion:Appreciating the Influence of Communities and Individual Actors on Hydrological Processes [SOURCE: Page_230]

The second major part of this thesis has addressed the history of Prek channels, as well as their current role in the provision of ecosystem services and LULC patterns in a case study area located ca. 70 km South of Phnom Penh. [SOURCE: Page_230]

The history of Preks was traced through historical engineering reports, starting in the early 20th century. According to French colonial engineers, Preks were originally constructed by the local population by breaching the elevated river banks to allow sedimentation in low-lying areas. Their aim was to raise land to create more elevated areas for high-value crops. French engineers adopted Prek construction and during the early 20th century the Cambodian Mekong delta saw a systematic extension of Preks along the banks of the Bassac and the Mekong. After the end of the French protectorate following World War II, records on the maintenance of Preks become sparse, though they are likely to have been maintained as agriculture held a high priority in the agenda of the government. During the Khmer Rouge regime in the 1970s, an extensive network of canals was constructed in the lowlands at the tail end of the Preks. Following the fall of the Khmer Rouge and the resettlement of displaced people, the focus of international [SOURCE: Page_230]

230 [SOURCE: Page_230]

development projects in this region of Cambodia fell on Preks and their rehabilitation. Since the 1990s, multiple projects have sought to restore their former functionality to enhance the prosperity and resilience of local agricultural communities. [SOURCE: Page_231]

The effectiveness of this approach as well as the high regard that local communities have for rehabilitation projects also became apparent during the surveys conducted with stakeholders in the case study area. Village chiefs and farmers at every Prek were interviewed and detailed data on cropping practices, irrigation, and the role of Preks for ecosystem services was collected. [SOURCE: Page_231]

This data showed that the primary use of Preks for local communities lies in the provision of irrigation water, especially during the dry season. Farmers use individual, mobile pumps to lift water from the Preks to their plots and distribute it either through gravity irrigation or using plastic pipes. In addition, Prek water is used to water cattle, and to meet non-dietary household needs. Furthermore, local inhabitants also fish in the Preks and in the flooded lowland areas during the wet season, though multiple interviewees noted a steep decline in fish catch over the past years, which they attribute to changes in inundations as well as illegal fishing practices. People also use the natural vegetation that grows along the banks of the Preks for food and fuel. To a certain extent, the interviewees also broached the issue of the role of Preks in catalyzing floods for regulating ecosystem services - such as pest regulation, especially by decimating rat populations, as well as soil- and groundwater recharge and sediment deposition. [SOURCE: Page_231]

Overall, this chapter has outlined the multiple ways in which local communities interact with the local agro-ecosystem in general, and with hydrological processes in general. From the historical initiation of Prek formation via artificial bank breaches, to modern-day rehabilitation projects and pumping practices, humans shape the Prek system as much as the Prek system shapes their livelihoods. [SOURCE: Page_231]

231 [SOURCE: Page_231]

232 [SOURCE: Page_232]

5 Assessing Landcover Dynamics through Supervised Classification Remote Sensing Approaches [SOURCE: Page_233]

As outlined in the previous chapter, the interviews yielded a detailed picture of local cropping practices.1 However, to assess ecosystem services on the level of the study area as a whole, a more spatialized understanding of land use / land cover (LULC) is necessary. For this reason, a remote sensing approach was chosen using Sentinel-1 and 2 and a supervised classification approach. Supervised classification allows the user to pre-define the classes into which images will be divided. Using a training dataset, a classifier learns to recognize each class and can then 1 This chapter has been published as a paper: Orieschnig, C.A., Belaud, G., Venot, J.P., Massuel, S. and Ogilvie, [SOURCE: Page_233]

A., 2021. Input imagery, classifiers, and cloud computing: Insights from multi-temporal LULC mapping in the Cambodian Mekong Delta. European Journal of Remote Sensing, 54(1), pp.398-416. [SOURCE: Page_233]

233 [SOURCE: Page_233]

delineate it in the images to be processes. For the purposes of this study, six broad land use classes are defined: open water surfaces, bare/fallow land, urban/village areas, fruit trees, rice fields, and vegetable fields. Out of these, urban areas - located along the main road that runs in parallel with the river - and fruit trees are relatively static over the course of a year (neglecting urban spread and the planting or cutting down of trees). The other classes are highly dynamic. During the wet season, large swaths of low-lying land in the west and southwest of the area are inundated. Subsequently, these areas see one or two cycles of rice cultivation, before lying fallow for part of the year. The higher terrain in the east of the study area sees a complex mosaic of fields lying fallow and being cultivated. Figure 5.1 shows an RGB overview of the LULC dynamics in the study area during the dry season. [SOURCE: Page_234]

Figure 5.1: Landcover dynamics in the study area during the dry season, RGB Image. [SOURCE: Page_234]

However, before land cover maps for the study area could be derived with any great certainty, it was necessary to test and compare the different methods available on the chosen earth observa- tion platform in this thesis, GEE. This meant comparing different classifiers, combinations of input imagery, and training data sets in order to achieve a classification with maximum accuracy on which further analyses could be based. [SOURCE: Page_234]

Like majority of LULC studies, this analysis uses supervised classification methods. Al- though some researchers have used unsupervised classification (Mohammady et al., 2015; O’Hara et al., 2003), supervised classification is often preferred due to the possibility of setting a pre- defined number of labelled output classes. To harness these advantages, a variety of classifiers [SOURCE: Page_234]

234 [SOURCE: Page_234]

is available for supervised classification. Among the most frequently used are machine learn- ing algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and K Nearest Neighbour (KNN) (Talukdar et al., 2020). Furthermore, advanced machine learning approaches such as artificial neural networks (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and deep neural networks (DNN) have seen more widespread use in recent years (Jozdani et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_235]

A number of papers compared these classifiers in LULC applications. Talukdar et al. (2020) compare RF and SVM, along with more advanced machine learning methods in a study area along the Ganga river in India. The authors conclude that the RF algorithm overall performs best. In contrast, Nery et al. (2016) find that SVM reaches the highest classification accuracies for LULC analyses after comparing it with KNN, RF, Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ), Recursive Partitioning Regression Trees (RPART), and Stochastic Gradient Boosting Methods (GBM) in a study area in Western Australia. The same conclusion was reached by Thanh Noi and Kappas (2017), who compared RF, KNN, and SVM classifications of Sentinel-2 imagery in the Red River Delta in Vietnam. Shelestov et al. (2017) weighed the merits of some of the classifiers available in GEE against external methods, including an ensemble neural networks, for crop classification using optical Landsat-8 images. They found decision-tree classifiers to perform best in GEE, though neural networks outperformed them. [SOURCE: Page_235]

Most of these comparison papers focus on contrasting the performance of classifiers applied to a single date rather than in a multi-temporal situation. In addition, none yet specifically compare classifiers in the context of cloud computing platforms, many of which only offer a limited number of native implementations. In addition, with a few notable exceptions (Hütt et al., 2016), many papers only approach the classifier comparison on the basis of a single imagery type, with a fixed set of bands, and a single source of training data. [SOURCE: Page_235]

However, no comparison existed so far for the classifiers available for LULC on GEE, nor for a multi-temporal situation in a highly dynamic area, as is necessary in the case of the case study area. To address this lack of knowledge, an assessment of the response of four supervised classifiers available in the online Javascript API of the GEE cloud computing platform, to the use of different combinations of input imagery, training data, and band sets for the purpose of land use and land cover analyses. These classifiers are Naive Bayes (NB), Classification and Regression Trees (CART), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machines (SVM). While it [SOURCE: Page_235]

235 [SOURCE: Page_235]

Table 5.1: Overview of image datasets used. Dataset Nr   Imagery          Band Set 1            Sentinel-1       Full 2            Sentinel-1       Reduced 3            Sentinel-1       Minimal 4            Sentinel-2       Full 5            Sentinel-2       Reduced 6            Sentinel-2       Minimal 7            Sentinel-1 & 2   Full 8            Sentinel-1 & 2   Reduced 9            Sentinel-1 & 2   Minimal [SOURCE: Page_236]

is possible to implement further supervised classification methods, such as fully convolutional neural networks (FCNN), or deep neural networks (DNN) in GEE, this requires the external training of the models on the TensorFlow platform (Abadi et al., 2016). Since this approach involves several billable components of Google Cloud, it is not included. [SOURCE: Page_236]

The comparisons are made using Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, both separately and in combination. In addition, the impact on classifier performance of the type of the training set, as well as the choice of bands, texture features, and spectral indices is tested. For this purpose, two different sets of training points (one based on field data, one derived from high-resolution satellite imagery) and three different sets of training bands (varying in the number of additional indexes and texture features used for classification) are used. [SOURCE: Page_236]

5.1     Data Used [SOURCE: Page_236]

A general outline of the classification workflow is given in Figure 5.3. Figure 5.2 gives an overview of the temporal distribution of images and training data points used in this thesis for the purposes of LULC classification. Following pre-processing, 9 datasets are generated on which the classifiers are tested. These datasets derive from the use of different imagery types alone and in combination, as well as different band sets (see Table 5.1). Parameter tuning, calibration, and validation is performed for each of the 9 datasets separately, using both the limited training points derived from fieldwork, and the extended training points generated on the basis of the SPOT-6 and 7 images, resulting in 18 different configurations of input data for each of the four classifiers. Finally, the best-performing algorithm is chosen and applied to the optical, radar, and combined dataset to generate a LULC classification spanning the entire period between 01/11/2019 and 31/10/2020. [SOURCE: Page_236]

5.2     Image Pre-Processing [SOURCE: Page_237]

To a certain degree, both Sentinel-1 and 2 images are already provided in pre-processed form in GEE. [SOURCE: Page_237]

Sentinel-1 images undergo pre-processing during ingestion in GEE based on the ESA’s Sentinel-1 toolbox. In this process, metadata is updated with a restituted orbit file, border noise [SOURCE: Page_237]

237 [SOURCE: Page_237]

and thermal noise is removed, and radiometric calibration and orthorectification are applied. The fact that images are provided in pre-processed form in GEE’s Javascript API removes one of the main hurdles many researchers face in using SAR data. In fact, several studies have used GEE as a source of SAR images, even though their analyses were subsequently conducted in different environments (Tamiminia et al., 2020; Amani et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_238]

As a basis for classification, additional bands are generated for SAR imagery using the original VV and VH bands (cf. Table 3.5). Three of these are based on arithmetic operations ( VV V H , VV   V H, VV +V 2 H ) which previous studies found to yield increased accuracies for LULC approaches (Slagter et al., 2020). The others are based on a classic Grey Level Co-occurence Matrix (GLCM), encompassing Haralick texture features (Haralick et al., 1973). These features describe image texture through interpretable descriptors and have been found to add valuable information for LULC analyses. (Clerici et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2020; Mishra et al., 2019). Texture features are calculated separately for both the VV and VH polarization, parameterized with a 5x^5 window size. Following previous studies (Nizalapur and Vyas, 2020), angular second moment (ASM), contrast (CONTRAST), correlation (CORR), inverse difference moment (IDM), entropy (ENT), dissimilarity (DISS), and variance (VAR) are used as added bands for classification. Following the calculation of the texture features, a refined Lee speckle filter (Yommy et al., 2015) is applied to smooth the original VV and VH bands in order to reduce speckle, since not all sdatasets use the generated texture bands. [SOURCE: Page_238]

Sentinel-2 images are available in pre-processed form in GEE. The sen^2cor algorithm (Main- Knorn et al., 2017) has been applied to transform Top of the Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance to surface reflectance (BOA). For this analysis, all bands are automatically re-sampled to 10 m resolution by the GEE processing algorithm. For the time series calculation, a cloudy pixel threshold of < 20% is introduced, and the remaining clouds are masked using a simple bit-mask based on the QA band. [SOURCE: Page_238]

Additional spectral indices (cf. Table 5.2) are calculated on the basis of native bands (cf. Table 3.6) o generate ancillary layers of information that serve as input for the classification algorithms, which past studies have found to be valuable in increasing classification accuracies (Godinho et al., 2016). These are based on a range of bands employed in past studies for various LULC analyses using different classification algorithms (Ouattara et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_238]

5.3        Creation of Image Datasets [SOURCE: Page_239]

In total, parameter tuning, calibration, and validation is performed on nine image datasets (cf. Table 5.1). [SOURCE: Page_239]

First, three main sets of images are created - one containing only SAR imagery, one containing optical imagery, and one in which images are created by stacking all available optical and SAR bands into a single image. Then, each of the three imagery sets is further subdivided into three tiers depending on how many bands are used for classification(see Table 5.3). One tier includes a band set that encompasses all native bands, spectral indices, and texture features. A reduced band set includes the native image bands as well as some indices and texture features. Finally, a minimal set consists only of the VV and VH bands for SAR, and the RGB bands for optical imagery. [SOURCE: Page_239]

5.4     Classifiers and Parameter Tuning [SOURCE: Page_240]

Each dataset is calibrated with 80% and validated with 20% of both the fieldwork and the SPOT-based training data, for each of the four classifiers. Preceding calibration, each classifier undergoes parameter tuning. A short description of each classifier as well as the associated tuning parameters is given below. [SOURCE: Page_240]

5.4.1    Naïve Bayes (NB) [SOURCE: Page_240]

This classifier relies on a simple probabilistic approach that is based on the Bayes theorem (John and Langley, 2013). It is referred to as naïve because it relies on the assumption of conditional independence between every pair of features, and a Gaussian probability distribution (Zhang, 2005). In reality, this condition is frequently not met, particularly in more complex situations and datasets. Nonetheless, several studies have found the simplistic approach to yield satisfying results (Johnson and Iizuka, 2016; Diengdoh et al., 2020), particularly in cases where only a limited number of input features is available. This may be due to the fact that, in general, even a small training set is sufficient to minimize the average risk of the classification error and compute the decision surface. Some studies have also argued that dependence distribution among classes could also account for the surprisingly good performance of NB (Kuncheva, 2006). In GEE’s implementation of NB, the only parameter that needs to be tuned for performance is the smoothing factor λ . [SOURCE: Page_240]

5.4.2    Classification and Regression Trees (CART) [SOURCE: Page_241]

CART classifiers belong to the family of decision tree classifiers. The basic approach of this type of classifier is to find the attribute or threshold that splits a training dataset most effectively into subsets. This split then becomes a node in the tree, with the two subsets forming branches. Each subset is then split into further subsets until only a non-splitable end node (also known as a ‘leaf node’) remains. The main criterion in performing every split is the normalized information gain (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014). Once grown using the training dataset, the decision tree can then be applied to new samples. A considerable disadvantage of this approach is its high sensitivity to the training dataset. Even globally negligible modifications in the training data can lead to fundamentally different tree structures (Shelestov et al., 2017). To improve classifier performance, the number of leaf nodes in each tree (maxNodes) is tuned. [SOURCE: Page_241]

5.4.3    Random Forest (RF) [SOURCE: Page_241]

Random Forest (RF) is a recursive partitioning technique that is based on the construction of an ensemble of classification and regression trees (hence the term forest). Each tree is trained using the same method as described above for CART. However, to increase computational efficiency, each tree only utilizes a random subset of features at each node – this step also reduces correlation (and accounts for the second element in the nomenclature of the classifier). Trees are bundled together computationally through bootstrap aggregating (“bagging”) (Breiman, 1996). The final classification result for a new sample is then obtained through a majority vote of individual tree results. Overall, this approach is less sensitive to overfitting and noisy data, two of the most considerable pitfalls of CART approaches (Breiman, 2001). For RF tuning, the number of trees (nTree) and the number of variables per split (mTry) have to be optimized. Past studies found that satisfactory, stable results could be produced with a number of trees ranging between 200 and 500 (Belgiu and Dragut, 2016). To find the optimal RF model, this study tested nTree = [50 : 750] with a step size of 50, and mTry = [1:15] with a step size of 1. [SOURCE: Page_241]

241 [SOURCE: Page_241]

5.4.4    Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB) [SOURCE: Page_242]

Like RF, Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB) algorithms utilize an ensemble of decision trees. How- ever, its basic approach differs in that it limits the complexity of trees, confining each individual tree to a weak prediction model. It achieves classification accuracy by iteratively combining an ensemble of these weak learners into strong ones by minimizing a differentiable loss function at every step, following a gradient descent procedure (Friedman, 2002). To reduce correlation between trees, each new tree is constructed on the basis of a stochastically selected subset of training data. Recent studies have shown GTB algorithms, such as XGboost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) to outperform classifiers such as SVM, RF, and KNN (Godinho et al., 2016), especially on unbalanced datasets. However, GTB are often prone to overfitting, a risk that can be minimized through parameter tuning. [SOURCE: Page_242]

In terms of parameters to be adjusted, the number of trees (nTree) is varied between 50 and 200, with a step size of 10. Furthermore, GTB requires a parameter to be specified to determine how many nodes a decision tree in the ensemble can have. Since GTB is based on weak learners, the maxNodes parameter is typically low, with a range of [2:10] with a step size of 1 being tested in this study. In addition, the sampling rate for stochastic gradient tree boosting, and the shrinkage rate, which controls the learning rate of the algorithm, need to be optimized. In this study, a range of [0.45:75] with a step size of 0.5 was tested for the former, and [0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5] for the latter. Finally, all three loss functions available in GEE for GTB were compared – least squares, least absolute deviation, and Huber. It must be noted that recommendations for nTree tuning usually include larger numbers of tree. Elith et al. (2008), for example, recommend nTree=1000 for tuning as a rule of thumb. However, the GEE implementation of GTB currently produces an error when more than 200 trees are employed for the data configuration in this study. This may be due to the fact that GTB was only recently implemented in GEE by the developers’ team and will be further discussed below. [SOURCE: Page_242]

5.4.5    Support Vector Machines (SVM) [SOURCE: Page_242]

The founding principle of this approach is to find the boundary that maximizes the distance from the nearest data point of all classes (Noble, 2006). These points are used for the construction [SOURCE: Page_242]

242 [SOURCE: Page_242]

of support vectors, which, in turn, form the basis for the computation of the maximum-margin hyperplane that serves as a boundary. The dimensionality of this hyperplane is determined by the number of features to be used for classification. For non-linear data, a kernel is applied to transform low-dimensional data to make it separable via the SVM approach in a higher- dimensional sphere (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995). Frequently used kernels include linear, Gaussian Radial Basis Function (RBF), sigmoid, and polynomial kernels (Amari and Wu, 1999). The main advantage of SVM is its high potential for generalization. [SOURCE: Page_243]

In terms of tuning SVMs, the first choice to make is to pick a kernel. For LULC approaches, RBF and Linear kernels are frequently used (Kavzoglu and Colkesen, 2009; Shi and Yang, 2015). Then the cost parameter C needs to be optimized, as well as the γ value in case the RBF kernel is used. The γ value determines the RBF kernel width and thus affects the smoothing of the hyperplane which divides classes. The C parameter sets the threshold for permitted misclassification of non-separable training data (Thanh Noi and Kappas, 2017). If it is too large, it can lead to over-fitting (Ghosh and Joshi, 2014). This study follows (Li et al., 2014) in using ten C values (2[-2;7] ) as well as ten γ values (2[-5;4] ) for parameter tuning. [SOURCE: Page_243]

5.5     Validation and Statistical Analysis [SOURCE: Page_243]

Finally, the classification results of each algorithm using each combination of imagery, band set, and training data is validated. For this, the remaining randomly selected 20% of the field work and SPOT-based datasets are used. Overall accuracy as well as producer and consumer accuracies are calculated (Congalton, 1991). To ascertain whether the choice of input imagery, training data, and band set has statistically significant impacts on classifier performance, the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis, 1952) is used. [SOURCE: Page_243]

243 [SOURCE: Page_243]

5.6     Results [SOURCE: Page_244]

5.6.1    Optimal Tuning Parameters [SOURCE: Page_244]

The tuning parameters that yielded the highest accuracies for each classifier and each of the 9 image subsets, and that are used in the remaining of the analysis, are given in Table 5.4, the full set of tuning parameters and their associated accuracies are given in the supplementary materials. The results show that the parameter values yielding the highest accuracies varied considerably for RF (nTree and mTry) and for SVM (C and γ ). For RF, the nTree used for the final analysis varies between 50 and 600, and nTry ranges from 1 to 14. For SVM, optimal classification accuracy is achieved using C values that vary along the full tuning spectrum. Similarly, the optimal γ value for the RBF kernel ranges from 2-5 to 24 . There are no discernible trends along the lines of imagery type, band sets, or training datasets. [SOURCE: Page_244]

In contrast to this, the optimal values for the tuning parameter λ for NB and CART’s maxNodes vary little. In the case of λ , most combinations of imagery, band sets, and training data show little sensitivity to value tuning. Where differences in accuracies depending on λ are observable, the highest accuracies can be reached with λ = 1 ⇤ 10 10 . As for maxNodes, the CART classifier globally reaches its highest accuracies using either 5 or 6 nodes. [SOURCE: Page_244]

As for GTB, parameter tuning revealed low sensitivities for some parameters, and higher discrepancies in accuracies for others. The type of loss function employed, for example, has a virtually untraceable effect on accuracies. The shrinkage function, on the other hand, showed optimal values between 0.01 and 0.25, and the sampling rate between 0.6 and 0.75. For nTree and maxNodes there was a noticeably larger variation for optimal parameter values for the fieldwork training set, than for the extended training set. In the former, values for nTree ranged between 50 and 190 and for maxNodes between 3 and 10. In the latter, the optimal value for nTree lay between 160 and 200, and for maxNodes between 9 and 10. [SOURCE: Page_244]

5.6.2        Overall Accuracy [SOURCE: Page_245]

The maximum overall accuracies achieved by each classifier depending on imagery type, band set, and training data, are given in Table 5.5. Accuracies over 85%, which previous studies have deemed satisfactory for LULC purposes (Denize et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2020; Steinhausen et al., 2018), are highlighted in bold. [SOURCE: Page_245]

The results show that GTB globally reached the highest overall accuracy, at 94%. This value is reached using combined imagery, the extended dataset derived from SPOT imagery, and both the full and the reduced band set. RF also yields similarly high values (93%) using the same combination of imagery, training dataset and bands. For the fieldwork dataset, the highest accuracies are also reached by GTB and RF. GTB yields an overall accuracy of 93% for the full and 92% for the reduced band sets using combined optical and SAR imagery. For the same input configuration, RF yields accuracies of 92% and 91% respectively. Furthermore, GTB and RF also reach accuracies of over 85% using all other combinations of bands and training sets for the combination of Sentinel-1 and 2 imagery, and for the use of the extended training set and the full and reduced band sets for optical-only imagery. [SOURCE: Page_245]

SVM using a linear kernel and combined optical and SAR imagery is third in terms of overall accuracy. Accuracies of up to 92% are achieved using the extended training dataset and the reduced band set. Like RF, SVM also yields high accuracies when trained using the fieldwork dataset and the reduced band set. It furthermore attains accuracies of 88% and 86% respectively [SOURCE: Page_245]

5.6.3      SAR- and Optical-Only vs. Combined Imagery [SOURCE: Page_246]

Overall, the results show a marked increase in accuracy for the majority of classifiers when combined imagery is used, as opposed to SAR and optical-only imagery. For RF, optical-only imagery led to an average accuracy of 78% across training and band sets. For SAR-only imagery, this average lay at only 67%. The combination of both imagery types, however, yielded an average accuracy of 90%. Similarly, the CART, SVM, and NB classifiers also yielded their best accuracies using the combined imagery. [SOURCE: Page_246]

As illustrated in Figure 5.4, the combined imagery yielded considerably higher accuracies for NB, CART, RF, and SVM using a linear kernel than optical or SAR images alone. For CART and RF, the improvement in accuracy when using combined imagery in comparison to optical-only imagery is statistically significant (p   0.95). In addition, the CART classifier using optical imagery shows considerable variability with respect to accuracies. The improvement in comparison to using SAR-imagery only is statistically significant for NB, CART, RF, and SVM using a linear kernel. However, for SVM using an RBF kernel, the reverse is true - the combined imagery yields considerably lower accuracy values than either optical- or SAR-only imagery. [SOURCE: Page_247]

Figure 5.4: Box plot of overall accuracies by imagery used and classifier, and significance of variation of accuracies depending on imagery type used. [SOURCE: Page_247]

247 [SOURCE: Page_247]

5.6.4    Choice of Training Data and Band Sets [SOURCE: Page_248]

In general, the extended training data yielded the highest overall accuracies for GTB, RF and SVM using both a linear and RBF kernel. For CART and NB, however, the training set based on fieldwork data led to higher accuracies. GTB, RF and SVM using a linear kernel also yielded accuracies of over 85% using the fieldwork dataset (cf. Table 5.5 and supplementary materials). It can be noted that the use of the extended data set leads to a higher accuracy improvement in optical and SAR-only imagery than in the combined imagery. For example, for RF applied to optical imagery, the average overall accuracy achieved using the fieldwork dataset lies at 74%, whereas the extended dataset yields an average overall accuracy of 82%. In contrast, for combined imagery the average RF using fieldwork training data lies at 89%. Using the extended dataset only increases this average overall accuracy to 90%. [SOURCE: Page_248]

As for the band set, it emerges that the extended and fieldwork datasets produce comparable accuracies for CART, RF, and GTB. SVM using a linear kernel, however, produces distinctly higher accuracies on the basis of the reduced band set. Furthermore, SVM using the RBF kernel produces its highest overall accuracies when the minimal band set is used. [SOURCE: Page_248]

5.6.5    Accuracy by Class [SOURCE: Page_248]

The accuracy with which each land cover class is classified by each algorithm varies considerably. Consequently, this impacts the overall classification accuracy at different points in the time series of images between 01/11/2019 and 31/10/2020, when the classes have a different predominance. [SOURCE: Page_248]

Water, for example, has a relatively high consumer and producer accuracy (cf. Table 5.6). While NB tends to errors of omission, mis-classifying water as urban areas, the other classifiers succeed in delineating surface water regions with fairly high confidence. RF and GTB in particu- lar delineate water well, with producer accuracies of 98% and 97%, and consumer accuracies of 97% and 98% respectively, followed by SVM (97% and 96% respectively). Consequently, inundated areas, as they can be observed in November, are represented well. [SOURCE: Page_248]

In contrast, the classifiers exhibit greater difficulties in separating bare/fallow land from urban areas, and vegetable fields from rice paddies. While CART, RF, GTB, and SVM succeed [SOURCE: Page_248]

Figure 5.6: Time series of areas classified as bare / fallow using the training point set based on SPOT-images and RF, CART and SVM (linear) between October 2019 and September 2020. NB and SVM (RBF) are not included due to low accuracies. [SOURCE: Page_250]

5.7     Discussion [SOURCE: Page_250]

5.7.1    Benefits of Combining Imagery [SOURCE: Page_250]

Most saliently, this study highlights the multiple benefits of combining Sentinel-1 and 2 imagery for various classifiers. For all classifiers except SVM using an RBF kernel, combined imagery yields the highest classification accuracy. Especially for SVM using a linear kernel, the combina- tion of optical and SAR imagery brings a relative increase in overall classification performance. This is in line with several studies that have found marked benefits in adding information from radar images to optical ones for LULC classification (Denize et al., 2018; Van Tricht et al., 2018). What is notable in this study is the consistent and considerable increase in accuracy that results from the combination of image sources. Tavares et al. (2019), for example, note a rise in accuracy from 89% using Sentinel-2 only to 91% using combined imagery. Similarly small accuracy improvements were reported by (Lu et al., 2018). In contrast, the present study finds increases in accuracy of up to 15 percentage points. In addition, it can be noted that the combination of imagery also leads to a reduction of the impact of the training dataset. It can be conjectured that this is due to the fact that additional layers of information counter-balance the noise in training data and make it more easily separable for classifiers. [SOURCE: Page_250]

250 [SOURCE: Page_250]

5.7.2    Configuring Input Parameters and Data for Optimal Results [SOURCE: Page_251]

Broadly, the results of the analysis illustrated the wide variations in the values of optimal param- eters leading to the best classification accuracies for RF and SVM, as well as the considerable impact of the choice of kernel for SVM. Regarding the RF parameter of nTree, for example, previous studies (e.g. (Thanh Noi and Kappas, 2017)) found that accuracies tended to increase with a rising number of classification trees in each random forest, and that further increasing the number of trees led to stability in the accuracy of the results, starting at ca. 250 trees. Others also note that forests with a larger number of trees do not necessarily perform better than those with fewer (Oshiro et al., 2012). The present analysis shows that optimal accuracy values for some data configurations can be reached at nTree = 50 already, and that increasing the number of trees can lead to a noticeable decrease in accuracy. This underscores the importance of performing parameter tuning prior to applying each of these classifiers in a new setting, with varying input data configurations. As the tuning results for GTB show, the importance of parameter tuning is also dependent on the quality of the training dataset. While optimal parameter values for nTree and maxNodes varied little for the extended training set, greater discrepancies in values needed to achieve optimal overall classification accuracies were observed using the fieldwork-based training dataset. [SOURCE: Page_251]

In terms of band sets and training data, this analysis illustrates the nuanced balance between adding additional layers of information through texture features and spectral indices, and intro- ducing noise that can detract from classification accuracies. Most prominently, it emerges that it isn’t necessarily the set of bands with the highest number of additional indices and texture features that yields the highest accuracies. Nor is it the minimalist approach taking as a basis of classification only the bare minimum of raw bands. Rather, it is the set of curated raw bands and spectral indices, as well as bands arithmetically calculated from the SAR imagery’s VV and VH bands, that leads to the highest classification performance. Most probably, this is due to the fact that any additional information offered by certain spectral indices is drowned out by the noise that other, less meaningful, indices produce. This result underlines findings from previous studies, such as da Silva et al. (2020), which concluded that the NDVI, EVI, and SAVI offer the highest additional values for LULC approaches. [SOURCE: Page_251]

251 [SOURCE: Page_251]

5.7.3    Overall Classifier Performance [SOURCE: Page_252]

When it comes to comparing algorithms in terms of accuracy, this analysis shows that the GTB and RF classifiers exhibit the consistently best performance under a number of different input data configurations, with GTB slightly exceeding RF in terms of accuracy. It must be highlighted that GTB achieved this performance, despite the fact nTree is currently limited to less than 200. Though SVM shows similarly high classification accuracies for combined imagery and the use of a reduced band set, GTB and RF performance is consistently superior with regard to all constellations of input data – imagery type, training dataset, and band set. It is only in certain land cover classes – such as the separation of urban areas and bare land – that SVM outperforms RF and GTB. Several previous studies have debated the compared performance of RF and SVM. Ma et al. (2017) found RF to be generally superior in a review of object-based LULC classification approaches, as did Talukdar et al. (2020) in a comparison of machine learning approaches for LULC classification. Rana and Venkata Suryanarayana (2020) by contrast, found SVM performance to be superior, especially in combination with a principal component approach. In addition, several studies have also factored GTB into the comparison. For example, Georganos et al. (2018) found the XGboost implementation of GTB to systematically outperform RF and SVM, especially on the basis of an extended feature set. Overall, it appears that SVM performs well when studies aim to fine-tune parameters and investigate specific applications, whereas RF offers more solid, generalizable applications for LULC approaches, and a lower sensitivity to various input data. This higher sensitivity of SVM to the types of input imagery and the training data set is in line with findings from earlier studies. Pelletier et al. (2017), for example, compared the effect of training data noise on supervised LULC classification using SVM and RF. The results found RF to be significantly more robust towards both random and systematic noise of training labels. [SOURCE: Page_252]

As for the other classifiers available in GEE that were tested in this study, it emerges that NB is ill-suited for LULC applications, with low overall accuracies. CART, on the other hand, yielded solid results for the combined imagery type. In particular, it can be noted that this classifier performed better when trained using only the fieldwork data. It can be conjectured that this may be due to the more precise nature of the points in this training data set. Even though there are fewer overall than in the extended dataset, and they are unevenly distributed between [SOURCE: Page_252]

252 [SOURCE: Page_252]

classes, their label attribution carries a higher certainty. As mentioned above, a higher label noise is likely to have been introduced in the extended dataset derived from SPOT during its creation (Frenay and Verleysen, 2014). CART appears to be more sensitive to noise of this kind in the input data, which can be related to the fact that, unlike RF, it only relies on a single threshold to define a node to split data into subsets. In RF, where this process is repeated multiple times, noise can be balanced out more easily. The discrepancy in the classification for CART depending on the training point set is illustrated starkly by contrasting Figures 5.5 and 5.6, the former of which was generated with the configuration of input parameters yielding the highest accuracies (meaning the fieldwork training point set for CART), and the latter of which used the extended dataset generated on the basis of SPOT images as input. In the former, the extents of bare land towards the end of the dry season are higher in the CART classification than in RF or SVM. In the latter, the reverse is true. [SOURCE: Page_253]

5.7.4     Final Classification Configuration and LULC Development Through- out the Year [SOURCE: Page_253]

Overall, the analysis so far has illustrated the the considerable benefits of using a combination of optical and SAR imagery in supervised multi-temporal LULC classifications in Google Earth Engine. When using GTB, the accuracies of these classifications can reach up to 94%, despite some current limitations in the classifier configuration. The results so far also reveal that combining Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery improves overall classification accuracy by 10 – 15 percentage points in comparison to analyses based on optical-only imagery. Furthermore, the results show that combining different sources of imagery reduces the impact of the size and quality of the training data set. This study also further highlights that out of all the classifiers available in Google Earth Engine, GTB yields the highest overall classification accuracies, performing best in a variety of combinations of input data, training points, and band sets. [SOURCE: Page_253]

In general, the use of the extended training data, with points set manually on the basis of high-resolution SPOT imagery, leads to higher accuracies, despite the higher label noise in comparison to the smaller fieldwork dataset. It can equally be concluded that a carefully selected set of native bands, spectral indices, and texture features used as a basis for classification [SOURCE: Page_253]

253 [SOURCE: Page_253]

results in equal or better classifier performance than either a minimalist set, or a large variety of additional bands, especially when using SVM. This underscores the delicate balance between adding indices and texture features as auxiliary layers of information for classification, and the noise that is introduced through their addition, which may impede classification accuracy. [SOURCE: Page_254]

Therefore, the final configuration of the LULC classifier chosen to characterize large-scale land use in the case study area is a GTB classifier, using a combination of Sentinel-1 and 2 imagery, the reduced band set, and the SPOT-based training set. [SOURCE: Page_254]

Using this classifier, twelve images covering the period between 2020 and 2021 were classified. The input Sentinel-1 and -2 images are mean composites of each month. In order to increase the accuracy of the detection of urban areas - which, as outlined above, is sometimes confused with fallow areas - and fruit trees a post-classification step was added. Permanent areas, defined as those that were mapped as either urban or fruit trees in 11 out of 12 images, were masked and the classification was then re-run over the remainder of each image. Finally, the re-classified images were exported and the relative percentage of each land cover class was calculated. [SOURCE: Page_254]

When possible, images recorded towards the middle of the month were selected in order to have equal temporal intervals between the land cover classification. However, due to cloud cover during the wet season in particular, this was not always possible. For June and October 2020, several images had to be composited in order to create a relatively cloud-free representation of the study area. [SOURCE: Page_254]

This classification provided the basis for the delineation of units for the model described in the next chapter. They were furthermore used to calculate various factors related to land cover, as will be outlined below. [SOURCE: Page_254]

254 [SOURCE: Page_254]

5.8     Conclusion - Understanding Ecosystem Services and Land- cover Dynamics on a Local Scale through Earth Observa- tion [SOURCE: Page_255]

This chapter has presented a thorough comparison of LULC classification methods using Sentinel- 1 and 2 optical and SAR imagery to derive a land cover classification for the case study area, with maximum accuracy. The considerable influence of the choice of classifier and its parametrisation, as well as of the selection of input bands, training data, and imagery has been highlighted. [SOURCE: Page_255]

As a final element in characterizing the Prek system in the case study area, a monthly LULC analysis was carried out using combined Sentinel-1 and -2 imagery and a supervised Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB) method. As training data, manually set points were used, which were based on both high-resolution SPOT and information on land use practices and the spatial configuration of crops gathered in the course of the field work presented in the previous chapter. [SOURCE: Page_255]

The monthly LULC maps derived from the land use analysis and the data on average crop distribution, irrigation practices, and yields, serves as input for the model outlined below. [SOURCE: Page_255]

255 [SOURCE: Page_255]

256 [SOURCE: Page_256]

6 Linking Hydrology and Ecosystem Services to Understand Current Challenges and Assess Future Perspectives [SOURCE: Page_257]

So far, this thesis has taken a close look at regional hydrological dynamics and trends in land cover, and has provided an assessment of agricultural practices, ecosystem services, and challenges related to hydrological processes and water management in the case study area. However, to answer the remaining research questions outlined in the beginning, a more abstract approach is necessary. The role of Preks and the related ES have been explored qualitatively, but to go further in a quantitative assessment, especially in the view of improving Prek design in adaptation to global changes, a new model formalizing the interactions between the hydrological system and the related services was constructed. [SOURCE: Page_257]

257 [SOURCE: Page_257]

To this end, an eco-hydrological model was constructed in the course of this thesis. It aims to make explicit the role of Prek channels in particular, as well as the Prek system in general, in providing the ecosystem services outlined in the previous chapter, and to simulate future scenarios. The model was built on the basis of data collected from local stakeholders in the course of fieldwork, and derived from the remote sensing analyses presented in Sections 3.4 and 5. It was then used to simulate four future scenarios relating to hydrological dynamics in the Mekong, temperature and precipitation patterns over the case study area, as well as different scenarios regarding the extent of Prek rehabilitation to assess whether this could help local communities adapt to global changes. The ecosystem services considered in the model were divided into two main categories - flood-related and not flood-related ES. [SOURCE: Page_258]

This chapter first expands on the ecosystem services to be modelled, the divide between flood- and not-flood-related ecosystem services, and their link to hydrological processes. Next, it provides an overview of the conceptual framework of the model, and how the hydrological processes in the area are modelled, including adaptations of methods described in previous chapters. It then outlines the modelling methodology used - the choice of modelling platform, the data, the delineation of modelling units, the calculation of flood- and not-flood related ES, as well as the parametrization of the model. Then, it explains how scenarios were constructed and on which data basis. Subsequently, results are outlined and discussed, and the limitations of the current modelling approach given. [SOURCE: Page_258]

6.1     Objectives: Representing the Links Between Hydrologi- cal Processes and Flood-Related and Not-Flood-Related Ecosystem Services [SOURCE: Page_258]

Ultimately, this model aims to represent the links between the hydrological processes at work in the case study area, and the ecosystem services from which the local population benefits. This section outlines these ecosystem services and explains in depth why they were divided into flood-related and not-flood-related ES. Furthermore, their links to hydrological processes are made explicit, and the scales at which they will be considered are outlined. [SOURCE: Page_258]

258 [SOURCE: Page_258]

As becomes evident from the description of the case study area in previous chapters and from the analysis of hydrological processes in the Cambodian Mekong delta, the annual monsoon floods are the defining characteristic of the region in terms of hydrology. Annual inundations form the basis for agricultural practices, by providing the necessary soil moisture and nutrients for lowland rice cultivation, recharge groundwater, regulate pests, and provide an environment for fish populations to regenerate. During the wet season, large swaths of land which are usually divided into smaller units by canals, small-scale dykes, and boundaries between individual fields, become one coherent body of water that is involved in the provision of all these ecosystem services. [SOURCE: Page_259]

In contrast, during the dry season, flow processes in the network of Prek channels and lowland canals are the determining factor for whether key ecosystem services can be provided or not. While some crops are rain-fed, relying solely on natural precipitation, the majority depends on irrigation, using the Preks and canals as a main source of water. For most of the farmers interviewed, the provision of irrigation water by the Prek system is the main benefit that they derive from it, and the primary reason they see rehabilitation projects and excavations in a positive light. [SOURCE: Page_259]

(a) Inundated parts of the study     (b) Receding flood water.      (c) The case study area during area.                                                               the dry season. [SOURCE: Page_259]

Figure 6.1: The case study area during different seasons. [SOURCE: Page_259]

For this reason, a fundamental distinction was made in the conceptualisation of the model - between ecosystem services directly related to the floods and those that are independent of them. [SOURCE: Page_259]

As a result of the division into flood-related and non-flood-related ES, the role of the Preks is conceptualised differently during the dry and the wet season. During the wet season, Preks and lowland canals act primarily as conduits of flooding and drainage. Water limitations are generally not a problem during these months, except in the case of the severely degraded Prek [SOURCE: Page_259]

259 [SOURCE: Page_259]

Put. In contrast, during the dry season, the Preks take on more of a storage function, providing the volumes of water necessary for irrigation, and establishing a flow connection between the lowland canal system and the Bassac mainstream. [SOURCE: Page_260]

The flood-related ecosystem services that are included in the model outlined below are soil- and groundwater recharge, the provision of habitats for fish reproduction, flood peak attenuation, pest regulation, and the deposition of sediments - and thus nutrients. [SOURCE: Page_260]

Most of these flood-related ecosystem services fall into the category of regulating ecosystem services. Sediment deposition could be argued to be provisioning to a certain extent, since some farmers and communities excavate sediments from their plots or the Prek channels and sell them so that others may actively raise their land. The provision of habitats for fish reproduction, though, more explicitly contributes to a provisioning service - especially since fish form an important element in the diet of the local population. However, as mentioned above, quantifying the average amounts of fish people derive from the system is difficult, not just due to the varying individual estimations given by interviewees, but also due to the fact that fish catch has declined dramatically in recent years according to many of them. The reasons given for this decline are numerous, such as overfishing and illegal fishing practices such as using electroshocks. Investigating the complex nexus of causality related to the decline in fish populations is beyond the scope of this thesis. Therefore, only one component - the existence of inundation-season habitats for reproduction - will be considered here. [SOURCE: Page_260]

It must also be noted that not all of the flood-related ecosystem services are felt by farmers in the case study area. Flood peak attenuation, for instance, through the storage of water volumes in the Boeung areas, benefits downstream communities, rather than the stakeholders in the area of interest. Similarly, groundwater recharge in the Boeungs is of little interest to the local population, since few of them have wells there and even fewer use them during the dry season. To a certain extent, groundwater recharge from the Preks during the period in which their water levels are high may be more important in this context (see below). However, since groundwater flow in the region is known to follow a North-South gradient (Kazama et al., 2007), and groundwater is an important resource in neighbouring Vietnam, groundwater recharge in the shallow aquifers of the Cambodian Mekong delta is still included in the model. [SOURCE: Page_260]

The calculation of flood-related ecosystem services is partially based on information provided [SOURCE: Page_260]
