by the interviewees during field work - such as the flood extents and duration necessary for pest regulation. Partially, however, they are estimated on the basis of literature values. This applies to rates of sedimentation, as well as groundwater recharge. Values from studies in adjacent areas were used and services calculated proportional to the inundated area at each time step, as outlined below. The general factors used to calculate each ES are given in Table 6.1. [SOURCE: Page_261]

The non-flood-related ecosystem services considered in this thesis are entirely of a provision- ing nature: provision of water for irrigation, livestock, and household needs, especially during the dry season. As will be outlined in more detail below, this ES is evaluated on the basis of the required volumes of water calculated from data gathered during the interviews, and the volumes of water available in the channel network at any time step. [SOURCE: Page_261]

Some non-flood-related provisioning ES are not considered numerically in the model. For instance, at non-rehabilitated Preks, many locals make use of the bank vegetation. They use branches from trees to construct fish traps and as fuel for their homes. They supplement their diets with ivy gourd and morning glory, and grow vegetables and fruit at banks of the Preks close to their houses. This is no longer possible at rehabilitated Preks, where banks are to be kept clean and free of vegetation - at least in theory. Consequently, these ES are lost in favour of better water provisioning capabilities. [SOURCE: Page_261]

One more significant difference between flood-related and not flood-related ecosystem services that needs to be outlined at this point is the scale at which they are calculated. Flood- related ecosystem services are provided by a continuous area of inundated floodplains. Though water depths vary, this area forms one coherent water body with properties that are assumed to [SOURCE: Page_261]

261 [SOURCE: Page_261]

be homogeneous, as will be outlined below. In contrast, the provision of not flood-related ES is highly variable across the study area, depending on the crops cultivated in each area and the availability of water in every single Prek and channel in the Boeung area. [SOURCE: Page_262]

Consequently, the calculation of flood-related and not-flood related ES was carried out at two different scales. Flood-related ES are calculated across the entire inundated area. For the calculation of not flood-related ES, the case study area was subdivided into separate modelling units - reach segments and surface units. Reach segments are Preks and Boeung channels, which function as conduits and sources of irrigation water. Surface units (SUs) are areas with a homogeneous elevation, land cover progression, and soil properties. As will be outlined in further detail below, SUs were delineated based on the monthly LULC maps derived from Sentinel-1 and 2 images. [SOURCE: Page_262]

6.2     Conceptualisation of the Model Configuration and De- scription of Calculation of Processes Relevant to ES [SOURCE: Page_262]

Now that the general ES to be modelled have been outlined, it is important to outline the spatial configuration and the general calculation of processes that are relevant to flood-related and not flood-related ES. This section provides an overview of all the elements necessary to the modelling process, and their general calculation, including the adaptation of methods presented in previous chapters. [SOURCE: Page_262]

In terms of flood-related ES, sediment deposition, groundwater recharge, the provision of habitats for fish reproduction, downstream flood peak attenuation, and pest regulation were considered. In terms of not-flood-related ES, the provision of irrigation water and thus crop production in the agro-ecosystem were calculated. [SOURCE: Page_262]

A simplified version of the model and calculation workflow is shown in Figure 6.2. As can be seen, there are two time steps for the calculation. At a daily time step, the case study area is divided into flooded and not flooded areas. At the same daily time step, flood characteristics such as its extent and volume are calculated for the later determination of flood-related ecosystem services. For not flood-related ES, the existence of a water deficit is determined using a [SOURCE: Page_262]

262 [SOURCE: Page_262]

combination of an inflow model and a water balance equation. To this end, the Preks and lowland canals were represented as a network of longitudinal reach segments (RS). Furthermore, for not-flood-related ecosystem services, the surface area were sub-divided into modelling units (referred to as surface units - SUs) based on elevation, slope, and land cover. [SOURCE: Page_263]

Figure 6.2: Simplified conceptual model. [SOURCE: Page_263]

At a seasonal time step, the ecosystem services are calculated based on the previously calculated daily values. A "season" in the context of the model is defined as one hydrological cycle starting and beginning at the height of the dry season in mid-April. As a baseline period, the year between 2020/04/15 and 2021/04/14 was used, as in-situ data is available during this time for calibration. [SOURCE: Page_263]

The main expected outputs of the model are a measure of the increases and decreases in [SOURCE: Page_263]

263 [SOURCE: Page_263]

ecosystem services for each future development scenario. [SOURCE: Page_264]

The overall spatial configuration of the case study area in terms of modelling units is shown in Figure 6.3. As the Figure shows, the systems consists of the Bassac mainstream to the right, with upstream and downstream boundary conditions, and the daily averaged water levels at the center of the river segment bordering the case study area. From there, individual RS branch out into the case study area, part of which is flooded. Water from these RS is lifted onto individual SUs along the length of the RS. The connections between RS are conceptualised as thresholds and calculated as weirs, as will be outlined in more detail in subsequent sections. This section now offers a description of the principal hydrological processes at work in each element of the conceptualisation. [SOURCE: Page_264]

Figure 6.3: Overall conceptualisation and relevant elements of the model. [SOURCE: Page_264]

6.2.1    Flooded Areas [SOURCE: Page_264]

To begin with, there are the annual monsoon inundations, which form one of the most significant hydrological processes in the area. Their recent dynamics can be observed from inundation maps derived from Sentinel-1 and -2 images using an unsupervised classifier in GEE, as outlined in Section 3.4.1.4. The progression of inundation extents in the case study area is shown in Figure [SOURCE: Page_264]

264 [SOURCE: Page_264]

During flood recession, the processes are reversed. Water drains from the elevated Chamkar areas both towards the inter-Prek areas and towards the tail ends of the Preks. From there, it further drains into the canal network and the Preks and towards the Prek Ambel, the Bassac, or the South of the case study area. [SOURCE: Page_266]

Flooded are modelled using the WAFL (cf. Section 3.4). Making an explicit, correlative link between upstream water levels and flooded areas at a daily time step, the WAFL makes it possible to overcome limitations such as a lack of knowledge about the exact geometric configuration of hydraulic links in the case study area, and exact terrain elevation. For the calculation of flood-related ecosystem services, variables such as the daily extents of inundations, average inundation depths, and overall inundation duration for each pixel are determined. [SOURCE: Page_266]

In addition, the inundation extents derived from Sentinel-1 and -2 images, were adapted and expanded to gain further insights into the hydrological processes in the case study area. First, they were used to determine maximum infiltration rates via pseudowaterlevels. Second, the applicability of the WAFL for predicting inundation extents in the case study area was tested. These calculations are outlined below in Section 6.3.5. [SOURCE: Page_266]

6.2.2     Non-Flood Areas [SOURCE: Page_266]

For the calculation of processes in not flooded areas, three types of elements were employed in the model - surface units, reach segments, and connection between reach segments. [SOURCE: Page_266]

6.2.2.1    Surface Units [SOURCE: Page_266]

The predominant hydrological processes in the not-flooded parts of the case study area are common processes observed in similar environments. The main terms of the hydrological balance are precipitation, evapotranspiration, deep percolation, and irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_266]

Regarding the latter, gravity irrigation^1 can frequently be observed in the area, with water 1 Gravity irrigation is the predominant irrigation method in the study area. Two instances of sprinkler irrigation [SOURCE: Page_266]

and three plots on which drip irrigation were implemented were observed during fieldwork, but mostly in close vicinity to village areas. [SOURCE: Page_266]

266 [SOURCE: Page_266]

flowing from the head of the plot at the bank of the Prek where it is pumped to lower-lying areas at the tail end of the plot, in inter-Prek area. As will be outlined in more detail in subsequent sections, inputs from pumping are estimated based on the fieldwork data and precipitation is taken from field measurements. [SOURCE: Page_267]

6.2.2.2   Reach Segments [SOURCE: Page_267]

In reach segments, the most significant processes are channel flow and pumping onto surface units, the latter of which has already been outlined above. [SOURCE: Page_267]

Channel flow refers to the flow of water between the Bassac, the Prek Ambel and the network of Preks and lowland channels in the Boeungs. Whether or not this flow happens at all is determined by the relative bed elevation of the channels, as well as threshold effects at their junctions. For instance, it is known from interviews with stakeholders that the heads of Preks - such as Prek Nou - preferentially see sediment deposition and thus hinder inflow of water from the Bassac into the Preks. Another regulatory element that exists on some Preks are gates. Installed at rehabilitated Preks, they can prevent inflow into and outflow from the Prek. In the case study area only one such gate exists - at Prek Chann. Its operational schedule, as outlined in the previous chapter, is somewhat uncertain and therefore not taken into consideration in the modelling of flows. [SOURCE: Page_267]

Along each Prek, there is a pronounced water level slope. This is illustrated by the near- realtime water level measurements provided by the loggers installed in Prek Chann and in Prek Touch. [SOURCE: Page_267]

In Prek Chann, a total of four loggers were installed starting in May 2020: two at the gate at its head, one up- and one downstream of it, one at a point where a smaller side channel drains into the Prek, and one at its western end. Furthermore, a logger is installed in the canal adjoining Prek Chann in the West. However, some of them - such as the logger at the western end - were out of order intermittently due to physical damage. The entirety of the data series is shown in Figure 6.6, and a selection of data from June and September 2020 is given in Figures 6.7 and 6.8 respectively. These illustrate a clear water level gradient between the Bassac and the interior floodplains, along the length of the Prek. During the dry season (represented by the June [SOURCE: Page_267]

267 [SOURCE: Page_267]

The changes in inflow are represented by water levels at Koh Khel and at the logger in the case study area, which are modified in the scenarios. The water level at Koh Khel is used for the calculation of WAFL-derived flooded areas, an the logger in the case study area serves as an input for the calculation of inflow in the system of RS. [SOURCE: Page_271]

6.3     Modelling Methodology [SOURCE: Page_271]

6.3.1    Choice of Modelling Platform [SOURCE: Page_271]

As outlined in the simplified conceptual model at the beginning of this chapter, the first step in the calculation is the division of the case study area into flooded- and not-flooded areas, before ecosystem services are calculated separately for each zone. This means that the modelling platform has to be capable of both representing the complex hydrological processes in the study area (cf. section 3.4) and their connection to ecosystem services. [SOURCE: Page_271]

A wide range of models and modelling platforms for hydrological processes is available, some even specifically designed for applications in deltaic environments. Furthermore, many of them also include some capabilities for the calculation of ecosystem services. In addition, there is also a wide range of models for the calculation of ecosystem services that incorporate the calculation of hydrological processes to a certain extent. Nonetheless, the model for this thesis was built from scratch in Python. The reasons for this lie in the spatial configuration and terrain characteristics of the study area, as well as the complexity of hydrological processes. [SOURCE: Page_271]

Many existing hydrological models adapted for floodplains environments are grid-cell-based, and aim to solve the shallow water equations in 2D environments, such as LISFLOOD-FP, Delft^3D, Mike Flood, ISIS-Infoworks, HEC-RAS 2D, and Telemac among others. However, to properly parametrize these models for the case study area, detailed geometric information would be necessary. This is due to the numerous small-scale dykes which delineate field borders and restrict flows. A dyke with a crest height of less than a meter and a width of only a few dozen centimeters can determine whether several hectares of land become flooded - or not. Such small-scale structures are difficult to represent, even in high-resolution DEMs such as TanDEM [SOURCE: Page_271]

271 [SOURCE: Page_271]

with a horizontal resolution of 12 m. Extensive manual adjustments and calibration might make it possible to represent flow processes in the case study area in hydrodynamic models, but that would still leave limitations with regard to the calculation and representation of ecosystem services, since many of these platforms don’t have dedicated modules to consider these processes. In contrast, models focused on the calculation of ES, such as InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services Tradeoffs, Sharp et al. (2020)) and ARIES (ARtificial Intelligence for Ecosystem Services, Villa et al. (2014)), lack the necessary functionalities to represent the complexity of flow processes in the area. [SOURCE: Page_272]

Another option that was considered for the modelling aspects of this thesis is the Soil Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), which offers great flexibility in terms of both hydrological processes and ecosystem services (Arnold, 1994; K. R. Douglas-Mankin et al., 2010; Francesconi et al., 2016). However, like LISFLOOD, it is based on grid cells, which makes it difficult to represent small-scale local terrain variations. While work-arounds exist for some aspects - such as super- imposing a channel system on the grid cells - a major limitation of SWAT is also that it is catchment-based and the model developed here is focused on a much smaller sub-section of a deltaic floodplain. [SOURCE: Page_272]

On larger scales, all of these limitations are of minor importance, and past studies have successfully applied all these tools for analyses in the Mekong Basin and Delta. Xing et al. (2017) used Delft^3D to analyse flow and sediment dynamics in the delta’s Song Hau channel. Shrestha et al. (2013) used SWAT to estimate the impact of climate change on sediment yield in a sub-basin of the Mekong in Laos, and Truong and Do (2018) used it together with MIKE-11 and MIKE HYDROBasin to estimate the cumulative impacts of hydropower projects on the delta floodplains. Hawker et al. (2017) used LISFLOOD for intermediate-scale inundation modelling in the delta, at a grid size of 540 m. More recently, Quoc Thanh et al. (2019) used Delft^3D to calculate the impact of dyke systems on downstream hydrodynamics in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta. In the Cambodian part of the delta, Heng et al. (2021) used a combination of the IWRM- Sub model, which was constructed by the MRC, SWAT, and the ISIS hydrodynamic model, to calculate the impact of future development and climate change on the floodplains at 1 km x 1 km resolution. Also in the Cambodian Mekong Delta and at the same scale, Horton et al. (2022) used a combination of the basin-wide IWRM model, MIKE-11, and IWRM-Sub to project flood extents in the entire delta in 2050. As can be seen from the scale and resolution of these models, [SOURCE: Page_272]

272 [SOURCE: Page_272]

local effects are not taken into consideration. [SOURCE: Page_273]

Another software option that was considered in the context of this thesis was OpenFLUID (Fabre et al., 2010, 2013). Developed by UMR LISAH in Montpellier, this modelling platform allows users to construct highly individualised, spatially explicit models depicting a variety of landscape processes. Its main advantage is that it is not grid-cell-based, but allows for the use of complex geometries of varying sizes. It has furthermore been used successfully in systems with multiple in- and outlets (Rudi, 2019). It distinguishes between surface areas (SU), which share common properties in terms of soil, land cover, slope, and elevation, and reach segments (RS), which are longitudinal elements used to represent channels (see Figure 6.11a). Each process to be modelled is encapsulated in a separate simulator, written in the C++ programming language, with inputs and outputs that allow simulators to be plugged together in various configurations (see Figure 6.11b). Much of the model outlined below took inspiration from the set-up and a simulator for overland flow was even coded on this platform. However, due to temporal constraints and a lack of familiarity with C++, the final model was constructed in Python. [SOURCE: Page_273]

(a) Spatial configuration of sample study area in (b) Simulator network for hydrological processes on OpenFLUID, using RS and SU.                       each unit of the case study area in OpenFLUID. [SOURCE: Page_273]

Figure 6.11: OpenFLUID interface. [SOURCE: Page_273]

The model outlined below was coded in Python 2.7.6 (Python Core Team, 2019) using the Anaconda Navigator (Anaconda, 2016) version of Jupyter Notebook. Jupyter Notebook was chosen since it supports literate programming, combining code, text, execution results, and visualisations such as figures and GIFs (see Figure 6.12). All of this contributes to the [SOURCE: Page_273]

273 [SOURCE: Page_273]

self-documenting Jupyter Notebook files, making them easily shareable and reproducible as long as dependencies are made explicit (Pimentel et al., 2019). [SOURCE: Page_274]

Figure 6.12: Code and visualisations of the module for non-flood-related ES in Jupyter Notebook. [SOURCE: Page_274]

6.3.2     Data Used [SOURCE: Page_274]

The data used for this model can be divided into two different categories: data used to delineate the modelling units and define their properties in the baseline scenario, and data that is varied depending on which scenario is modelled and that is used for calibration, validation, and sensitivity testing. [SOURCE: Page_274]

6.3.2.1   Land Cover Data [SOURCE: Page_274]

Into the former category fall the TanDEM-X elevation model, the WAFL-derived flood ex- tents described in Section 3.4, and the LULC classification outlined in Section 5. The LULC classification was further used to determine land-use related coefficients for the calculation of evapotranspiration and the determination of overall yield (cf Sections 6.3.6.4 and 6.3.6.5). In addition, the agricultural characteristics depending on the crops in the SUs - average irrigation hours, average and maximum yield, as well as price per unit - were calculated from the data gathered in interviews. They are shown in Table D.3 in Appendix D. [SOURCE: Page_274]

274 [SOURCE: Page_274]

6.3.2.2    Soil Data [SOURCE: Page_275]

Furthermore, various existing soil classifications in the study area were taken into consideration. This included classifications by Crocker (1962), White et al. (2000), and the FAO (1997). However, these classifications were all conducted at large scales - country-wide in the case of Crocker (1962) and White et al. (2000) and worldwide in the case of the FAO. The delineations of soil types therefore have limited accuracies in the study area. According to the FAO classification, the Chamkar areas in the vicinity of the Bassac are Eutric Fluvisols, which indicate medium clayey soils, and the Chamkar areas further towards the Boeungs, the transition zones, as well as the Boeungs themselves are Eutric Gleysols, which correspond to sandy clay loam to clay. Crocker (1962) draws a similar border, with Bassac-adjacent Chamkar areas classified as Alluvial Lithosols and the remaining case study area simply as Brown Alluvial Soils (loamy or clayey soils). According to White et al. (2000), who proposed a soil classification specifically for rice-growing areas in Cambodia, the study area falls under the category of Prateah Lang soils, which denote sandy soils over clay.2 Unfortunately, no systematic in-situ survey of soils could be carried out due to fieldwork being cut short. From field observations, also reflected in Vandôme (2020), it appears that Chamkar areas are characterized by more sandy soils, while Boeung areas feature deeper, more clayey soils. In transition zones, soils were observed to vary from silty-clay in the lower-lying areas that are more frequently flooded to silty-sand in more elevated zones that only rarely see floods. In contrast, a borehole created with an auger drill at Prek Chann, near the water level in the center of the Prek (see Figure 3.2 indicated the presence of brown clay up until a depth of 1 m, and grey clay at a depth of 1-3 m. Due to the uncertainty in the soil typology of the area and its delineation, soil properties were assumed to be uniform over the area in the model for simplicity’s sake. However, three different soil types were compared in the sensitivity testing stage of the modelling process: silty clay, sandy clay loam, and clay loam. Their average hydraulic values according to Carsel and Parrish (1988) and Saxton and Rawls (2006) are given in Table D.4 in Appendix D. In addition, the infiltration rates determined from the analysis of pseudowaterlevels in Section 6.3.5.2 below were taken into consideration. 2 Unfortunately, no high-resolution map is available and from the map provided in White et al. (2000), it might [SOURCE: Page_275]

also be that the case study area falls under Orung soils, which have a very similar colour as Prateah Lang soils in the legend. Orung soils denote loam or clay over sand. However, since they only make up 1-2% of the entire area under consideration in the map, Prateah Lang soils are the more likely candidate. [SOURCE: Page_275]

275 [SOURCE: Page_275]

6.3.2.3   Water Levels: Hydraulic Boundary Conditions [SOURCE: Page_276]

The case study area is bracketed by two hydrological stations maintained by the MRC - Koh Khel upstream and Chau Doc downstream. In addition, a pressure logger was installed in the Bassac in 2020 in order to have local water measurements, taking account of the superimposed of upstream influences of upstream inflow and backwater effect (cf. Section 3.2.3). [SOURCE: Page_276]

As an external boundary condition, water level data from the station at Koh Khel and the logger at the Bassac in the study area was used. For the calculation of inundated areas, the values at Koh Kehl are used, together with WAFL. The values from the logger are used as input for the calculation of water levels in the network of RS. Values from both sources are modified for scenario simulation to represent upstream shifts due to climate change, hydropower infrastructure, and land use change. [SOURCE: Page_276]

Furthermore, the data from the loggers in the Preks and the channels (see Figure 3.2) was used to validate the water levels calculated in the course of each model run. [SOURCE: Page_276]

6.3.2.4   Climate Data: Temperature and Precipitation [SOURCE: Page_276]

For precipitation and temperature data, in-situ data from the meteorological station installed in the case study area was used. For the determination of long-term averages, CHIRPS and ERA$_5$ Daily Aggregates were extracted from GEE (see Section 3.3 for details). ERA$_5$ is a climate reanalysis product produced by ECMWF - Copernicus Climate Change Service. It provides consistent global data on meteorological parameters such as air temperature, wind speed, air pressure, and dew point temperature since 1979, though at a moderate resolution of 27 830 meters. Sediment concentrations measured by the MRC at Koh Khel and Phnom Penh were used to establish a baseline and then varied in accordance with estimations for future developments according to the literature. Finally, the geometry of the Prek channels and canal network was estimated based on the in-situ measurements taken during the fieldwork, as well as values provided in engineering reports such as SOFRECO (2017) and MoWRAM and AFD (2022). For rehabilitated Preks, a bed level of 0 m asl is assumed. For not rehabilitated Preks, a level of 2.5 m is assumed. The exception to this is Prek Put, which has a considerably higher bed [SOURCE: Page_276]

276 [SOURCE: Page_276]

level, estimated for the purposes of this calculation at 4 m. [SOURCE: Page_277]

6.3.3    Delineating the Prek System into Modelling Units [SOURCE: Page_277]

Before the actual calculation workflow could be defined, the study area needed to be divided into smaller modelling units. As outlined above, the model presented here follows OpenFLUID in delineating a network of reach segments (RS) in the form of Preks and lowland canals, and subdividing the study area into surface units (SU) which share similar properties. [SOURCE: Page_277]

Delineating the RS - which correspond to the Preks and primary lowland canals - could be carried out on the basis of already available geometry files as well as high-resolution SPOT satellite imagery. A choice was made not to delineate smaller drains as little is known about their geometry or location. Overall, 30 such segments were delineated, shown in Figure 6.14a. In contrast, delineating the SUs was a more difficult endeavour. A balance had to be struck between a higher spatial resolution, allowing for the representation of small-scale terrain features, and limiting the number of units for the sake of computational complexity. As a first step, RS were considered as separating lines between SU. Beyond that, the division into Boeungs (flooded annually), transition areas (sometimes flooded), and Chamkars (never flooded) was considered, as well as the average elevation and slope. Finally, a progression of land use was considered by overlaying the results of the LULC classification for each month for the season 2020-2021 (see Figure 6.13). This made it possible to identify areas that share a similar cropping schedule, such as single rice cropping, double rice cropping, or single rice cropping followed by a crop such as maize. On this basis, 129 SUs were delineated manually in QGIS. The results are shown in Figure 6.14b. This latter aspect, the inclusion of cropping practices based on both interviews and remote sensing also arguably adds an socio-hydrological dimension to the model, though merely a basic one that could be extended, as will be outlined later on. While based on physical data and the results of quantitative numerical analyses, the process of delineating units was based on individual judgement and the visual assessment of area similarity. [SOURCE: Page_277]

277 [SOURCE: Page_277]

Figure 6.13: Delineation of RS and SUs, carried out manually in QGIS. [SOURCE: Page_278]

(a) Delineation of reach segments.                       (b) Delineation of surface units. [SOURCE: Page_278]

Figure 6.14: Delineation of modelling units. Background image: Google Earth. [SOURCE: Page_278]

Once the delineation of SUs was concluded, the characteristics for each unit were calculated. From the TanDEM-X elevation model, an area-elevation-curve for each unit was extracted. Similarly, in each unit, the area percentages of each land cover class in each month were extracted from the LULC classification. Finally, the average KC , KY and CN values, as well as irrigation requirements and optimal yields for each crop, were calculated for each unit, based on the relative area share of each land cover class in each unit. The result of these calculations were [SOURCE: Page_278]

278 [SOURCE: Page_278]

saved to two separate CSV files to characterize each unit - one containing the area-elevation curve, the other the land-use-related parameters. [SOURCE: Page_279]

A final element related to the spatial delineation of the Prek system is the definition of a network of irrigation sources. Each SU was assigned one RS that serves as its source of irrigation water. This assignment was clear for some units - such as those surface units bordering directly on a Prek. For others, though, it was a more difficult matter and often based on knowledge of the study area or common farming practices. For instance, it emerged from the interviews that for some areas adjoining Prek Put, Prek Nou served as a source of irrigation water. Since Prek Put is practically dry year-round and Prek Nou contains water several months into the dry season, farmers have organized a distribution network containing a double-pumping system. However, it must nonetheless be noted that this assignment of RS to SU as irrigation sources is a simplification and the origin of uncertainties. For instance, in the Boeung areas, several canals might serve as irrigation sources, rather than just one. Similarly, alternative sources such as wells or ponds located at the end of plots are neglected. However, it appears from the interviews that these sources of irrigation water are used only by a small minority of farmers. [SOURCE: Page_279]

6.3.4    Choice of Modelling Period, Time Step, and Baseline Scenario [SOURCE: Page_279]

Each model run spans the duration of one year, to allow the comparison of the impact of the monsoon inundations on the annual provision of ES. For this reason, the modelling period begins and ends at the height of the dry season, when there are no flood-related ES and the provision of not-flood-related ES is at a minimum. The 15th of April was chosen as a starting and end date for each simulation. [SOURCE: Page_279]

As a time step for the simulation, a daily interval was chosen. Partially, this is due to considerations of keeping the computational efforts involved in the calculation limited. The water levels used in the scenarios outlined in Section 6.4 are based on these long-term values. [SOURCE: Page_279]

In terms of baseline scenario, the season 2020-21 was chosen, meaning the period between April 15 2020 and April 14 2021. The reason for this is that the meteorological station and the water level loggers were installed in the case study area in spring 2020. This means that for the season 2020-21, in-situ data in the Preks and canals is available for calibration and validation. [SOURCE: Page_279]

279 [SOURCE: Page_279]

Similarly, sufficient Sentinel-1 and 2 images for a monthly LULC were available during this period. In addition, the majority of survey data used to characterize agricultural practices stems from spring 2020. However, there are a few drawbacks to choosing this period as a reference, especially with regard to flood-related ecosystem services. As outlined briefly in section 3.2.3 and visible in Figure 3.27, the 2020 monsoon inundations were far shorter than typical, and had far lower extents. From this point of view, it would be better to use a hydrologically average year, based on the time series of the past 30 years. Otherwise, future changes in flood-related ES are evaluated in comparison to a situation that is already less than ideal, as can partly be seen in the descriptions of the decrease in fish populations given by interviewees. However, for the moment, the value of available in-situ data outweighs these considerations. [SOURCE: Page_280]

6.3.5     Preliminary Calculations [SOURCE: Page_280]

A final step before the calculation of the model could commence was to complete two preliminary calculations to verify data and methods used in the model. These calculations are, on the one hand, the validation of the estimation of inundation surfaces using the WAFL, and, on the other hand, the estimation of maximum infiltration rates using pseudowaterlevels. The former verifies that the WAFL, a methodology developed at the scale of the Cambodian Mekong delta, yields relevant results at the local level. The latter uses inundation dynamics during the recession phase to identify an average infiltration rate in the area. [SOURCE: Page_280]

6.3.5.1   Validating the WAFL in the case Study Area [SOURCE: Page_280]

As outlined in Chapter 3.4, this method was developed to re-construct past inundation extents on the basis of water levels. In this chapter, however, the WAFL is used to predict inundation extents. Therefore, a further analysis to determine the predictive capabilities of WAFL had to be conducted before it could be used to determine inundation extents for future scenarios. [SOURCE: Page_280]

For this purpose, the water levels measured during the 2021 monsoon inundations, which were not used in the original WAFL development, were used to predict inundation extents. These predicted extents were then compared to those observed from Sentinel-1 and -2 images. The [SOURCE: Page_280]

280 [SOURCE: Page_280]

results are shown in Figures 6.15 and 6.16. Figure 6.15 provides a visual comparison of WAFL- and Sentinel-derived inundation extents at the beginning of June, July, August, September, October, and November. It shows that the overall evolution is reproduced with acceptable levels of accuracy in terms of amplitude and timing of the flood, information which is essential for the purpose of the model. However, the figures also show that at the beginning and end of August, the WAFL tends to underestimate inundation extents in the Boeung slightly. This is mirrored in Figure 6.15, which compares the size of the overall inundated areas derived from both approaches. After an initial peak in mid-August, the WAFL-derived extents decline much faster than the observed ones. As outlined in Section 3.2.3, this pattern of an initial peak followed by a decline in river water levels and then the main flood season peak is typical in the hydrological dynamics in the Bassac. From initial examination it appears that the WAFL registers a much faster flood recession than was actually observed, both after the initial peak and the main one. This is logical, as water retained by local structures, such as dykes around rice fields, is not considered in its calculation. In addition, there is the fact that after the main flood peak, rice cultivation begins in those plots that are no longer flooded. Since the classification of Sentinel images was carried out for only two classes - not flooded and flooded - irrigated rice fields with young plants are often detected as flooded, even though this state is brought about by irrigation, not natural dynamics. In those instances where this latter issue is the reason for the mismatch between calculated and observed inundation extents, the fact that the WAFL does not register it as flooded is actually beneficial to the accuracy of calculations, because the water needed for irrigating rice fields is extracted from the canal network. [SOURCE: Page_281]

A final point that needs to be raised is that calculated inundation extents rarely follow the boundary lines of SUs. Therefore, different SUs might be partially flooded at each time step, according to the WAFL. To decide whether they are considered for the calculation of not-flood- related ES, a simple threshold was implemented. If less than 20% of a SU are flooded it is taken into consideration for the calculation of not-flood-related ES. Part of the reason for this choice are local patterns of cultivation. In many cases, farmers begin to cultivate the elevated areas of their Chamkar plots while those located in the direction of inter-Prek areas are still flooded. [SOURCE: Page_281]

281 [SOURCE: Page_281]

evaporation, open-channel outflow from the case study area, precipitation, and irrigation. Irri- gation can make the flooded areas appear larger than they naturally are. Farmers pump water onto their fields to irrigate their crops, using channels as water sources. These irrigated fields, especially rice fields, can be mistaken as naturally flooded surfaces by the Sentinel-classification, as a simple binary classifier was employed to delineate inundation extents. In addition, it can also be assumed that, as the water level decreases, it reaches the thresholds at which connections are cut. The outflow to neighboring water bodies is then largely reduced and tends to zero as the flood recedes. [SOURCE: Page_283]

To derive infiltration rates from the curve of inundated areas, pseudowaterlevels were used. This concept was already introduced in Section 3.4, for instance in Figure 3.33. It calculates the assumed average water level (in m asl) in the flooded areas of the study area by linking its area-elevation curve with the extent of inundations observed from Sentinel-1 and -2 images. The pseudowaterlevel calculated for the case study area for the period 2017-2022 is shown in Figure 6.17. Marked in red is the quasi-linear phase of flood recession. For the 2016/17 - 2020/21 recession phases, this quasi-linear section is between ca. 2.5 and 0.7 m, for the 2015/16 and 2021/22 phases, it is between approximately 1.7 and 0.5 m. For each year, a linear trendline was calculated to determine the daily rate of flood recession. On average, recession is calculated to occur at a decrease in pseudowaterlevel of 2.57 cm/day, with a standard deviation of 0.41 cm. For the purposes of this model, it is assumed that this recession is accounted for mostly by infiltration. [SOURCE: Page_283]

Not included in these estimates are the effects of precipitation and irrigation, which increase inundated areas, and evaporation and outflow, which decrease them. It is assumed that, to a certain extent, these effects have a lower magnitude and compensate for each other to some extent. Nevertheless, this estimation of infiltration rates provides an idea of an order of magnitude, rather than exact values. [SOURCE: Page_283]

283 [SOURCE: Page_283]

6.3.6     Calculation Workflow [SOURCE: Page_285]

6.3.6.1   Overview of Calculation Workflow [SOURCE: Page_285]

The detailed calculation workflow is given in Figure 6.18. It consists of two main parts: one is the calculation of flood-related ecosystem services, the other the calculation of not-flood-related ecosystem services. That means that the first principal step in the model is to determine which parts of the case study area are flooded at each time step. At the same time, the total inundated area and, on the basis of the area-elevation curve extracted from TanDEM, the total water volume in the study area are calculated at each time step. [SOURCE: Page_285]

Subsequently, the inundated areas are treated as a single unit, rather than separate SUs and RS, as these distinctions all but disappear during the flood. This flooded area is calculated for each time step and, at the end of the simulation, the overall average inundation duration is determined. On this basis, the seasonal flood-related ecosystem services are then calculated. The variables used and the rationale behind them is outlined in Section 6.3.6.3 and Figure 6.2. [SOURCE: Page_285]

The second major branch of the model is the calculation of not-flood-related ES. This involves more complex calculations at a daily time step, which are spatially explicit for each SU and RS. First, inflow into the RS from the Bassac and the Prek Ambel is calculated. Then, the irrigation volume required for each SU is determined on the basis of the table that characterizes its land use pattern. Then, the water balance for each SU is calculated. Water inputs are precipitation and irrigation volumes. They are added to the surface storage. Infiltration transfers water from the surface to the soil storage. From there, the volume of water plants use for evapotranspiration (ET) is detracted. If soil storage is exceeded, percolation adds water to groundwater storage. At the end of each time step in each SU, it is registered whether sufficient water was available to meet crop water requirements. If this was not the case, the water deficit is noted. Then, to conclude the calculations at each time step, the new water volumes in the reach segments after abstractions for irrigation purposes are calculated. [SOURCE: Page_285]

At this point, several limitations need to be highlighted. For one thing, surface runoff is not considered in the current version of the model. As noted previously, most Chamkar plots slope away into two directions: towards the Boeung in the West and towards the inter-Prek area in the [SOURCE: Page_285]

285 [SOURCE: Page_285]

North or South. Yet overland flow towards these areas is not currently part of the model because of two factors. First, there is the fact that it would involve considerable complexity, even more so due to the small gradients, multiple connections with other units, and small-scale structures such as mini-dykes constructed to delineate plots and prevent runoff. Second, not-flood-related ES are of primary importance mostly during the dry season, when available water volumes are restricted. It was thus assumed that runoff would for that reason be limited in importance. [SOURCE: Page_286]

The second major element of the water balance that is neglected are groundwater dynamics and possible associated flows back to open channels. From measurements in a well at Prek Chann as well as circumstantial evidence such as bank collapses, it is clear that it happens that the groundwater table in the Chamkar areas is elevated above the bed level of the Preks, though its exact elevation varies. It can be conjectured that during the wet season, when water levels in the Preks are typically high, an influent situation dominates, with Prek water infiltrating into the surrounding banks and Chamkar areas. After the flood, this situation reverses into an effluent one, with water that was stored in the banks exfiltrating back into the Prek. During the dry season, excess irrigation water that raises the groundwater table might also contribute to this. By not including this process in the model, a source of Prek water other than the inflow from the Bassac and the Prek Ambel is neglected. The primary reason why this process is not considered so far is the severely limited knowledge of subsurface dynamics and aquifer configurations in the area. Grain size distribution and dimensions of aquifers and aquitards are unknown. At some Preks, especially rehabilitated ones, it is possible that the bed penetrates the aquitard and is thus in permanent connection with the groundwater table. However, no sufficient information on these processes is available. For this reason, it was assumed that the contributions of groundwater to the water level in the Preks remains relatively limited. Whether the calculation is robust in spite of this assumption will be discussed in subsequent sections. [SOURCE: Page_286]

Once the calculations at the daily time step for the non-flood-related ES is finished, the overall effect on provisioning services is determined on the basis of water deficits. As noted previously, these provisioning services relate solely to agricultural production. The use of natural vegetation, for instance for dietary, medicinal, and fuel purposes, is not taken into consideration except on a qualitative basis. For all crops, the likely yield reduction as a response of water stress is calculated, as is outlined in detail in Section 6.3.6.4. [SOURCE: Page_286]

286 [SOURCE: Page_286]

287 [SOURCE: Page_287]

Figure 6.18: Model architecture and calculation workflow. [SOURCE: Page_287]

The final modelling step puts both flood- and not-flood-related ES into perspective by comparing them to the baseline scenario of the 2020-21 cultivation season. [SOURCE: Page_288]

Currently, the model takes between 20 and 30 minutes to run one simulation. So far, the computational efficiency has not been optimized, since the main objective was to make an explicit link between hydrological variables and ES, assessed at the season scale, rather than having an accurate determination of flows at every time step. [SOURCE: Page_288]

6.3.6.2   Calculation of Inundation Extents using WAFL [SOURCE: Page_288]

As noted in the description of the overall workflow of the model, the first crucial step is to delineate flooded areas in the case study area at every time step. In this version of the model, this is achieved using the WAFL, which is described in detail in Section 3.4. The WAFL provides a straightforward, though not very nuanced, estimation of inundation extents. Complex local flow processes and small-scale terrain variations that lead to large-scale variations in inundated areas are already implicitly considered in this approach due to its derivation from observed inundation extents and measured water levels. [SOURCE: Page_288]

6.3.6.3   Calculating Flood-Related Ecosystem Services [SOURCE: Page_288]

Calculating the Inundated Area and Stored Volume Inundated areas, inundation volumes, and inundation durations are calculated for the WAFL. Based on the daily water levels measured at Koh Khel station, it is calculated which pixels are flooded at every time step. Their areas are then added up to calculate the entire flooded area. To calculate the stored volumes, the area-elevation curve of the case study area, derived from TanDEM-X is used. [SOURCE: Page_288]

Provision of Habitats for Fish Reproduction           To calculate the impact of hydrological pro- cesses on the provision of fish habitats, this thesis evaluates the average duration, extent, and depth of inundations on the floodplain and compares it to to the baseline scenario. These values are calculated by computing the average water level during the flood, then calculating the corre- sponding inundation extent, duration, and depth. The latter is computed on the basis of the study [SOURCE: Page_288]

288 [SOURCE: Page_288]

area’s elevation-area curve. [SOURCE: Page_289]

Pest Regulation      According to information from the interviews, rat populations are decimated when sufficient water levels are achieved for sufficient durations. Two interviewees stated that the water levels needed to reach at least the middle of the Preks at which they were being interviewed, for at least two weeks. [SOURCE: Page_289]

To calculate whether a pest regulation effect would be achieved, the areas described by the farmers were delineated in a shape file, and the average WAFL value of the pixels in question was calculated, at 6.43 m. If this value was exceeded for over 14 days, the condition for pest regulation was set to be satisfied in the model. [SOURCE: Page_289]

Soil and Groundwater Recharge As a simplistic approach to groundwater recharge, the maximum infiltration at Ksat was assumed over the entire flooded area for the entire duration of the inundation period. Initial variations in the infiltration speed could be calculated, including a more physical determination of the movement of the wetting front according to Heber Green and Ampt (1911). However, since the initial infiltration time until saturated conditions are reached takes up a comparatively small amount of time in the majority of the area, these variations are neglected for now. [SOURCE: Page_289]

A further assumption that is made with regard to groundwater recharge is that there is no limit with regard to the amount that can infiltrate. Some field data collected in the course of the COSTEA project indicates that there might be an aquitard at 5-6 m below ground level, measured at Prek Chann. This would mean that it is a mere 2-4 m below ground level in the Boeung, depending on the location under consideration, if the aquitard were horizontal. What is known, however, is that there is groundwater flow along a North-South axis, towards Vietnam (Kazama et al., 2007). It is therefore assumed that the aquifer is either sufficiently deep to absorb all water that is infiltrated during the flood, or that groundwater flow transports excess water to Vietnam before it can lead to limits on infiltration. [SOURCE: Page_289]

Sediment and Nutrient Deposition         Sediment deposition - and thus nutrient input in the study area - are estimated on the basis of inundation extents and durations, as well as average sediment [SOURCE: Page_289]

289 [SOURCE: Page_289]

concentrations during the flood season. Sedimentation rates are assumed to be homogeneous across the study area, and to set in as soon as a pixel becomes flooded. The total sedimentation in the case study area over the course of the wet season is thus calculated by multiplying daily sedimentation rates with the inundation extent at each time step. As can be seen from the overview Table in Appendix A, the MRC maintained multiple stations at which sediment concentration or Total Suspended Solids (TSS) were measured. However, many of these stations ceased their activities in 2017, 2018, or 2019. For this reason, two values are examined more closely to determine at baseline: the TSS concentration measured at Koh Khel between 1993 and 2017 and the suspended sediment concentration (SSC) measured at a station called OSP-MRC, located in Phnom Penh just upstream of the diffluence of the Bassac, between 2011 and 2018. Other, more recent or complete measurements at upstream stations could be considered, for instance at Kratie, but the further away a station is located, the larger the likelihood that sediment concentrations have changed in the interim due to deposition or erosion - especially due to the flow into the Tonle Sap Lake - to a higher degree than the changes over time at Koh Khel. [SOURCE: Page_290]

The TSS series at Koh Khel has the advantage that it offers a long-term view of the develop- ment of the concentrations of suspended solids. However, TSS alone cannot serve as a proxy for sediment concentrations due to differences arising from the sampling methods for TSS and SSC. TSS was originally conceived as a water quality parameter. In the MRC data, it is based on a water sample taken in the top 0.3 m of the stream. Since heavier sediments tend to be present at deeper water depths, they are often underrepresented in TSS samples, which leads to an overall underestimation of sediment concentrations. In contrast, SSC samples are based on the depth-integrated method and thus give more accurate results (Kummu and Varis, 2007; Gray et al., 2000). Therefore, TSS is used merely as a way to estimate the temporal development of overall sediment dynamics, whereas the SCC values in Table 6.2 are used to calculate average sediment deposition. [SOURCE: Page_290]

The TSS concentrations at Koh Khel, measured by the MRC between 1993 and 2017 are given in Figure 6.19. As can be seen, concentrations in the 1990s reached much higher peaks during the wet season months than in the 2000s or 2010s. Furthermore, it is known from the analysis of the hydrological series outlined in Section 3.2.3 that the year 2008 can be seen as a break point. Therefore, the values measured between 2010 and 2017 were used to calculate average monthly TSS concentrations in the Bassac at Koh Khel. They are given in Table 6.2. [SOURCE: Page_290]

290 [SOURCE: Page_290]

The calculation of sedimentation rates is implemented using the formula outlined in Winter- werp (2007): D = cb ⇤Ws                                         (6.1) [SOURCE: Page_292]

where D is the deposition rate, cb is the suspended sediment concentration and Ws is the settling velocity. The parameter cb is assumed to be the same as the SSC measured in the main stream of the Bassac. This is a considerable simplification and neglects the spatial distribution of sedimentation, and the fact that differing concentrations have been reported between river mainstreams and laterals (Belaud and Paquier, 2000, 2001). It will be discussed further in subsequent sections. [SOURCE: Page_292]

Ws is calculated following Zhiyao et al. (2008), as: [SOURCE: Page_292]

ν 3               12/7 Ws =     d⇤ [38.1 + 0.93d⇤ ] 7/8                              (6.2) d [SOURCE: Page_292]

where ν is the kinematic viscosity, d is the particle median diameter, and d⇤ is a dimensionless particle diameter calculated as: [SOURCE: Page_292]

(s    1) ⇤ g 1/3 d⇤ = (               ) d                               (6.3) ν2 [SOURCE: Page_292]

where s is the relative particle density (sediment density / fluid density, ρs /ρ ), g is the acceleration of gravity (Camenen, 2007). [SOURCE: Page_292]

As a particle diameter, the values measured by Hung et al. (2014) in the Vietnamese Mekong delta were used, which gives the median at 12.5 µ m. The same study gave an average value for s of 2.65. Furthermore, the average water temperature for the calculation of the kinematic viscosity ν is also taken from Hung et al. (2014), at approximately 30 degrees C during the wet season. These results were echoed by Gratiot et al. (2017). [SOURCE: Page_292]

Finally, erosion needs to be taken into account. While sediments are being deposited on the floodplains, erosion leads to a certain degree of resuspension, reducing the final overall sediment deposition. The magnitude of resuspension depends on the cohesiveness of the sediments, [SOURCE: Page_292]

292 [SOURCE: Page_292]

as well as on the shear stress exacted by the flow of water across the floodplains. Since the inundation process is, for the moment, estimated from the WAFL and the flow processes within the floodplains are thus not being considered, the erosion rate is estimated as a proportion of the deposition rate based on the average values given for 83 different parameter sets in Hung et al. (2014), at an average resuspension factor of 0.8. [SOURCE: Page_293]

Flood Peak Attenuation           Finally, flood peak attenuation as a benefit to downstream commu- nities is calculated on the basis of the water volumes retained in the case study area during the flood rise. Following Chapter 3.2.2, the start of the inundation period is defined as the date with the highest daily water level variation during the season, while the flood peak is defined as the date with the highest water level (after the implementation of a 3-day rolling mean to eliminate spikes due to measurement errors or local variations). [SOURCE: Page_293]

6.3.6.4    Calculating Not-Flood-Related Ecosystem Services [SOURCE: Page_293]

Not-flood-related ecosystem services were calculated for all SUs at any one time step. As a first step, the water levels in all Preks and lowland channels are calculated based on inflow from neighbouring RS as well as the Bassac and the Prek Ambel. Then, it is determined whether the water volumes contained in these channels fulfill the irrigation water demand of SUs that use them as sources. Subsequently, the water balance is calculated in each individual SU, using precipitation and irrigation as inputs, percolation and evapotranspiration as outputs, and updating the surface and soil storage terms, with the transport between them being calculated as infiltration. As a last step, the water volumes post-irrigation are updated in all channels and Preks. [SOURCE: Page_293]

Calculating Prek and Channel Water Volumes                    The inflow and outflow of water into RS is calculated based on the weir equation (cf. Section 6.2.2.3. The reason for this choice of equation is that it is known from field trips that there is often a threshold, formed by an accumulation of sediments, between the Preks and the Bassac as well as the channels and the Preks. This arises from the fact that increased rates of sedimentation can be observed in these areas. 3 3 This was furthermore confirmed during interviews. Several village chiefs, for instance at Prek Nou, explained [SOURCE: Page_293]

that local excavations were organized at the Prek heads because inflow was restricted due to sedimentation there. [SOURCE: Page_293]

293 [SOURCE: Page_293]

Furthermore, the weir equation is able to account for the link between water levels and flow between adjoining RS even where parameters like geometry and roughness are uncertain. The higher the denivelation between two water bodies, the larger the flow rate. Two situations are typical: free flow and submerged flow. In the former, the RS having the higher water levels empties into the RS without a downstream influence to consider. In this case, the standard equation used is: [SOURCE: Page_294]

p          3 Q = α ⇤Cd ⇤        2g ⇤ h^12 ⇤ l                             (6.4) [SOURCE: Page_294]

In the case of submerged flow, the flow is limited due to the small denivellation between water levels in the RS. The corresponding equation is: [SOURCE: Page_294]

p         p Q = α ⇤Cd$_2$ ⇤    2g ⇤ h^2 ⇤ h^1            h^2 ⇤ l                    (6.5) [SOURCE: Page_294]

p Cd$_2$ = 1.5 ⇤ 3 ⇤Cd                                        (6.6) [SOURCE: Page_294]

in which Q is the discharge, h^1 is the higher water level above the weir crest, h^2 is the lower water level above the weir crest, g is the gravitational acceleration, l, is the weir length, Cd is the discharge coefficient for non-submerged weirs, assumed at the standard value of 0.385, Cd$_2$ is the discharge coefficient for submerged weirs (here taken as unity, allowing continuity of discharge at the limit between free and submerged flows), and α is a correction factor to be optimized through calibration to account for the fact that both Cd and the weir length are estimations. Whether a weir is submerged or not is decided on the basis of the difference between h^1 and h^2 : If h^1 > 1.5 ⇤ h^2 , the weir counts as in free flow (Eq. 6.3.6.4), otherwise it is submerged (Eq. 6.3.6.4). [SOURCE: Page_294]

The term α needs to be subject to calibration, validation, and sensitivity testing. This is outlined in Section 6.3.7.2. Actual connections in the study area are often complex and [SOURCE: Page_294]

294 [SOURCE: Page_294]

unmeasured, so geometry (weir length and crest height) as well as discharge coefficients are unknown a priori. Therefore, standard weir lengths were estimated from SPOT high-resolution satellite imagery, and both α and the crest height were subjected to calibration (see below). Since α ⇤Cd values include all unmeasured effects, they can deviate considerably from the theoretical value of 0.385. [SOURCE: Page_295]

The input water level in the Bassac and the Prek Ambel is calculated on the basis of the in-situ data that the logger in the Bassac has been registering since June 2020, and the upstream water level at Koh Khel. Unfortunately, the logger has not yet registered a complete April-to-April seasonal cycle and thus can’t serve as direct input. However, the water levels it records were correlated to those at Koh Khel to make an estimate of local water levels possible. As the results of the hydrological analysis have shown (cf. Section 3.2.3), the relationship between upstream and downstream water levels varies considerably between the wet and the dry season. To compensate for this, a method analogous to the Lamagat approach (cf. Section 3.4.1) was used, and the optimal correlation for each month was calculated. [SOURCE: Page_295]

Using the equations above, a flow between RS a new water volume is calculated in each RS at the start of every time step. Based on the assumed geometry, this volume is then converted into a new water level. The corresponding mathematical expression is given below in Equation 6.3.6.4. Here, Vt denotes the volume of water in a RS, with a water level z^2,t at time t, supplied by the river or another RS where water level z^1,t is known. The flow Qt given by the weir equation (see Equations 6.3.6.4 and 6.3.6.4) and is equal to [SOURCE: Page_295]

dVt        dz^2 Qt =       = At ⇤                                       (6.7) dt         dt [SOURCE: Page_295]

The area A is a function of z^2 , as well as Q in the case of submerged flow, giving a differential equation that is solved with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme (see Appendix F). [SOURCE: Page_295]

In the code, the calculation is carried out through a loop over the different RS, starting from the upstream boundary condition (the water level in the Bassac), and iterating across the different RS according to the flow direction during flood rise and recession. Variations during a time step are bounded so that z^1 = z^2 at most. At the end of this loop, the volume is available in each RS. [SOURCE: Page_295]

295 [SOURCE: Page_295]

Following this, the irrigation volumes abstracted from each RS in the ideal scenario are calculated. If these volumes aren’t available, the magnitude of the water restrictions is noted and the water input into the SUs drawing water from the RS affected reduced in the next time step. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Water Balance Loop Over SUs The central element of the calculation of not-flood-related ES is the water balance on every SU that is calculated in a loop at every time step. Precipitation and irrigation serve as inputs to the surface storage volume. Water from surface storage is transferred to soil storage through infiltration. From soil storage, plants can abstract water for evapotranspiration (ET)4 . If soil moisture is above field capacity, percolation occurs as input to groundwater layers. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Precipitation [SOURCE: Page_296]

The precipitation data used as an input for initial calculations of the baseline scenario is taken from meteorological station installed by the UNDP in Koh Thom, since it has made data available over the entirety of the baseline period (2020-04-15 - 2021-04-14). To evaluate future scenarios, precipitation data was modified in accordance with projections in the literature, see Section 6.4. Furthermore, the data used was compared with CHIRPS for the purpose of sensitivity testing. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Irrigation [SOURCE: Page_296]

Irrigation data is based on the information gathered during the interviews on the frequency of irrigation sessions for every crop, as well as the average duration of session. It furthermore uses data collected by Pratx (2017) and in the course of the field trip in February - March 2020 by Vandôme (2020) on the average configuration of the irrigation systems and capacity of pumps, which was found to lie at 60 m^3 /h. Building on this information, average irrigation requirements in m^3 /d were calculated for each land cover class. Then, the average daily irrigation needs in every month were calculated for each SU based on the percentage of LULC classes that cover it at each time step. [SOURCE: Page_296]

Actual Evapotranspiration 4 Calculation follows the FAO methodology (Allen et al., 1998), for each of the crops in the SU at the time of [SOURCE: Page_296]

simulation. [SOURCE: Page_296]

296 [SOURCE: Page_296]

Potential evapotranspiration (PET) was calculated using the PyETo Python package using the Thornthwaite (1948) empirical method. This was used rather than the standard FAO Penman- Monteith method Allen et al. (1998) because it has comparatively minimalistic input data requirements. PET is calculated based on monthly air temperature and monthly mean daily daylight hours, estimated from latitude. Future applications may want to consider a refinement through a transition to the standard Penman-Monteith method. [SOURCE: Page_297]

To calculate actual ET (AET), PET is multiplied with a crop coefficient Kc . This crop coefficient was based on the crop detected in the LULC classification, with values for individual crops taken from the literature (see Table D.1). For the vegetable LULC category calculated through the remote sensing approach, an average for the vegetables found in the interviews was calculated and weighted according to their relative area. KC values were based on the tables provided by the FAO (Allen et al. (1998), Steduto et al. (2012)). [SOURCE: Page_297]

Infiltration [SOURCE: Page_297]

Infiltration is calculated on the basis of the curve number method, which was developed by the US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Soil Conservation Service (SCS). It is an empirical method to calculate the amount of infiltration and runoff from rainfall events and irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_297]

Where R is the accumulated runoff depth (mm), P is the accumulated input volume (mm), S is the potential maximum retention (mm), and Ia is the initial abstraction. In application, S is calculated from the curve number CN (see Equation 6.3.6.4 above). CN itself is taken from literature values, based on the soil group and land cover (Boughton, 1989; Choi et al., 2019; Hawkins et al., 2008). Furthermore, it is modified depending on antecedent moisture conditions (AMC), meaning that where soils have seen particularly large or particularly sparse irrigation [SOURCE: Page_297]

297 [SOURCE: Page_297]

or rainfall amounts, CN is modified. When the accumulated 5-day antecedent water input is below 36 mm, CN       I is used, when it is above 53 mm CN       III is used. Otherwise, the standard CN     II is used (Bos et al., 2009; Silveira et al., 2000). All CN values used in the calculations for this thesis are given in table D.5. For the purposes of this thesis, hydrological soil group C (moderately fine to fine soil texture) was chosen. The curve numbers corresponding to the different land cover classes are given in Table D.5 in Appendix D. It also includes the variations (CN-I and CN-III) depending on the antecedent soil moisture at the start of the time step. [SOURCE: Page_298]

To calculate infiltration, the theoretical runoff R is subtracted from the existing volume of water stored at the surface (Vsur f ), as well as the inputs in the form of precipitation (Precip) and irrigation (Irrig): [SOURCE: Page_298]

In f = Precip + Irrig +Vsur f     R                           (6.10) [SOURCE: Page_298]

Since overland flow is currently not considered in this simulation, as outlined above, the calculated Q is simply added to the surface water volume Vsur f [SOURCE: Page_298]

Percolation [SOURCE: Page_298]

To calculate percolation, another simplifying assumption was made - namely that it occurs if the soil storage capacity in the root zone is exceeded. The depth of the root zone is estimated at 1 m, based on literature about the average principal rooting depths of paddy rice, mango trees, and various vegetables grown in the area Uga et al. (2013); Feldman (1994); CARR (2014) Evidently, the average rooting depth is highly dependent on the LULC categories. For now, no differentiation between SUs was implemented for the sake of simplicity. However, future applications should spatialise this variable. Potential soil storage (Ssoil ) is calculated simply on the basis of soil storage capacity, derived from Table D.4. Soil storage volumes at every time step (Vsoil as the total volume of water par unit area, in and below the root depth), as well as percolation (Perc), are then calculated on the basis of infiltration, previous soil storage volumes, [SOURCE: Page_298]

298 [SOURCE: Page_298]

and AET. [SOURCE: Page_299]

Vsoil = In f +Vsoil,t 1    AET                               (6.11) [SOURCE: Page_299]

Perc = max(Vsoil     Ssoil ; 0)                            (6.12) [SOURCE: Page_299]

Outputs Calculated at Every Time Step [SOURCE: Page_299]

At every time step, several parameters are calculated and stored to memory. These are the Vsur f , Vsoil , combined inputs from irrigation and precipitation (Precip + Irrig, for the calculation of AMCs), water deficits arising from insufficient water volumes in the channel network, and percolation volumes (Perc). These are saved to a data frame and then treated further once the calculation of daily water balances has been concluded. [SOURCE: Page_299]

Calculation of Seasonal Provisioning Services The calculation of seasonal provisioning services follows the approach implemented in the FAO’s CROPWAT software (see Allen et al. (1998)), in using a yield response factor Ky to characterize the effect of water scarcity on the yield of various crops: [SOURCE: Page_299]

Ya            AET 1       = Ky (1        )                                  (6.13) Yx            ETx [SOURCE: Page_299]

where Yx is the maximum yield without limiting factors, based on crop variety, ETx is the evapotranspiration in case crop water requirements are fully met (ETx = Kc ⇤ PET ), and AET is the actual evapotranspiration possible under given conditions. Ya , then, is the actual yield. The Ky values used in this thesis (see Table D.1 were taken from the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 (cf. Allen et al. (1998) and Steduto et al. (2012)). Furthermore, KY values for some crops, which were not available in the original FAO publication, were taken from Karanja (2006), Sekendur (2017), Azevedo et al. (2018), Lovelli et al. (2007), and Sezen et al. (2005). For some vegetables, such as long bean, wax gourd, and bittermelon, no data specifically for the [SOURCE: Page_299]

299 [SOURCE: Page_299]

species could be found. In such cases, it was substituted with data from a species in the same family. Bittermelon, for instance (Momordica charantia) belongs to the family of Cucurbitaceae. Thus, data for squash (genus Curcurbita) is used (see Table D.2). [SOURCE: Page_300]

Yx is estimated on the basis of the data gathered in interviews, taking the average of the upper 25th percentile, after the removal of outliers. Once the calculation of the daily water balance is concluded, and the proportion of actual to maximum evapotranspiration known for each time step, a final yield calculation loop is run over every unit to determine the overall response. For now, this is done on a monthly basis, to account for the different kinds of rice cultivation, for instance. It is furthermore assumed that each month contributes equally to final crop yield. Evidently, this is a simplifying assumption and with a view towards improving the model, different growth stages of the various crops ought to be taken into consideration. [SOURCE: Page_300]

6.3.6.5   Summary of Model Outputs [SOURCE: Page_300]

Overall, at the end of the model run, the following outputs are provided: [SOURCE: Page_300]

• Flood-Related ES [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Area extent, average duration, and average depth of habitats for fish reproduction. In m^2 , d, and m, and as percentage change compared to the baseline scenario. [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Total volume stored in the case study area during the flood rise, which contributes to flood peak attenuation in m^3 , and as percentage change compared to the baseline scenario. [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Average seasonal sediment deposition in kg/m^2 and as percentage change compared to the baseline scenario. [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Seasonal groundwater recharge in m^3 and as percentage change compared to the baseline scenario. [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Pest regulation as a binary parameter - whether it happens or not. [SOURCE: Page_300]

• Non-flood-related ES [SOURCE: Page_300]

– Average crop yield in all SUs and the case study area as a whole, in % of optimal yield and as percentage change compared to the baseline scenario. [SOURCE: Page_300]

6.3.7     Parametrization and Sensitivity [SOURCE: Page_301]

For calibration and validation, data that the loggers in Prek Chann collected during the 2021 wet season was used. Due to the relative data sparsity in the area, merely the water level in the Preks could be subjected to these steps. Other important output parameters, such as yield, sediment deposition, or groundwater recharge could not be assessed so far. [SOURCE: Page_301]

Sensitivity analysis, to gauge the relative impact of different parameters on model outputs and thus its overall performance, was performed on soil parameters, channel geometry - particularly bed elevation - and the use of different precipitation data. Soil parameters and channel geometry are two parameters that were estimated on the basis of knowledge of the study area gathered during field work, as well as existing literature in the form of studies carried out in the wider region and engineering reports written about Preks. However, they are nonetheless estimations and it was necessary to gauge how small variations in them could affect the overall model output. [SOURCE: Page_301]

It has to be noted that calibration, validation, and sensitivity testing were only carried out to a preliminary degree so far. Due to temporal restrictions and a lack of data, these steps were only implemented manually, rather than automatically using regression, variance-based, or entropy-based methods, as is recommended for hydrological modelling (Song et al., 2015; Devak and Dhanya, 2017). [SOURCE: Page_301]

6.3.7.1   Parametrization and Validating Channel Flow Through In-Situ Water Levels [SOURCE: Page_301]

To calibrate the flow function in the model, water levels measured by the loggers in Prek Chann and Prek Touch were used (cf. Figure 3.2), as well as those of the logger in the Bassac. [SOURCE: Page_301]

To calibrate the flow module in the simulation, the coefficient α in Equation 6.3.6.4 was manually adjusted, alongside the assumed weir height. Since the aim is to find a water level that is representative for the entirety of the Prek, a mean value of all the loggers in Prek Chann was calculated for each date, and the RMSE (cf. Equation 3.1) between this mean and the simulated water level in the Prek was calculated. Since only one water level is measured in Prek Chann this calculation was not necessary, but apart from that the same procedure was observed. The values tested, in each combination, as well as their RMSE are given in Table 6.3. Examples of a [SOURCE: Page_301]

Values lie between 530 l/m^2 and, assuming high permeability, 33285 l/m^2 . This illustrates the high uncertainty arising from assumptions made about soil properties in the area, with variations of several orders of magnitude to be expected depending. For the purposes of the simulation, a Ks value of 0.026 m/d was retained, as estimated from the flood recession analysis. [SOURCE: Page_304]

parameters - temperature, precipitation, river stages, and Prek configuration. Temperature and precipitation are likely to change in the study area itself due to climate change over the coming years. River stages will evolve based on upstream factors such as the construction of hydropower plants and the variation of precipitation patterns due to climate change. The configuration of Preks, finally, might be modified through rehabilitation projects or locally organized excavations. [SOURCE: Page_309]

The change in temperatures and precipitation is taken from Supharatid et al. (2022). This study uses the 18 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMPI$_6$) to project the local manifestations of climate change in mainland Southeast Asia under two SSP-RCP (shared socioeconomic pathway-representative concentration pathway) scenarios: RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. It provides estimates for temperatures and monthly precipitation amounts in Cambodia by 2050. [SOURCE: Page_309]

Similarly, future projections for river water levels are simulated in this thesis based on Hoang et al. (2019). This study modelled the impact of climate change, hydropower, and irrigation schemes on the flow of the Mekong by the 2050s. It assumes maximum hydropower development, with all currently projected dams being in operation, as well as an expansion of irrigated areas. As for climate change, both RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 are modelled. The study also provides projections of flow changes at several MRC stations, including Kratie in Cambodia. In order to use these projections, a correlative link was established on a monthly basis between Kratie, Koh Khel, and the logger in the case study area. A visual comparison of the water level elevation at the three stations is provided in Figure 6.27. This follows the same procedure as described above, based on the methodology of the Lamagat method. Scenarios: [SOURCE: Page_313]

• Scenario 1: RCP 4.5, full dam and irrigation development, no rehabilitation [SOURCE: Page_313]
