It has to be noted that this implementation of scenarios still leaves considerable room for refinement. For the moment, only average changes for temperatures and precipitation on a national scale were implemented, and a blanket rehabilitation of Preks - not taking into account the installation of gates or the different types of rehabilitation projects - was assumed. In reality, far more nuanced scenarios ought to be considered, with variations in upstream dam and irrigation development, as well as the number of Preks rehabilitated and the type of rehabilitation. Furthermore, the scenario data used was taken from only two relatively recent studies, rather than compared between different ones at different scales. All of these aspects could be improved still in the further development of the model. The results presented below are therefore initial projections to give an idea of both future development and model capabilities. [SOURCE: Page_313]

6.5     Results and Discussion: Different Scenario Impacts on the Prek System and the Ecosystem Services it Provides [SOURCE: Page_313]

The results of the calculation of not-flood related ecosystem services are shown in Figures 6.31 and 6.32 as well as Table 6.6 below. They show that, without rehabilitation, conditions in 2050 would result in consistent yield reductions, both under Scenario 1 and 2. Both scenarios are similar with regard to the magnitude of yield reductions - between 1% and just over 16%, with [SOURCE: Page_313]

313 [SOURCE: Page_313]

scenario. This is likely due to the shift in the flood peak, which is discussed below, and the fact that the LULC properties in the model are, as of now, static. This limitation is discussed in detail in the next section. [SOURCE: Page_316]

With regard to flood-related ecosystem services, it emerges that the flood in the scenarios projected on the basis of data collected between 1971 and 2000 is still more extensive than the flood observed in 2020-21. As shown in Table 6.7, the maximum water level would increase from 5.89 to 6.35 m, and it would occur later - in early November. Furthermore, both average and maximum inundation extents would increase - by 7.57% and 17.98% respectively in Scenario 1 and by 8.01% and 16.85% respectively in Scenario 2. As can be seen in Figure 6.33, the maximum flood extents are very similar, with RCP 4.5 having slightly more inundated areas in the Western part of the case study area. Similarly, the maximum volume retained would increase considerably, by 40.80% and 35.15% in either scenario. In contrast, the amount of groundwater recharge increases only slightly (by 7.57% and 8.01% respectively) and neither scenario results in water levels high enough to result in pest regulation. Sediment deposition even decreases slightly, from 16.52 kg/m^2 to 13.23 kg/m^2 and 13.64 kg/m^2 respectively. This is due to the relationship between overall flood duration and the average flooded area. [SOURCE: Page_316]

volumes for irrigation. Yet the elevation used in the simulation for not rehabilitated canals is a mere estimation, based on qualitative observations during fieldwork as well as on engineering reports using data from other Preks in the wider region. Topographic surveys along the length of several Preks - for instance during the dry season when they are devoid of water - could greatly improve the accuracy of simulations for not rehabilitated scenarios. [SOURCE: Page_318]

Similarly, the lack of detailed knowledge on soil and subsurface properties, especially infil- tration coefficients, porosity values, and the presence and depth of aquitards, poses a substantial limitation with regard to the simulation. Not only does it limit the accuracy of infiltration estimates - and thus the availability of water for evapotranspiration from the soil storage term - it also obscures possible groundwater interactions to the point where it became unfeasible to include them in this prototype model. A distributed soil survey across the case study area as well as soil cores could provide these key pieces of information and clarify at which order of magnitude the subsurface system operates. As mentioned above, there are some indications, for instance, that excess irrigation water filtrates back to the Prek during extensive dry-season irrigation. Yet this is hardly reflected in the groundwater storage term in the current model. Once information on soil and subsurface properties becomes available, adding a simulation module to represent filtration processes in Chamkar areas would become possible. [SOURCE: Page_318]

Another aspect that has been neglected so far and that imposes limitations is surface storage and flow. With the current assumed infiltration properties, the surface storage term has shown that the amounts that fail to infiltrate on a daily basis during the dry season are comparatively small. However, field observation indicate that there is some exchange between individual plots. Since the SUs that serve as the basis for this model comprise multiple plots, this effect is somewhat dampened, as a lot of the water that is transferred between plots through surface runoff may still stay within the same SU. Without doubt, though, some exchange occurs between the areas delineated SUs in reality. Once the soil properties are better-known and the infiltration rates can thus be calculated with a greater degree of certainty, it would be advisable to take surface flow processes into account. [SOURCE: Page_318]

Furthermore, more sensitivity testing ought to be carried out with regard to the spatial configuration of simulation units, both surface units and reach segments. Currently, the model is based on a delineation grounded in knowledge acquired during fieldwork. However, it is [SOURCE: Page_318]

318 [SOURCE: Page_318]

likely that the subdivision of reach segments, for instance, leads to uncertainties, especially when segments are relatively short. The reason for this is that flow is currently calculated at a daily time step. For example, reach segment 16 is a mere 0.5 km in length and, as a lowland canal, fairly shallow. If it is used as an irrigation source, it is possible that the entire volume in the segment is used up in a single calculation time step and a lack of water registered. In reality, however, water would flow into this segment from neighbouring, larger segments, at the same time as farmers’ pumps extract it, thus preventing the channel from falling dry. Simultaneously, however, a limitation is also imposed by not dividing longer RS into multiple units. This is clearly illustrated by the validation data at Prek Chann, which shows the water level slope between the head of the Prek and its tail. Furthermore, field observations have shown that even individual pumping activities in one part of the Preks can influence its flow direction during the height of the dry season. During the same period, some villages have erected temporary earthen dams across their Preks to concentrate what little water is available in one of its sections. This is not to mention the gate that currently exists at Prek Chann and which regulates in- and outflow during some months of the year. All of these complexities have been neglected so far. For future simulations, it would be beneficial to further subdivide RS, to take account of inhomogeneities along their lengths as well as of water level slopes. At the same time, the time step of the flow calculation would have to be downscaled to avoid the unrealistic emptying of shorter segments. [SOURCE: Page_319]

Next, a considerable limitation of the current model is that it is solely based on the LULC dynamics of the 2020-2021 season. While grounded in extensively tested remote sensing analyses using field data as input, the classification used to characterize areas is nonetheless static. That means that currently, future farmer decisions with regard to planting different crops at different times of the year depending on hydrological framework conditions varying between scenarios are not taken into consideration. Instead, it is assumed that the monthly crop distribution remains static. It is known from interviews that this is not the case, and that there are already some plans by farmers to switch away from the cultivation of mango, for instance, in the medium term. On a smaller temporal scale, farmers unquestionably adjust cultivation practices - planting and harvesting earlier or later - depending on the hydrological situation in the area. This means the spatial distribution of the crops doesn’t stay the same. Such decisions too are currently not represented. For instance, rice planting on low-lying units would commence later if floods retreat later in future scenarios. However, since these areas are registered as flooded in the 2020-21 [SOURCE: Page_319]

319 [SOURCE: Page_319]

LULC classification, these delayed crops cannot be represented. This model configuration thus precludes the modelling of LULC responses to future scenarios. To address this issue, it might be feasible to add a LULC decision model. Using information from the surveys and the 2020-21 LULC categorization, it could identify cultivation pathways and decision and timing factors. Furthermore, larger economic considerations could also be taken into account. For the moment it is assumed that water availability is the only constraint farmers in the region face. However, the availability of pesticides and fertilizers, as well as labour force also play crucial roles in the calculation of overall yield. [SOURCE: Page_320]

A further aspect that represents a major limitation of the model in its current form is the simplistic estimation of flooded areas on the basis of WAFL. While it serves as a quick and efficient means of calculation and has been shown to represent reality with an acceptable degree of accuracy, it still comes with considerable caveats. For one thing, it is a black box model with regard to the flow processes in the floodplain, which engenders uncertainty with regard to processes such as sediment deposition.5 Crucially, however, the WAFL fails to take into account the influence of Prek rehabilitation on inundation processes. By default, this method assumes that the hydraulic link between a river and its floodplains remains relatively static. However, Prek rehabilitation alters that very link. So far, it has been assumed that the rehabilitation of one or two Preks has a negligible impact on this link. To a certain extent, this is supported by the validation procedure WAFL was subjected to (cf. Section 3.4.3). Among others, the comparison with inundation maps based on historical Landsat images showed a fairly good match, even though no Preks were rehabilitated at the time that these images were taken, and two were rehabilitated during the period that WAFL is based on. Nonetheless, it is extremely likely that the blanket rehabilitation of Preks in the case study area would modify this link to the point where WAFL estimates are no longer accurate. Furthermore, in the current model, the impact of outflow from the Boeung areas to the Bassac on Prek water levels is also neglected due to the use of WAFL. It is assumed that since this occurs at the end of the wet season, when river water levels are still fairly, high, sufficient water is still available in Preks to meet irrigation requirements and the exact contribution from outflow is therefore relatively negligible. However, these issues cold be addressed by refining the calculation of inundations by employing a more 5 When it comes to sediment deposition, it would also be beneficial to install sediment traps at a few points in the [SOURCE: Page_320]

floodplain to provide validation data for deposition processes. Hung et al. (2014) carried out such measurements in the Vietnamese delta, but as has been noted, sedimentation is likely to be higher on the Cambodian floodplains due to a lack of regulation infrastructure. [SOURCE: Page_320]

320 [SOURCE: Page_320]

complex, dedicated flow model, such as Delft^3D or LISFLOOD. The challenge of using these models, and the principal reason why they have not been implemented so far, are their extensive parametrization requirements. Especially terrain characteristics such as small-scale dykes would necessitate intensive calibration before reliable results could be produced.6 [SOURCE: Page_321]

Another simplification that poses constraints on the validity of the current model are the assumptions with regard to sedimentation. For one thing, the spatial distribution of sedimentation is being neglected - instead sediment concentrations in the inundated floodplains are assumed to be the same as in the river mainstream. In future versions of the model, a statistical relationship could be established to account for the known discrepancies between these concentrations. Furthermore, if an advanced flow model were to be used, it would also be possible to calculate parameters such as shear stress in the floodplain to calculate resuspension rather than having to estimate it as a fraction of deposition on the basis of previous studies. [SOURCE: Page_321]

Another aspect that must be highlighted with regard to model limitations and uncertainty is the construction of scenarios, specifically future water level projections. As outlined above, the water level scenarios used in this analysis are based on a single study by Hoang et al. (2019), which provides estimates only for an upstream station at Kratie, which are further based on the period 1971-2000. Applying this scenario and transferring it to the water levels in the case study area resulted in a loss of the typical multi-peaking pattern observed in the area, likely because the multi-year average of daily water levels was used, rather than one particular year. In addition, the future water levels projected in the scenarios on the basis of this data were already exceeded by the water levels observed in recent years. They are therefore to be taken with a measure of scepticisim and refined when possible. Furthermore, there were doubts pertaining to the data provided by the MRC, specifically to issues such as gauge elevation and changes in the rating curve. When a rating curve was constructed using the full series of water levels and discharge measurements given at Kratie, for instance, the back-calculation of discharge yielded unrealistic results. For future model applications, a greater number of scenarios ought to be compared, taking into account projections that allow for the conservation of typical local flow patterns. Furthermore, factors such as projected changes in sediment concentration, and different rehabilitation scenarios (deep vs. shallow calibration, number of Preks to be rehabilitated etc.) 6 Unfortunately, topographic data are required at a vertical resolution and accuracy which are not currently [SOURCE: Page_321]

available. Future satellite missions may partially solve this lack of information,but it is likely that small interventions by farmers, such as building small dykes to retain water, would affect the flow distribution. [SOURCE: Page_321]

321 [SOURCE: Page_321]

should be taken into account. [SOURCE: Page_322]

Finally, there are several limitations that must be noted with regard to the conceptual com- plexity of the model. Several aspects of local water management that are well-known from the results of the field work have been neglected, such as the practice of double-pumping, building temporary dams across Preks, and gate operation at Prek Chann. If a RS network with more sub-segments were to be delineated, these processes could be taken into consideration - provided, of course that sufficient information is available on their temporal dynamics. Alternatively, it could be envisioned to represent these aspects through an agent-based decision model. For instance, a condition could be added that double-pumping at non-rehabilitated Preks becomes feasible once a certain percentage of SUs along the Prek is experiencing acute water stress. [SOURCE: Page_322]

6.7     Conclusion: Deriving a Systematic Understanding and Possible Future Outlooks from Numerical Modelling [SOURCE: Page_322]

This chapter has outlined a numerical modelling approach towards representing flood-related and not-flood-related ecosystem services in the case study area. Based on the insights gained and data collected during field work, as well as on remote sensing analysis and literature values, a workflow was constructed to allow the simulation of future scenarios with regard to shifts in precipitation and temperatures, water level, and the rehabilitation of Preks. [SOURCE: Page_322]

The results have shown that under the future scenarios simulated, not-flood-related ecosystem services would decline by 2050, with yields of rice, fruit, and vegetables decreasing by up to 16% with the current Prek configuration. If blanket rehabilitation were to be implemented, in contrast, they would increase by up to 43%. Under the simulated water levels, flood-related ecosystem services would increase, with higher inundation extents, retention volumes, and and groundwater recharge. Only average sediment deposition would decrease, and pest regulation would remain the same as in the baseline scenario - lacking due to insufficiently high water levels. [SOURCE: Page_322]

However, the process of model construction, validation, and sensitivity testing has also highlighted a number of issues with the current setup that remain to be resolved. First, there are the uncertainties resulting from a lack of data in the study area related to factors such as soil [SOURCE: Page_322]

322 [SOURCE: Page_322]

properties and the elevation of channel beds, as well as the fact that surface flows between units and subsurface flows were neglected. Furthermore, there are the limitations imposed by using the LULC characteristics from the 2020-2021 season as a baseline for yield calculation, as well as the use of WAFL as a blackbox model for flood calculation. Another issue is the data used for the construction of scenarios. The water levels for future scenarios, for instance, don’t account for the regionally typical multi-peaking pattern, since they are based on a multi-year average. In addition, the baseline period on which are used to calculate future water levels lies several years in the past, calling into question the accuracy of simulations. [SOURCE: Page_323]

Overall, it can be summarized that the model outlined above presents a promising prototype to be refined further as information becomes available and scenarios are more clearly constructed. [SOURCE: Page_323]

323 [SOURCE: Page_323]

324 [SOURCE: Page_324]

7 Conclusion, Discussion, Perspectives [SOURCE: Page_325]

The Cambodian Mekong delta is a unique area in terms of hydrological processes and agro- ecosystems. Distinct from its Vietnamese counterpart through a lack of hydraulic infrastructure, it is a focal point for cascading effects of upstream developments, yet also one of the most productive areas in Southeast Asia in terms of agriculture and fisheries. Yet it has also offered a gateway towards exploring more universal processes, shared by deltaic areas worldwide, developing transferable methods, and drawing more generic conclusions. [SOURCE: Page_325]

This thesis has sought to explore the link between ecosystem services and hydrological processes, to explore the impact of large-scale changes and their translation to the regional level, as well as to examine how canal networks can be used to respond to these changes at a local level. In particular, it has aimed to elucidate the role of the Prek channels, which are characteristic for the Cambodian Mekong delta. Taking one case study area just North of the border to Vietnam as their focus, the analyses outlined in this thesis have attempted to shed light on the complex [SOURCE: Page_325]

325 [SOURCE: Page_325]

set of ecosystem services from which the local population benefits, as well as their connection to Prek channels and large-scale hydrological processes. Finally, this thesis laid the foundation for estimating the impact of future projected developments on local hydrological processes and ecosystem services. Through these analyses, it has become possible to answer the research questions first outlined in the introduction. [SOURCE: Page_326]

What are the current patterns of regional hydrological dynamics at the scale of the Cam- bodian upper Mekong delta, and which trends have manifested themselves over the past three decades?     In terms of the hydrological dynamics at the scale of the Cambodian upper Mekong delta, three components have been considered - water levels in the Mekong and the Bassac, precipitation over the area, and inundation extents and dynamics. They were analyzed over two large zones of interest - one on the right bank of the Bassac and one bracketed by the Bassac and the Mekong. [SOURCE: Page_326]

A statistical analysis identified the year 2008 as a hydrological break point in the water level series of the past thirty years, provided at four stations maintained by the Mekong River Commission (MRC). Overall, the annual monsoon floods have been found to arrive later and recede sooner, amounting to shorter durations and sharper peaks in water levels. Furthermore, a comparison of both daily and near-realtime measurements taken at stations along the Bassac between Phnom Penh and Chau Doc has highlighted typical bi-daily and bi-monthly water level variations linked to tides and moon phases, as well as a characteristic pattern of multiple flood peaks during the wet season, which might be related to hydraulic thresholds for floodplain connections and upstream processes such as the reverse flow into the Tonle Sap Lake. [SOURCE: Page_326]

A comparison of precipitation data, measured locally at three in-situ stations and estimated through remote sensing products in the form of CHIRPS has revealed that remotely sensed data typically overestimates frequent low-intensity rainfall events and underestimates high-intensity events. However, an inter-station comparison showed that considerable heterogeneity also exists between in-situ stations and that CHIRPS is still valuable due to the consistent long-term data it provides. A trend (and break point) analysis on the CHIRPS data for the region did not yield any significant break points in the precipitation time series. It also did not reveal many significant trends in long-term precipitation. A decadal comparison of monthly rainfall sums has shown [SOURCE: Page_326]

326 [SOURCE: Page_326]

that precipitation amounts in September and October were slightly higher in the 2010s than in previous decades. The only statistically significant trend, however, is the increase in precipitation in December. [SOURCE: Page_327]

A final element of the analysis of hydrological processes at regional scales has been the development of a methodology to construct a novel water level - flood link (termed WAFL), in order to re-construct past inundation extents and assess long-term changes in the spatial pattern and timing of monsoon floods. By linking locally measured water levels to inundation maps derived from Sentinel-1 and 2 images taken between 2017 and 2020, a foundation was established on the basis of which inundation extents can be estimated using historical water levels. The robustness of this approach has been assessed using the TanDEM-X 12 m elevation model and inundation maps as well as LULC classifications derived from historical Landsat-5 and -8 images. Overall, this approach showed that WAFL is capable of estimating inundation extents with overall accuracies of 87% to 93% in comparison to historical inundation maps. It also revealed that the incidence of inundations has decreased sharply in the early traditional wet season in July and the first half of August (at an average of -21%) and that the average duration of inundations has decreased by 19 days in comparison to the pre-2008 period. [SOURCE: Page_327]

How are regional and local hydrological processes being affected by reported basin- and delta-wide changes? A comparison of the results obtained at the scale of the Cambodian Mekong Delta with insights derived from a literature review show that basin-wide trends brought about by the extensive development of hydropower infrastructure, climate change, and land use change are reflected closely in the regional and local water level dynamics. [SOURCE: Page_327]

The hydrological break point identified in the Cambodian Mekong delta in the year 2008, for instance, mirrored the results of large-scale studies. Yun et al. (2020) examined the impact of both climate change and hydropower development on the entirety of the Mekong basin, including its Chinese part and attained the break point of 2008 through a Mann-Kendall test at Yun Jing Hong station in China. Han et al. (2019), focusing on the impacts of climate change and human activities on the flow regime of the Lancang, found the same break point for the same station and noted that this corresponding to the interception of river flow by the Nuozhadu reservoir, the largest to be constructed on the river at that time. Li et al. (2017), investigating flow changes [SOURCE: Page_327]

327 [SOURCE: Page_327]

across the entire Mekong basin detected a slightly later change point in 2009 at Chiang Saen station in Northern Thailand, near the border to Myanmar and Laos, also using the Mann-Kendall test. [SOURCE: Page_328]

Furthermore, the trends towards shorter food durations and sharper flood peaks have also been evidenced in studies conducted at larger scales. In a review of the impact of dams on the Mekong’s hydrology, Hecht et al. (2018) noted the reduction of the annual flood pulse as one of the main negative effects, especially in terms of floodplain ecology and fisheries. Similarly, Pokhrel et al. (2018) found that the annual flood pulse in the lower basin would be dampened by 50% and delayed by one month. This is also echoed by Chua et al. (2022), who found the duration of the flood season to have decreased by 26 days at Kampong Cham and by 40 days at Phnom Penh due to a later start and an earlier end. [SOURCE: Page_328]

The attribution of the causes of these changes is tilted towards hydropower infrastructure having larger impacts than other drivers, such as land use change or climate change. Binh et al. (2020), for instance, found that the relative impact of infrastructure outweighs that of climate change in their study of long-term alterations in the Mekong’s flow regime adaptation resulting possible strategies for the Vietnamese part of the delta. Similarly, Shin et al. (2020) found that historically, it was climate variability that governed variations in surface water dynamics in the Mekong basin. Since 2009, however, the authors find that the impacts of dams have increased steadily in their influence and have come to dominate. [SOURCE: Page_328]

What are the roles that Preks play in catalyzing these processes at the local level?         At the local level of the case study area, the Preks’ primary role in catalyzing hydrological processes is to act as a vector of flooding and drainage during the wet season, though the extent to which they can fulfill this functionality depends on their rehabilitation status to a large degree. At the beginning of the flood season, when river water levels rise, Preks begin to flood as soon as water levels in the Bassac exceed the bed elevation at the head of the Preks. Frequently, this head elevation is higher than in other parts of the Prek, as the head is a hotspot for sedimentation. Consequently, threshold effects are observable and focused excavations are sometimes organized by communities, such as at Prek Nou. During the flood rise, Preks serve as conduits for water from the Bassac towards the floodplains in the Boeung areas. This dynamic inverses once the [SOURCE: Page_328]

328 [SOURCE: Page_328]

flood peak has passed. Then, water drains through the Preks back into the river mainstream. [SOURCE: Page_329]

Another component of the system the importance of which must not be underestimated, though, is the network of smaller lowland canals in the Boeung at the tail end of the Preks, which was constructed during the Khmer Rouge regime. It appears that the bed elevation of these canals is often lower than that of Preks, especially non-rehabilitated ones. Consequently, they can serve as a vector for both flooding and drainage even when Preks have fallen dry. For instance, it can be observed that at the tail end of some non-rehabilitated Preks, inundations actually begin before the Prek itself is flooded, as water is transported through rehabilitated Preks, such as Prek Chann, and then flows north and south through the canal network before overspilling the banks of the canals. Similarly, at the end of the wet season, water continues to drain through the canals - especially towards the South - even after not-rehabilitated Preks have fallen dry. [SOURCE: Page_329]

Finally, it must be noted that the role of the Preks during the dry season in terms of hydrology differs considerably from its role during the wet season. In the months between November and June, the Preks’ main functionality is no longer as a conduit of water, but rather as a reservoir from which anthropogenic flows originate. Farmers pump Prek water onto their fields to irrigate their crops, thereby creating a steady flow of water from the Prek "reservoir" onto the surrounding surface areas. This, in turn, contributes to surface runoff, infiltration, and evapotranspiration flows. [SOURCE: Page_329]

The role of Preks for sub-surface flows is harder to estimate due to a lack of data. As noted in Chapter 6, it can be conjectured that during the wet season, when water levels in the Preks are typically high, an influent situation dominates, with Prek water infiltrating into the surrounding banks and Chamkar areas. After the flood, this situation reverses into an effluent one, with water that was stored in the banks exfiltrating back into the Prek. To some extent, this is evidenced by bank collapses, which appear to be partially due to high soil water pressure. Furthermore, there is some evidence that water infiltrating from irrigation during the dry season filtrates back to the Prek. At some rehabilitated Preks, it appears that the Prek is even in direct connection with the groundwater table. [SOURCE: Page_329]

What are the ecosystem services from which people in the Prek area benefit? How are these linked to hydrological processes? Broadly, the ecosystem services from which people [SOURCE: Page_329]

329 [SOURCE: Page_329]

benefit in the area can be delineated into flood-related and not-flood related ones. Flood-related ecosystem services are largely of a regulating nature. The annual monsoon inundations, catalyzed by the Preks, deposit valuable nutrient-laden sediments on the plots in the Boeung area. Further, they recharge soil- and groundwater, providing a basis for recession rice cultivation. During the wet season, floods provide valuable shallow-water habitats on the floodplains in which populations of fish, which form an integral part of the local diet, can regenerate. Another regulating service that can be felt immediately by the population in the area is the regulation of pests. Rat populations especially are reduced provided that the flood level is high enough for a sufficient duration. On a larger scale, inundations in the Cambodian Mekong delta also provides flood attenuation, though it is downstream communities who benefit from this regulating service. [SOURCE: Page_330]

In terms of not-flood-related ecosystem services, the Preks serve as valuable sources of water. Primarily, this water is used for irrigation, but several people interviewed in the case study area also use it to water their cattle and for non-dietary household needs. Furthermore, it is a common practice to fish in the Preks - though catches have declined recently - and to collect natural vegetation along their lengths, which is then used for food, fuel, or, in some cases, medicinal purposes. At non-rehabilitated Preks, where no regulations to the contrary exist, people also plant fruit and vegetables on the banks of the Prek and use the branches of the trees that grow along their banks as construction material and for fish traps. While there is water in the Prek, locals further use them as routes for transport, though this practice seems to be in decline, particularly at rehabilitated Preks, where better roads were constructed on the banks. [SOURCE: Page_330]

How will future developments and trends impact hydrology in the Prek area, and in con- sequence, the ecosystem services to which it is linked? What measures can be taken to mitigate or prevent negative impacts?        The regional hydrological analysis and the newly constructed model for not-flood-related and flood-related ecosystem services in the case study area have shown that river water levels are the principal driver of inundations in the area. Flood- related ecosystem services are thus largely dependent on upstream developments, including climate change-induced shifts in precipitation patterns over the Mekong basin, and hydropower development on the Mekong mainstream and its tributaries. Going by the overall consensus in the literature (Hoang et al., 2016; Yun et al., 2020; Binh et al., 2020), which points towards shorter floods, and lower flood peaks, flood-related ecosystem services would thus be set to [SOURCE: Page_330]

330 [SOURCE: Page_330]

decline. In contrast, this was not reflected in the modelled scenarios, as they use projections from a study by Hoang et al. (2019), which are based on the average of the pre-2000 period in Kratie. This further illustrates the importance of reliable upstream projections - and the comparison of different projections - when estimating future flood-related ecosystem services in the Prek area. [SOURCE: Page_331]

In contrast, the availability of water in the Preks during the dry season and thus the provision of the majority of not-flood-related ecosystem services is dependent on two factors: river water levels and the bed elevation of Preks and canals, which governs when natural inflow from the river becomes possible. Most future projections (Hoang et al., 2019; Hecht et al., 2018; Yun et al., 2020) see an increase in dry season flows due to the impact of both climate change and hydropower development. However, the simulations carried out using the eco-hydrological model developed in the course of this thesis show that they would still be too low to provide sufficient inflow of water into the Preks at their current bed level to fulfill water needs, especially in combination with climate change drivers over the case study area. However, the model also shows that rehabilitation is an effective counter-measure to these developments. Lowering the bed level of the Preks ensures inflow and thus water provisioning services. Consequently, agricultural production increases in the modelled scenarios in which Prek levels were lowered, despite other negative drivers. [SOURCE: Page_331]

Possibilities for Further Development While the methods presented in the course of this thesis have largely succeeded in answering the research questions outlined at the beginning of this thesis, there are several possibilities for further improvement. [SOURCE: Page_331]

Most fundamentally, the methods could be refined if more detailed information about the case study area became available. As outlined above, only a limited amount of information available in the case study area. Part of this is due to the fact that fieldwork was cut short, for instance with regard to the number of interviews that could be conducted. In part, it is also because only little information on aspects such as soil properties and subsurface configurations could be collected so far. Similarly, the training dataset for the LULC classification was limited for the same reason. The data that does exist from secondary sources had to be scrutinized carefully. For instance, while the MRC data was invaluable in the course of its thesis, it was also a source of uncertainty since metadata was unavailable and aspects such as gauge elevation and rating curve changes [SOURCE: Page_331]

331 [SOURCE: Page_331]

over the course of the time series remained opaque. [SOURCE: Page_332]

Furthermore, the current setup of the numerical model presented in the last chapter of this thesis is, as emphasized, a prototype with room for improvement in multiple ways - from refining scenarios and inundation calculation to adding modules for subsurface and overland flow. Its use of LULC and cropping data from the 2020-21 season further limits its flexibility with regard to future developments, and especially the responses of the local communities to these developments. Similarly, the WAFL only offers a limited capability for estimating inundation extents for future scenarios and thus flood-related ecosystem services, contingent on the static nature of river-floodplain connections. While developed at a regional scale, it proved to apply well at a finer scale, due, in large part, to the resolution of Sentinel products. However, its application at finer scales could be refined through adapted delay times according to the distance of pixels to the reference gauge. [SOURCE: Page_332]

Other studies conducted in the Cambodian Mekong delta have faced similar limitations and issues, even though many of them were conducted at a larger scale. Horton et al. (2022), for instance, used MIKE-11, a 1D flood propagation model, and IWRM-Sub, a 2D flood duration and extent model to assess the impacts of future development scenarios on the Cambodian Mekong delta. However, this study used the digital elevation model derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM), which is of limited use in the case study area due to the fact that its data was recorded prior to 2009, it has a limited accuracy in particularly flat areas, and its 90 m resolution would not be enough to represent the low terrain gradients and small-scale topography features in the case study area. Possible alternatives are the use of TanDEM-X (12m), though this has also been shown to have limitations in the course of this thesis, as well as the error-reduced version of SRTM - Multi-Error-Removed-Improved-Terrain (MERIT) DEM (cf. Hawker et al. (2019)). With more accurate DEM information, the use of models that use the full St. Venant’s equations - such as Delft^3D, MIKE21, and LISFLOOD - could be envisioned in the case study area. However, even then the sheer number of connections to be represented would make these models difficult to parametrize. To this end, data assimilation from remote sensing and airborne data acquistion could be explored. [SOURCE: Page_332]

Finally, there are aspects of large-scale developments that have not yet been taken into account conceptually, such as the impact of sea level rise and sediment starvation. These current [SOURCE: Page_332]

332 [SOURCE: Page_332]

shortcomings offer avenues towards possible improvements in multiple ways. For instance, agent-based decision modules could be added to take into account adaptation processes in local communities and their land-use practices in response to drivers of change (cf. Richard et al. (2022)). Similarly, further modules based on socio-hydrology and eco-hydrology could be added to refine the representation of processes and future simulations. [SOURCE: Page_333]

Overall, however, the initial performance of the model is promising. It offers an innovative, multi-method approach to modelling the interactions between ecology and water, also taking account of the human dimension by integrating agricultural practices such as integration. [SOURCE: Page_333]

Transferability and Larger Context A final aspect of this thesis that needs to be highlighted is that it carries implications for the larger conceptual context in which it was presented, and that several of its results are transferable to similar areas worldwide. This applies particularly to the results pertaining to LULC classification, the WAFL, and the newly developed eco-hydrological model. [SOURCE: Page_333]

The LULC analysis conducted in the course of this thesis has provided a widely applicable comparison of the performance of supervised classification methods on the cloud computing platform Google Earth Engine. Future studies can benefit from these results with regard to their choice of input imagery, band selection, and training dataset - as well as the process of optimizing their tuning parameters. [SOURCE: Page_333]

The WAFL provides an avenue towards re-constructing historical inundation extents and changes in inundation processes in otherwise data-sparse areas. The ultimate aim of the developed methodology is to provide long-term insights into the spatial dynamics of inundations in tropical deltas. Applying the approach to the Mekong delta showed that this is possible with acceptable average accuracies of 87% in comparison to historical inundation maps derived from Landsat. Such comparisons have also highlighted the limitations of the WAFL with regard to long-term changes in local terrain configuration, and the challenges posed by LULC characteristics such as the presence of natural vegetation. For an application in other study areas, this means that a basic knowledge of changes in local conditions is a prerequisite for the development and application of the WAFL. An awareness of landcover dynamics - which can be assessed through historical LULC analysis - or significant shifts in terrain elevations and the river-floodplain [SOURCE: Page_333]

333 [SOURCE: Page_333]

connections, notably due to the construction of water control infrastructures, is crucial. It must also be noted that the WAFL is primarily applicable in areas where inundations are correlated largely with dynamics in river water levels. This refers to areas in which the influence of local precipitations and groundwater is limited and where there are few obstacles to the flow of water into and out of the floodplain. This can be mostly the case in semi-arid places but also in tropical areas like in the Mekong delta, as demonstrated in this study by the comparison of water level dynamics and Sentinel-derived inundation extents. Where historical records of water levels are available, as a first step in the application of WAFL, such an analysis should be used to elucidate the applicability of the methodology. However, in areas where inundations are significantly correlated with processes such as local precipitation or groundwater logging, adjustments to the correlation model can be made by introducing new input variables, provided time-series are available. Another possible extension of the WAFL is its use to detect the influence of hydraulic infrastructures by illustrating discrepancies between expected and observed inundation extents. A similar application of the Lamagat correlation model was already proposed by Bader et al. (2016). [SOURCE: Page_334]

The eco-hydrological model, finally, demonstrates the importance of small-scale observations and modelling approaches. Despite significant simplifications and limitations, it can represent local processes well, and is well-adapted to a data sparse environment. While it can be improved with regard to further quantification, a better description of various components, and possible further validation with in-situ data, it offers a transferable alternative approach to the down- scaling of coarser modelling data. This could offer interesting opportunities to represent local processes and explore scenarios in similar study areas across the globe, especially in (tropical) delta floodplains characterized by irrigation channels where similar questions of upstream influences and local development scenarios prevail, such as in the Tana river delta in Ethiopia and Kenya (Mwamlavya et al., 2021), the Indus river delta in Pakistan (Irfan et al., 2019; Kravtsova et al., 2009; Atif et al., 2021; Syvitski et al., 2013), and the Inner Niger Delta in Mali (Neal et al., 2012; O’Brien et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_334]

With regard to the larger conceptual context, this thesis has harnessed concepts from both ecohydrology and socio-hydrology and illustrated ways in which the two disciplines can be inte- grated, also with regard to the use of the framework of ecosystem services. The ecohydrological model presented in this thesis integrates a human dimension in multiple ways. First, it uses the [SOURCE: Page_334]

334 [SOURCE: Page_334]

anthropocentric ES framework. Second, it partly bases the delineation of its modelling units on human agricultural practices. The information necessary to do so partially stems from first-hand information given by the actors involved. To spatialize it, this first-hand information was used as the basis of a supervised remote sensing classification. This approach illustrates how actor-based data can be used to inform numerical approaches, and how the conceptual distance between socio- and ecohydrology can be bridged. In addition, potential future developments in the model further explore this interstitial sphere, such as the incorporation of retroactions between land use and sociological dynamics into the ecohydrological model. [SOURCE: Page_335]

Overall Conclusion      Overall, this thesis provides an innovative look at the ecohydrological approach to deltaic agro-ecosystems such as those present on the floodplains of the Cambodian Mekong delta. It combines multiple methods and uses them to articulate the processes in the Prek system from diverse angles, as any single method would provide only a limited, partial view. In addition, it can be seen as a contribution to ecohydrology as a whole that the model in this thesis accounts explicitly for the human element of agro-ecosystems by integrating information on cultivation practices gathered in the course of fieldwork, and delineating homogeneous surface units on this basis. [SOURCE: Page_335]

The results presented in this thesis have illustrated that the Cambodian Mekong Delta is tied closely into the developments, both hydrological and ecological, in the larger Mekong region. Basin-wide trends in hydrological dynamics are reflected in both local water levels and the incidence and duration of monsoon inundations on the deltaic floodplains. Large-scale developments such as the decrease in fish populations are keenly felt by local communities, as has emerged from interviews. Most of the local stakeholders who were interviewed demonstrated a deep awareness of the larger nexus of cause and effect into which their communities are tied. Several of them talked about how they saw upstream hydropower development shift the rhythm of the river. Others drew the link between dwindling inundation extents and soil water deficiencies and the abundance of rat populations. However, it has also emerged that they see local measures, in particular the rehabilitation of the Preks, as a way to address the negative impacts that they are facing as a result of these developments. [SOURCE: Page_335]

The Preks themselves tie the floodplains of the Cambodian Mekong Delta much more closely [SOURCE: Page_335]

335 [SOURCE: Page_335]

to the river and its distributaries than its Vietnamese counterpart. Largely devoid of gates and dykes, they act as a vector for flooding and drainage, as a conduit for sedimentation and fish, as a route for transport and a source of irrigation water. Rehabilitating them to make water inflow possible year-round is perceived as uniformly positive by the stakeholders who were interviewed, despite issues such as bank collapses and re-settlements of individual families. The increased availability of irrigation water as well as the accompanying roads on the Prek banks are seen as the biggest benefits, as they increase the production potential of farmers’ plots as well as the ease of accessing them. [SOURCE: Page_336]

The challenges that the Cambodian Mekong Delta faces are symptomatic for, if not identical to, the situation of numerous deltas worldwide. Some methods presented in this thesis, such as the WAFL and LULC classification, and - to a certain extent - the numerical model can be transferred to similar deltaic areas to shed light on the shifts in hydrological processes and their impacts. Universally, though, it can be stated that deltaic areas are at the mercy of developments that happen at much larger scales - upstream hydropower development, basin-wide climate change impacts, and global sea level rise to name but a few. There is little deltaic communities can do to influence these developments. They can, however, adapt - and in this local infrastructure such as the Preks play a crucial role, as this thesis has demonstrated. For over a century, Preks have contributed to the enhancement of agriculture in the Cambodian Mekong Delta, raising land for the cultivation of high-value crops, and providing irrigation water when it is needed most. Despite the social and political upheavals of the 20th century, they have remained integral to the community structure and agricultural practices in the region. With sufficient care, maintenance, and the beneficial effects of rehabilitation projects, they will be able to catalyze crucial ecosystem services to support local communities well into an as of yet uncertain future. [SOURCE: Page_336]

B Description and Documentation of Each Prek in the Case Study Area [SOURCE: Page_393]

This chapter provides a brief description of each Prek as well as photographic documentation. It is primarily based on fieldwork conducted in June 2019, but has been updated with information from later field trips where necessary. [SOURCE: Page_393]

B.1      Prek Cham Kroum [SOURCE: Page_393]

The head of Prek Cham Kroum, the northernmost Prek in the study area, is located close to the 7th Cambodia-China Friendship bridge across the Tonle Bassac. Water can flow freely from the Bassac into the Prek. Directly along the head of the Prek, there is a tight agglomeration of [SOURCE: Page_393]

393 [SOURCE: Page_393]

houses. The Prek itself, though filled with water along its whole length, is overgrown with water hyacinths (Eichhornia crassipes). The profile of the Prek is well-defined, though erosion effects are visible in some places. Vegetation is lush along its whole length, with Mango trees being the dominant crop over large stretches. [SOURCE: Page_394]

A particularity of this Prek are a number of cylindrical containers, probably used for the storage of liquids, that can be found in several places along the Prek (though whether those liquids are water, growth enhancers for mango trees, or pesticides could not yet be determined). [SOURCE: Page_394]

It was visible in several places that vegetation along the Prek is being removed. In some spots, cut-down branches of banana and bamboo trees could be seen. In others, there were charred spots on the ground where dried vegetation had been burned. [SOURCE: Page_394]

For the majority of its length, the course of Prek Cham Kroum is very straight. However, at its tail end, it takes a sharp turn to the North and then curves towards its junction with the Prek Ambel in a wide bend. Here the area is covered by grassland and a small settlement is located along the Prek Ambel. According to the information of local inhabitants, the community in this settlement is predominately composed of Cham people. [SOURCE: Page_394]

The junction of the Prek with the Prek Ambel is not easily accessible since several houses are located directly on its banks and no open path leads to the waterfront. In itself, the junction is wide and open, but at the time of observation (June 2019), it was entirely overgrown with water hyacinths to the point where no open water surface was visible anymore. According to interviewees, there is an annual water shortage in the Prek in April and May. Water from the Prek is used for irrigation during both the dry and the rainy season when it is available. Furthermore, people fish in the Prek during the rainy season and use the vegetation found on the banks for their diet – predominantly morning glory (Ipomoea aquatica) and ivy gourd (Coccina grandis). In addition, some also plant vegetables and fruit on the banks of the Prek – bananas and papayas among others. In the past, the Prek was also commonly used as a source of domestic water, water for livestock and transport by boat during the rainy season. However, these uses ceased because clean water is now available from a communal supply pipe and a new road was constructed, rendering the waterway superfluous as a transport route. On an additional note, one farmer stated that fishing used to be possible in the Prek during both the dry and the rainy season, but that fish populations have declined in the past 10 years. [SOURCE: Page_394]

394 [SOURCE: Page_394]

Furthermore, a Farmer’s Water User Community (FWUC) appears to exist at Prek Cham Kroum, and an interviewed farmer is the deputy head of this association. According to him, its chief aims are to prevent the littering of the Prek, to prevent the unauthorized removal of sediments (which can lead to bank collapses) and to coordinate the clearing of vegetation on the bank of the Prek. According to the interviewee the association was created by his excellency Choa Tol, who works in the Ministry of the Interior, and its Khmer name is Pro Chea Kapea. Every farmer who has plots along the Prek belongs to the association. The interviewee’s duties as deputy head of the association include patrolling the Prek every 3-5 days to spot any illicit activities. The head of the FWUC is not elected, but chosen by the chief of the village. [SOURCE: Page_395]

The Prek has not been rehabilitated, though it appears that it would be welcomed by the local residents in order to supply sufficient water for irrigation. In 2018, the FWUC coordinated an effort to supply water during the dry season because there was less than usual in the Prek. They asked the commune to assist them in renting a big pumping station to pump water into the Prek as well as to acquire sandbags so that the spread of the irrigation water on the fields could be channeled to crops that have the largest water requirements. According to the interviewee, the effort succeeded and together with the funding the FWUC received from the commune, the individual farmers only had to contribute 2000 Riel each to cover the costs of the operation. [SOURCE: Page_395]

395 [SOURCE: Page_395]

(a) Head of the Prek and China Friendship              (b) Mango trees and liquid storage containers. Bridge. [SOURCE: Page_396]

(c) Grassland and Cham settlement at tail end.           (d) Junction of the Prek and Prek Ambel. [SOURCE: Page_396]

(e) Dense water hyacinth vegetation.                 (f) Charred spots from burned vegetation. [SOURCE: Page_396]

Figure B.1: Visual documentation of Prek Cham Kroum. [SOURCE: Page_396]

396 [SOURCE: Page_396]

B.2      Prek Me Srok [SOURCE: Page_397]

At the head of Prek Me Srok, water can flow freely into the Prek. A wooden bridge spans the head of the Prek, a small concrete-paved path leading along the bank of the Bassac. Several boats could be seen navigating the Prek in June 2019 and the water surface was relatively free of water hyacinths. Water is present throughout the Prek and at the time of the visit (ca. 11:30 a.m.), a slight current towards the Prek Ambel was visible. [SOURCE: Page_397]

The profile of the Prek is well-defined throughout and the roads along the Prek are passable. [SOURCE: Page_397]

In some places, charred patches were bank vegetation was removed through burning can be observed. Locally, erosion effects and bank collapses are visible. [SOURCE: Page_397]

Similar to the Prek Cham Kroum, the course of the Prek Me Srok is straight for the majority of its length, but takes a sharp turn to the North at its end, to join with the Prek Ambel after a double curve. At this point, erosion effects are clearly visible on a larger scale and some presence of water hyacinths could be noted. [SOURCE: Page_397]

For comparison purposes, the pumping stations along the Prek Me Srok were georeferenced. Unfortunately, the majority of the pumps had already been removed by farmers in preparation for the inundations during the monsoon season. What remained were blue PVC pipes leading from the Prek to the top of the bank and under the road to the fields. It has to be noted that not all those pumping stations are equipped with individual pumps during the dry season – rather one pump is shifted between several pumping stations. However, while the numbers of pumps and pumping stations might not correspond entirely, the large number of pumping stations still bears testimony to extensive irrigation activities during certain times of the year. Overall, a total of 69 pumping stations could be counted on the Prek’s length of 4.700 m. This equals ca. 1.5 pumping stations per 100 m. [SOURCE: Page_397]

Water from the Prek is used for irrigation during the dry season, to water and wash livestock and, for domestic water supply (though not for drinking water). Several interviewees also stated that they use the bank vegetation – specifically, morning glory. One of the interviewees also fishes regularly in the Prek, though he noted that this activity was limited due to declining fish populations. [SOURCE: Page_397]

397 [SOURCE: Page_397]

The Prek has recently been rehabilitated – and several interviewees expressed satisfaction in this regard, appreciating the year-round availability of water in the Prek. The Prek was deepened and the excavated material was used to raise the road on the bank. Before the Prek was rehabilitated, there was a shortage of water during several months of the year for seven years. [SOURCE: Page_398]

(a) Head of the Prek, with bridge.                (b) Boat used to transport goods along the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_398]

(c) Bank collapses along the Prek.                      (d) Road and profile along the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_398]

(e) Junction of the Prek with Prek Ambel, erosion effects along the banks. [SOURCE: Page_398]

Figure B.2: Visual documentation of Prek Me Srok. [SOURCE: Page_398]

398 [SOURCE: Page_398]

B.3      Prek Lok [SOURCE: Page_399]

The head of Prek Lok shows extensive sediment deposits separating the current level of the Bassac from the mouth of the Prek, constricting the inflow into the Prek. This area is actually being used as a recreational area by the local population and several people could be observed sunbathing on the sandbanks and swimming in the Bassac. Furthermore, extensive macrophyte floating vegetation covers the water surfaces at the head of the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_399]

Nevertheless, water is present in many parts of the Prek, though water hyacinths cover large areas of the water surface. At one point, there is a ford where a road crosses the Prek [SOURCE: Page_399]

Like Prek Cham Kroum and Prek Me Srok, Prek Lok’s tail connects with the Prek Ambel, though without the curve that characterizes this area of the other two Preks. Beside the junction of the Prek Ambel and the Prek Lok, there is a small agglomeration of houses. [SOURCE: Page_399]

Along the Prek, but especially at its tail end, extensive erosion effects are visible. [SOURCE: Page_399]

Two people were interviewed in June 2019 at this Prek – one of them a fisherman who lives at the junction of Prek Ambel and Prek Lok, the other one a farmer who has four plots along the Prek. According to their information, the Prek has never been rehabilitated, but they would welcome such a rehabilitation. The farmer noted that if water were in the Prek year-round, not only would it allow him to grow a second crop of rice, but also to use his boat on the Prek. The farmer, who lives in the village at the head end of the Prek, uses the municipal pipe for the supply of domestic water, but the fisherman uses water from the Prek and Prek Ambel, though he boils it first. The water from the Prek is furthermore used for the watering of livestock. Both interviewees also use the vegetation found along the banks of the canal, especially morning glory, though the fisherman also noted that his family sometimes eats the flowers of the water hyacinths. [SOURCE: Page_399]

At this Prek too the number of visible pumping stations was counted to compare it to Prek Me Srok. Only a total of 8 pumping station over the whole length of the Prek could be observed in June 2019. While this is probably also due to the fact that many pumping stations were removed entirely for the duration of the wet season, it also shows that irrigation activity at this Prek is lower than at Prek Me Srok. [SOURCE: Page_399]

399 [SOURCE: Page_399]

(a) Head of the Prek, with sediment deposits               (b) Bridge across the Prek in the village area. preventing inflow. [SOURCE: Page_400]

(c) Erosion at the tail end of Prek Lok.               (d) Junction of Prek Lok and the Prek Ambel. [SOURCE: Page_400]

(e) Ford across Prek Lok at its tail end. [SOURCE: Page_400]

Figure B.3: Visual documentation of Prek Lok. [SOURCE: Page_400]

B.4      Prek Pok [SOURCE: Page_400]

The head of Prek Pok allows for free inflow into the Prek, although there are some sediment deposits. It has to be noted that the head of Prek Pok and Prek Hom do not lie directly at the Bassac, but rather at another man-made channel. An island with a Pagoda on it separates the heads of these Preks from the Bassac. The channel connecting the heads of Prek Pok and Prek [SOURCE: Page_400]

400 [SOURCE: Page_400]

Hom to the Bassac is called Wat Koh channel and begins just beside the head of Prek Lok. As with Prek Lok, there are sediment deposits and macrophyte floating plant vegetation constricting the free inflow of water into the channel and thus into the Preks it supplies. [SOURCE: Page_401]

Water is present in some parts of the Prek, but there are two fords cutting through it, creating barriers for the water. In the farmer interviews it was stated that this was intentional so that the little water that there is in the Prek would be concentrated in the areas closer to the village to enable the farmers there to irrigate their crops. Consequently, the plots along the tail-half of the Prek are lying fallow during the dry season, as no water for irrigation is available. The ford closer to the village, which dams up the majority of the water present in the Prek, was apparently built in the early months of 2019, and, according to statements made by interviewees, is removed before the rainy season to enable a free flow of water during the annual monsoon inundation. [SOURCE: Page_401]

This Prek, unlike the others described so far, does not end in the Prek Ambel, but rather in a dead end. There is a ford at the end of the Prek, another road crossing through, but no further channels to which it is connected. [SOURCE: Page_401]

The two farmers interviewed at this Prek in June 2019 grow beans, corn and dry season rice on their plots and use the Prek as source for irrigation water and for livestock. One of them also uses it for transport by boat, to fish in occasionally and, in the month of June, to harvest morning glory and ivy gourd on its banks. The Prek has not been rehabilitated and both farmers report a lack of water in the Prek from November to June. Both also agree that they would welcome a rehabilitation project and the increased availability of water throughout the year, especially since some of their plots are currently lying fallow. As noted above, a ford including a small dam was built to concentrate the little water that is available during the dry season in one half of the Prek. Furthermore, there is a coordination among farmers to pump water from the Bassac into the Prek when it is needed. Two or three farmers possess bigger pumps and take on the task of pumping water on demand, charging 10.000-20.000 Riel per hour (open to negotiation) to cover labour and operational costs as well as to make a small profit. The chief of the village is responsible for Prek maintenance and asks the farmers to take care of the Prek vegetation in front of their houses and plots. Apparently, the village chief also coordinated the removal of sediments with a private company. From what the interviewees could say, the company dredged parts of the canal where road accessibility was possible, and used some of the sediments to repair minor bank collapses. [SOURCE: Page_401]

401 [SOURCE: Page_401]

It appears that the company accepted part of the sediments as payment for their services, because they can sell the excavated material to farmers who wish to raise their land. If the company is asked to also dredge parts of the Prek that are more difficult to access, the village chief would have to collect money from the farmers to pay the charges, and that is apparently rather difficult. [SOURCE: Page_402]

(a) Beginning of Wat Koh channel, with                     (b) Wat Koh channel with Prek Pok de- sediment deposits.                                         branching. [SOURCE: Page_402]

(c) Ford across the Prek, with dammed up                   (d) Bridge across the Prek in the village water on the right and dry channel on the                  area. left. [SOURCE: Page_402]

(e) Fields lying fallow at the tail end of the               (f) Ford across the tail-end of the Prek. Prek due to lack of irrigation water. [SOURCE: Page_402]

Figure B.4: Visual documentation of Prek Pok [SOURCE: Page_402]

402 [SOURCE: Page_402]

B.5      Prek Hom [SOURCE: Page_403]

Prek Hom, like Prek Pok is connected to the Bassac through the Wat Koh channel. However, while Prek Pok debranches from the Wat Koh channel, Prek Hom is its continuation. Effectively, the Wat Koh channel takes a sharp turn to the West and becomes Prek Hom. In this transitional area, a large pool of water exists. [SOURCE: Page_403]

Prek Hom’s profile is well-defined throughout. The Prek is broad and apparently of consider- able depth, for there is water in the channel throughout. In some places, water hyacinth vegetation is dense. Furthermore, several bank collapses and other, more minor, erosion sites were observed. In several places, people appear to have taken steps to prevent erosion by fortifying the bank with cut-off tree branches . [SOURCE: Page_403]

While its course is mostly straight, Prek Hom takes several turns at its tail end, before ending in a perpendicular irrigation/drainage channel. On the other side of this channel, a smaller water course continues in the direction of Prek Ambel. [SOURCE: Page_403]

At Prek Hom, two farmers were interviewed in June 2019. They grow mangoes, rice, corn, beans and sugarcane along the Prek. The Prek has not been rehabilitated and in this case the two farmers disagree on whether it would be a good idea to do so. The current system is that farmers coordinate among themselves to hire machines to remove sedimentary deposits at the head of the Prek when it is necessary to do so. The costs are split amongst themselves. One of the interviewed farmers is satisfied with this system while the other finds that it is rather expensive and would welcome a rehabilitation of the Prek that would ensure free inflow all year-round. Furthermore, he also stated that an even greater advantage of rehabilitation for him would be the construction of a better road along the Prek. He currently finds it very difficult to transport his equipment and crop from his house at the head of the Prek to his plots at its tail. [SOURCE: Page_403]

Both interviewees use the Prek for irrigation and domestic water supply. One of them also uses it for transport by boat, to water his livestock, for fishing and as a source of food in the form of bank vegetation such as morning glory. [SOURCE: Page_403]

B.6      Prek Nou [SOURCE: Page_405]

Unlike Prek Hom and Prek Pok, the head of Prek Nou lies directly on the Bassac, though it does not debranch in a straight line, but rather in a backwards curve. Nonetheless, a free inflow of water is possible and the Prek is supplied with water throughout. Water hyacinths are abundant in certain places. The Prek’s profile is well-defined but erosion is very pronounced in some places. It ends in the same perpendicular channel as Prek Hom. [SOURCE: Page_405]

Two farmers were interviewed on this Prek in June 2019. Both of them use the water from the Prek for irrigation. One of them also uses it for his domestic water supply, to water his livestock and sometimes as a source of food in the form of vegetation that grows on its banks. The other farmer also uses the Prek for transport by boat and fishes in it, though only for domestic use. Beans, mangoes, corn and rice are grown on the plots. Two years ago, the Prek was rehabilitated and consequently, there is enough water in the Prek year-round. Both farmers feel that the rehabilitation was a success and appreciate the continuous availability of water in the Prek. The farmers agree that there used to be a FWUC, more than ten years ago. However, it was dissolved due to conflicting interests. The FWUC put up a blockade so that the Chamkar would not be flooded during the rainy season, but there were other farmers who needed the water. Nowadays, it is the chief of the village who is in charge of Prek maintenance, though according to the information by the interviewees, no strict rules are observed. The farmers are responsible for clearing the vegetation on the banks of the Prek in front of their houses and their plots. [SOURCE: Page_405]

(a) Head of the Prek.                            (b) Water hyacinth vegetation. [SOURCE: Page_405]

Figure B.6: Visual documentation of Prek Nou [SOURCE: Page_405]

405 [SOURCE: Page_405]

B.7        Prek Put [SOURCE: Page_406]

Out of all the Preks in the study area, Prek Put is in the worst state of disrepair. Its head is entirely disconnected from the Bassac by sediment deposits. The concrete foundations of an old pumping station that was used to lift water from the Bassac to the Prek are still visible, but the endeavour was abandoned several years ago and the pump has been removed. A dirt road crosses in front of the abandoned pumping station, further separating the head of the Prek from the Bassac. [SOURCE: Page_406]

In itself, the Prek is filled with waste and vegetation and in several places, earthen dams have been erected across what remains of the channel in order to let streets and paths cross over. In some cases, these incorporate pipes in order to let water pass, should it enter the Prek. But even these pipes are often clogged with vegetation or missing entirely. In one case the brick foundation of a garden wall cuts through the Prek completely without any possibility of water passage. [SOURCE: Page_406]

From what remains of it, it can be deduced that Prek Put’s original profile was already considerably smaller than that of the other Preks in the study area. Furthermore, it is also the shortest Prek. From what was observed during the field trip, the Prek hardly qualifies as such anymore. Its sedimentation has reached levels to leave it hardly more than a longitudinal depression in the landscape. [SOURCE: Page_406]

According to the information gained in the interview with a local, hardly any water is present in the Prek even in the high period of flooding during the wet season. It does not serve for irrigation purposes – the interviewee stated that it is easier to use water from nearby Prek Nou if it is possible to do so and to abandon the plots if it is not. The only use that can be derived from the Prek is the use of vegetation such as morning glory and bitter melon. Furthermore, the interviewee stated that a rehabilitation of the Prek would entail major conflicts of interest, since several local residents have built their houses directly on the banks of the Prek or very close to it and would have to be resettled. [SOURCE: Page_406]

406 [SOURCE: Page_406]

(a) Head of Prek Put at the Bassac.                    (b) Remains of the old pumping station. [SOURCE: Page_407]

(c) Earthen dam across Prek Put.                          (d) Prek Put, entirely overgrown. [SOURCE: Page_407]

Figure B.7: Visual documentation of Prek Put [SOURCE: Page_407]

B.8      Prek Chann [SOURCE: Page_407]

Prek Chann diverges perpendicularly from the Bassac and has a straight course all the way to its end. It was rehabilitated in 2017 and the Prek was broadened, deepened and a new road and gate were constructed. The gate is located ca. 700 m inland from the head of the Prek. However, a few hundred meters West of the gate, major bank collapses have occurred since the rehabilitation, posing a constriction on the amount of water that can flow through the Prek. Prek Chann ends in a perpendicular irrigation channel. [SOURCE: Page_407]

407 [SOURCE: Page_407]

Two farmers were interviewed at this Prek in July 2019, one of them being the head of the local FWUC. Both interviewees use the Prek as a source for irrigation water all year round and as a source of water for their livestock. Furthermore, one of them fishes in the Prek all year round. Both of them also state that they use the vegetation that grows on the banks, and one of them plants certain vegetables such as lemongrass, garlic, bitter lemon and Chinese cabbage on the banks himself. They were furthermore in agreement that the rehabilitation of the Prek, which was carried out in 2017, has been a positive change for them, enabling them to use their plots more effectively. One of the interviewees had to move her entire house back by 3 m during the rehabilitation, but still stated that it had been worth it. [SOURCE: Page_408]

Regarding the operation of the gate, the interviewees did not mention any particular conflicts. The head of the FWUC, who was interviewed, is in charge of the operation of the gate. He states that he leaves the gate open between November and June, when there is a shortage of water in the Prek but closes it between June and October in order to prevent soil erosion. While he did not discuss this operation schedule with all the members of the FWUC, he did consult with one other farmer before deciding on it. He also noted that the gate is opened very slowly, since there was an accident in 2018 when the gate was opened abruptly. A farmer who had been fishing in the Prek at the time was swept away by the suddenly rising water and almost drowned. [SOURCE: Page_408]

One major issue at the Prek Chann are the bank collapses that occurred after rehabilitation. As mentioned above, they constrict the flow of water. The head of the FWUC states that he has already contacted the pertinent authorities, but has not yet heard back from them. Apart from deciding on the schedule for gate operation and managing the repair of the bank collapses, the head of the FWUC also coordinates the clearing of the vegetation on the banks of the Prek. The system is that every farmer is responsible for clearing the vegetation that borders on their plots, which seems to work so far. The head of the FWUC said that if someone did not meet their duties, he would consider making them pay for the water from the Prek. All the farmers who have plots along the Prek are in the FWUC. The head is elected democratically. [SOURCE: Page_408]

408 [SOURCE: Page_408]

(c) Concrete fortification of banks behind the                (d) View towards tail end of the Prek. gate. [SOURCE: Page_409]
