409 [SOURCE: Page_409]

B.9      Prek Touch [SOURCE: Page_410]

Prek Touch is an unrehabilitated, heavily overgrown Prek with hardly any water present. What water there was seems to have been pumped not from the head of the Prek but from its tail-end, where another irrigation channel, this one filled with water, is located, separated from the Prek by an earthen mound. There is a pump and a plastic pipe to transport water from one channel to the other. This channel at the end of the Prek branches off from a perpendicular drainage/irrigation channel. Furthermore there is a half-sunken, but still operational bridge located at the junction of these two channels that allow for a relatively dry crossing. [SOURCE: Page_410]

The lack of water was evident in the agricultural practices and general vegetation that could be observed along the Prek. A great number of fields lay fallow, though some farmers could be seen attempting to cultivate fruit and vegetables such as cucumbers. [SOURCE: Page_410]

Two farmers were interviewed at this Prek in June 2019. They have crops consisting of mango trees, mung beans and dry season rice in plots along the Prek. The Prek has never been rehabilitated and both interviewees state that there is not sufficient water for them to irrigate crops during the dry season months. (Though one of the farmers stated that there was no water in the Prek between November and July, while the other reported such a lack only between December and April.) Both farmers use the Prek for irrigation and transport by boat during the rainy season. One of them further uses it for domestic water supply and watering his livestock, while the other fishes in the Prek whenever possible. Both of them also report using the vegetation found on the banks, especially morning glory. Furthermore, they stated that there is a private water seller, who supplies the Prek with water when there is no natural inflow during the dry season at the price of 100 $ per ha per crop cycle. [SOURCE: Page_410]

According to the interviewees, there used to be a FWUC until 9 years ago, which was founded and coordinated by the village chief. However, when the village chief died, the association fell apart. Now, it is the current village chief who is nominally in charge of Prek maintenance, but it appears that no measures are being taken. Both farmers seem very enthusiastic about the possibility of Prek rehabilitation and would welcome the extended presence of water in the Prek to grow another cycle of crops. [SOURCE: Page_410]

410 [SOURCE: Page_410]

After the interviews with the farmers, a third interview was conducted at this Prek – namely with the private water seller who uses a big pump to supply the Prek during the dry season when no natural inflow is possible. He is a farmer himself, but has been taking the additional responsibility of pumping water from the Bassac into the Prek for five years. According to him, he started this activity to supply his own family’s plots but was approached by other farmers soon after. He bases his pricing policy on the plot size and the crop type and charges between 150 000 and 300 000 Riel per ha per season. Payment is collected at the end of the season, generally without many problems, even though there are currently several people who owe him money. When the pumps are running, he leaves them on for 24 h/day. When water is required in the Prek, he pumps for one week and then takes a break of 2-3 days before beginning again. At the moment, he supplies the plots of ca. 20 farmers with water during the dry season. Asked about the possibility of Prek rehabilitation, the private water seller stated that he would still welcome it. According to him, it would be a big advantage for his own plots if water were available without the necessity of additional pumping activities, which are not a big source of additional income for him. [SOURCE: Page_411]

411 [SOURCE: Page_411]

(a) Pump that is used to lift water into the Prek.         (b) Fields lying fallow at the tail end of the Prek due to lack of water. [SOURCE: Page_412]

(c) Head of the Prek, with pumping station to lift water from the Bassac into the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_412]

(d) Junction of the two irrigation channels, with the half submerged bridge that can be used for crossing. [SOURCE: Page_412]

Figure B.9: Visual documentation of Prek Touch [SOURCE: Page_412]

B.10 Prek Thom [SOURCE: Page_412]

Prek Thom forms the southern border of the study area. It diverges directly from the Bassac and its tail end connects to the Prek Ambel. During this field trip in June 2019 only ca. half the length of the Prek could be visited, as road conditions on the second half were too difficult to continue. At the furthest point of the Prek that was visited, an old concrete construction [SOURCE: Page_412]

412 [SOURCE: Page_412]

is located. It appears that it used to be a gate to regulate the flow through the perpendicular irrigation channel that crosses the Prek at this point, but parts of the construction have been dismantled. The construction that remains seems to serve as a bridge across the perpendicular channel to continue the path along the Prek. [SOURCE: Page_413]

Along the tail-half of the Prek, a second Prek (Prek Khsae 500), which originates at Prek Ambel, runs in parallel to Prek Thom. In the area that was visited during this field trip, only a road on a dam separates those two channels. In some places, pipes have been installed through which water can be transferred from one Prek to the other. [SOURCE: Page_413]

According to the information gathered in the interviews in June 2019, at this Prek, the last rehabilitation took place in 1993. However, since then, sedimentation has clogged up the canal again. The interviewed farmers expressed a very positive attitude towards possible future rehabilitation, since year-round water availability would be a boon to their farming activities. In 2019, the farmers state that they lack water between January and August. There was a private water supplier who pumps water from the Bassac into the Prek for farmers along the Prek to use for their plots. He charges them at varying rates depending on the crop they want to irrigate and the diameter of the pipe that they are using to irrigate. The interviewees use the water from the Prek for irrigation and the vegetation found on the banks for their regular diets both during the dry and the rainy season. [SOURCE: Page_413]

The head of Prek Thom shows considerable sediment deposits and a regular inflow of water currently was not possible possible in 2019 during the first field survey. There is a ferry station at the head of this Prek, which offers the possibility to cross the Bassac. [SOURCE: Page_413]

However, significant changes occurred at Prek Thom during the duration of this thesis. In 2020, the Prek was excavated through a local initiative. The bed was deepened significantly, and the banks straightened, as is outlined in Chapter 4.3. [SOURCE: Page_413]

414 [SOURCE: Page_414]

C Translations of Quotations from Archival Research in Cambodia [SOURCE: Page_415]

In this study, we have taken the greatest account of the observations of the inhabitants, they have been excellent guides for us, this question of the drilling of sealing canals is of great interest to them, not only have they always agreed to inform us when we have had recourse to them, but more often than not they have come to us themselves to ask us to include in our projects the Preks which they have indicated to us to show us the best locations and the most economic way of carrying out the work. - First Mekong sealing studies, File Nr. 25754, p.7 1 [SOURCE: Page_415]

The Tiams had once found a way to obtain this precious land; this is the legend 1 See Appendix C for translations. [SOURCE: Page_415]

415 [SOURCE: Page_415]

that was told to me by old Cambodians. Che Tiam Ania Khou, aunt of Governor Tiam of Kanchor, lived a century ago in the small village of Dey Dos, on the right bank of the Mekong; his house overlooked the river and behind it was a large beng which filled up every year at the time of the floods, but rather late. Ania Khou had bought a beautiful, heavy dugout canoe in Sambor province, and his idea was to take it into the large beng behind his house and use it to transport the wood and white huts that he would fetch from the mountain across the beng. But the sides of the bank are almost sheer at Dey Dos, and all his efforts to hoist the dugout canoe, to get it over the hump, were in vain; it was too heavy and the bank too steep on the river side. Ania Khou then had the idea of digging a channel seven or eight cubits deep and of a width equal to that of the heavy dugout, thinking of taking advantage of the moment of the highest flood of the year to make his dugout penetrate by this channel into the great Beng. Ania Khou’s plan succeeded marvellously and when the flood had reached the level of the bottom of the canal, the waters of the river rushed into the Beng whose level was still several meters below, the priogue was violently pushed towards the still water table and flatted there, but it happened that the waters of the river rushed with so much force that they widened the canal which, in two months, reached a width of sixty coudée (NB: ca. 30 m). Moreover, the silty waters of the river, rushing into clearer waters which were not at the same temperature, quickly deposited their silt and when the floods came, old Tiam was not a little surprised to see that the area of cultivable land had considerably increased behind his house and that a double bulge of fertile land was clearly marked out at the outlet of the new prek into the Beng. [SOURCE: Page_416]

It is therefore not a question here of conquering, for a people who cannot exploit them, new lands suitable for cultivation, but simply of regulating, by means of irrigation, a harvest which depends only on the quantity of annual rainwater and also on its distribution during the development of the various phases of the crop. - Rapport au sujet d’un programme de travaux d’hydraulique agricole (10th of May 1910, FileNr 5654), Direction Générale des Travaux Publics [SOURCE: Page_416]

416 [SOURCE: Page_416]

F Runge Kutta Solution [SOURCE: Page_467]

The fourth-order Runge-Kutta solution is calculated as follows. [SOURCE: Page_467]

dy(t) For :         = y^0 (t) = f (y(t),t), with y(t^0 ) = y^0   (F.1) dt [SOURCE: Page_467]

k^1 = f (y⇤ (t^0 ),t^0 )                 (F.2) [SOURCE: Page_467]

h     h k^2 = f (y⇤ (t^0 ) + k^1 ,t^0 + )               (F.3) 2     2 [SOURCE: Page_467]

h     h k^3 = f (y⇤ (t^0 ) + k^2 ,t^0 + )               (F.4) 2     2 [SOURCE: Page_467]

467 [SOURCE: Page_467]

k^4 = f (y⇤ (t^0 ) + k^3 h,t^0 + h)                          (F.5) [SOURCE: Page_468]

k^1 + 2k^2 + 3k^3 + k^4 y⇤ (t^0 + h) = y⇤ (t^0 ) +                       h                 (F.6) 6 [SOURCE: Page_468]

This method uses an initial condition y(t^0 ) = y^0 as well as intermediary slope estimates k^1 , k^2 , k^3 , and k^4 as well as their eventual weighted sum to estimate the slope at time step t^0 + h. Here, k^1 is the slope at the beginning of the time step, k^2 and k^3 are estimates of the slope at mid-point, used to cover the first and second half of the time step respectively, and k^4 is the estimate of the slope at the endpoint (Carpenter et al., 2005). Input imagery, classifiers, and cloud computing: Insights from multi- temporal LULC mapping in the Cambodian Mekong delta [SOURCE: Page_471]

Abstract [SOURCE: Page_471]

The increased availability of open-access Synthetic Aperture Radar and optical earth observation data has engendered numerous land use and land cover (LULC) analyses combining these types of imagery. In parallel, the computational capabilities of cloud platforms have enabled a wider community to perform LULC classifications over long periods and large areas. However, an explicit assessment of how the performance of classifiers available on these cloud platforms responds to and can be optimized for the use of multi-imagery data, has been lacking for multi-temporal LULC approaches. This study carries out such an assessment for the supervised classifiers natively available in the open-access cloud computing platform Google Earth Engine: Naïve Bayes (NB), Classification and Regression Trees (CART), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB), and Support Vector Machines (SVM). A multi-temporal LULC analysis using Sentinel-1 and 2 is implemented for a study area in the Cambodian Mekong delta. Classifier performance is compared for different combinations of input imagery, band sets, and training datasets. The results show that GTB and RF yield the highest overall accuracy, at 94% and 93% respectively. Combining optical and SAR imagery boosts classification accuracy for CART, RF, GTB, and SVM by 10-15 percentage points. Furthermore, it also reduces the impact of limited training dataset quality for RF, GTB, and SVM. [SOURCE: Page_471]

Keywords: CART, Google Earth Engine; Gradient Tree Boosting, LULC; Random Forest; Sentinel-1 and -2; SVM [SOURCE: Page_471]

Introduction [SOURCE: Page_471]

Over the past years, there has been continuous progress in the availability of [SOURCE: Page_471]

satellite products environmental studies. Analyses of long time-series have become [SOURCE: Page_471]

possible through the now fully available Landsat archives, which span back to 1972 [SOURCE: Page_471]

(Saunier et al., 2017). Simultaneously, high-frequency, high-resolution imagery, [SOURCE: Page_471]

provided by the Sentinel constellation enable a wider community of researchers to gain [SOURCE: Page_471]

471 [SOURCE: Page_471]

insights into complex, long-term, large-scale states and processes. Consequently, these [SOURCE: Page_472]

products find applications in various disciplines, from archaeology (Schreier, 2020) to [SOURCE: Page_472]

marine biology (Foo & Asner, 2019). Particularly analyses in the domain of land use [SOURCE: Page_472]

and land cover (LULC) have benefited from the increased availability of imagery. These [SOURCE: Page_472]

analyses provide crucial insights into interactions between human populations and their [SOURCE: Page_472]

environment, from tracing a crop cover history across the United States (Johnson, 2019) [SOURCE: Page_472]

and assessing the impacts of dam construction on land use (Li et al., 2017), to mapping [SOURCE: Page_472]

rice cropping in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta (Kontgis, Schneider, & Ozdogan, 2015), [SOURCE: Page_472]

and evaluating changes in habitat quality and composition in conservationally [SOURCE: Page_472]

significant areas (López, López-Sandoval, Gerique, & Salazar, 2020; Yohannes, [SOURCE: Page_472]

Soromessa, Argaw, & Dewan, 2021) and ecosystem service provision (Kusi, Khattabi, [SOURCE: Page_472]

Mhammdi, & Lahssini, 2020). Especially the Sentinel constellation by the European [SOURCE: Page_472]

Space Agency (ESA), with its spatial resolution of up to 10 m, return frequency of [SOURCE: Page_472]

upwards of 6 days, and provision of both optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) [SOURCE: Page_472]

data provides attractive insights into LULC dynamics. Since its launch in 2014 (Potin et [SOURCE: Page_472]

al., 2019), Sentinel has been used for LULC analyses relating to smallholder maize in [SOURCE: Page_472]

Africa (Jin et al., 2019), monsoon inundations (Dinh, Elmahrad, Leinenkugel, & [SOURCE: Page_472]

Newton, 2019) and rice paddy extents (Minh, Avtar, Mohan, Misra, & Kurasaki, 2019) [SOURCE: Page_472]

in the Mekong Delta, and wetland mapping in Canada (Mahdianpari et al., 2018). [SOURCE: Page_472]

However, a considerable hindrance to many analyses has been the computational [SOURCE: Page_472]

power required to perform them. LULC studies covering long periods of time, large [SOURCE: Page_472]

areas, or high resolutions and image frequencies often exceed the computational [SOURCE: Page_472]

resources at individual researchers’ disposal. In response, cloud-based services and [SOURCE: Page_472]

computing platforms have been developed (Carretero & Blas, 2014). Open-access cloud [SOURCE: Page_472]

472 [SOURCE: Page_472]

computing platforms such as Google Earth Engine (GEE) (Gorelick et al., 2017), [SOURCE: Page_473]

OpenEO (Gomes, Queiroz, & Ferreira, 2020), or Open Data Cube (Killough, 2018) now [SOURCE: Page_473]

enable any user to cope with the massive amounts of available data. Among the [SOURCE: Page_473]

different platforms, GEE is the most widely-used to conduct analyses at large scales and [SOURCE: Page_473]

for long time series (Kumar & Mutanga, 2018). Early high-profile applications include [SOURCE: Page_473]

Hansen et al. (2013) mapping global forest cover change, and Pekel et al., (2016) [SOURCE: Page_473]

creating a dataset of global surface water occurrence, change, and seasonality since the [SOURCE: Page_473]

1980s. More recently, studies have used GEE to map irrigation on the US High Plains [SOURCE: Page_473]

over three decades (Deines et al., 2019), to track global annual impervious areas since [SOURCE: Page_473]

1985 (Gong et al., 2020), and to follow wildfire progression in British Columbia [SOURCE: Page_473]

(Crowley, Cardille, White, & Wulder, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_473]

However, while the progress with regard to the availability of images and [SOURCE: Page_473]

sufficient computational capacity for analyses has yielded fascinating insights, the [SOURCE: Page_473]

choice of algorithm for land use classification purposes carries an often-neglected [SOURCE: Page_473]

weight. As Thanh Noi & Kappas (2017) point out, the overall accuracy of a LULC [SOURCE: Page_473]

analysis depends ‘not just on the quantity and quality of the images, but also on the [SOURCE: Page_473]

right choice of classification method.’ [SOURCE: Page_473]

The majority of LULC analyses use supervised classification methods. Although [SOURCE: Page_473]

some researchers have used unsupervised classification (Mohammady, Moradi, [SOURCE: Page_473]

Zeinivand, & Temme, 2015; O’Hara, King, Cartwright, & King, 2003), supervised [SOURCE: Page_473]

classification is often preferred due to the possibility of setting a predefined number of [SOURCE: Page_473]

labelled output classes. To harness these advantages, a variety of classifiers is available [SOURCE: Page_473]

for supervised classification. Among the most frequently used are machine learning [SOURCE: Page_473]

algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Gradient [SOURCE: Page_473]

473 [SOURCE: Page_473]

Tree Boosting (GTB), Maximum Likelihood Classifiers (Orimoloye, Mazinyo, Nel, & [SOURCE: Page_474]

Kalumba, 2018; Orimoloye & Ololade, 2020), and K Nearest Neighbour (KNN) [SOURCE: Page_474]

(Talukdar et al., 2020). Furthermore, advanced machine learning approaches such as [SOURCE: Page_474]

artificial neural networks (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and deep [SOURCE: Page_474]

neural networks (DNN) have seen more widespread use in recent years (Jozdani, [SOURCE: Page_474]

Johnson, & Chen, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_474]

A number of papers compared these classifiers in LULC applications. Talukdar [SOURCE: Page_474]

et al. (2020) compare RF and SVM, along with more advanced machine learning [SOURCE: Page_474]

methods in a study area along the Ganga river in India. The authors conclude that the [SOURCE: Page_474]

RF algorithm overall performs best. In contrast, Nery et al. (2016) find that SVM [SOURCE: Page_474]

reaches the highest classification accuracies for LULC analyses after comparing it with [SOURCE: Page_474]

KNN, RF, Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ), Recursive Partitioning Regression [SOURCE: Page_474]

Trees (RPART), and Stochastic Gradient Boosting Methods (GBM) in a study area in [SOURCE: Page_474]

Western Australia. The same conclusion was reached by Thanh Noi & Kappas (2017), [SOURCE: Page_474]

who compared RF, KNN, and SVM classifications of Sentinel-2 imagery in the Red [SOURCE: Page_474]

River Delta in Vietnam. Shelestov et al. (2017) weighed the merits of some of the [SOURCE: Page_474]

classifiers available in GEE against external methods, including an ensemble neural [SOURCE: Page_474]

networks, for crop classification using optical Landsat-8 images. They found decision- [SOURCE: Page_474]

tree classifiers to perform best in GEE, though neural networks outperformed them. [SOURCE: Page_474]

Most of these comparison papers focus on contrasting the performance of [SOURCE: Page_474]

classifiers applied to a single date rather than in a multi-temporal situation. In addition, [SOURCE: Page_474]

hardly any compare classifiers in the context of cloud computing platforms, many of [SOURCE: Page_474]

which only offer a limited number of native implementations. In addition, with a few [SOURCE: Page_474]

notable exceptions (Hütt, Koppe, Miao, & Bareth, 2016), many papers only approach [SOURCE: Page_474]

474 [SOURCE: Page_474]

the classifier comparison on the basis of a single imagery type, with a fixed set of [SOURCE: Page_475]

bands, and a single source of training data. [SOURCE: Page_475]

In view of the proliferation of studies addressing research questions through [SOURCE: Page_475]

multi-temporal analyses using cloud computing platforms, this paper aims to [SOURCE: Page_475]

systematically address these knowledge gaps. It presents an assessment of the response [SOURCE: Page_475]

of four supervised classifiers available in the online Javascript API of the GEE cloud [SOURCE: Page_475]

computing platform, to the use of different combinations of input imagery, training data, [SOURCE: Page_475]

and band sets for the purpose of land use and land cover analyses. These classifiers are [SOURCE: Page_475]

Naive Bayes (NB), Classification and Regression Trees (CART), Random Forest (RF), [SOURCE: Page_475]

Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB), and Support Vector Machines (SVM). While it is [SOURCE: Page_475]

possible to implement further supervised classification methods, such as fully [SOURCE: Page_475]

convolutional neural networks (FCNN), or deep neural networks (DNN) in GEE, this [SOURCE: Page_475]

requires the external training of the models on the TensorFlow platform (Abadi et al., [SOURCE: Page_475]

2016). Since this approach involves several billable components of Google Cloud, it is [SOURCE: Page_475]

not included in this paper, which focuses on entirely open-access solutions. [SOURCE: Page_475]

The comparisons are made using Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical [SOURCE: Page_475]

imagery, both separately and in combination. In addition, the impact on classifier [SOURCE: Page_475]

performance of the type of the training set, as well as the choice of bands, texture [SOURCE: Page_475]

features, and spectral indices is tested. For this purpose, two different sets of training [SOURCE: Page_475]

points (one based on field data, one derived from high-resolution satellite imagery) and [SOURCE: Page_475]

three different sets of training bands (varying in the number of additional indexes and [SOURCE: Page_475]

texture features used for classification) are used. [SOURCE: Page_475]

475 [SOURCE: Page_475]

Study Area [SOURCE: Page_476]

For the purposes of this study, a study area on the floodplains of the Mekong delta in [SOURCE: Page_476]

Cambodia was chosen. The region is well known for intra- and inter-annual land use [SOURCE: Page_476]

changes (Liu et al., 2020; Ngo, Lechner, & Vu, 2020), making it adapted to test the [SOURCE: Page_476]

multi-temporal capacity of classifiers. The area is subject to annual monsoon [SOURCE: Page_476]

inundations, which typically last from July until November. For the rest of the year, the [SOURCE: Page_476]

floodplain is intensively cultivated, in one to three cropping cycles. [SOURCE: Page_476]

Specifically, an area of 44 km^2 on the right bank of the Bassac river, one of the [SOURCE: Page_476]

Mekong’s deltaic distributaries, was chosen (see Figure 1). Located about 70 km south [SOURCE: Page_476]

of the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh, this area exhibits rapid changes in land use [SOURCE: Page_476]

following flood rise and recession, and strong annual variability in cropping calendars [SOURCE: Page_476]

and cultivated areas. In the north, it is dominated by fruit trees, especially mango trees, [SOURCE: Page_476]

while the south is a patchwork of fields where rice and vegetables like tomatoes, [SOURCE: Page_476]

cucumbers, and aubergines are grown. During the dry season, these crops are either [SOURCE: Page_476]

irrigated with water pumped from canals, or rely on sparse amounts of rainfall. The [SOURCE: Page_476]

rainfall distribution in the area is bimodal, with peaks in the early and late wet season. [SOURCE: Page_476]

Overall, six broad land use classes are defined: open water surfaces, bare/fallow [SOURCE: Page_476]

land, urban/village areas, fruit trees, rice fields, and vegetable fields. Out of these, urban [SOURCE: Page_476]

areas – located along the main road that runs in parallel with the river – and fruit trees [SOURCE: Page_476]

are relatively static over the course of a year (neglecting urban spread and the planting [SOURCE: Page_476]

or cutting down of trees). The other classes are highly dynamic. During the wet season, [SOURCE: Page_476]

large swaths of low-lying land in the west and southwest of the area are inundated. [SOURCE: Page_476]

Subsequently, these areas see one or two cycles of rice cultivation, before lying fallow [SOURCE: Page_476]

for part of the year. The higher terrain in the east of the study area sees a complex [SOURCE: Page_476]

476 [SOURCE: Page_476]

mosaic of fields lying fallow and being cultivated. Figure 2 shows an RGB overview of [SOURCE: Page_477]

the LULC dynamics in the study area during the dry season. [SOURCE: Page_477]

[Figure 1 about here: Location of the study area on the floodplains of the Cambodian Mekong delta.] [SOURCE: Page_477]

[Figure 2 about here: Landcover dynamics in the study area during the dry season, RGB image.] [SOURCE: Page_477]

Data Used [SOURCE: Page_477]

The data used in this study stems from three sources: the Sentinel satellite constellation [SOURCE: Page_477]

maintained by the European Space Agency (ESA), high-resolution SPOT-6 and 7 [SOURCE: Page_477]

imagery, and fieldwork in Cambodia. For classifier training, images from three time [SOURCE: Page_477]

points in November 2019, February 2020, and April 2020 were used. At all time points, [SOURCE: Page_477]

both Sentinel-1 and 2 data are available on either the same or adjacent dates. These [SOURCE: Page_477]

dates fall at the beginning, middle, and end of the dry season and account for the main [SOURCE: Page_477]

changes in cultivation practices and LULC dynamics (cf. Figure 2). The SPOT-6 and 7 [SOURCE: Page_477]

images and the fieldwork data are used for parameter tuning, calibration, and validation. [SOURCE: Page_477]

Details on the satellite images used are given in Table 1. [SOURCE: Page_477]

Sentinel-1 [SOURCE: Page_477]

The ESA’s Sentinel-1 constellation consists of two satellites, Sentinel-1A and [SOURCE: Page_477]

Sentinel-1B, which were launched in 2014 and 2016 respectively. Both satellites have a [SOURCE: Page_477]

477 [SOURCE: Page_477]

return period of 12 days, resulting in a combined Sentinel-1 overpass frequency of 6 [SOURCE: Page_478]

days. They collect C-band synthetic aperture radar imagery in a variety of polarizations, [SOURCE: Page_478]

instrument modes, and resolutions. For this study, interferometric wide swath (IW) [SOURCE: Page_478]

images in the form of co-polarized VV and cross-polarized VH bands at 10 m resolution [SOURCE: Page_478]

are used, as the most widely-spread type of imagery for LULC approaches using SAR [SOURCE: Page_478]

(Khan, Govil, Kumar, & Dave, 2020; Ranjan & Parida, 2019; Tavares, Beltrão, [SOURCE: Page_478]

Guimarães, & Teodoro, 2019). [SOURCE: Page_478]

In total, six Sentinel-1A and B images taken in descending orbits are used to [SOURCE: Page_478]

train and validate the classifiers for three different dates. The study area is located at an [SOURCE: Page_478]

intersection area of two Sentinel-1 tiles. To reduce random speckle noise, mean [SOURCE: Page_478]

composites of Sentinel-1 images taken on subsequent days were created for each [SOURCE: Page_478]

training time point (cf. Table 1). To test the trained classifier and create a LULC time [SOURCE: Page_478]

series, 117 SAR images between 01/11/2019 and 31/10/2020 are used. As can be seen in [SOURCE: Page_478]

Figure 3, these images are distributed regularly throughout the year. [SOURCE: Page_478]

Sentinel-2 [SOURCE: Page_478]

Like Sentinel-1, the ESA’s Sentinel-2 collection consists of a pair of satellites. [SOURCE: Page_478]

Sentinel-2A was launched in 2015, followed by Sentinel-2B in 2017. Both satellites [SOURCE: Page_478]

have a return period of 10 days, resulting in a combined Sentinel-2 image frequency of [SOURCE: Page_478]

5 days. The constellation provides multi-spectral optical imagery for a total of 12 [SOURCE: Page_478]

spectral bands ranging from the blue to the short wave infrared spectrum. [SOURCE: Page_478]

Like for Sentinel-1, overlapping Sentinel-2 tiles are available in the study area. [SOURCE: Page_478]

To train the classifiers, three composites of six cloud-free optical images are used (cf. [SOURCE: Page_478]

Table 1). For the land use time series classification, 47 images between 01/11/2019 and [SOURCE: Page_478]

478 [SOURCE: Page_478]

31/10/2020 are used. However, it must be noted that these images are not distributed [SOURCE: Page_479]

regularly across the year. As shown in Figure 3, multiple images are available for every [SOURCE: Page_479]

month during the dry season. During the wet season, when cloud cover is high, this is [SOURCE: Page_479]

not the case. [SOURCE: Page_479]

### 3.3. Data for Calibration and Validation

This study uses SPOT-6 and 7 images to generate training points for the classification [SOURCE: Page_479]

algorithms. SPOT (Satellite Pour l’Observation de la Terre) is a high-resolution satellite [SOURCE: Page_479]

operated commercially by Spot Image. It provides panchromatic and multi-spectral [SOURCE: Page_479]

images at 1.5-6 m resolution. Complemented by knowledge of the general LULC [SOURCE: Page_479]

distribution patterns in the study area, points are set manually where land use classes are [SOURCE: Page_479]

discernible with reasonable certainty on the high-resolution images. Overall, 9,000 [SOURCE: Page_479]

training points are set – 1500 per training class (cf. Table 2). While this procedure yields [SOURCE: Page_479]

an extensive set of training data, it also introduces some class noise. This describes [SOURCE: Page_479]

training points that carry erroneous labels, which can impact the quality of the [SOURCE: Page_479]

classification. However, it is still salient to harness a dataset generated in this way for [SOURCE: Page_479]

comparative purposes, as noise is a common problem in supervised remote sensing [SOURCE: Page_479]

approaches (Frenay & Verleysen, 2014; Pelletier et al., 2017). [SOURCE: Page_479]

A final component of the data setup of this paper is ground-truth training data [SOURCE: Page_479]

collected at the study site in autumn 2019 and spring 2020. In total, 1,712 training [SOURCE: Page_479]

points were collected. The majority were set on site using a manual GPS device [SOURCE: Page_479]

(horizontal accuracy: 10 m). In addition, some were set manually using geo-referenced [SOURCE: Page_479]

in-situ images from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). However, unlike for the training [SOURCE: Page_479]

479 [SOURCE: Page_479]

data derived from SPOT-6 and 7 images, the training points from the field surveys are [SOURCE: Page_480]

not distributed equally between classes. For example, while the November fieldwork [SOURCE: Page_480]

training set includes 630 points, its April equivalent only contains 491 (cf. Table 2). [SOURCE: Page_480]

While this training sample is smaller and its points are unevenly distributed between [SOURCE: Page_480]

classes and dates, the confidence of its label attribution is considerably higher. [SOURCE: Page_480]

[Table 2 about here: Distribution of training data points across the multi-temporal images.] [SOURCE: Page_480]

Methodology [SOURCE: Page_480]

A general outline of the classification workflow is given in Figure 4. Following pre- [SOURCE: Page_480]

processing, 9 datasets are generated on which the classifiers are tested. These datasets [SOURCE: Page_480]

derive from the use of different imagery types alone and in combination, as well as [SOURCE: Page_480]

different band sets (see Table 3). Parameter tuning, calibration, and validation is [SOURCE: Page_480]

performed for each of the 9 datasets separately, using both the limited training points [SOURCE: Page_480]

derived from fieldwork, and the extended training points generated on the basis of the [SOURCE: Page_480]

SPOT-6 and 7 images, resulting in 18 different configurations of input data for each of [SOURCE: Page_480]

the four classifiers. Finally, the best-performing algorithm is chosen and applied to the [SOURCE: Page_480]

optical, radar, and combined dataset to generate a LULC classification spanning the [SOURCE: Page_480]

entire period between 01/11/2019 and 31/10/2020. [SOURCE: Page_480]

[Table 3 about here: Overview of image datasets used.] [SOURCE: Page_480]

[Figure 4 about here: Classification workflow.] (updated) [SOURCE: Page_480]

Image Pre-Processing [SOURCE: Page_480]

To a certain degree, both Sentinel-1 and 2 images are already provided in pre-processed [SOURCE: Page_480]

480 [SOURCE: Page_480]

form in GEE. [SOURCE: Page_481]

Sentinel-1 images undergo pre-processing during ingestion in GEE based on the [SOURCE: Page_481]

ESA’s Sentinel-1 toolbox. In this process, metadata is updated with a restituted orbit [SOURCE: Page_481]

file, border noise and thermal noise is removed, and radiometric calibration and [SOURCE: Page_481]

orthorectification are applied. The fact that images are provided in pre-processed form [SOURCE: Page_481]

in GEE’s Javascript API removes one of the main hurdles many researchers face in [SOURCE: Page_481]

using SAR data. In fact, several studies have used GEE as a source of SAR images, [SOURCE: Page_481]

even though their analyses were subsequently conducted in different environments [SOURCE: Page_481]

(Amani et al., 2020; Tamiminia et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_481]

As a basis for classification, additional bands are generated for SAR imagery [SOURCE: Page_481]

using the original VV and VH bands (cf. Table B$_2$). Three of these are based on [SOURCE: Page_481]

arithmetic operations (VV/VH, VV-VH, (VV+VH)/2) which previous studies found to [SOURCE: Page_481]

yield increased accuracies for LULC approaches (Slagter, Tsendbazar, Vollrath, & [SOURCE: Page_481]

Reiche, 2020). The others are based on a classic Grey Level Co-occurence Matrix [SOURCE: Page_481]

(GLCM), encompassing Haralick texture features (Haralick, Shanmugam, & Dinstein, [SOURCE: Page_481]

1973). These features describe image texture through interpretable descriptors and have [SOURCE: Page_481]

been found to add valuable information for LULC analyses.(Clerici, Valbuena Calderón, [SOURCE: Page_481]

& Posada, 2017; Lin, Zhang, Lin, Gamba, & Liu, 2020; Mishra, Prasad, Rai, [SOURCE: Page_481]

Vishwakarma, & Arora, 2019). Texture features are calculated separately for both the [SOURCE: Page_481]

VV and VH polarization, parameterized with a 5x^5 window size. Following previous [SOURCE: Page_481]

studies (Nizalapur & Vyas, 2020), angular second moment (ASM), contrast [SOURCE: Page_481]

(CONTRAST), correlation (CORR), inverse difference moment (IDM), entropy (ENT), [SOURCE: Page_481]

dissimilarity (DISS), and variance (VAR) are used as added bands for classification. [SOURCE: Page_481]

Following the calculation of the texture features, a refined Lee speckle filter (Yommy, [SOURCE: Page_481]

481 [SOURCE: Page_481]

Liu, & Wu, 2015) is applied to smooth the original VV and VH bands in order to reduce [SOURCE: Page_482]

speckle, since not all data datasets use the generated texture bands. [SOURCE: Page_482]

Sentinel-2 images are available in pre-processed form in GEE. The sen^2cor [SOURCE: Page_482]

algorithm (Main-Knorn et al., 2017) has been applied to transform Top of the [SOURCE: Page_482]

Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance to surface reflectance (BOA). For this analysis, all [SOURCE: Page_482]

bands are automatically resampled to 10 m resolution by the GEE processing algorithm. [SOURCE: Page_482]

For the time series calculation, a cloudy pixel threshold of < 20% is introduced, and the [SOURCE: Page_482]

remaining clouds are masked using a simple bit-mask based on the QA band. [SOURCE: Page_482]

Additional spectral indices (cf. Table 4) are calculated on the basis of native [SOURCE: Page_482]

bands (cf. Table B$_1$) to generate ancillary layers of information that serve as input for [SOURCE: Page_482]

the classification algorithms, which past studies have found to be valuable in increasing [SOURCE: Page_482]

classification accuracies (Godinho, Guiomar, & Gil, 2016). These are based on a range [SOURCE: Page_482]

of bands employed in past studies for various LULC analyses using different [SOURCE: Page_482]

classification algorithms (Ouattara et al., 2020). [SOURCE: Page_482]

[Table 4 about here: Spectral indices calculated for optical Sentinel-2 imagery ] [SOURCE: Page_482]

Creation of Image Datasets [SOURCE: Page_482]

In total, parameter tuning, calibration, and validation is performed on nine image [SOURCE: Page_482]

datasets (cf. Table 3). [SOURCE: Page_482]

First, three main sets of images are created – one containing only SAR imagery, [SOURCE: Page_482]

one containing optical imagery, and one in which images are created by stacking all [SOURCE: Page_482]

available optical and SAR bands into a single image. Then, each of the three imagery [SOURCE: Page_482]

sets is further subdivided into three tiers depending on how many bands are used for [SOURCE: Page_482]

classification(see Table 5). One tier includes a band set that encompasses all native [SOURCE: Page_482]

482 [SOURCE: Page_482]

bands, spectral indices, and texture features. A reduced band set includes the native [SOURCE: Page_483]

image bands as well as some indices and texture features. Finally, a minimal set consists [SOURCE: Page_483]

only of the VV and VH bands for SAR, and the RGB bands for optical imagery. [SOURCE: Page_483]

[Table 5 about here: Band sets of spectral indices and texture features. For the combined imagery set, these bands are stacked. ] [SOURCE: Page_483]

Parameter Tuning and Classification [SOURCE: Page_483]

Each dataset is calibrated with 80% and validated with 20% of both the fieldwork and [SOURCE: Page_483]

the SPOT-based training data, for each of the four classifiers. Preceding calibration, [SOURCE: Page_483]

each classifier undergoes parameter tuning. A short description of each classifier as well [SOURCE: Page_483]

as the associated tuning parameters is given below. [SOURCE: Page_483]

Naïve Bayes (NB) [SOURCE: Page_483]

This classifier relies on a simple probabilistic approach that is based on the Bayes [SOURCE: Page_483]

theorem (John & Langley, 1995). It is referred to as naïve because it relies on the [SOURCE: Page_483]

assumption of conditional independence between every pair of features, and a Gaussian [SOURCE: Page_483]

probability distribution (Zhang, 2005). In reality, this condition is frequently not met, [SOURCE: Page_483]

particularly in more complex situations and datasets. Nonetheless, several studies have [SOURCE: Page_483]

found the simplistic approach to yield satisfying results (Diengdoh et al., 2020; Johnson [SOURCE: Page_483]

& Iizuka, 2016) particularly in cases where only a limited number of input features is [SOURCE: Page_483]

available. This may be due to the fact that, in general, even a small training set is [SOURCE: Page_483]

sufficient to minimize the average risk of the classification error and compute the [SOURCE: Page_483]

decision surface. Some studies have also argued that dependence distribution among [SOURCE: Page_483]

classes could also account for the surprisingly good performance of NB (Kuncheva, [SOURCE: Page_483]

483 [SOURCE: Page_483]

2006). In GEE’s implementation of NB, the only parameter that needs to be tuned for [SOURCE: Page_484]

performance is the smoothing factor λ . [SOURCE: Page_484]

Classification and Regression Trees (CART) [SOURCE: Page_484]

CART classifiers belong to the family of decision tree (DT) classifiers. The basic [SOURCE: Page_484]

approach of this type of classifier is to find the attribute or threshold that splits a [SOURCE: Page_484]

training dataset most effectively into subsets. This split then becomes a node in the tree, [SOURCE: Page_484]

with the two subsets forming branches. Each subset is then split into further subsets [SOURCE: Page_484]

until only a non-splitable end node (also known as a ‘leaf node’) remains. The main [SOURCE: Page_484]

criterion in performing every split is the normalized information gain (Shalev-Shwartz [SOURCE: Page_484]

& Ben-David, 2014). Once grown using the training dataset, the decision tree can then [SOURCE: Page_484]

be applied to new samples. A considerable disadvantage of this approach is its high [SOURCE: Page_484]

sensitivity to the training dataset. Even globally negligible modifications in the training [SOURCE: Page_484]

data can lead to fundamentally different tree structures (Shelestov et al., 2017). To [SOURCE: Page_484]

improve classifier performance, the number of leaf nodes in each tree (maxNodes) is [SOURCE: Page_484]

tuned. [SOURCE: Page_484]

Random Forest (RF) [SOURCE: Page_484]

Random Forest (RF) is a recursive partitioning technique that is based on the [SOURCE: Page_484]

construction of an ensemble of classification and regression trees (hence the term [SOURCE: Page_484]

forest). Each tree is trained using the same method as described above for CART. [SOURCE: Page_484]

However, to increase computational efficiency, each tree only utilizes a random subset [SOURCE: Page_484]

of features at each node – this step also reduces correlation (and accounts for the second [SOURCE: Page_484]

element in the nomenclature of the classifier). Trees are bundled together [SOURCE: Page_484]

484 [SOURCE: Page_484]

computationally through bootstrap aggregating (“bagging”) (Breiman, 1996). The final [SOURCE: Page_485]

classification result for a new sample is then obtained through a majority vote of [SOURCE: Page_485]

individual tree results. Overall, this approach is less sensitive to overfitting and noisy [SOURCE: Page_485]

data, two of the most considerable pitfalls of CART approaches (Breiman, 2001). For [SOURCE: Page_485]

RF tuning, the number of trees (nTree) and the number of variables per split (mTry) [SOURCE: Page_485]

have to be optimized. Past studies found that satisfactory, stable results could be [SOURCE: Page_485]

produced with a number of trees ranging between 200 and 500 (Belgiu & Dragut, [SOURCE: Page_485]

2016). To find the optimal RF model, this study tested nTree = [50 : 750] with a step [SOURCE: Page_485]

size of 50, and mTry = [1:15] with a step size of 1. [SOURCE: Page_485]

Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB) [SOURCE: Page_485]

Like RF, Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB) algorithms utilizes an ensemble of decision [SOURCE: Page_485]

trees. However, its basic approach differs in that it limits the complexity of trees, [SOURCE: Page_485]

confining each individual tree to a weak prediction model. It achieves classification [SOURCE: Page_485]

accuracy by iteratively combining an ensemble of these weak learners into strong ones [SOURCE: Page_485]

by minimizing a differentiable loss function at every step, following a gradient descent [SOURCE: Page_485]

procedure (Friedman, 2002). To reduce correlation between trees, each new tree is [SOURCE: Page_485]

constructed on the basis of a stochastically selected subset of training data. Recent [SOURCE: Page_485]

studies have shown GTB algorithms, such as XGboost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) to [SOURCE: Page_485]

outperform classifiers such as SVM, RF, and KNN (Godinho et al., 2016), especially on [SOURCE: Page_485]

unbalanced datasets. However, GTB are often prone to overfitting, a risk that can be [SOURCE: Page_485]

minimized through parameter tuning. In terms of parameters to be adjusted, the number [SOURCE: Page_485]

of trees (nTree) is varied between 50 and 200, with a step size of 10. GTB further [SOURCE: Page_485]

requires a parameter to be specified to determine how many nodes a decision tree in the [SOURCE: Page_485]

485 [SOURCE: Page_485]

ensemble can have. Since GTB is based on weak learners, the maxNodes parameter is [SOURCE: Page_486]

typically low, with a range of [2:10] with a step size of 1 being tested in this study. In [SOURCE: Page_486]

addition, the sampling rate for stochastic gradient tree boosting, and the shrinkage rate, [SOURCE: Page_486]

which controls the learning rate of the algorithm, need to be optimized. In this study, a [SOURCE: Page_486]

range of [0.45:75] with a step size of 0.5 was tested for the former, and [0.005, 0.01, [SOURCE: Page_486]

0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5] for the latter. Finally, all three loss functions available in GEE for [SOURCE: Page_486]

GTB were compared – least squares, least absolute deviation, and Huber. [SOURCE: Page_486]

Support Vector Machines (SVM) [SOURCE: Page_486]

The founding principle of this approach is to find the boundary that maximizes the [SOURCE: Page_486]

distance from the nearest data point of all classes (Noble, 2006). These points are used [SOURCE: Page_486]

for the construction of support vectors, which, in turn, form the basis for the [SOURCE: Page_486]

computation of the maximum-margin hyperplane that serves as a boundary. The [SOURCE: Page_486]

dimensionality of this hyperplane is determined by the number of features to be used for [SOURCE: Page_486]

classification. For non-linear data, a kernel is applied to transform low-dimensional data [SOURCE: Page_486]

to make it separable via the SVM approach in a higher-dimensional sphere (Cortes & [SOURCE: Page_486]

Vapnik, 1995). Frequently used kernels include linear, Gaussian Radial Basis Function [SOURCE: Page_486]

(RBF), sigmoid, and polynomial kernels (Amari & Wu, 1999). The main advantage of [SOURCE: Page_486]

SVM is its high potential for generalization. [SOURCE: Page_486]

In terms of tuning SVMs, the first choice to make is to pick a kernel. For LULC [SOURCE: Page_486]

approaches, RBF and Linear kernels are frequently used (Kavzoglu & Colkesen, 2009; [SOURCE: Page_486]

Shi & Yang, 2015). Then the cost parameter C needs to be optimized, as well as the γ [SOURCE: Page_486]

value in case the RBF kernel is used. The γ value determines the RBF kernel width and [SOURCE: Page_486]

thus affects the smoothing of the hyperplane which divides classes. The C parameter [SOURCE: Page_486]

486 [SOURCE: Page_486]

sets the threshold for permitted misclassification of non-separable training data (Thanh [SOURCE: Page_487]

Noi & Kappas, 2017). If it is too large, it can lead to over-fitting (Ghosh & Joshi, 2014). [SOURCE: Page_487]

This study follows (Li et al., 2014) in using ten C values (2[-2;7]) as well as ten γ values [SOURCE: Page_487]

(2[-5;4]) for parameter tuning. [SOURCE: Page_487]

Validation and Statistical Analysis [SOURCE: Page_487]

Finally, the classification results of each algorithm using each combination of imagery, [SOURCE: Page_487]

band set, and training data is validated. For this, the remaining randomly selected 20% [SOURCE: Page_487]

of the field work and SPOT-based datasets are used. Overall accuracy as well as [SOURCE: Page_487]

producer and consumer accuracies are calculated (Congalton, 1991). To ascertain [SOURCE: Page_487]

whether the choice of input imagery, training data, and band set has statistically [SOURCE: Page_487]

significant impacts on classifier performance, the non-parametric Kruskal Wallis test [SOURCE: Page_487]

(Kruskal & Wallis, 1952) is used. [SOURCE: Page_487]

Results [SOURCE: Page_487]

Optimal Tuning Parameters [SOURCE: Page_487]

The tuning parameters that yielded the highest accuracies for each classifier and each of [SOURCE: Page_487]

the nine image subsets, and that are used in the remaining of the analysis, are given in [SOURCE: Page_487]

Table 6. The full set of tuning parameters and their associated accuracies are given in [SOURCE: Page_487]

the supplementary materials. The results show that the parameter values yielding the [SOURCE: Page_487]

highest accuracies varied considerably for RF (nTree and mTry) and for SVM (C and γ). [SOURCE: Page_487]

For RF, the nTree used for the final analysis varies between 50 and 600, and nTry [SOURCE: Page_487]

ranges from 1 to 14. For SVM, optimal classification accuracy is achieved using C [SOURCE: Page_487]

values that vary along the full tuning spectrum. Similarly, the optimal γ value for the [SOURCE: Page_487]

487 [SOURCE: Page_487]

RBF kernel ranges from 2-5 to 24 . There are no discernible trends along the lines of [SOURCE: Page_488]

imagery type, band sets, or training datasets. [SOURCE: Page_488]

In contrast to this, the optimal values for the tuning parameter λ for NB and [SOURCE: Page_488]

CART’s maxNodes vary little. In the case of λ, most combinations of imagery, band [SOURCE: Page_488]

sets, and training data show little sensitivity to value tuning. Where differences in [SOURCE: Page_488]

accuracies depending on λ are observable, the highest accuracies can be reached with λ [SOURCE: Page_488]

= 1*10-10. As for maxNodes, the CART classifier globally reaches its highest accuracies [SOURCE: Page_488]

using either 5 or 6 nodes. [SOURCE: Page_488]

As for GTB, parameter tuning revealed low sensitivities for some parameters, [SOURCE: Page_488]

and higher discrepancies in accuracies for others. The type of loss function employed, [SOURCE: Page_488]

for example, has a virtually untraceable effect on accuracies. The shrinkage function, on [SOURCE: Page_488]

the other hand, showed optimal values between 0.01 and 0.25, and the sampling rate [SOURCE: Page_488]

between 0.6 and 0.75. For nTree and maxNodes there was a noticeably larger variation [SOURCE: Page_488]

for optimal parameter values for the fieldwork training set, than for the extended [SOURCE: Page_488]

training set. In the former, values for nTree ranged between 50 and 190 and for [SOURCE: Page_488]

maxNodes between 3 and 10. In the latter, the optimal value for nTree lay between 160 [SOURCE: Page_488]

and 200, and for maxNodes between 9 and 10. [SOURCE: Page_488]

[Table 6 about here: Tuning parameters for optimal accuracies for each classifier and band set. ] (updated) [SOURCE: Page_488]

Overall Accuracy [SOURCE: Page_488]

The maximum overall accuracies achieved by each classifier depending on imagery [SOURCE: Page_488]

type, band set, and training data, are given in Table 7. Accuracies over 85%, which [SOURCE: Page_488]

previous studies have deemed satisfactory for LULC purposes (Denize et al., 2018; [SOURCE: Page_488]

488 [SOURCE: Page_488]

Khan et al., 2020; Steinhausen, Wagner, Narasimhan, & Waske, 2018) are highlighted in [SOURCE: Page_489]

bold. [SOURCE: Page_489]

The results show that GTB globally reached the highest overall accuracy, at [SOURCE: Page_489]

94%. This value is reached using combined imagery, the extended dataset derived from [SOURCE: Page_489]

SPOT imagery, and both the full and the reduced band set. RF also yields similarly high [SOURCE: Page_489]

values (93%) using the same combination of imagery, training dataset and bands. For [SOURCE: Page_489]

the fieldwork dataset, the highest accuracies are also reached by GTB and RF. GTB [SOURCE: Page_489]

yields and overall accuracy of 93% for the full and 92% for the reduced band set using [SOURCE: Page_489]

combined optical and SAR imagery. For the same input configuration, RF yields [SOURCE: Page_489]

accuracies of 92% and 91% respectively. Furthermore, GTB and RF also reach [SOURCE: Page_489]

accuracies of over 85% using all other combinations of bands and training sets for the [SOURCE: Page_489]

combination of Sentinel-1 and 2 imagery, and for the use of the extended training set [SOURCE: Page_489]

and the full and reduced band sets for optical-only imagery. [SOURCE: Page_489]

Third in terms of overall accuracy is SVM, using a linear kernel and combined [SOURCE: Page_489]

optical and SAR imagery. Accuracies of up to 92% are achieved using the extended [SOURCE: Page_489]

training dataset and the reduced band set. Like RF, SVM also yields high accuracies [SOURCE: Page_489]

when trained using the fieldwork dataset and the reduced band set. It furthermore attains [SOURCE: Page_489]

accuracies of 88% and 86% respectively for the use of the full band set and both [SOURCE: Page_489]

training data sets. For the variation of SVM using an RBF kernel, the overall [SOURCE: Page_489]

classification accuracy does not surpass 63%. [SOURCE: Page_489]

The CART classifier reaches overall accuracies of up to 88%, when trained [SOURCE: Page_489]

using combined imagery, the fieldwork dataset and either the full or reduced band sets. [SOURCE: Page_489]

Far below this mark is the Naive Bayes classifier. Its highest overall accuracies, at 72%, [SOURCE: Page_489]

is reached using the combined optical and SAR imagery. [SOURCE: Page_489]

489 [SOURCE: Page_489]

training set, and band set. OA values of over 85 are marked in bold.] (updated) [SOURCE: Page_490]

SAR- and Optical-Only vs. Combined Imagery [SOURCE: Page_490]

Overall, the results show a marked increase in accuracy for the majority of classifiers [SOURCE: Page_490]

when combined imagery is used, as opposed to SAR and optical-only imagery. For RF, [SOURCE: Page_490]

optical-only imagery led to an average accuracy of 78% across training and band sets, [SOURCE: Page_490]

for GTB to 76%. For SAR-only imagery, this average lay at only 67% and 63% [SOURCE: Page_490]

respectively. The combination of both imagery types, however, yielded an average [SOURCE: Page_490]

accuracy of 90% for RF, and of 91 for GTB. Similarly, the CART, SVM, and NB [SOURCE: Page_490]

classifiers also yielded their best accuracies using the combined imagery. [SOURCE: Page_490]

As illustrated in Figure 5, the combined imagery yielded considerably higher [SOURCE: Page_490]

accuracies for NB, CART, RF, GTB, and SVM using a linear kernel than optical or SAR [SOURCE: Page_490]

images alone. For CART, RF, and GTB the improvement in accuracy when using [SOURCE: Page_490]

combined imagery in comparison to optical-only imagery is statistically significant (p < [SOURCE: Page_490]

0.05). In addition, the CART classifier using optical imagery shows considerable [SOURCE: Page_490]

variability with respect to accuracies. The improvement in comparison to using SAR- [SOURCE: Page_490]

imagery only is statistically significant for NB, CART, RF, and SVM using a linear [SOURCE: Page_490]

kernel. However, for SVM using an RBF kernel, the reverse is true – the combined [SOURCE: Page_490]

imagery yields considerably lower accuracy values than either optical- or SAR-only [SOURCE: Page_490]

imagery. [SOURCE: Page_490]

[Figure 5 about here: Box plot of overall accuracies by imagery used and classifier, and significance of variation of accuracies depending on imagery type used.] [SOURCE: Page_490]

490 [SOURCE: Page_490]

Choice of Training Data and Band Sets [SOURCE: Page_491]

In general, the extended training data yielded the highest overall accuracies for GTB, [SOURCE: Page_491]

RF and SVM using both a linear and RBF kernel. For CART and NB, however, the [SOURCE: Page_491]

training set based on fieldwork data led to higher accuracies. GTB, RF and SVM using [SOURCE: Page_491]

a linear kernel also yielded accuracies of over 85% using the fieldwork dataset (cf. [SOURCE: Page_491]

Table 7 and supplementary materials). It can be noted that the use of the extended data [SOURCE: Page_491]

set leads to a higher accuracy improvement in optical and SAR-only imagery than in the [SOURCE: Page_491]

combined imagery. For example, for RF applied to optical imagery, the average overall [SOURCE: Page_491]

accuracy achieved using the fieldwork dataset lies at 74%, whereas the extended dataset [SOURCE: Page_491]

yields an average overall accuracy of 82%. In contrast, for combined imagery the [SOURCE: Page_491]

average RF using fieldwork training data lies at 89%. Using the extended dataset only [SOURCE: Page_491]

increases this average overall accuracy to 90%. [SOURCE: Page_491]

As for the band set, it emerges that the extended and fieldwork dataset produce [SOURCE: Page_491]

comparable accuracies for CART, RF, and GTB. SVM using a linear kernel, however, [SOURCE: Page_491]

produces distinctly higher accuracies on the basis of the reduced band set. Furthermore, [SOURCE: Page_491]

SVM using the RBF kernel produces its highest overall accuracies when the minimal [SOURCE: Page_491]

band set is used. [SOURCE: Page_491]

Accuracy by Class [SOURCE: Page_491]

The accuracy with which each land cover class is classified by each algorithm varies [SOURCE: Page_491]

considerably. Consequently, this impacts the overall classification accuracy at different [SOURCE: Page_491]

points in the time series of images between 01/11/2019 and 31/10/2020, when the [SOURCE: Page_491]

classes have a different predominance. [SOURCE: Page_491]

491 [SOURCE: Page_491]

Water, for example, has a relatively high consumer and producer accuracy (cf. [SOURCE: Page_492]

Table 8). While NB tends to errors of omission, mis-classifying water as urban areas, [SOURCE: Page_492]

the other classifiers succeed in delineating surface water regions with fairly high [SOURCE: Page_492]

confidence. RF and GTB in particular delineate water well, with producer accuracies of [SOURCE: Page_492]

98% and 97%, and consumer accuracies of 97% and 98% respectively, followed by [SOURCE: Page_492]

SVM (97% and 96% respectively). Consequently, inundated areas, as they can be [SOURCE: Page_492]

observed in November, are represented well. [SOURCE: Page_492]

In contrast, the classifiers exhibit greater difficulties in separating bare/fallow [SOURCE: Page_492]

land from urban areas, and vegetable fields from rice paddies. While CART, RF, GTB, [SOURCE: Page_492]

and SVM succeed well in classifying the permanent urban areas in the East of the study [SOURCE: Page_492]

area, they also tend to misclassify fields lying fallow during the dry season as urban [SOURCE: Page_492]

areas. The discrepancy between the size of the areas classified as fallow across the year [SOURCE: Page_492]

depending on which classifier is used is also shown in Figure 7. In terms of consumer [SOURCE: Page_492]

accuracy, SVM using a linear kernel can boast the best performance in delineating [SOURCE: Page_492]

urban and fallow land. In contrast, RF and GTB exhibit a better performance in [SOURCE: Page_492]

separating rice paddies and vegetable plots, both in terms of producer and consumer [SOURCE: Page_492]

accuracies. [SOURCE: Page_492]

Discussion [SOURCE: Page_493]

Benefits of Combining Imagery [SOURCE: Page_493]

Most saliently, this study highlights the multiple benefits of combining Sentinel-1 and 2 [SOURCE: Page_493]

imagery for various classifiers. For all classifiers except SVM using an RBF kernel, [SOURCE: Page_493]

combined imagery yields the highest classification accuracy. Especially for SVM using [SOURCE: Page_493]

a linear kernel, the combination of optical and SAR imagery brings a relative increase in [SOURCE: Page_493]

overall classification performance. This is in line with several studies that have found [SOURCE: Page_493]

marked benefits in adding information from radar images to optical ones for LULC [SOURCE: Page_493]

classification (Denize et al., 2018; Van Tricht, Gobin, Gilliams, & Piccard, 2018). What [SOURCE: Page_493]

is notable in this study is the consistent and considerable increase in accuracy that [SOURCE: Page_493]

results from the combination of image sources. (Tavares et al., 2019), for example, note [SOURCE: Page_493]

a rise in accuracy from 89% using Sentinel-2 only to 91% using combined imagery. [SOURCE: Page_493]

Similarly small accuracy improvements were reported by (Lu, Tao, & Di, 2018). In [SOURCE: Page_493]

contrast, the present study finds increases in accuracy of up to 15 percentage points. In [SOURCE: Page_493]

addition, it can be noted that the combination of imagery also leads to a reduction of the [SOURCE: Page_493]

impact of the training dataset. It can be conjectured that this is due to the fact that [SOURCE: Page_493]

additional layers of information counter-balance the noise in training data and make it [SOURCE: Page_493]

more easily separable for classifiers. [SOURCE: Page_493]

Configuring Input Parameters and Data for Optimal Results [SOURCE: Page_493]

Broadly, the results of the analysis illustrated the wide variations in the values of [SOURCE: Page_493]

493 [SOURCE: Page_493]

optimal parameters leading to the best classification accuracies for RF, GTB, and SVM, [SOURCE: Page_494]

as well as the considerable impact of the choice of kernel for SVM. Regarding the RF [SOURCE: Page_494]

parameter of nTree, for example, previous studies (e.g. Thanh Noi and Kappas, 2017) [SOURCE: Page_494]

found that accuracies tended to increase with a rising number of classification trees in [SOURCE: Page_494]

each random forest, and that further increasing the number of trees led to stability in the [SOURCE: Page_494]

accuracy of the results, starting at ca. 250 trees. Others also note that forests with a [SOURCE: Page_494]

larger number of trees do not necessarily perform better than those with fewer (Oshiro, [SOURCE: Page_494]

Perez, & Baranauskas, 2012). The present analysis shows that optimal accuracy values [SOURCE: Page_494]

for some data configurations can be reached at nTree = 50 already, and that increasing [SOURCE: Page_494]

the number of trees can lead to a noticeable decrease in accuracy. This underscores the [SOURCE: Page_494]

importance of performing parameter tuning prior to applying each of these classifiers in [SOURCE: Page_494]

a new setting, with varying input data configurations. As the parameter tuning results [SOURCE: Page_494]

for GTB show, the importance of parameter tuning is also dependent on the quality of [SOURCE: Page_494]

the training dataset. While optimal parameter values for nTree and maxNodes varied [SOURCE: Page_494]

little for the extended training set, greater discrepancies in values needed to achieve [SOURCE: Page_494]

optimal overall classification accuracies were observed using the fieldwork-based [SOURCE: Page_494]

training dataset. [SOURCE: Page_494]

Broadly, in terms of band sets and training data, this analysis illustrates the [SOURCE: Page_494]

nuanced balance between adding additional layers of information through texture [SOURCE: Page_494]

features and spectral indices, and introducing noise that can detract from classification [SOURCE: Page_494]

accuracies. Most prominently, it emerges that it isn’t necessarily the set of bands with [SOURCE: Page_494]

the highest number of additional indices and texture features that yields the highest [SOURCE: Page_494]

accuracies. Nor is it the minimalist approach taking as a basis of classification only the [SOURCE: Page_494]

bare minimum of raw bands. Rather, it is the set of curated raw bands and spectral [SOURCE: Page_494]

494 [SOURCE: Page_494]

indices, as well as bands arithmetically calculated from the SAR imagery’s VV and VH [SOURCE: Page_495]

bands, that leads to the highest classification performance. Most probably, this is due to [SOURCE: Page_495]

the fact that any additional information offered by certain spectral indices is drowned [SOURCE: Page_495]

out by the noise that other, less meaningful, indices produce. This result underlines [SOURCE: Page_495]

findings from previous studies, such as (da Silva et al., 2020), which concluded that the [SOURCE: Page_495]

NDVI, EVI, and SAVI offer the highest additional values for LULC approaches. [SOURCE: Page_495]

Overall Classifier Performance [SOURCE: Page_495]

When it comes to comparing algorithms in terms of accuracy, this analysis shows that [SOURCE: Page_495]

the GTB and RF classifiers exhibit the consistently best performance under a number of [SOURCE: Page_495]

different input data configurations, with GTB slightly exceeding RF in terms of [SOURCE: Page_495]

accuracy. Though SVM shows similarly high classification accuracies for combined [SOURCE: Page_495]

imagery and the use of a reduced band set, GTB and RF performance is consistently [SOURCE: Page_495]

superior with regard to all constellations of input data – imagery type, training dataset, [SOURCE: Page_495]

and band set. It is only in certain land cover classes – such as the separation of urban [SOURCE: Page_495]

areas and bare land – that SVM outperforms RF and GTB. Several previous studies [SOURCE: Page_495]

have debated the compared performance of RF and SVM. Ma et al. (2018) found RF to [SOURCE: Page_495]

be generally superior in a review of object-based LULC classification approaches, as [SOURCE: Page_495]

did Talukdar et al. (2020) in a comparison of machine learning approaches for LULC [SOURCE: Page_495]

classification. Rana & Venkata Suryanarayana (2020) by contrast, found SVM [SOURCE: Page_495]

performance to be superior, especially in combination with a principal component [SOURCE: Page_495]

approach. In addition, several studies have also factored GTB into the comparison, [SOURCE: Page_495]

though their number is lower due to the fact that this algorithm has only more recently [SOURCE: Page_495]

seen widespread use in LULC. For example, Georganos et al. (2018) found the [SOURCE: Page_495]

495 [SOURCE: Page_495]

XGboost implementation of GTB to systematically outperform RF and SVM, especially [SOURCE: Page_496]

on the basis of an extended feature set. Overall, it appears that SVM performs well [SOURCE: Page_496]

when studies aim to fine-tune parameters and investigate specific applications, whereas [SOURCE: Page_496]

RF offers more solid, generalizable applications for LULC approaches, and a lower [SOURCE: Page_496]

sensitivity to various input data. This higher sensitivity of SVM to the types of input [SOURCE: Page_496]

imagery and the training data set is in line with findings from earlier studies. Pelletier et [SOURCE: Page_496]

al. (2017), for example, compared the effect of training data noise on supervised LULC [SOURCE: Page_496]

classification using SVM and RF. The results found RF to be significantly more robust [SOURCE: Page_496]

towards both random and systematic noise of training labels. [SOURCE: Page_496]

As for the other classifiers available in GEE that were tested in this study, it [SOURCE: Page_496]

emerges that NB is ill-suited for LULC applications, with low overall accuracies. [SOURCE: Page_496]

CART, on the other hand, yielded solid results for the combined imagery type. In [SOURCE: Page_496]

particular, it can be noted that this classifier performed better when trained using only [SOURCE: Page_496]

the fieldwork data. It can be conjectured that this may be due to the more precise nature [SOURCE: Page_496]

of the points in this training data set. Even though there are fewer overall than in the [SOURCE: Page_496]

extended dataset, and they are unevenly distributed between classes, their label [SOURCE: Page_496]

attribution carries a higher certainty. As mentioned above, a higher label noise is likely [SOURCE: Page_496]

to have been introduced in the extended dataset derived from SPOT during its creation [SOURCE: Page_496]

(Frenay and Verleysen, 2014). CART appears to be more sensitive to noise of this kind [SOURCE: Page_496]

in the input data, which can be related to the fact that, unlike RF, it only relies on a [SOURCE: Page_496]

single threshold to define a node to split data into subsets. In RF, where this process is [SOURCE: Page_496]

repeated multiple times, noise can be balanced out more easily. The discrepancy in the [SOURCE: Page_496]

classification for CART depending on the training point set is illustrated starkly by [SOURCE: Page_496]

contrasting Figures 6 and 7, the former of which was generated with the configuration [SOURCE: Page_496]

496 [SOURCE: Page_496]

of input parameters yielding the highest accuracies (meaning the fieldwork training [SOURCE: Page_497]

point set for CART), and the latter of which used the extended dataset generated on the [SOURCE: Page_497]

basis of SPOT images as input. In the former, the extents of bare land towards the end [SOURCE: Page_497]

of the dry season are higher in the CART classification than in RF or SVM. In the latter, [SOURCE: Page_497]

the reverse is true. [SOURCE: Page_497]

Conclusion [SOURCE: Page_497]

Overall, this study illustrates the considerable benefits of using a combination of optical [SOURCE: Page_497]

and SAR imagery in supervised multi-temporal LULC classifications in Google Earth [SOURCE: Page_497]

Engine. When using GTB, the accuracies of these classifications can reach up to 94%. It [SOURCE: Page_497]

reveals that combining Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery improves overall [SOURCE: Page_497]

classification accuracy by 10 – 15 percentage points in comparison to analyses based on [SOURCE: Page_497]

optical-only imagery. Furthermore, the results of the analysis show that combining [SOURCE: Page_497]

different sources of imagery reduces the impact of the size and quality of the training [SOURCE: Page_497]

data set. This study also further highlights that out of all the classifiers available in [SOURCE: Page_497]

Google Earth Engine, GTB yields the highest overall classification accuracies, [SOURCE: Page_497]

performing best in a variety of combinations of input data, training points, and band [SOURCE: Page_497]

sets. [SOURCE: Page_497]

In general, the use of the extended training data, with points set manually on the [SOURCE: Page_497]

basis of high-resolution SPOT imagery, leads to higher accuracies, despite the higher [SOURCE: Page_497]

label noise in comparison to the smaller fieldwork dataset. It can equally be concluded [SOURCE: Page_497]

that a carefully selected set of native bands, spectral indices, and texture features used [SOURCE: Page_497]

as a basis for classification results in equal or better classifier performance than either a [SOURCE: Page_497]

minimalist set, or a large variety of additional bands, especially when using SVM. This [SOURCE: Page_497]

497 [SOURCE: Page_497]

underscores the delicate balance between adding indices and texture features as [SOURCE: Page_498]

auxiliary layers of information for classification, and the noise that is introduced [SOURCE: Page_498]

through their addition, which may impede classification accuracy. Finally, this study [SOURCE: Page_498]

also highlights the importance of tuning various input parameters prior to classification, [SOURCE: Page_498]

and of comparing basic classifier settings such as the choice of SVM kernel. [SOURCE: Page_498]

Overall, this study showcases the considerable differences in the outputs of [SOURCE: Page_498]

LULC analyses on the GEE cloud computing platform that can result from the choice of [SOURCE: Page_498]

imagery, input bands, classifiers, and parametrization – which can lead to vast [SOURCE: Page_498]

disparities when applied to larger areas. These results can provide preliminary guidance [SOURCE: Page_498]

to researchers to improve the accuracy of LULC analyses, which provide essential [SOURCE: Page_498]

inputs into studies ranging from agriculture to hydrology. [SOURCE: Page_498]

Abstract [SOURCE: Page_514]

As in many tropical deltas globally, annual floods shape the livelihoods of the largely rural population in the Cambodian Mekong delta. Agricultural cycles are keyed to the flood arrival, peak, and recession, and fish populations depend on inundated floodplains for their regeneration. However, as factors like climate change and hydropower infrastructure development are altering the Mekong’s hydrology, the inundation dynamics of its deltaic floodplains are shifting as well. Several studies have assessed the general changes of river discharge and flood extent on a basin- or delta-wide scale. Yet the sustainable development of this region is relying on dynamics at more local and specific scales, which have not been addressed so far. This paper presents a methodology to track the evolution of hydrological regimes and associated inundations in tropical deltas such as the upper Mekong delta in Cambodia, where it is applied over the past 30 years. Data scarcity and heterogeneity of the environment in this region necessitated the use of combined approaches. We established a link between water levels measured in-situ and [SOURCE: Page_514]

Email address: [EMAIL_REDACTED] (Christina Orieschnig ) [SOURCE: Page_514]

Preprint submitted to Journal of Hydrology                                   June 8, 2022 [SOURCE: Page_514]

514 [SOURCE: Page_514]

flood maps derived from optical and radar satellite images (Sentinel-1 and - 2).The robustness of the link was assessed using Sentinel, Landsat imagery and the TanDEM-X (12m) elevation model. This water level-flood link (WAFL) was then used to reconstruct a daily time series of inundation extents reaching back to the beginning of hydrological measurements in 1991 (30 years). On this basis, changes in the incidence, duration, and spatial distribution of floods were analysed. The results indicated that WAFL can be used to reconstruct inundation maps with an overall robustness of 87% in comparison to historical inundation maps derived from remote sensing imagery. Comparisons of WAFL-derived flood extents with Landsat images further underscored the significant role of local infrastructure, sedimentation dynamics, and land cover to explain changes in inundation dynamics. WAFL-based analyses revealed that inundation du- rations have decreased by an average of 19 days when comparing the periods before and after 2008, which was identified as a break point in the hydrological time series. Furthermore, a drastic decrease in inundation the annual frequency with which individual pixels are flooded can be detected during the first half of the traditional flood season, with an average of -21% in early August, negatively impacting water-based livelihoods, from agriculture to fisheries. Keywords: Mekong delta, Cambodia, inundations, Sentinel-1 and -2, water levels [SOURCE: Page_515]

1   1. Introduction [SOURCE: Page_516]

2      Tropical deltas worldwide are fundamentally influenced by regional and local 3   hydrological regimes (Kuenzer and Renaud, 2012; Loucks, 2019). Given low 4   terrain gradients, inundation processes are central to their populations’ water- 5   based livelihoods. Yet it is often not well-understood what impact large-scale, 6   basin-wide changes have on more local systems, often due to a lack of data. 7   This is illustrated perfectly by the Cambodian Mekong Delta. 8      As the largest trans-boundary river in Southeast Asia, the Mekong plays a 9   crucial role in the socioeconomic development of the region, with agriculture 10   and fisheries highly dependent on its flow regime (Kondolf et al., 2018; Boretti, 11   2020; Kummu and Sarkula, 2008). However, recent years have seen considerable 12   shifts in the Mekong’s hydrology (Yun et al., 2020; Trung et al., 2020). Its 13   seasonal hydrological regime, defined by a flood pulse - a strong unimodal flow 14   pattern induced by the annual Monsoon precipitation - has altered in terms of 15   timing and magnitude. On a basin-wide scale, numerous studies have traced 16   the reasons for this to a variety of factors, especially hydropower development 17   and climate change (Hecht et al., 2018; Lacombe et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2019; 18   Yun et al., 2020; Li et al., 2017; Pokhrel et al., 2018). For example, Hoang et al. 19   (2019) project that dry season flows in the basin will more than double as a 20   result of hydropower development, while wet season flows will decrease by 16% 21   by 2050. Similarly, Hoang et al. (2016) conclude that climate change will result 22   in a decrease of wet season flows by 7%, and an increase in dry season flows by 23   33% by 2065. 24      These basin-wide changes have a particularly adverse impact on downstream 25   hydro-ecological systems in the Cambodian and Vietnamese Mekong Delta (In- 26   tralawan et al., 2018; Yoshida et al., 2020). In these areas, the annual inunda- 27   tions^1 fundamentally shape the livelihoods of the local population. They deposit 28   nutrient-rich sediments on the floodplains, benefiting flood-recession agriculture, [SOURCE: Page_516]

1 This paper uses the terms ”flood” and ”inundations” synonymously. [SOURCE: Page_516]
